John 6:28's question is asked of Jesus by a crowd that has just been fed and wants to know 'that we might work the works of God', and John 6 has no other contact with Helaman 5. Acts 2:37 has the same question in a passage whose next verse is Aminadab's answer at 5:41 ('Repent'), whose opening clause is reproduced at 5:48 ('And now when they heard this'), and whose surrounding chapter supplies the descent of the Spirit, the fire and the marvellous words at 5:45. The link is written at Acts 2:37; John 6:28 is the longer run and the shallower one.

The n-gram stream matched Nehemiah 9:12 here and the Exodus original stands behind it. 'Pillar of fire' is CONVENTIONS §4's own example of a phrase common to every English Bible, so kjvSpecific could not be claimed for it in any case; but the greater objection is that the image is doing different work. Exodus's pillar goes before a marching people to give them light in the way; Helaman's encircles a stationary crowd inside a prison and does not move. The chapter's fire is Daniel 3's — fire that stands around people and does not burn them — and that link is written at 5:23. A reader arriving at 5:43 expecting the Exodus pillar is sent there.

Jeremiah in the dungeon of Malchiah is a genuine KJV prophet-in-prison story and therefore a tempting association for this chapter, but the match is on 'of the prison and they', four function words and a noun. Jeremiah's prison has mire and cords and no miracle; Helaman's has fire that does not take hold on the walls. The verse's real borrowing is 1 Peter 1:8, linked.

Ranked first in the verse at rarity 2.00 on a five-word run of function words, where Hosea's next words are 'great wickedness' and Helaman's are 'faith in my well beloved'. The sense is not merely different but opposite: Hosea 10:15 is Bethel's judgement, Helaman 5:47 is the voice's absolution. The verse's borrowings are John 20:19's greeting and Revelation 13:8's clause, both recorded on the link.

A five-word verbatim run and the closest single string in the chapter to Acts 2:37 — closer than the 'what shall we do' at 5:40 where the Acts link is written. It is filed here rather than linked because the two halves belong to one borrowing: Acts 2:37 is a single verse containing both the crowd's hearing and the crowd's question, and Helaman has split it across 5:40 and 5:48 with the Pentecost itself (5:45) between them. Adjudicating both would double-count one source. A reader arriving at 5:48 is sent to 5:40, and to 5:45 for the descent of the Spirit.

Five words shared with the shepherds returning from the manger, 'glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen'. The phrase is also Acts 4:20's ('we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard'), which is nearer in sense — witnesses compelled to testify — and neither can be isolated. 'Heard and seen' is the KJV's ordinary pair for eyewitness report, and Helaman 5:50 is an ordinary report.

'Weapons of war' is the Book of Mormon's own standing military term and the laying down of them is its own recurring conversion image, established long before Helaman. Ezekiel 32:27 is the descent of the uncircumcised mighty into hell with their weapons of war laid under their heads — a burial, not a repentance. The gesture is superficially the same (weapons put down) and the meaning is the reverse.

Considered and declined. 'The stedfastness of your faith' is a KJV singleton at Colossians 2:5 and Helaman 6:1 has 'their firmness, and their steadiness in the faith' — but the Book of Mormon's noun is 'steadiness', not 'stedfastness', and the 1830 does not spell it Paul's way. 'Steadiness' occurs in no KJV verse at all. What the two share is a doctrine and a preposition. Recorded because the singleton is real and the near-miss on the noun is the kind of thing that reads as a match at a glance.

The verse's top candidate at rarity 2.10 on a six-word run, and every word of it is the Book of Mormon's ordinary way of saying what missionaries do. Acts 10:42 is Peter at Cornelius's house on the ordination of Christ as judge of quick and dead; Helaman 6:6 is a one-clause travel notice. Covered as formulaic rather than argued.

A six-word run of a KJV list formula. Daniel 11:43 is the king of the north having power over the treasures of Egypt; Helaman 6:9 is a prosperity notice. 'Gold and silver' in that order with 'and of' between is how the KJV inventories wealth everywhere from Genesis 24:35 to Revelation 18:12, and it carries no signal. Recorded once here for the several similar matches across 6:9-11.

Matched here and at Mark 13:3 on a five-word run, and the run ends one word early in the way ADJUDICATING §4 describes: the Gospels' next words are 'mount of Olives' and Helaman's are 'judgement seat'. Matthew 24:3 opens the Olivet discourse; Helaman 6:15 reports the assassination of a chief judge by an unknown hand. Sitting somewhere is not a shared idea. The verse has no biblical source that this adjudication can identify.

Matched at 6:17's 'the riches of the world' (the dossier keys it to the 6:16 block). Romans 11:12 uses the phrase of Israel's fall being the riches of the world — a metaphor for the Gentiles' gain — and Helaman uses it of literal wealth. The verse's real borrowing is Psalm 62:10's 'set not your heart upon', a KJV singleton the n-gram stream did not rank, which is CONVENTIONS §9's point again: the stream sees the four-word noun phrase and misses the clause split across 'set their hearts upon their riches'.

A five-word verbatim run at rarity 2.00, and the sense is opposed in a way worth stating. 'Exceeding sorrowful' occurs in three KJV verses, and all three are the passion: the disciples at the last supper asking 'Lord, is it I?', and twice Christ in Gethsemane, 'my soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death'. Helaman 6:20 is the Lamanites' reaction to discovering robbers among them, and their sorrow issues immediately in a manhunt — 'they did use every means whatsoever was in their power, to destroy them off the face of the earth'. The KJV's phrase names a grief that submits; the Book of Mormon's names one that acts. The verse's own concern, a nation discovering a conspiracy in its midst, has nothing to do with either Gethsemane or the betrayal.

'Entered into the covenant' is a KJV singleton and it is the wrong covenant. Jeremiah 34:10 is Zedekiah's princes covenanting to free their Hebrew slaves — a covenant made before the LORD, in the right, and then broken (34:11, 'afterward they turned'). Helaman 6:21 is the Nephites entering the Gadianton oaths, a covenant made in the wrong and kept scrupulously; its whole content is that it will not be broken, since 6:22-24 exist to punish anyone who reveals it. The two verses are exact inversions on both axes, the covenant's morality and its durability, which is why the singleton cannot be used. Recorded at length as a model of the trap: a KJV singleton whose one occurrence is the opposite case.

exclusions.sharedText: over all the face of the
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and one of the Book of Mormon's own commonest formulas — 'all the face of the earth' and its variants occur in dozens of verses of the 1830 text and are covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1. Genesis 41:56's famine has no contact with Helaman 6:28's tower. Noted only because the verse it lands in is one this catalogue does link, to Genesis 11:4, on entirely different words.

'He which is the author of all sin' invites the KJV's two 'author of' constructions — Hebrews 5:9's 'author of eternal salvation' and 1 Corinthians 14:33's 'God is not the author of confusion' — and the second is the more interesting, since Helaman's sentence is its exact negative counterpart applied to the adversary. But 'author of' is two words, the KJV never uses the construction of the Devil, and neither verse shares anything else with Helaman 6:30. The formula is more likely English theological usage of the period than a borrowing. Recorded because a reader who knows 1 Corinthians 14:33 will hear it here and should be told the catalogue considered it.

The n-gram stream ranked Matthew 21:32 here on 'the way of righteousness', a phrase occurring in five KJV verses. The link is written at 2 Peter 2:21 instead, on the sequence rather than the phrase: 2 Peter has the way of righteousness known and then the holy commandment turned from — a KJV singleton — and Helaman 6:31 has 'turned out of the way of righteousness, and did trample under their feet the commandments of God' in that order. Matthew 21:32 is about John the Baptist coming in the way of righteousness and being disbelieved, which supplies neither the turning nor the commandment.

Helaman 6:31's 'did trample under their feet the commandments of God' contains Matthew 7:6's KJV singleton 'under their feet' and is the second of three occurrences in this batch of chapters. It is registered here rather than linked because 6:39, eight verses later, has both halves of Matthew 7:6 in one sentence — the trampling and the rending — and adjudicating the phrase twice inside one chapter would double-count a single borrowing. A reader arriving at 6:31 is sent to 6:39, and to Helaman 4:22 for the first occurrence in this book.

'Keep his statutes' occurs in two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 26:17 and 1 Kings 2:3, and both extend the list to 'and his commandments, and his judgments'. Helaman 6:34 has 'keep his statutes and commandments, and to walk in truth and uprightness before him', which is the Deuteronomic formula in the abstract rather than either verse in particular — the second half, 'walk in truth and uprightness', matches neither and is nearest 1 Kings 3:6's 'in truth, and in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart', which is a third verse again. With three candidates and no distinguishing wording, no source is identifiable.

A five-word run of function words. Exodus 5:19 is the Israelite officers seeing they were in evil case over the brick quota; Helaman 6:38 is the Gadianton band overspreading the Nephites. Nothing but the clause skeleton is shared.

Regnal-year boilerplate. The Book of Mormon dates by 'the sixty and ninth year of the reign of the Judges' throughout Helaman, and any KJV verse dating a king's reign will share four words with any of them. Asa's diseased feet have no other contact. 2 Chronicles 36:20's 'the reign of the' is excluded on the same evidence and is not given a separate entry.

The chapter's top-ranked candidate at verse 1 and worthless. 'Returned to the land of' is the KJV's ordinary way of saying a man went home; Exodus 4:20 has Moses going back to Egypt with the rod of God, Helaman 7:1 has Nephi coming south from the land northward, and the two share nothing but the verb and the preposition. The verse's one real contact with the KJV is two verses later, at 'the land of his nativity'.

exclusions.sharedText: commit adultery, and steal, and kill
exclusions.reason: A reader meeting 'commit adultery, and steal, and kill' at 7:5 will hear the Decalogue, and rightly. The link is not filed here because the fuller and more diagnostic list is sixteen verses later at 7:21 — 'murder, and plunder, and steal, and bear false witness against your neighbor' — where the neighbour clause identifies Exodus 20:16 and the order of the list identifies Matthew 19:18. 7:5's three verbs are in no KJV order (Exodus and Deuteronomy both run kill, adultery, steal) and carry no version signal on their own. See the adjudication at 7:21.

Considered and declined at the level of a link, though it is close. Isaiah 5:23's woe against judges who 'justify the wicked for reward, and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him' states both halves of Helaman 7:5 — the wicked let go for money, the righteous condemned because of their righteousness — and Helaman 7:25-27 is a woe series like Isaiah 5:20-23. But not one content word is shared: Helaman has condemning, unpunished and money against Isaiah's justify, reward and righteousness. Proverbs 17:15's 'he that condemneth the just' is a KJV singleton and closer in one verb, but is a proverb rather than an indictment of a bench. The chapter's judicial complaint is adjudicated instead at 7:10, where Habakkuk 1:4 supplies the same charge and Habakkuk 2:1 supplies the tower.

'Keep the commandments of God' is the Book of Mormon's most frequent single formula and matches dozens of KJV verses. Deuteronomy 10:13 was ranked here only because the five-word window happened to close on it; nothing else in the verse touches Deuteronomy 10.

Four words of narrative connective. Saul being fetched and found a head taller than the people has no contact with men running to report a praying prophet. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 and recorded only because it was ranked in a verse that does have a real link, to Isaiah 53:12.

Ranked because Jeremiah 46:16 contains 'the land of our nativity' and the chapter has already used 'the land of his nativity' at 7:3. The two are not the same borrowing: 7:22 reads 'the land of our possession', which shares only the article-noun-preposition frame, and Jeremiah 46:16 is a rout of Egyptian mercenaries. The nativity link is at 7:3 and its source is Genesis 11:28, which is the KJV's only verse with the singular masculine form.

A four-word run inside a divine first-person speech, and the temptation is that Deuteronomy 18:15-19 is the prophet-like-Moses oracle the Book of Mormon uses elsewhere and at length. Nothing else at 7:23 points there: Deuteronomy 18:19 threatens the man who will not hearken, Helaman 7:23 promises strength to the man who does, and the Book of Mormon verse has no prophet-raised-up, no 'in my name', and no requiring it of him. The phrase is the KJV's ordinary complement to 'thus saith the Lord'.

The 1830 spelling 'shew' is preserved here and makes the match look better than it is. Jeremiah 16:13 withholds favour from exiles in a foreign land; Helaman 7:23 withholds a demonstration of strength from the wicked while granting it to the penitent. The shared string is a negated verb and a pronoun. Worth an entry only because 'shew' is exactly the kind of KJV orthography that carries real evidence elsewhere in this catalogue (CONVENTIONS §8), and here it carries none.

Five words of connective tissue joining a woe to its ground, which Helaman 7:25-27 does three times in three verses. Hosea 10:15's subject is Bethel and its verdict is the cutting off of the king of Israel; nothing else is shared. The threefold woe formula itself is closer to Isaiah 5:20-23 and Habakkuk 2:6-12 than to Hosea, and neither is proposed as a source here because the wording is the Book of Mormon's own.

The highest-scoring candidate at the chapter's last verse and an accident of English word order. 1 John 5:16's 'I do not say that he shall pray for it' declines to command intercession for a sin unto death; Helaman 7:29's 'I do not say that these things shall be, of myself' disclaims the prophecy's origin, not its content. Same five words, opposite grammatical function — the Book of Mormon's clause is a denial of authorship and John's is a refusal to instruct. Luke 1:20's 'these things shall be' is excluded on the same evidence and is not given a separate entry.

A serious candidate, displaced on one noun. Matthew 21:46 — 'when they sought to lay hands on him, they feared the multitude, because they took him for a prophet' — has all three of Helaman 8:4's elements, including the reason, which the Book of Mormon does not state and which fits (8:9, 'if he had not been a prophet he could not have testified'). It is excluded because Matthew reads 'multitude' where Helaman and Acts 5:26 read 'people', and Acts 5:26 supplies nine consecutive words against Matthew's four. Luke 20:19 has the right noun and is retained as composite on the link. ADJUDICATING §4's warning about pronouns applies to nouns too: Matthew's crowd word is not Luke's, and the Book of Mormon has Luke's.

The n-gram stream's top candidate in the verse, on a six-word run, and the sense is unrelated. David says 'he is a good man, and cometh with good tidings' of a runner he has recognized at a distance by his gait; the phrase means a reliable messenger, not a righteous teacher, and nothing in 2 Samuel 18 involves a crowd, a division of opinion, or a threat to the man being discussed. John 7:12 has the same six words in the mouth of a divided multitude arguing about a preacher some believe and some think a deceiver, which is Helaman 8:7 exactly.

Five words of relative-clause connective. Mark 11:23 is the mountain cast into the sea and the believer who 'shall believe that those things which he saith shall come to pass'; the shared string is the frame around the content, and the content is a faith saying about prayer rather than a crowd's estimate of a prophet. Recorded because the run is long and because the verse's real second source, 1 Kings 13:32's 'surely come to pass', is a KJV singleton the n-gram stream ranked below this.

Ranked on the name of the sea, which the Book of Mormon has to use and which occurs across two dozen KJV verses. Exodus 15:22 is Moses bringing Israel from the Red Sea into the wilderness of Shur, three days without water; it shares no event with Helaman 8:11. The verse's genuine Exodus contact is 14:22's 'upon the dry ground', and its most distinctive phrase comes from 2 Kings 2:14.

Four words spanning a title and a verb. Luke 17:20 is the Pharisees asking when the kingdom of God should come, and the shared string is 'of God should come' with 'kingdom' amputated on one side and 'Son' on the other. Matthew 27:40's 'the Son of God come', ranked at 8:20, is excluded on the same evidence and is not given a separate entry — it is the mocking 'if thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross', where 'come' belongs to the next clause. Both are the window closing one word early (ADJUDICATING §4).

'The Son of God' is one of the KJV's commonest titles and one of the Book of Mormon's; the extra word that raised the score, 'with', begins an unrelated clause in each. Romans 1:4 declares Christ Son of God by the resurrection; Helaman 8:15 has men looking upon him with faith. No contact beyond the title.

The Book of Mormon's standing discourse formula, matching hundreds of KJV verses; John 4:35 was ranked only because its own 'Behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes' happens to place the words in the same order. It is proposed again at 8:16 and 9:23 and passed over there in silence. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Exodus 10:11 is Pharaoh expelling Moses and Aaron from his presence in the middle of the plague negotiations — 'and they were driven out from Pharaoh's presence'. Helaman 8:21 has the seed of Zedekiah driven out of the land of Jerusalem, which is an exile, not an ejection from a room. Four shared words, opposite scale. The verse's real source is the Zedekiah slaughter at Jeremiah 39:6 and 2 Kings 25:7, both of which Hardy's apparatus also cross-references.

Five words of pure connective tissue. Mark 6:3 is the Nazareth crowd listing Jesus's sisters, 'are they not all here with us? And they were offended at him'; the run crosses the sentence boundary and joins two unrelated clauses. Isaiah 59:12's 'are with us and' is excluded on the same evidence and is not given a separate entry.

Four words of connective. Zechariah 10:5's mighty men treading down enemies in the mire share nothing with God manifesting himself to the prophets. Psalm 18:38, Exodus 13:8, 1 Samuel 9:6 and Jonah 3:10 are all ranked at this verse on runs of the same kind and are excluded on the same evidence; none is given a separate entry. The verse is the chapter's densest patch of Book of Mormon formula and its lowest-signal one.

Considered because 'ye are ripening … for everlasting destruction' is a harvest-judgment figure and Joel 3:13 ('put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe') is the KJV's clearest source for one, with Revelation 14:18 restating it. Declined because the Book of Mormon uses 'ripe' and 'ripening' for iniquity throughout, from 1 Nephi onward, as a formula of its own with no sickle, no harvest and no vine anywhere near it. The verse's borrowing is the two-word 'everlasting destruction' from 2 Thessalonians 1:9, and that is where the link is filed.

Five words of narrative connective, and the resemblance is closer than it deserves to be: Mark 16:3's women say among themselves, as they go, 'Who shall roll us away the stone?' and Helaman 9:1's five men say among themselves, as they go, that they will know of a surety whether Nephi is a prophet. Both parties are walking toward a body they have not yet seen. But the shared words are all frame and no content, the KJV uses 'said among themselves' of half a dozen crowds, and nothing else in Helaman 9 touches the resurrection narrative. Recorded because the situational parallel is the kind a careful reader would stop over.

A genuine temptation, considered and declined. 'Know of a surety' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 15:13 and Acts 12:11, and Acts 12:11 is attractive because Peter says it having just been brought out of prison by an angel, which is where the five men of Helaman 9 are about to end up. The contact is four words of idiom with no other element in common: Helaman's speakers use it of a test they are about to run, Peter of a deliverance already accomplished, and there is no angel, no chains and no gate in the Book of Mormon chapter. The chapter's prison borrowings are at 9:9, from Acts 16:23 and Matthew 14:3, and they are verbally much stronger.

Four words of which three are auxiliaries and a pronoun. Hebrews 11:6's 'he that cometh to God must believe that he is' concerns believing that God exists; Helaman 9:2's 'we do not believe that he is a prophet' concerns an office. The window closes one word early in the way ADJUDICATING §4 describes — Hebrews' next word is 'and', Helaman's is 'a'.

Six words of subordinating tissue joining a verb to its result clause. 2 Samuel 22:39 is David consuming his enemies so that they could not arise; Helaman 9:8 is the crowd supposing God smote the five so that they could not flee. Recorded rather than passed over because the run is long and because a reader might hear a divine-smiting parallel in it; there is none, and the Book of Mormon clause is the crowd's mistaken inference, which the chapter then refutes.

exclusions.sharedText: it came to pass that on the morrow
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run and the longest in the chapter, and it is worth nothing. 'And it came to pass that on the morrow' is the Book of Mormon's standard temporal transition and the KJV's; Numbers 17:8 is Aaron's rod budding in the tabernacle. This is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names first — a long run means nothing on its own — and it is the clearest instance of it in Helaman 7-9. Malachi 4:5's 'of the great and' and 1 Kings 13:29's 'to mourn and to' are ranked at the same verse and excluded on the same evidence; neither is given a separate entry.

Five words of reported-speech frame. Luke 9:10 is the apostles returning and telling Jesus all that they had done; Helaman 9:13 is five prisoners telling the judges all that they had done. The construction is the KJV's ordinary way of summarizing a report and carries no signal. The chapter's real Gospel borrowing at this point in the trial is at 9:19.

exclusions.sharedText: the man that hath done this
exclusions.reason: A five-word run and a real temptation, because 2 Samuel 12:5 is David's furious verdict on the rich man of Nathan's parable — 'the man that hath done this thing shall surely die' — and it is famously a verdict the speaker has unwittingly passed on himself. Helaman 9:20's judges ask Nephi 'who is this man that hath done this murder?', and 9:27-38 will reveal that the murderer is one of their own band. The parallel is real and the wording is not: Helaman's clause is an interrogative asking for a name, 2 Samuel's a demonstrative pronouncing a sentence, and the Book of Mormon has no parable, no Nathan, and no self-conviction. Filed as wrong-sense with the note that a reader who wants the Nathan resonance should have it as resonance, not as a source.

Five words of pure direction-giving. Ecclesiastes 7:2's 'It is better to go to the house of mourning' is an aphorism about mortality; Helaman 9:26 sends men to a named man's house to ask him a question. Nothing else shared.

One of the KJV's commonest theological phrases and one of the Book of Mormon's. Ephesians 3:7's 'given unto me by the effectual working of his power' and John 6:65's 'except it were given unto him of my Father' were ranked alongside it and are excluded on the same evidence; none is given a separate entry. The verse's interesting relation is not to any of them but to Acts 8:10's 'the great power of God', which the Samaritans say of Simon Magus and which Nephi here refuses to let stand of himself — that is argued on the link at 9:16.

Four words, of which the content is a passive verb every prophet in both testaments uses of himself. John 3:28 is the Baptist disclaiming the Christ and saying he is sent before him; Helaman 9:36 is Nephi claiming honesty and divine commission. The disclaimer structure is superficially similar and the vocabulary is not distinctive enough to adjudicate.

exclusions.sharedText: the words which he had said unto them
exclusions.reason: Seven words of reported-speech frame, ranked highest at the verse. Genesis 45:27 is the brothers telling Jacob all Joseph's words; the run is the frame and the content is elsewhere in both verses. 1 Kings 13:11, Judges 20:40 and 2 Peter 3:15 are ranked at the same verse on runs of the same kind and are excluded on the same evidence; none is given a separate entry.

'Set at liberty' occurs in four KJV verses — Jeremiah 34:16, Luke 4:18, Acts 26:32 and Hebrews 13:23 — and Luke 4:18's 'to set at liberty them that are bruised' is the memorable one. It is declined as a source because Luke's phrase renders a programmatic quotation of Isaiah 61 and Helaman's is a procedural note about five men leaving a cell; Acts 26:32's 'this man might have been set at liberty' is closer in setting and equally undecidable. Three words of legal idiom with four candidate verses and no way to choose. The release is recorded instead on the Acts 16:23 link at 9:9, where the whole prison sequence is argued.

A five-word run of covenant-curse boilerplate. Deuteronomy 28:20 threatens vexation 'because of the wickedness of thy doings'; Helaman 10:3 explains why a prophet is depressed. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase constantly and it carries no source. The real contact in this verse is the rare verb 'pondering', catalogued at the link.

exclusions.sharedText: this people and thou hast not
exclusions.reason: The six-word run is an artifact of two independent boilerplate strings meeting at a clause boundary — 'unto this people' ends one sentence and 'and thou hast not' begins the next. Exodus 33:12 is Moses complaining that God has not told him whom he will send; Helaman 10:4 is God commending Nephi for not fearing men. Nothing else of Exodus 33 is present, and the window is blind to the fact that it spans a full stop.

The machine's top-ranked source for the phrase is the messianic judge of Isaiah 11:4, who smites the earth 'with the rod of his mouth'. It should not be taken. “smite the earth” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, and only one of them — Revelation 11:6 — also contains 'have power over', which Helaman 10:6 has immediately before it and in the same order. The link is written at Revelation 11:6, where the rest of the grant (shutting heaven against rain) is spent in Helaman 11. Malachi 4:6, the third instance, is a curse on the land at the end of the prophets and has no other contact here.

A genuine five-word match and the senses are opposed. In Jeremiah 38:15 the prophet refuses to speak — 'If I declare it unto thee, wilt thou not surely put me to death?' — and the clause is the protasis of a refusal made by a man in a dungeon to the king who put him there. In Helaman 10:6 God declares to Nephi, in the presence of angels, a grant of power. The same five words face in opposite directions, and there is an ironic near-miss worth naming: Helaman 10:15 has the crowd trying to put Nephi in prison, which is where Jeremiah is speaking from. It is a coincidence of narrative furniture, not a borrowing.

“in the presence of mine” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is why it ranked, and the singleton is real but empty: Psalm 23:5's noun is 'enemies' and Helaman 10:6's is 'angels', and everything the phrase shares is the preposition and the possessive. Nothing else of Psalm 23 is anywhere in the chapter. The possible Lukan source of the phrase (Luke 15:10) is recorded as a low-confidence link at the verse.

A temptation worth naming because the chapter has just been talking about a temple. “the Lord God Almighty” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Revelation 21:22, 'I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it' — three verses after Helaman 10:8 gave Nephi power to rend a temple in twain, which is a pairing a careful reader would want. It will not bear the weight. The determiner is what makes Revelation 21:22 a singleton, and the shorter 'Lord God Almighty' occurs in five KJV verses, all in Revelation (4:8, 11:17, 15:3, 16:7, 21:22). Helaman 10:11 does not have even that: it has 'the Lord God, who is the Almighty', a relative-clause periphrasis matching no KJV verse. The commonplace was available to any nineteenth-century writer without Revelation 21.

exclusions.sharedText: the Lord had spoken these words unto
exclusions.reason: “had spoken these words unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and the singleton is worthless, exactly as CONVENTIONS §9 says of this same verse — Job 42:7 was the pilot's standing example of rare boilerplate outranking real links. The construction is a speech-closing formula ('when X had spoken these words unto Y') that the KJV writes a dozen ways and the Book of Mormon writes constantly; the rarity measures the KJV's preference for 'when he had thus spoken', not any relation between Job and Nephi. Job's clause introduces God's rebuke of Eliphaz; Helaman's introduces a prophet turning back toward a crowd.

The window closes one word early, in the way ADJUDICATING §4 warns about: Luke 4:29's next word is 'down headlong' off a cliff, Helaman 10:15's is 'into prison'. But the machine is pointing at the right episode for the wrong reason, and the register should say so. Luke 4:29-30 is the Nazareth crowd that tries to destroy the prophet and out of whose midst he passes untouched, which is precisely Helaman 10:15-16 — and the link for that is written at 10:16, on John 5:13's 'conveyed' and Acts 8:39-40's Spirit-borne removal, where the verbal evidence actually is. Luke 4:30 is recorded there as a composite.

The five words agree and the object does not: Luke 20:26's verb is 'take hold of his words' — the spies fail to catch Jesus in speech — while Helaman 10:16's is 'take him', a failed physical arrest. The scene the Book of Mormon is actually running here is the failed arrest of John 7:44-46 (opened at 10:1) and the escape of John 5:13, both catalogued. Luke 20:26 shares a negated auxiliary and a very common verb.

Refusal-to-hearken is one of the Book of Mormon's most-used formulas and one of the KJV's; the phrase appears in Helaman 10:13, 10:15 and 10:18 alone. Covered by the standing exclusion for connective matches (CONVENTIONS §5); recorded once here because Ezekiel 20:8 was ranked, and passed over in silence at its other occurrences.

Four words spanning a phrase boundary in a date formula the Book of Mormon prints eight times in this chapter alone ('the reign of the Judges'). 2 Kings 23:22 is dating Josiah's passover against the period of the Israelite judges. Nothing but the noun is shared, and the noun means a different office in each book.

“there was a great famine” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the singleton is more tempting than it looks: 2 Kings 6:25 is the famine in besieged Samaria, an Elisha chapter, in a Helaman chapter that is running the Elijah-Elisha drought material hard, and it ends (2 Kings 7:1) with a prophet announcing the famine's end and being believed only after the fact. A reader would be right to notice it. It should still be declined: the shared string is five words of the plainest possible narrative English, the 2 Kings famine is caused by a siege rather than by drought or by any prophet's word, and every phrase in this chapter that is actually distinctive points at 1 Kings 17-18 instead — 'according to my word' (17:1) at this same verse, 'thou art a man of God' (17:24) at 11:8, 'send rain upon the earth' (18:1) at 11:13. The link is written at 1 Kings 17:1.

Genesis 11:1's 'the whole earth was of one language' and Helaman 11:6's 'the whole earth was smitten' share a subject and a copula. Babel has nothing to do with a drought, and the Book of Mormon's 'whole earth' here means the whole of a local land, as the next clause ('even among the Lamanites as well as among the Nephites') makes explicit.

“remember the words of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, so the rank is earned, and the sense is nonetheless opposed. Acts 20:35 is Paul's farewell at Miletus urging the Ephesian elders to remember a saying of Jesus about generosity, quoted approvingly and voluntarily. Helaman 11:7 has a starving people remembering the words of a prophet because the destruction he threatened is arriving. One is a treasured maxim, the other a returning threat. The formula 'remember the words of X' is also among the Book of Mormon's own stock phrases and needs no source.

The four words match and the grammar does not: 2 Chronicles 29:10 asks that God's fierce wrath 'may turn away from us', with wrath as the subject, while Helaman 11:8 asks that God 'turn away from us this famine', with God as subject and the famine as object. The prayer that God turn away his anger does appear in this chapter, three times, at 11:11, 11:12 and 11:16 — and its source is Jonah 3:9, the only KJV verse with 'turn away from his fierce anger', which is where the link is written. Hezekiah's covenant is a plausible-looking near miss.

'The people began to' is Book of Mormon narrative connective tissue; it occurs twice in verse 7 alone. Numbers 25:1 is Israel's whoredom with the daughters of Moab at Shittim. Covered by the standing exclusion for connective matches (CONVENTIONS §5) and recorded once because the machine ranked it.

The temptation here is large and should be named rather than passed over. Nephi quotes himself in the creation fiat's exact form — 'when I said, Let there be a famine' — and the narrator has already reported the result in the creation account's own idiom: 'and so it was done, according to the words of Nephi' (11:5), against Genesis 1's 'and it was so'. A prophet who has just been told at Helaman 10:8-10 that whatever he says will be done, saying 'Let there be', is a reading a careful editor would want. It is declined for two reasons. “let there be” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses and is not confined to Genesis 1; and the whole phenomenon — a prophet's word determining the weather — has an exact and much rarer source that this chapter is demonstrably using, 1 Kings 17:1's 'there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word', where “according to my word” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The link is written at 11:5. If the creation echo is there, it is riding on the Elijah borrowing rather than competing with it.

The obvious place to look for the end of an Elijah drought is the Kings narrative, and mediation-check.py even scores one decisive point for it here. That point is an artifact: it rests on 'it came to pass', which is the Book of Mormon's universal connective and not evidence of anything. Weighed rather than counted, 1 Kings 18:45 has no fruit, no earth and no feminine possessive, and offers instead clouds, wind and Ahab riding to Jezreel, none of which is here. The verse the Book of Mormon actually has is James 5:18, both of whose halves are KJV singletons, and the link is written there.

'The whole face of the land' is one of the Book of Mormon's most-used geographical formulas and appears twice within three verses here (11:18, 11:20). Genesis 2:6's mist watering 'the whole face of the ground' shares the formula and nothing else. Covered by the standing exclusion at CONVENTIONS §5; recorded once for the chapter and passed over at its other occurrences.

Leviticus 26:6, 'I will give peace in the land, and ye shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid', is the covenant blessing that answers the covenant curses of Leviticus 26:19-20 ('I will make your heaven as iron, and your earth as brass … neither shall your land yield her increase') — which is a drought-and-famine sequence resolving into peace, exactly the shape of Helaman 11. A reader could reasonably want the link. The wording will not support it: four common words, no shared clause, and the Book of Mormon's own year-summary formula ('did have exceeding great peace in the land') accounts for the sentence. Recorded so that the Leviticus 26 shape is on the register even though no verse of it is quoted.

A five-word match with the catalogue's most-cited New Testament sentence, and it is empty here. John 18:14 is Caiaphas's counsel 'that it was expedient that one man should die for the people', which the Book of Mormon does use — at 1 Nephi 4:13, where Nephi justifies killing Laban in Caiaphas's words and the link is adjudicated. Helaman 11:28 has no man dying for anyone: 'it was expedient that there should be a stop put to this work of destruction' is an administrative decision to send an army after bandits. 'Expedient' is one of the Book of Mormon's commonest adjectives and this is the impersonal construction, not the sacrificial one. A reader who arrives here from 1 Nephi 4:13 should be told the resemblance is the idiom only.

exclusions.sharedText: upon all the face of the
exclusions.reason: Six words of the same geographical formula excluded at 11:18. ADJUDICATING §4 names 'scattered upon all the face of the earth' as the type case of a phrase the narrator has adopted as his own; Ezekiel 34:6's scattered flock is a shepherd oracle and has no other contact with a chapter about robbers in the mountains.

Four words, and the temptation is thematic rather than verbal: Psalm 34:8's 'O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him' has both of Helaman 12:1's ideas — God's goodness and trust in him — in one line. It should still be declined. 'We can see that the Lord' is Mormon's own editorial idiom throughout this chapter ('and thus we see', 12:3), the psalm's imperative is a call to trust while Helaman 12:1's indicative is a complaint that trust does not last, and “put their trust in him” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, none of them Psalm 34.

exclusions.sharedText: in gold, and in silver, and in
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run shared with three KJV verses at once (Exodus 31:4, 35:32 and 2 Chronicles 2:7), which is itself the sign that it is a list-formula rather than a borrowing: all three are specifications for a craftsman able to work in gold, silver and brass, for the tabernacle or the temple. Helaman 12:2's gold and silver are agricultural prosperity, and the phrase's real source is three verses away — Deuteronomy 8:13's 'thy silver and thy gold is multiplied', catalogued at the link.

A six-word run, and the pairing is genuinely biblical, but Genesis 46:32 and 47:1 are Joseph presenting his brothers to Pharaoh and have no relation to the argument of Helaman 12. The flocks-and-herds pair belongs to this verse by way of Deuteronomy 8:13, 'when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, and thy silver and thy gold is multiplied' — where all four of Helaman 12:2's nouns occur together, in the same two pairs, inside the passage that also supplies the verse's 'forget the Lord their God'. The link is written at Deuteronomy 8:13.
Four words of connective tissue. Jeremiah 11:14 forbids the prophet to intercede; Helaman 12:2 marks the turn of a cycle ('then is the time that they do harden their hearts'). No content is shared.

Recorded because a reader will think of it. 'Whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth' (Hebrews 12:6, quoting Proverbs 3:12) and 'As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten' (Revelation 3:19) are the New Testament's statements of exactly Helaman 12:3's doctrine — that affliction is corrective and is a mark of favour. But “chasten” occurs in exactly six KJV verses and “chasten his people” occurs in exactly zero, no clause is shared, and Helaman 12:3's warrant is empirical rather than affectionate: not that God chastens those he loves, but that without chastening 'they will not remember him'. The structural source of that claim is Judges 2:14-19, filed as a figural link at 12:3. Note the 1830 reads 'all manner of pestilences' where 1920 has the singular.

exclusions.sharedText: (the nothingness of man weighed against dust)
exclusions.reason: 'O how great is the nothingness of the children of men; yea, even they are less than the dust of the earth' is close in thought to Isaiah 40:15-17, where the nations are 'as a drop of a bucket', 'counted as the small dust of the balance', and 'all nations before him are as nothing'. Isaiah 40:12 even has 'comprehended the dust of the earth in a measure'. The wording will not carry it: “the dust of the earth” occurs in exactly nine KJV verses and is a stock phrase, 'nothingness' is not a KJV word at all, and the comparative 'less than' — which is the whole of Mormon's rhetorical point — has no counterpart in Isaiah, where man is nothing rather than less than something. Recorded so the Isaiah 40 background is on the register without being claimed.

Four words of a prepositional phrase. Ezekiel 48:28 is a boundary description running to 'the waters of strife in Kadesh'; Helaman 12:16 addresses 'the waters of the great deep'. The distinctive phrase in the verse is the KJV singleton at Isaiah 51:10, where the link is written.

Five words of judgment boilerplate. Ezekiel 9:9's 'the iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah is exceeding great' is a general indictment; Helaman 12:18's phrase specifies whose iniquity attaches the curse to a particular buried object. Covered by the standing exclusion for connective matches (CONVENTIONS §5).

The senses are opposed and instructively so. Luke 12:33's 'a treasure in the heavens that faileth not' is precisely what a buried treasure is not, and the saying exists to contrast the two; Matthew 13:44's treasure hid in a field is likewise a thing found and rejoiced over. Helaman 12:18-19's treasure is hidden, cursed, and never recovered by anyone. The episode behind it is Achan's, where “hid in the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 7:21, and where the buried valuables bring a curse on the man who buried them. The link is written at Joshua 7:21.

Four words opening a conditional. Helaman 12:18-21 is a series of four such conditionals in a row and the machine ranked one at random; Deuteronomy 19:8's is about enlarging the borders and adding cities of refuge. The verse's real material is the KJV singleton 'cut off from my presence', catalogued at the link.

exclusions.sharedText: of the Lord their God, for
exclusions.reason: Six words that are entirely 'the Lord their God' plus two connectives. That title occurs three times in Helaman 12 alone and is among the Book of Mormon's commonest phrases. Jeremiah 43:1 is a narrative transition. Covered by the standing exclusion at CONVENTIONS §5.

A five-word match worth writing up, because a careless reader could take it and because the two sentences are about entirely different things. 1 Corinthians 7:7 is Paul on celibacy — 'For I would that all men were even as I myself' — a wish about marital state, immediately qualified by 'but every man hath his proper gift of God'. Helaman 12:25 is Mormon on universal salvation: 'And I would that all men might be saved. But we read that in that great and last day, there are some which shall be cast out.' The optative construction is identical and the content shares nothing. What the verse does borrow is at its end: 'cast off from the presence of the Lord' is the KJV's judgment idiom of 2 Thessalonians 1:9, recorded as a composite at the 12:26 link. Note the 1830's two 'which' where 1920 reads 'who'.

“everlasting life” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses, seven of them in John, so the machine's pick of John 6:40 is arbitrary among a large set. The verse is quoting John 5:29, whose eleven-word frame ('they that have done good … and they that have done evil') Helaman 12:26 reproduces under an explicit citation formula, and whose 'resurrection of' it replaces with Daniel 12:2's 'everlasting'. The link is written at John 5:29 with Daniel 12:2 as a composite; Hardy's apparatus cross-references John 5:29 at this verse.

The standing exclusion for this chapter. Samuel's sermon is delivered in the KJV's narrative and homiletic boilerplate throughout, and the n-gram stream returns it at a dozen verses: 13:2 (Acts 10:42 and 1 Kings 19:21, 'preach unto the people' / 'unto the people and they did'), 13:4 (Job 34:23, 'that he should enter into'), 13:16 (Deuteronomy 20:15, 'all the cities which are'), 13:17 and 13:32 (Haggai 1:9 and Isaiah 19:20, both scoring only on 'saith the Lord of hosts'), 13:18 (Ezekiel 21:7 and Jeremiah 25:27, 'to pass saith the Lord' and 'no more because of the'), 13:20 (Joshua 7:12, 'before their enemies because they'), 13:22 (Exodus 8:28, 'the Lord your God in'), 13:26 (Hebrews 13:7 and 11:6, 'unto you the word of' and 'that he is a') and 13:33 (Isaiah 12:4, 'in that day shall ye say'). Every one is the connective tissue covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5, and none shares a content word that construes. Deuteronomy 10:13 is listed here as the representative because 13:1's 'keep the commandments of God, according to the law of Moses' is the Book of Mormon's own summary formula for Lamanite observance and is used identically at 15:5.

Worth saying plainly that Samuel's opening image has no King James source. 'The sword of justice hangeth over this people … the sword of justice falleth upon this people' is the Book of Mormon's own phrase: 'sword of justice' occurs in no KJV verse at all. The KJV's sharpened-and-furbished sword of Ezekiel 21:9-11 is the nearest thing to a personified sword of judgment and shares nothing but the noun; the hanging sword is Damocles, not scripture. Filed because a reader who goes looking for the biblical background of the sermon's first image should be told there is none, and because the phrase is one of the Book of Mormon's most distinctive coinages (Alma 26:19, 60:29 and elsewhere).

A five-word run and the wrong fourth generation. 2 Kings 10:30 is the Lord's reward to Jehu — his children to the fourth generation will sit on Israel's throne — which is a promise of dynastic continuity, the opposite of what 13:10 threatens. 'Fourth generation' occurs in seven KJV verses; the four that matter are the jealous-God formula of Exodus 20:5, Exodus 34:7, Numbers 14:18 and Deuteronomy 5:9, because those alone pair the span with the verb 'visiting', and Helaman 13:10 uses 'visit' three times in one sentence. The link is at Exodus 20:5.

A genuine King James idiom with no King James passage behind it. 'The more part' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 19:32 (the confused assembly at Ephesus) and Acts 27:12 (the ship's council at Fair Havens), and the Book of Mormon uses it three times in this sermon alone (13:12, 15:5, 15:6) in senses that have nothing to do with either. This is the kind of evidence that bears on the project's general claim — the text's English is Jacobean down to its quantifiers — without being evidence of dependence on any verse. Recorded so that the phrase is countable rather than accepted as a link.

The obvious match on the fire clause, and it is superseded. 'Fire come down from heaven' occurs in three KJV verses, two of them Elijah calling down fire on the captains of fifty (2 Kings 1:10, 1:12) and one the beast's false wonder (Revelation 13:13). None involves a city, and none involves sparing. Helaman 13:13-14 is built on the other proposition entirely — a city destroyed unless righteous people are found inside it, and spared 'for the righteous' sake' — and the only KJV sentence that states it is Genesis 18:26, 'then I will spare all the place for their sakes', a KJV singleton. The fire itself is Sodom's, Genesis 19:24. Filed because Elijah's fire is the phrase a reader will find first and the wrong answer.

exclusions.sharedText: for the righteous' sake, that it is spared
exclusions.reason: Cross-reference, not a rejection. 13:14's 'it is for the righteous' sake, that it is spared' is the closest verbal contact in the passage with Genesis 18:26's 'I will spare all the place for their sakes', but the argument the two verses share begins at 13:13 and the link is adjudicated there. A reader browsing verse by verse should be sent one verse back rather than shown nothing.

exclusions.sharedText: hath not hearkened unto the words of him who gave them unto you
exclusions.reason: Cross-reference. The Deuteronomy 8 material — the God who gives the power to get wealth, and the forgetting that follows prosperity — runs across 13:21-22 and is adjudicated at 13:22, where 'ye do not remember the Lord your God' supplies the verb that makes the identification. The machine's own proposal here, 2 Kings 22:13 ('because our fathers have not hearkened unto the words of this book'), is a six-word run on 'hearkened unto the words of' whose object is Josiah's rediscovered law-book and not a giver of riches; it is not the source.

A KJV singleton in the wrong direction. 'Cast stones at' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 16:6, where Shimei casts stones at David — a private cursing of a king in flight, not a judicial stoning and not the killing of a prophet. Helaman 13:24's 'cast stones at them, and do slay them' belongs with the prophet-killing complex of Matthew 23:37 ('thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them'), which is what 13:25 goes on to quote. Recorded because an absolute rarity is the strongest kind of evidence this catalogue uses and it has to be able to say when one does not count.

'As the Lord liveth' is the King James oath formula and occurs across Judges, Samuel, Kings, Ruth, Jeremiah and Hosea; the stream returns 1 Samuel 14:39 and Judges 8:19 here because both continue 'as the LORD liveth, if …', which is Samuel's construction too. It is a formula, not a source. Noted separately from the chapter's standing exclusion only because it is a formula with real Hebraic weight — the text's use of it is evidence about its register, and about nothing else.

The other New Testament indictment for killing the prophets, and it loses. Stephen's speech has almost everything Helaman 13:24-29 has — 'Ye stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart and ears … as your fathers did, so do ye. Which of the prophets have not your fathers persecuted? and they have slain them' — and Helaman 13:29 even has 'ye hardened and ye stiffnecked people'. But 'stiffnecked' occurs in nine KJV verses, eight of them Mosaic, so it points at Exodus 32-34 as readily as at Acts; and the two decisive phrases in this passage are Matthew's and only Matthew's. 'In the days of our fathers' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 23:30, and 'blind guides' in exactly two, Matthew 23:16 and 23:24. Stephen's speech has no counterfactual disclaimer and no guides. Filed at length because Acts 7 is the reference a well-read editor would reach for and the wording will not support it.

tools/kjv-rarity.py returns two verses for 'weep and howl', and one of them is an artifact of punctuation. Joel 1:5 reads 'Awake, ye drunkards, and weep; and howl, all ye drinkers of wine' — two imperatives to two audiences across a clause break, addressed to drunkards over the failure of the wine. James 5:1 has the phrase as a unit and addresses rich men whose riches are about to fail, which is Helaman 13:32's situation exactly, and James 5:2-3 then supplies three further KJV singletons that the lament at 13:33-35 works through. The link is at 13:32.

exclusions.sharedText: we have hid up our treasures, and they have slipped away
exclusions.reason: Cross-reference. The lament at 13:33-36 is where the chapter's two strongest links actually pay off — James 5:1-3, adjudicated at 13:32, and Psalm 73:18, adjudicated at 13:31 — and neither is a fresh borrowing here. A reader who arrives at these verses looking for the source of 'our riches are gone from us' and of the slipperiness should be sent to both.

Filed for what it shows about the text's vocabulary rather than about a source. 'Behold we are surrounded by demons' has no King James background at all: the word 'demons' occurs in no KJV verse, the King James Bible always saying 'devils' (Revelation 12:9's dragon is 'called the Devil, and Satan'). This is one of the few points in the sermon where the English is not the KJV's, and it is worth having in the register precisely because the catalogue's claim is about the places where it is. The following clause, 'encircled about by the angels of him who hath sought to destroy our souls', is likewise the Book of Mormon's own idiom.

exclusions.sharedText: and it shall come to pass that ye shall
exclusions.reason: The standing exclusion for this chapter, and the one place in the book where it needs saying twice, because chapter 14 is a list of prophecies and every item begins with the same connective. The stream's longest run in the chapter is nine words at Ezekiel 47:22 and every word of it is 'and it shall come to pass that ye shall'. The same applies to 14:2 (2 Corinthians 11:25, 'a night and a day' — Paul's shipwreck), 14:7 (Ezekiel 38:20, 'shall fall to the'), 14:11 and 14:12 (Psalm 141:6 and 2 Corinthians 2:4, 'shall hear my words' and 'that ye might know the'), 14:12 (Luke 1:3 and Isaiah 48:3, both scoring only on 'all things from the beginning'), 14:15 (John 11:24 and John 20:9, 'he shall rise again' and 'again from the dead'), 14:20 and 14:27 (Acts 19:8, 'for the space of three'), 14:21 (Genesis 1:29, 'upon the face of'), 14:22 and 14:28 (Zechariah 5:3 and Ezekiel 34:6, 'the face of the whole earth' and 'upon all the face of'), 14:26 (Revelation 17:7, 'and the angel said unto me') and 14:30 (Joshua 23:16, 'he hath given unto you'). None shares a content word that construes; all are covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: believe on the Son of God
exclusions.reason: The machine's top match at this verse, and it is the wrong Johannine verse. John 9:35 is a question put to one man — 'Dost thou believe on the Son of God?' — with no promise attached. Helaman 14:8 is a universal conditional with everlasting life as its apodosis, which is the form of John 3:36 ('He that believeth on the Son hath everlasting life'); the fuller subject 'the Son of God' comes from 1 John 5:10. The link is at John 3:36 with 1 John 5:10 as composite. Worth an entry because 'believe on the Son of God' is the longer run and the weaker match, which is the pilot's standing lesson about run length (CONVENTIONS §9).

exclusions.sharedText: cut off from the presence of the Lord
exclusions.reason: The chapter's densest theological sentence has no King James source, and the reason is worth recording: 'cut off from the presence of the Lord', 'the fall of Adam', 'the first death' and 'spiritual death' are the Book of Mormon's own settled vocabulary, worked out at 2 Nephi 9 and Alma 12, and Samuel is using it as received doctrine rather than reaching for scripture. The KJV's expulsion from Eden (Genesis 3:22-24) has the driving out but not the formula, and 'spiritual death' occurs in no KJV verse at all. Filed so the register can show where the sermon stops quoting; the borrowings resume at 14:18 with the Baptist's axe.

The Old Testament half of a mediation test, recorded as a negative result so the negatives stay countable. 'The sun shall be darkened' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 13:10 and Mark 13:24, the second quoting the first. mediation-check.py returns two decisive points, both against Isaiah: the Book of Mormon reproduces neither 'in his going forth' nor 'to shine', the two clauses Isaiah has and Mark drops. The order confirms it — Isaiah runs stars, sun, moon; the Book of Mormon runs sun, moon, stars with Mark. The link is at Mark 13:24.

Cross-reference. 'Yea, they shall be rent in twain' is the closest verbal contact in the chapter with the KJV's account of the crucifixion signs — the phrase occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 27:51 and Mark 15:38, both of the temple veil — but the sentence begins at 14:21 with the yielding up of the ghost and the shaking of the earth, and the link is adjudicated there. A reader arriving at 14:22 should be sent one verse back rather than shown nothing.

A real prophetic commonplace with no verse behind it. Cities laid waste and left without inhabitant are Isaiah's, Jeremiah's and Ezekiel's stock — Isaiah 6:11's 'until the cities be wasted without inhabitant' is the nearest — and 'many highways shall be broken up' has no KJV analogue at all, the King James Bible's highways being either built up (Isaiah 40:3, already in view at 14:9) or lying waste (Isaiah 33:8). The verse is a list of earthquake damage in the Book of Mormon's own words. Filed rather than passed over because a reader who has just been shown Isaiah 40:3-4 at 14:9 and 14:23 will reasonably expect the highway of 14:24 to belong to the same block, and it does not.

Close, and it does not land. John 3:18-19 — 'he that believeth not is condemned already … And this is the condemnation, that light is come into the world' — is the KJV's nearest statement of self-incurred condemnation for unbelief, and Helaman 13:29 has already borrowed from John 3:19, which makes the temptation real. But 14:29's 'if they are condemned, they bring upon themselves their own condemnation' shares only the noun, and the doctrine it states is the Book of Mormon's own agency argument, completed at 14:30-31 out of Deuteronomy 30 rather than out of John. Recorded so the John 3 borrowing at 13:29 is not silently extended to a verse that does not carry it.

A tempting tie-breaker that will not hold. Helaman 15:2's woe on those with child is verbally identical in Matthew 24:19, Mark 13:17 and Luke 21:23, so a reader looking for a way to choose between the three will notice that Luke alone continues, one verse later, with 'Jerusalem shall be trodden down of the Gentiles' — and that Helaman 15:2 ends 'therefore they shall be trodden down, and shall be left to perish'. It does not decide anything: 'trodden down' occurs in ten KJV verses, seven of them Isaiah's, and the Book of Mormon uses it again seven verses later at 15:9 of the Lamanites lying down before their enemies, where no Olivet context is in view. The link is at Matthew 24:19, on the sequence argument from 15:1, and this row records why the apparently decisive detail was not allowed to overturn it.

The standing exclusion for this chapter. Lamentations 4:6 scores on 'of the iniquity of the' and shares no content word with 15:4's 'the iniquity of the tradition of their fathers'; the same applies to 15:6 (Leviticus 17:5, 'that they may bring'), 15:7 (1 John 3:19 and Revelation 22:6, 'of the truth and' and 'of the holy prophets'), 15:9 (Acts 27:12, 'by any means they'), 15:11 (John 16:4 and 1 Kings 16:7, 'the time shall come' and 'and also by the'), 15:12 (Leviticus 16:29, 'unto you that in the') and 15:17 (Judges 2:18 and 1 Samuel 29:6, 'the Lord because of their' and 'as the Lord liveth'). All are the connective boilerplate covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

The verse a reader will expect, and it is not being quoted. 'They have buried their weapons of war … and will not lift their swords against them' looks like Isaiah 2:4's 'nation shall not lift up sword against nation' (and Micah 4:3's), but the Book of Mormon's own narrative supplies everything here: the burial of the weapons is Alma 24:17-19, told at length, and Samuel is reminding a Nephite audience of an event in their own recent history rather than of a prophecy. The machine's proposal, Ezekiel 32:27 ('their weapons of war'), is the phrase but not the act — Ezekiel's fallen mighty go down to the grave WITH their weapons under their heads, which is the opposite gesture. Filed because the Isaiah expectation is strong and the passage is one of the Book of Mormon's most famous, and because getting it wrong would put a swords-into-ploughshares reading on a text that is about martyrdom.

A five-word run and the sense is opposed. In 1 Samuel 15:9 Saul and the people 'would not utterly destroy' the best of the Amalekite livestock — a disobedience for which Saul loses the kingdom in the same chapter. Helaman 15:16's 'I will not utterly destroy them' is God announcing mercy on his own initiative. The verb phrase is shared and the theology is inverted. 2 Chronicles 12:7 is the more interesting near miss and is filed separately.

exclusions.sharedText: I will not destroy them but I will
exclusions.reason: The closest thing in the KJV to Helaman 15:16's structure, and it loses on one adverb. 2 Chronicles 12:7 — 'They have humbled themselves; therefore I will not destroy them, but I will grant them some deliverance' — has the withheld destruction, the adversative 'but I will', and a mercy granted on account of repentance, which is the whole shape of the Book of Mormon verse. What it does not have is 'utterly', and 'I will not utterly destroy' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Amos 9:8. Amos also supplies what Chronicles cannot: a remnant preserved through a sifting among all nations (9:9), which is what 'in the day of my wisdom, they shall return again unto me' describes and what Chronicles' short reprieve from Shishak does not. Filed at length because the two candidates are genuinely close and the rarer phrase is what settles it.

'Utterly destroy' occurs in twelve KJV verses and the first-person future form is spread across Numbers 21:2, Jeremiah 25:9 and Jeremiah 50:21 without any one of them being distinctive. The stream returns Jeremiah 25:9 and Numbers 21:2 here on four-word runs. 15:17's borrowing is not the threat but its counterpart in the preceding verse: Amos 9:8 is the KJV's one sentence holding both verdicts together, and the link is at 15:16.

The stream's top match in the chapter at rarity 2.00, and it scores on five words of connective tissue that the Book of Mormon uses continuously. 2 Kings 17:14 is about Israel hardening their necks like their fathers; Helaman 16:2 and 16:6 are about a crowd that did not believe in the words of Samuel. Nothing but the negated verb and its preposition is shared, and 'believe in' is among the commonest constructions in either book. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; recorded here only because it outranked every real link in the chapter.

A genuine KJV singleton — 'cast stones at' occurs only at 2 Samuel 16:6, where Shimei stones David and his servants as the king flees Absalom — and tempting for exactly that reason. It is the wrong story. Shimei's stones are an insult thrown at a fleeing king by a partisan of the house he displaced, and they land; the stones at Helaman 16:2 are thrown by a whole city at a prophet standing still on a wall, and they miss, which is the point of the verse. The KJV passage that is doing the work here is Matthew 23:37, the city that stones the prophets sent to it, which Samuel had already put to this same city at Helaman 13:25; the link is filed there. The singleton is a coincidence of a common verb and a common noun, and is a good illustration of why a rarity count is evidence and not a verdict.

Five words shared and the senses are unrelated. In Jeremiah 8:7 the stork, the turtle, the crane and the swallow 'observe the time of their coming' — bird migration, cited as a reproach to a people who do not know the LORD's judgment. In Helaman 16:5 'the time of their coming' is the arrival of prophesied events, so that hearers may remember they were told beforehand. The pronoun does not even refer to persons in the same way: Jeremiah's 'their' is the birds', the Book of Mormon's is the things'. An artifact of English word order, and a clean example of the trap at ADJUDICATING §4.

'Cast himself down' is a KJV singleton and it is not this. At 1 Kings 18:42 Elijah goes up to the top of Carmel and casts himself down upon the earth, putting his face between his knees to pray for rain — a prostration, not a fall. Samuel casts himself down from the wall to escape a mob. Checked because the singleton would have made a strong-looking row; the link at this verse goes instead to Luke 4:9, whose 'cast thyself down from hence' is the right act and the right preposition even though it is second person. Recorded so that a reader who runs the rarity count themselves finds the Elijah verse already accounted for.

The stream's best match at this verse (rarity 2.00), and the resemblance is entirely in a narrative formula. Matthew 4:17 begins Jesus' Galilean ministry, 'From that time Jesus began to preach, and to say, Repent'; Helaman 16:7 ends Samuel's, sending him home to 'begin to preach and to prophesy among his own people'. The pairing in the Book of Mormon is preach-and-prophesy, not preach-and-say, and 'began to preach' carries no distinctive KJV colour. The chapter's real Matthew contact is at 16:6.

A batch entry covering the chapter's regnal formula, which the stream matches at 16:9 (Ezra 6:15, 1 Kings 16:8, 2 Chronicles 36:20), 16:11, 16:12 and 16:24. 'The eighty and sixth year of the reign of the Judges' is the Book of Mormon's own dating formula, used through Alma and Helaman without variation, and it happens to share its skeleton with every regnal date in Kings, Chronicles and Ezra because both are King James English for the same thing. The rare words the scorer rewards — 'reign', 'sixth' — are supplied by the calendar, not by a source. No entry in this family is a borrowing.

exclusions.sharedText: their own strength ... their own wisdom
exclusions.reason: 'Began to depend upon their own strength, and upon their own wisdom' reads like wisdom literature and is not traceable to any of it. 'Own strength' occurs in two KJV verses (Psalm 21:13, Amos 6:13) and 'own wisdom' in one (Proverbs 23:4, 'cease from thine own wisdom'), and none of them pairs the two or supplies the verb. Proverbs 3:5's 'lean not unto thine own understanding' is the sentiment but not the noun, and Isaiah 5:21's 'wise in their own eyes' is neither. A real conceptual resemblance with too little verbal contact to adjudicate. The chapter's argument about wisdom and folly is carried instead by the Ephesians 5:15 link at 16:10.

The stream's only match at this verse, on 'them all the days of'. Isaiah 63:9 is the angel of God's presence bearing and carrying Israel all the days of old; Helaman 16:21 is a fear of being kept in servitude 'all the days of our lives'. The shared string is a time adverbial that occurs across the KJV in every genre and completes differently in the two verses — 'of old' against 'of our lives'. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

Worth recording because of what it shows about the Book of Mormon's English rather than about a source. 'The evil one' is not a King James phrase: the KJV's designation is 'the wicked one' (Matthew 13:19, 13:38, 1 John 2:13, 2:14), and the only string match for 'evil one' in the whole King James Bible is the word-boundary artifact at James 4:11, 'Speak not evil one of another'. So Helaman 16:21's 'the cunning and the mysterious arts of the evil one' is a place where the text is not following the KJV even where a KJV equivalent was available. No link; the observation belongs in the register.

A batch entry for the connective matches at 16:22 and 16:23. 'Upon all the face of the land' is a Book of Mormon geographical formula used scores of times from 1 Nephi onward and adjudicated at its first use; the machine matches it here against Ezekiel 34:6's scattered flock, and matches the same two verses against Exodus 14:17 and Joshua 7:5 on 'harden the hearts of' and 'hearts of the people', against 2 Chronicles 14:2 and 31:20 on 'that which was good and', against Luke 1:66 on 'up in their hearts', and against Deuteronomy 1:36 on 'the land that he'. None shares a content word that construes with its match. The real source at 16:22 is Psalm 2:1, which the stream did not propose, because the agreement is split across the sentence and contiguous windows cannot see it (CONVENTIONS §9).

The stream's highest-scoring candidate at this verse (rarity 2.00, a six-word run) and the wrong one. Deuteronomy 34:11 shares the formula 'the signs and the wonders' with Helaman 16:23, and so, on the stream's own list, do Deuteronomy 7:19 and twelve other KJV verses; the phrase identifies nothing. What identifies the source is the clause the stream ranked last, at rarity 1.00: 'wrought among the people' is a KJV singleton at Acts 5:12, which is also the only verse in the Bible carrying the whole of 'signs and wonders wrought among the people'. Deuteronomy's signs are Moses' plagues on Pharaoh; Helaman's are worked among the Lord's own people and fail to hold them, which is Acts 5:12's situation inverted. The link is filed at this verse to Acts 5:12.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references both 2 Kings 25:7 and Jeremiah 39:6 at this verse; both report the sons of Zedekiah slain, and neither leaves the exception the Book of Mormon claims. The adjudicated link is filed at Jeremiah 39:6, whose immediately preceding verses (39:1-5) are the ones the surrounding argument (8:20) names Jeremiah's own fulfilled prophecy about — the context that makes one of the two witnesses the proximate one. 2 Kings 25:7 carries the identical clause and is not a distinct finding.

'There shall be no night there' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 21:25 and 22:5, and describes the new Jerusalem, where night is abolished permanently because the Lamb is its light. 3 Nephi 1:8's night is abolished for one night as a birth sign, and its wording — 'which shall be as one day, as if there were no night' — reproduces two KJV singletons from Zechariah 14:7 instead ('shall be one day', 'not day, nor night'), which Revelation does not have. The link is filed at this verse to Zechariah 14:7. Revelation's phrase is recorded here because it is the passage a reader is likelier to think of first, and because Revelation 21-22 is itself reworking Zechariah 14.

The machine's only candidate at this verse, and a pure artifact of 'and it came to pass'. Luke 2:15 is the shepherds going to Bethlehem — a nativity verse proposed at a nativity chapter, which is exactly the coincidence the standing connective exclusion exists to absorb. Nothing but the narrative formula is shared: the Book of Mormon has a day appointed for executions and Luke has shepherds leaving a field. Recorded rather than passed over in silence only because the apparent aptness of the reference would tempt a reader who did not look at the shared string.

The four-word run construes in opposite directions. In Isaiah the yoke is destroyed because of the anointing — a deliverance; in 3 Nephi the believers are about to be destroyed because of their faith — a persecution. 'Because of' is doing all the work and it is a connective. The real source at this verse is 1 Kings 18:42, which the same stream ranked first on a genuine KJV singleton.

Proverbs 23:17 is 'be thou in the fear of the LORD all the day long', an exhortation to a settled disposition; 3 Nephi 1:12 is 'he cried mightily unto the Lord, all the day', a duration of one day's prayer. The five shared words are 'the Lord all the day' and the sixth word of the Proverbs phrase, 'long', is what makes it mean something different. Jeremiah 8:19 was proposed at the same verse on 'behold the voice of', which occurs across the King James Bible in every register; neither candidate identifies anything.

A batch entry for the connective matches at this verse. 'I have caused to be' in Jeremiah 29:4 is followed by 'carried away from Jerusalem unto Babylon' and is part of an exile formula; in 3 Nephi it is followed by 'spoken by the mouth of my Holy Prophets'. Hebrews 2:3 was proposed at the same verse on 'to be spoken by', which is the same auxiliary chain. The verse's real borrowings — John 18:37, Acts 3:18 and Luke 21:28 — are all adjudicated as links, and two of the three were invisible to the stream.

exclusions.sharedText: of the Father, and of the Son
exclusions.reason: The stream's top candidate here, a seven-word run, and the wrong construction. Matthew 28:19's phrase is a coordinate list — Father, Son, Holy Ghost — that any trinitarian sentence in English reproduces, and the Book of Mormon uses it dozens of times. What is distinctive in 3 Nephi 1:14 is the genitive that follows, 'the Son of the Father', which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 John 1:3, and the link is filed there.

exclusions.sharedText: and they knew that it was
exclusions.reason: A six-word run of pure recognition-narrative. Acts 3:10 is the crowd recognising the lame man at the Beautiful gate; 3 Nephi 1:19 is the people recognising the day of the Lord's birth. The clause is what any English narrator writes when a crowd identifies something, and the words that carry the verse — the night as light as mid-day, the sun rising in its proper order — have no contact with Acts 3 at all. The 1 Samuel 11:11 candidate at the same verse is 'and it came to pass'.

'Harden their hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 11:20, where it is the LORD hardening the Canaanites so that Israel may destroy them utterly. That is a King James singleton and would ordinarily be strong evidence, but hardness of heart is the Book of Mormon's most heavily used idiom, running from 1 Nephi onward in every book and every voice, and it is adjudicated at its first use. Joshua 11:20's sense is also the reverse of this verse's: there God hardens, here Satan does. The real source at 3 Nephi 1:22 is John 12:40, whose 'hardened their heart' and 'blinded their eyes' are both singletons and whose 'be converted' decides the mediation.

exclusions.sharedText: the words of the prophecy of
exclusions.reason: A genuine King James singleton — 'the words of the prophecy' occurs only at Revelation 22:18 — and a good illustration of why a singleton is not by itself a link. Revelation 22:18's phrase is completed by 'of this book' and belongs to the curse on anyone who adds to it; 3 Nephi 1:26's is completed by 'of all the Holy Prophets' and belongs to a year-end summary of fulfilled signs. What the Book of Mormon's clause actually reproduces is the Luke-and-Acts holy-prophets formula (Luke 1:70, Acts 3:21), already adjudicated in this chapter at 1:13 and in earlier books at 1 Nephi 3:20 and Mosiah 13:33. The link at 1:26 is filed to Luke 1:19 on 'glad tidings'.

The stream's top candidate at this verse. Ezra 3:13 is the crowd at the second temple's foundation, where the people could not distinguish the shouting from the weeping; 3 Nephi 1:27 is a people who could not overpower the Gadianton robbers. Only the negated modal is shared. The adjudicated source at this verse is Psalm 10:8, which the stream could not see because the agreement is split between 'their secret places' and 'many murders' twenty words apart.

A batch entry for the two candidates at this verse. 'Remain in the land' (Joshua 1:14) and 'did remain in the' (Obadiah 1:14) are four-word runs of ordinary territorial English, and the Book of Mormon uses 'remain in the land' continuously from Mosiah onward. Neither Joshua's Reubenite families nor Obadiah's Edomite survivors has any contact with Nephite dissenters fleeing to the robbers.

A KJV singleton — 'flattering words' occurs only at 1 Thessalonians 2:5, where Paul denies using them — and the Book of Mormon's standing term for demagoguery from Mosiah 11:7 onward, where it is adjudicated. The occurrences at Alma 46:7 and Alma 50:35 were registered here the same way, and this one follows them: the phrase has become Mormon's own word for the practice rather than a fresh reach for Paul, and the narrating hand at 3 Nephi 1:29 is the same hand that abridged Mosiah. The reader is sent to Mosiah 11:7 for the argument.

A five-word causal connective that the Book of Mormon uses in every historical book. Deuteronomy 28:20's clause is 'because of the wickedness of thy doings, whereby thou hast forsaken me', a covenant curse in the second person; 3 Nephi 1:30 has 'because of the wickedness of the rising generation'. Nothing beyond the connective is shared, and 'the rising generation', which is what the verse is actually about, is in no KJV verse at all.

'The people began to wax strong in wickedness and abominations.' “wax strong in” occurs in no KJV verse and the past form “waxed strong in” occurs in exactly two, Luke 1:80 and Luke 2:40 — and both of them are the same sentence about a child growing: 'And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit', said of John the Baptist and then of Jesus. The coincidence is tempting because this chapter is counting the years since the nativity, so the KJV's only 'waxed strong in' verses are describing the childhood the Nephite calendar is measuring. It is still a coincidence. Luke's idiom takes a virtue as its object and describes growth toward a ministry; 3 Nephi 2:3 takes wickedness and abominations as its object and describes a population's decay. 'Wax strong' with an abstract object is ordinary King James English and the Book of Mormon uses it repeatedly on its own account. Recorded because a reader who notices the Luke verses will want to know the catalogue noticed them.

A six-word run and the highest-ranked candidate in this stretch of the chapter, and it is a title. 2 Kings 9:6 is Jehu's anointing — 'I have anointed thee king over the people of the LORD, even over Israel' — and 3 Nephi 2:5 is a dating note: 'since the days of Mosiah, which was king over the people of the Nephites.' The shared words are the KJV's ordinary way of saying that a man ruled a nation, and the Book of Mormon uses the same construction of Benjamin, Mosiah, Noah and Lamanite kings throughout. Nothing of the anointing scene is present.

A four-word run consisting entirely of a number. Genesis 11:19 is Peleg's entry in the postdiluvian genealogy; 3 Nephi 2:6 is the Nephite chronology — 'six hundred and nine years had passed away, since Lehi left Jerusalem.' The KJV writes out large numbers this way constantly and simply had occasion to write this one at Genesis 11:19. This entry covers the whole run of dating formulas in 2:4-8, which are not listed individually; compare the standing entry at Helaman 1:1.

The best-looking verbal candidate in the chapter and it has to be declined in full, because a reader working with the 1830 text will find it. 1830 reads 'could no where be found in all the land', two words, which 1920 collapsed to 'nowhere' and thereby erased; the first edition preserves the KJV's orthography here as it does at shew and marvellous, and the phrase it preserves is a singleton. “no where” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 10:14 — Saul's uncle asking where he has been, 'To seek the asses: and when we saw that they were no where'.
