Better still, “could not be found” occurs in exactly three KJV verses and one of them is 1 Samuel 10:21, seven verses later in the same chapter: Saul taken by lot at his own coronation and 'when they sought him, he could not be found.' The Book of Mormon's clause fuses both phrases and both come from one KJV chapter about a man who could not be located. The sense is nevertheless wrong at every point that matters. 1 Samuel 10:14 is about livestock, and its 'no where' is predicated of the asses, not of a person; 1 Samuel 10:21 is about a man hiding among the stuff who is produced two verses later. Neither is a disappearance, nobody is taken up, and the searches end. 3 Nephi 2:9's man is never produced and the record passes to his son. The link at this verse is filed at 2 Kings 2:17, where the search does fail; this entry records that the sharper verbal candidate was seen, that the 1830 reading is what makes it visible, and that it was refused on sense.

“which had the charge of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is why the machine ranked it, and the verse is a good deal more interesting than the phrase: Jeremiah 52:25 is the deportation after the fall of Jerusalem, and it lists among the captives 'an eunuch, which had the charge of the men of war' and 'the principal scribe of the host'. A Nephite who had the charge of the records disappearing might be thought to answer that. It will not carry. “had the charge of” occurs in exactly four KJV verses and the construction is plain administrative English; the object in Jeremiah is an army, not an archive; and the clause here is the Book of Mormon resuming its own sentence from seven verses earlier, 3 Nephi 1:2, where this Nephi departs 'giving charge unto his son Nephi … concerning the plates of brass, and all the records', which is Mosiah 1:16's idiom for the same handover. The link at this verse is elsewhere — see 2 Kings 2:17.

“utter destruction” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 20:42 and Zechariah 14:11, and neither is in view. 1 Kings 20:42 uses it of a man Ahab was to have devoted and let go — the herem, a thing appointed to destruction, not a fate threatened; Zechariah 14:11 promises there shall be no more of it in a restored Jerusalem. 3 Nephi 2:13 uses the phrase as the Book of Mormon uses it everywhere from Alma 9:18 to Helaman 13:10, as a standing term for the annihilation of a people by war. Rare in the KJV, formulaic in this corpus, and a rarity count that measures the King James Bible's vocabulary rather than any borrowing.

A model case for this category, and it needs writing out because the resemblance is at the level of the image and the meaning is exactly reversed. 'Their curse was taken from them, and their skin became white like unto the Nephites.' In the King James Bible a skin turning white is itself the curse and never its removal: Miriam becomes 'leprous, white as snow' for speaking against Moses (Numbers 12:10), Moses's own hand is made 'leprous as snow' as a sign (Exodus 4:6), and Gehazi goes out from Elisha 'a leper as white as snow' for his greed (2 Kings 5:27). “white as snow” occurs in eight KJV verses and the three that describe a human skin are all judgements. The Book of Mormon's whitening is the lifting of a judgement. There is besides no shared wording — no 'snow', no 'leprous', no 'white as' — and the passage's real antecedents are internal, 2 Nephi 5:21 and Alma 3:6, not biblical. Recorded so that the register shows the catalogue considered the leprosy verses and found the polarity opposed.

A five-word run and the top-ranked candidate for the verse, and the two sentences say opposite things. Psalm 78:63 is a line of the historical psalm's catalogue of judgements — 'The fire consumed their young men; and their maidens were not given to marriage' — where the young men die and the young women do not marry. 3 Nephi 2:16 has 'their young men and their daughters became exceeding fair, and they were numbered among the Nephites', which is a blessing, a flourishing and an incorporation. 2 Kings 8:12, the other candidate on the same run, is Hazael foreseeing that he will slay Israel's young men with the sword. The pairing of young men with daughters or maidens is one of the KJV's commonest parallelisms and points nowhere by itself.

A five-word run of the plainest causal boilerplate. Deuteronomy 28:20 is the covenant curse — 'because of the wickedness of thy doings, whereby thou hast forsaken me' — and 3 Nephi 2:18 reads 'because of the wickedness of the people of Nephi'. The construction occurs across the KJV and is the Book of Mormon's default explanation of a military reverse; it recurs in this very chapter at 2:19 ('this because of their iniquity'). No content word is shared beyond 'wickedness'.

exclusions.sharedText: (a drawn sword suspended over a people)
exclusions.reason: Typology pulls hard here and the wording will not bear it, which is the Judges 3 case at Helaman 1:10 over again. 'The sword of destruction did hang over them, insomuch that they were about to be smitten down by it, and this because of their iniquity.' The King James Bible has one image of a sword held in suspension over a people who are about to be struck for a sin: 1 Chronicles 21:16, where David sees the angel of the LORD 'having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem', the plague already running because of the census. “stretched out over” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is that one. But the Book of Mormon has 'hang over', not 'stretched out over', and “hang over” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 26:12 and 26:13, both about the curtains of the tabernacle. “the sword of destruction” occurs in no KJV verse at all. There is no angel here, no plague, no confession, and no shared distinctive word. Recorded so that a reader who sees the Chronicles image is told the catalogue saw it and declined to catalogue it as dependence.

“utter destruction” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 20:42 and Zechariah 14:11, so a reader who checks the rarity will be tempted, and the entry is here to say the catalogue checked it too. Neither verse will do. 1 Kings 20:42 is a prophet condemning Ahab for having spared a king he was to have devoted to destruction — the phrase there renders the ban, the herem, a thing decreed by God and carried out on his behalf. Zechariah 14:11 promises the abolition of the ban from a restored Jerusalem. Giddianhi uses the words as a commander's threat about what his troops would do if released: “they would visit you with utter destruction”. Two words, one of them the ordinary intensifier, in a sense the KJV never has for them, and nothing else of 1 Kings 20 anywhere near.

A five-word run and one of the higher machine scores in the chapter. The senses are opposed in the way that matters most. Exodus 22:24 is the LORD's threat against Israelites who afflict the widow and the fatherless — “I will kill you with the sword; and your wives shall be widows, and your children fatherless” — that is, a judgment on oppressors, executed by God, on behalf of the defenceless. 3 Nephi 3:6 is an oppressor's threat against a people who have done him no wrong, and the sword is his own army's. The Book of Mormon's clause is in any case “visit you with the sword”, which is not Exodus's verb; “kill you with the sword” it does not have. The shared string is the preposition and its object.

“extinct” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Job 17:1 (“my days are extinct”) and Isaiah 43:17, and Isaiah's is the apposite one: an army and its power that “shall lie down together, they shall not rise: they are extinct, they are quenched as tow”, which is Pharaoh's host at the sea. Giddianhi threatens to bring an army down until a people “shall become extinct”. One rare word, used in the same domain, and that is the whole of it: no shared construction, no shared syntax, and the direction is reversed — in Isaiah the army is what is extinguished, here the army is what extinguishes. Recorded because the word is genuinely rare in the KJV and a rarity check alone would make this look stronger than it is.

The chapter's second-highest n-gram score (2.00), and it is a bare conditional. Numbers 32:20 is Moses's terms to Reuben and Gad — “If ye will do this thing, if ye will go armed before the LORD to war” — and Giddianhi's is an ultimatum with the same hinge repeated in both polarities two clauses apart (“if ye will do this … but if ye will not do this”). The construction is the King James Bible's ordinary way of stating a condition and the Book of Mormon uses it continuously. This entry also covers Genesis 34:15's “unto you if ye will”, which the machine ranked at the same verse: Genesis 34 is genuinely in play in this chapter, but at 3:7 and as a narrative form, where it is catalogued — not through this string.

This is the entry the Exodus 2:2 “goodly” case in 1 Nephi is the model for: a typology pulls hard and the wording will not bear it. “was a just man” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 6:9 (Noah) and Mark 6:20 (Herod's estimate of John the Baptist). The Noah reading is the seductive one, because what this just man immediately does is gather a whole population together with their flocks and their herds and all their substance into one place, seal it round with fortifications, and preserve them alive through a destruction that carries off everyone outside. But there is no ark, no water, no covenant and no remnant language anywhere in the chapter, and “just man” is a stock KJV commendation — the shared string is four words of which three are function words. Mark 6:20 fits the situation better than Genesis does (a ruler confronted with a man he cannot intimidate) and it fits it backwards, since there the ruler fears the just man and here the just man is the ruler. Declined at any confidence, and recorded so that a reader who sees the flood type is told the catalogue saw it too.

exclusions.sharedText: sent a proclamation … that they should gather together … unto one place
exclusions.reason: Not a rejection of the source but a redirection to where its wording actually lands. Lachoneus' proclamation is issued here, and the Ezra 10:7 link is real — but 3:13 reads “that they should gather together”, without the reflexive, while 3:22 and 3:24 both read “that they should gather themselves together”, which is Ezra's five-word run verbatim, and 3:22 supplies “throughout all the face of the land” against Ezra's “throughout Judah and Jerusalem”. CONVENTIONS §6a: put the link where the wording is. The adjudication is at 3 Nephi 3:22 and a reader who arrives at 3:13 should go there.

exclusions.sharedText: their flocks and their herds and all their substance
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run at 3:13 and again at 3:22, and the highest-scoring candidate in the chapter after it is repeated (Numbers 31:9, rarity 3.50, is the same list in a different order and is covered by this entry). “Flocks and herds” with “all their substance” is the King James Bible's standing inventory for a household on the move — Genesis 12:5, 13:5, 24:35, 46:32, 47:1, Exodus 10:9, 12:38, Numbers 31:9, 32:1 and many more — and the Book of Mormon uses it for every migration it narrates. Genesis 46-47 scores highest only because Joseph's brothers happen to bring the same three items in the same order. Nothing of the Goshen settlement is present here, and the machine's other proposals against this string (Genesis 12:5, Genesis 47:1) fall with it.

“as the Lord liveth” occurs in exactly 27 KJV verses and is the Bible's standard oath formula; Judges 8:19 ranked only because the machine's window caught the following “if” as well. The Book of Mormon uses the formula throughout and this chapter uses it twice, here in Lachoneus' warning and again in Gidgiddoni's answer at 3:21. The second occurrence is catalogued, and not for this phrase's own sake: at 3:21 it stands in one speech with “the Lord forbid”, and 1 Samuel 26:10-11 is the only place in the KJV where those two idioms are adjacent. Nothing of that argument applies at 3:15, where the oath stands alone.

exclusions.sharedText: into the wilderness that we may
exclusions.reason: The top-scoring candidate in the chapter (rarity 3.00, a six-word run) and worthless, which is CONVENTIONS §9's point about the n-gram stream being a recall floor rather than a ranking. Exodus 3:18 is Moses and the elders asking Pharaoh for leave to go “three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God”: a request made by slaves to their master, for a religious purpose, in order to leave. 3 Nephi 3:20 is a free people asking their own commander for leave to go into the wilderness that they may fall upon robbers and destroy them: an offensive military proposal. The shared six words are the destination and a purpose clause, and every content word after them differs. The real source-question at this verse is the type-scene of Deuteronomy 1:41-44, which is catalogued as a figural link and shares no wording at all — an instructive pairing, since the machine's best string here points nowhere and the link that is worth having was invisible to it.

“bucklers” occurs in exactly five KJV verses and is a rare enough word to be worth checking, but “shields and bucklers” as a phrase occurs in exactly 0 — the KJV pairs them only in lists that also carry spears, bows or habergeons (2 Chronicles 23:9, Ezekiel 38:4, Ezekiel 39:9), and Song of Solomon 4:4 and Job 15:26 are not armouries at all. Ezekiel 39:9 is the closest (“both the shields and the bucklers, the bows and the arrows”) and is a prophecy of Israel burning the weapons of a defeated invader for seven years, which is the opposite of arming. “Buckler” is simply the King James word for a small shield and the Book of Mormon's armament lists use it throughout the war chapters. The link that this verse does carry is at its first clause, to Matthew 26:22.

The chapter’s top-ranked candidate, on a five-word run that the verse then repeats twice more. 1 Kings 21:15-16 is Ahab going down to take possession of Naboth’s vineyard after Jezebel has had Naboth stoned, and the surface attraction is real: in both texts a party seizes land whose owners are gone. But the transaction is inverted at the point that matters. Naboth’s vineyard is seized from a man judicially murdered for it, and the seizure is the crime the chapter exists to condemn; the robbers take lands the Nephites have deliberately abandoned under Lachoneus’s proclamation (3 Nephi 3:13, 3:22), which is why the lands are empty and why, four verses later, the robbers are starving in them. Ahab gets a vineyard; Giddianhi gets a desert. Nothing of 1 Kings 21 beyond the idiom is present, and “take possession of” is the ordinary King James phrase for occupying land.

exclusions.sharedText: their flocks, and their herds, and all their substance
exclusions.reason: A genuine composite of two Genesis migrations sits under this clause — “and all their substance” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 12:5, where Abram leaves Haran for Canaan with it, and “flocks and their herds and all” occurs in exactly two, Genesis 46:32 and 47:1, where Jacob’s household goes down into Egypt. But 3 Nephi 4:3 is not where the Book of Mormon says it. The phrase enters at 3 Nephi 3:13, in Lachoneus’s proclamation commanding the gathering (“their flocks and their herds, and all their substance, save it were their land, unto one place”), and is executed at 3:22. 4:3 is the narrator recalling a movement already narrated. Adjudicate the Genesis composite at 3 Nephi 3:13; this row exists so that a reader who meets the phrase here is sent there.

A five-word run, and the highest-scoring candidate on the verse, on a phrase the catalogue has good reason to take seriously: John 18:14 is Caiaphas’s counsel that it was expedient that one man should die for the people, and 1 Nephi 4:13 borrows precisely that sentence to justify the killing of Laban. So the temptation here is not naive. It fails on sense. Caiaphas’s expediency is a calculation that one death will save a nation, and the Gospel glosses it as unwitting prophecy; Giddianhi’s is a supply problem — “there was no way that they could subsist, save it were to plunder, and rob, and murder”. Nothing dies for anyone, nobody prophesies, and “expedient” is among the most worn words in the Book of Mormon’s vocabulary, appearing across every book with no biblical colouring at all. The Caiaphas link stands at 1 Nephi 4:13 and does not extend here.

This is the closer verbal match of the two and it still loses. “fallen to the earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 26:14 and 2 Chronicles 20:24, and Acts has the Book of Mormon’s “all” as well — “when we were all fallen to the earth”, against “had all fallen to the earth”. What Acts does not have is anything else. Paul is recounting his own conversion on the Damascus road, struck down by a light while travelling to arrest Christians, and hears a voice; the Nephite armies fall down deliberately, in prayer, at the sight of an approaching enemy. 2 Chronicles 20:24, by contrast, sits inside the one KJV narrative whose entire sequence 3 Nephi 4 reproduces — the gathering, the prostration, the ambush the Lord sets, the field of dead, the return with singing. The link is written there; see the note at 4:8 for the argument, including the admission that Chronicles supplies the pattern and Acts the extra word.

“threatenings” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 4:29 and Acts 9:1, and in no Old Testament verse — a genuine New-Testament-only word turning up in a first-century-BC Nephite war narrative, which is the kind of datum this catalogue exists for. It is not adjudicated here for two reasons. First, the word enters this book at 3 Nephi 3:12, of Lachoneus refusing to be frightened by “the demands and the threatenings of a robber”, so 4:12 is a repetition inside one book (ADJUDICATING §4). Second, and decisively, the full Acts 9:1 collocation appears one chapter later: 3 Nephi 5:5 reads “as many as were found breathing out threatenings against their brethren”, against Acts 9:1’s “Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord”. That is where the borrowing is demonstrable and that is where it should be catalogued. Noted here so a reader of 4:12 is sent to 5:5.

A five-word run of pure geographical connective. Joshua 13:4 is a boundary list — “all the land of the Canaanites… unto Aphek, to the borders of the Amorites” — and 3 Nephi 4:13 is a pursuit order bounded by the wilderness. No content word is shared beyond the idiom itself, and the Book of Mormon uses “the borders of” for every frontier it has. This entry covers the other boundary-formula candidates in the chapter; they are not listed individually.

“with boldness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 4:31, where the disciples filled with the Holy Ghost “spake the word of God with boldness” — and the temptation is sharpened by the fact that Acts 4:29, two verses earlier, is one of the King James Bible’s only two “threatenings” verses, and 3 Nephi 4:12 has “threatenings”. Two words from one short Acts paragraph, two verses apart in the Book of Mormon, is a coincidence worth stating. It is not enough. In Acts the threatenings belong to the persecutors and the boldness to the persecuted, and both words are about speech; in 3 Nephi 4 both belong to Giddianhi, and the boldness is a robber chief’s courage in a losing fight. Boldness is also among the Book of Mormon’s most common virtues, and it is never Acts’s. Recorded so that the convergence is on the books, and declined.

“lay siege” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Isaiah 29:3 and Ezekiel 4:2-3, so Ezekiel is a real candidate on the phrase alone. Isaiah 29:3 takes it because it is the only one of the three that has the Book of Mormon’s “round about” attached — “I will camp against thee round about, and will lay siege against thee with a mount”, against “they came up on all sides to lay siege round about the people of Nephi”. Ezekiel 4:2 is a symbolic action performed on a tile with a model fort and battering rams, and none of its furniture is present. The link is written at 4:16 with Isaiah 29:3 in composite alongside Luke 19:43.

A five-word run consisting entirely of function words plus “people”. 1 Chronicles 23:25 is David’s reason for settling the Levites’ duties, “The LORD God of Israel hath given rest unto his people, that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever”; 3 Nephi 4:23 is Zemnarihah ordering a retreat northward. Opposed in sense — rest granted against a siege abandoned — and sharing no distinctive vocabulary. Covered in principle by the standing connective-tissue exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob
exclusions.reason: The obvious source for the patriarchal triad, and the one the Book of Mormon does not use. Exodus 3:6, 3:15 and 4:5 all read “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”, with no conjunction before Isaac; 3:16 compresses to “of Isaac, and of Jacob”. 3 Nephi 4:30 has the conjunction, which puts it with Matthew 22:32, Mark 12:26, Luke 20:37 and Acts 7:32 — the four New Testament verses that are the only KJV verses reading it that way. Registered here because a reader who assumes Exodus should be told that the wording rules it out, and because tools/mediation-check.py cannot make the call: it ignores single common words, and “and” is the only word at which the two forms differ. Same discrimination as 1 Nephi 6:4 and Alma 36:2.

“most high God” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses, spread from Melchizedek in Genesis 14 to Daniel to the Gerasene demoniac in Mark 5:7, and no one of them can be picked out as a source. Psalm 78:56 ranked only because it is the shortest verse containing the phrase. It is also the wrong sense: “Yet they tempted and provoked the most high God, and kept not his testimonies” is about apostasy, and 3 Nephi 4:32 is a doxology. The title is doing real work in the verse — see the link at 4:32, where it answers Matthew 21:9’s “Hosanna in the highest” — but it is doing it as generic KJV vocabulary, not as a citation of any verse that has it.

The machine’s top candidate at 4:8, 4:31 and 4:33 alike, on a six-word run, and it is exactly backwards. Judges 2:14 is a judgment: “the anger of the LORD was hot against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of spoilers… and he sold them into the hands of their enemies round about.” Every occurrence in 3 Nephi 4 is a deliverance OUT of those hands — 4:8 petitions it, 4:31 and 4:33 celebrate it. Judges 8:34, which has the Book of Mormon’s direction and its plural “hands”, is the verse the link is written on at 4:33; “delivered them out of the hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and that is it. This entry covers the Judges 2:14 candidate wherever it recurs in the chapter.

The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter and it scores for a real reason: “must needs be that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 18:7, and the Book of Mormon reproduces it twice, at 5:1 and 5:2. But Matthew 18:7 is about the inevitability of offences — 'Woe unto the world because of offences! for it must needs be that offences come' — and 3 Nephi 5:1-2 is about the inevitability of prophecy being fulfilled. The verse that joins this idiom to fulfilment is Acts 1:16, 'this scripture must needs have been fulfilled', and the link is written there. Recorded here because a reader who runs the string and finds a singleton will land on Matthew, and should be told the catalogue landed there too and moved.

A five-word run of pure connective tissue — 'and they knew that it' — matched against a verse about the lame man at the Beautiful gate. Nothing else of Acts 3:10 is present, and 5:2's own 'they knew it must needs be' is adjudicated at 5:1. Covered in principle by the standing boilerplate exclusion; listed because it ranked second in the chapter.

A genuine and tempting singleton: “with all diligence” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 4:23, 'Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.' The temptation is doubled by the fact that 3 Nephi 5:5 sorts the unrepentant precisely by what they 'still continue to have … in their hearts', so a reader could construct a contrast in which those who serve God with all diligence have kept their hearts and those who did not have not. The wording will not bear it. In Proverbs the phrase governs guarding an inward thing; in 3 Nephi it governs an outward practice of worship, and the noun 'heart' is two verses away and attached to the opposite party. The Book of Mormon uses 'with all diligence' as a standing formula of its own — Jacob 1, Enos 1, Mosiah 7, Alma 21, 2 Nephi 6 among others — which is what a phrase looks like when it has stopped being a borrowing. The real sources of 5:3 are Acts 26:7 and Luke 2:37, adjudicated at the verse.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when they had
exclusions.reason: An eight-word run and the longest in the chapter; it is the Book of Mormon's narrative hinge matched against Amos's locust vision. Covered by the standing exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 2:1, and listed here only because its length will draw a reader's eye.

Four connective words, but the inversion is neat enough to be worth denying explicitly. Revelation 13:15 is 'as many as would not worship the image of the beast should be killed'; 3 Nephi 5:4 is 'as many as would repent of their sins … were set at liberty'. Compulsory worship on pain of death against voluntary repentance rewarded with release — a reader could build something here. There is nothing to build it out of: no shared vocabulary beyond the four-word connective, and 5:4's actual source, Luke 4:18, accounts for the whole sentence.

Worth a register entry as a caution about rarity counts. The machine ranks this because “the will of God that” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — but the count is an artifact of punctuation. 1 Peter 2:15 reads 'For so is the will of God, that with well doing ye may put to silence…', where 'that' opens a new clause; the string is only rare because the KJV happens to place a comma there and nowhere else. The Book of Mormon's phrase is the ordinary one: “according to the will of God” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Romans 8:27, Galatians 1:4, 1 Peter 4:19), and the corpus uses it constantly. No other contact with 1 Peter 2 — no well doing, no foolish men, no silence.

The strongest thing the catalogue declined in this chapter, and it is declined on a count. 3 Nephi 5:13-17 assembles the whole Johannine eyewitness apparatus in order: a disciple who has been 'called of him to declare his word … that they might have everlasting life' (5:13), and then 'a record of the things which I have seen with mine own eyes' (5:17). 1 John 1:1-3 has the same three moves — 'which we have seen with our eyes … declare we unto you … that eternal life, which was with the Father'. But the verbal test fails where it should pass. “seen with our eyes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 1:1, and the Book of Mormon does not have it: “mine own eyes” occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses, and the possessive-plus-'own' construction is the corpus's own idiom, not the King James Bible's. The dossier's proposal here, John 8:38, fails for the same reason and is worse — 'I speak that which I have seen with my Father' is about the Son's origin, not about testimony. Recorded so a reader who sees the Johannine shape is told the catalogue saw it and would not put a link on it.

“make an end of” occurs in exactly five KJV verses and in every one of them it means to destroy or to finish off — Ezekiel 20:17 'neither did I make an end of them in the wilderness', Isaiah 38:13, Daniel 9:24 'to make an end of sins'. 3 Nephi 5:19 means to stop talking: 'now I make an end of my saying which is of myself'. The Book of Mormon's own 'make an end' formula for closing a discourse runs from 1 Nephi to Moroni and has no biblical parent; the KJV never uses the phrase of speech.

A five-word run and a singleton — “hath blessed the house” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and it is still arithmetic rather than evidence. “blessed the house of” occurs in exactly two verses, 2 Samuel 6:12 and 1 Chronicles 13:14, and they are the same episode: the ark lodging three months with Obededom the Gittite and prospering his household. 3 Nephi 5:21 is 'Surely he hath blessed the house of Jacob, and hath been merciful unto the seed of Joseph' — a national covenant formula, where the KJV verse is a domestic anecdote about a man who kept a box. 'The house of Jacob' itself occurs in eighteen KJV verses and is Isaiah's phrase, which is where this chapter's peroration is drawing from; see the Isaiah 11:12 link at 5:26.

Five connective words. The machine proposes 2 Timothy 3:7 here and 1 Timothy 2:4 at 5:25 for the same string, and both KJV verses complete it as 'the knowledge of the truth' — a fixed Pastoral-epistle collocation — while 3 Nephi completes it as 'the knowledge of the Lord their God' (5:23) and 'the knowledge of the covenant' (5:25). The one that completes differently is the one that matters: the Book of Mormon's phrase belongs with Isaiah 11:9, 'the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD', which is the chapter Isaiah 11:12 comes from and which the peroration is already using. One entry covers both verses.

“the Lord liveth” occurs in exactly 37 KJV verses and is the King James Bible's standard oath. 1 Samuel 29:6 ranks only because Achish happens to precede it with 'surely', as 3 Nephi 5:24 does; the verse is a Philistine king certifying David's good conduct and has no other contact with a gathering prophecy. The formula recurs at 5:26 ('as the Lord liveth, so shall it be') and is not evidence at either verse.

exclusions.sharedText: scattered upon all the face of the earth
exclusions.reason: A genuine KJV singleton — “upon all the face of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and by 3 Nephi it is the Book of Mormon's own dispersion formula, adjudicated as a composite element at 1 Nephi 10:12 and excluded as a repeat at 1 Nephi 13:39, 1 Nephi 14:14, Alma 29:2 and Helaman 11 among others. What is worth adding here is where the formula stops: the clause is 'which are scattered abroad upon all the face of the earth', and its first four words are a different KJV singleton, James 1:1's address to the twelve tribes of the dispersion. The link is written on that half at 5:24; this half is standing formula.

Ranked at both 5:24 and 5:26, and it is the wrong half of the phrase. Jeremiah 49:36 reads 'the four quarters of heaven', not of the earth, and it is a scattering rather than a gathering: 'I will scatter them toward all those winds; and there shall be no nation whither the outcasts of Elam shall not come.' The Book of Mormon has 'of the earth', which is Revelation 20:8's, and gathers rather than scatters. Recorded because Jeremiah 49:36's 'outcasts' is a word this chapter's real Isaian source, Isaiah 11:12, also uses, and a reader could be drawn across on it.

exclusions.sharedText: the four quarters of the earth
exclusions.reason: The same KJV singleton the machine ranks first at 5:24, and it is the same borrowing two verses later within one sentence of argument. Adjudicated at 5:24, where the mediation test against Isaiah 11:12 is run and 'quarters' rather than 'corners' is shown to be decisive. What 5:26 adds is Isaiah's own word, 'dispersed', which 5:24 lacks, and the link on that is written at 5:26.

exclusions.sharedText: in the twenty and sixth year
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter, on a six-word run, and it is regnal-year dating and nothing else. 1 Kings 16:8 dates the accession of Elah of Israel; 3 Nephi 6:1 dates the return of the Nephites to their lands after the robber war. The Book of Mormon dates every paragraph of this chapter the same way — 6:4 'the twenty and sixth and seventh years', 6:9 'the twenty and eighth year', 6:10 'the twenty and ninth year', 6:14 and 6:17 'the thirtieth year' — so the rarity that made the phrase rank is arithmetic rather than intertextual: the KJV had occasion to write 'twenty and sixth' about a reign once, and this chapter had occasion to write it about a year of the judges once. This entry covers every regnal-dating candidate in the chapter, including Ezekiel 1:1 at 6:14 ('in the thirtieth year') and Revelation 21:1 at 6:4 ('passed away, and there was'), which are the same phenomenon reached through different numerals and different connectives.

“entered into a covenant” occurs in exactly two KJV verses — 2 Chronicles 15:12, Asa's national covenant to seek the LORD, and Ezekiel 16:8, the LORD's marriage covenant with Jerusalem — which is rare enough to be worth checking and not enough to be a source. The Book of Mormon uses the phrase for a treaty with surrendered robbers here and, twenty-five verses later, for the secret oath of the judges: 'they did enter into a covenant one with another, yea, even into that covenant which was given by them of old, which covenant was given and administered by the Devil' (6:28). One chapter using the phrase in both senses, one of them diabolical, is a phrase the book owns, not one it is borrowing. Nothing else of 2 Chronicles 15 is present.

This one is genuinely tempting and it is being declined on the preposition. “lifted up with pride” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 3:6 — 'Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil' — and the fit with this chapter is uncomfortably good, since 3 Nephi 6:15 says in so many words that 'Satan had great power' over exactly these people, which is Paul's 'condemnation of the devil' arriving five verses later. But the Book of Mormon never once writes 'with'. It writes 'lifted up unto pride' here, 'lifted up in pride' three verses later, and 'lifted up in the pride of their hearts' or 'of their eyes' dozens of times from 2 Nephi onward, in books adjudicated before this one. A formula the corpus has used continuously for four hundred pages, with a preposition the KJV verse does not have, is the corpus's own; the singleton is a coincidence of the two words that surround it. Recorded at length because a reader who runs the rarity check will find the singleton and should be told the catalogue found it too and why it declined.

A four-word run and pure homography. In Joshua 4:18 what is lifted up is the soles of the priests' feet, out of the Jordan onto dry land, and the clause is a physical description of the end of a miracle. In 3 Nephi 6:10 what is lifted up is the people, into pride and boastings because of their riches. The verb is not even the same verb in sense — one is elevation of a body, the other is a moral state — and the preposition 'unto' governs a place in Joshua and an abstraction in the Book of Mormon. The real source of the pride language in this verse is discussed at the James 4:16 link and at the 1 Timothy 3:6 entry below.

exclusions.sharedText: (social rank distinguished by wealth inside a congregation)
exclusions.reason: The thematic pull is strong and the wording will not bear it. James 2:1-9 is the New Testament's one sustained passage on a church that sorts its members by wealth — the gay clothing and the good place, the poor man under the footstool, 'are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts' — and 3 Nephi 6:12 is a church sorted by wealth into ranks, immediately followed by the church being broken up. The catalogue does link this verse's neighbourhood to James, but through James 4:13-5:6 at 6:10, where three KJV singletons and a preserved sequence carry the case. At 6:12 itself there is not one shared distinctive word: James has respect of persons, apparel, and a synagogue; the Book of Mormon has ranks, riches, learning and poverty. Filed here so that the reading is recorded as considered rather than missed.

A four-word run in opposite senses, and the difference is a matter of English idiom rather than of theology. Matthew 24:43's goodman 'would not have suffered his house to be broken up' — that is, broken into, burgled by the thief who comes in the night; the KJV's 'broken up' there translates the digging through of a mud wall. 3 Nephi 6:14's church 'was broken up in all the land', which is dissolution, a body ceasing to hold together. Nothing else of the Olivet discourse is in the verse, and the eschatological setting that might have made the parallel interesting cuts the wrong way: Matthew's householder fails to watch and loses his goods, while the Nephite church fails and loses itself.

exclusions.sharedText: (a conspirator drawing away the hearts of a people to seize a throne)
exclusions.reason: “stole the hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse: 'so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel', and the narrative it opens is the closest biblical analogue to what 3 Nephi 6 describes — a subversion worked through the judgment-seat (2 Samuel 15:2-4, Absalom promising better justice to every man who came to the king for judgment), ending in a conspiracy to displace the ruler and take the crown, which is 3 Nephi 6:30 exactly. But the Book of Mormon writes 'lead away the hearts of the people', which shares with 2 Samuel 15:6 only the noun 'hearts', and 'lead away' is itself a KJV singleton belonging to an unrelated verse (Isaiah 20:4, the Assyrian deporting Egyptians). Typology without wording, and the Ehud entry at Helaman 1:10 is the model for how the catalogue handles that: record it, decline it, and let the reader see the type was seen.

“the hearts of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is the kind of fact that ought to settle a link and here does not. Joshua 7:5's hearts melt and become as water: it is a description of national terror after the defeat at Ai. 3 Nephi 6:16's hearts are led away by Satan into iniquity: it is a description of national seduction. The verb governs the noun in opposite directions — fear that paralyses versus desire that moves — and the two verses share no other word. The near miss is worth naming: Joshua 7 is a story about a man who coveted silver, gold and a goodly garment and brought the whole people down with him, which is almost the argument of 3 Nephi 6:10-16, and a catalogue that recorded the singleton without recording that it is the wrong half of Joshua 7 would be making a false economy.

exclusions.sharedText: (ignorance as the plea for those who kill the just)
exclusions.reason: The most interesting thing declined in this chapter. Acts 3:17 is Peter's excuse for the men who had just killed Jesus — 'I wot that through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers' — and it stands behind Luke 23:34's 'they know not what they do'. 3 Nephi 6:18 says of a people who are about to kill their prophets, and who are four chapters from the crucifixion in the other hemisphere, that they 'did not sin ignorantly'. The plea Peter grants Jerusalem is refused to Zarahemla, and the refusal is placed immediately before the killings. That is a real reading and the catalogue believes it, but it is not a verbal dependence: Acts 3:17 has 'through ignorance', a phrase the KJV uses eight times and always in the Levitical law, while 3 Nephi 6:18 has the adverb 'ignorantly', whose Book of Mormon setting is the sacrificial law of Numbers 15:28 and whose paired term 'wilfully' comes from Hebrews 10:26. The link at 6:18 is written there, against Hebrews and Numbers; this entry records the Acts reading and says why it is not the source.

A five-word run and the wrong governor. John 2:8's governor is the ruler of the feast at Cana, the master of ceremonies who tastes the water made wine; the word renders architriklinos and has no judicial content at all. 3 Nephi 6:23's governor is the head of state whose warrant is required before an execution, and whose ignorance of the killings is the point of the verse. The KJV's eight 'governor of the —' phrases are of a city, a house, the country, the Jews and the feast, and none of them is 'the governor of the land', which occurs in no KJV verse. The chapter's real debt on this point is to John 18:31 and is catalogued at 6:22; the coincidence is that both come from John.

exclusions.sharedText: any man should be put to death
exclusions.reason: Cross-reference, not a rejection. This is the verse with the closest verbal contact in the chapter — “put any man to death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 18:31's 'It is not lawful for us to put any man to death', and 6:24 reads 'this was contrary to the laws of the land, that any man should be put to death, except they had power from the governor of the land', which is the same rule stated from the other side of the passive. The link is nevertheless catalogued two verses earlier, at 6:22, where the rule is given together with the personnel it binds — lawyer, judge, high priest — because that is where a reader meets the whole of what John 18:31 supplies. A reader arriving at 6:24 is sent there.

A five-word run opening the verse, and it is a false friend of an unusually exact kind. “all this was done” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 1:22, 21:4 and 26:56 — and in all three it is the front half of a fulfilment formula: 'that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet', 'that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled'. The clause exists in the KJV only to attach an event to a prophecy. 3 Nephi 7:5 uses the identical words to attach the event to a cause of the opposite kind: 'Now all this was done, and there was no wars as yet among them; and all this iniquity had come upon the people, because they did yield themselves unto the power of satan.' Matthew's formula explains a happening by God's word; the Book of Mormon's explains it by Satan's power. Nothing else of Matthew 1 is present, and the Book of Mormon has its own fulfilment formula ('that the word might be fulfilled') which it does not use here.

The strongest string match in the first half of the chapter after the dog and the sow, and it inverts. “entered into a covenant” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 15:12 and Ezekiel 16:8, and the Chronicles verse continues with the infinitive of purpose the Book of Mormon also has — 'entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers'. But 3 Nephi 7:11's covenanters have 'entered into a covenant to destroy the government', and they are the object of the sentence's hatred, not its subject: the tribes are 'united in the hatred of those who had entered into a covenant'. Asa's covenant is a national oath to seek God, sworn publicly and enforced on pain of death; this is the secret combination's oath to destroy a government, and 7:6 has already named it 'the secret combination'. The catalogue does have a link to Asa's covenant assembly, and it is a good one — Alma 46:35, where the whole structure of 2 Chronicles 15:8-15 is rebuilt including the death penalty for refusing the oath. A reader who arrives at 3 Nephi 7:11 by way of that row should be told that the phrase here is the same and the covenant is its opposite.

exclusions.sharedText: (a kingdom in the north obtained by flattery)
exclusions.reason: Typology pulls hard here and the wording will not bear it — the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry in 1 Nephi is the model for this kind of refusal. Daniel 11:21 is the King James Bible's one portrait of a man who is not entitled to a kingdom and gets one anyway: 'in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom: but he shall come in peaceably, and obtain the kingdom by flatteries.' 3 Nephi 7:9-12 crowns a man the tribes have not chosen, over a band rather than a nation, who takes flight 'into the northernmost part of the land, and there build up unto themselves a kingdom' — Daniel 11's king of the north, established by flattery. The verbal case collapses on inspection. “flatteries” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all of them in Daniel 11 (21, 32, 34), and the Book of Mormon does not use the word: “flattered” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses, and the Book of Mormon's clause is 'he flattered them that there would be many dissenters', which is flattery used to recruit, not to corrupt. No other word of Daniel 11:21 is present. Recorded so that a reader who sees the type is told the catalogue saw it and declined it.

exclusions.sharedText: in the thirty and first year
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the highest n-gram score in the second half of the chapter, and it is arithmetic. “thirty and first year” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 16:23, for the simple reason that the KJV dates by regnal year constantly and had occasion to write this particular numeral once. 1 Kings 16:23 is the accession of Omri; 3 Nephi 7:14 is a year in the Nephite reckoning from the sign of Christ's birth, and the same book dates its chapters this way throughout (7:1, 7:13, 7:21, 7:23, 7:26 and onward). The candidate ranks again at 7:21 and is covered here rather than listed twice. This entry follows the standing treatment of regnal dating filed at Helaman 1:1.

A five-word run scoring 2.00, and the coincidence is grammatical rather than lexical: the Book of Mormon's clause is 'they were established according to the minds of them which was their chiefs and their leaders', where 'the minds of' means the opinions of the tribal leaders and 'them which' is the ordinary 1830 relative that 1920 changed to 'those who'. 2 Corinthians 4:4 is about minds blinded by the god of this world. The Pauline verse is nevertheless in this chapter, two verses later and in its proper sense: see the link at 7:16, where 'the blindness of their minds' fuses 2 Corinthians 4:4's blinded minds with Ephesians 4:18's blindness of heart. The run here is a decoy that happens to point at the right epistle for the wrong reason.

“written in this book” occurs in exactly twelve KJV verses, of which 2 Kings 23:3 is one and five are Deuteronomic curse formulae; in all of the Old Testament instances the book in question is the book of the law and the point is that its contents bind. 3 Nephi 7:17's point is the reverse — what is not in the book. The negative form settles it: “not written in this book” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 20:30, and that is where the link is written.

The chapter's most tempting silent parallel. 3 Nephi 7:19 says that Nephi, in the name of Jesus, 'even his brother did he raise from the dead, after he had been stoned and suffered death by the people' — and the King James Bible has exactly one narrative of a named man raised from the dead whom the text repeatedly identifies as somebody's brother, John 11, where Lazarus is 'the brother' of Mary and Martha at 11:2, 11:19, 11:21, 11:23 and 11:32. The verbal contact is nil. “raise from the dead” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses; John 11:44 reads 'And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes'; the Book of Mormon supplies a stoning that John has no counterpart for, and its raised man is the raiser's own brother rather than a friend's. What is worth recording, and is recorded at 7:17 instead, is that the sentence sits inside a passage built on John's two colophons — so a reader who feels John's presence here is feeling something real and finding it in the wrong verse.

The same five-word window ranks at 7:21, 7:22 and 7:25 and is the commonest candidate in the chapter, which is exactly what a connective run does. Acts 14:18 is 'with these sayings scarce restrained they the people, that they had not done sacrifice unto them' — the crowd at Lystra being talked out of offering to Barnabas and Paul. The Book of Mormon's three occurrences are 'did truly signify unto the people that they had been visited', 'did truly manifest unto the people that they had been wrought upon', and 'unto the people, that they had repented'. In every case the words are the seam between a verb of declaring and its content clause, and the seam is the whole of the match. Covered here for all three verses under the standing exclusion for connective runs (CONVENTIONS §5).

Not a machine candidate but worth catching by eye, because the arithmetic is inviting: “evil spirits and infirmities” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 8:2, and that verse also has devils going out of a woman, so it holds in a single clause both halves of 3 Nephi 7:22's 'as many as had devils cast out from them, and were healed of their sicknesses and their infirmities'. The singleton is not reproduced. The Book of Mormon has 'sicknesses and their infirmities' where Luke has 'evil spirits and infirmities', and “their infirmities” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 5:15 and 7:21, neither of them Luke 8:2 — so the phrase the Book of Mormon actually writes points at two other verses than the one the rare pairing suggested. The verse is adjudicated instead as part of the Mark 16:17-20 signs-list borrowing recorded at 7:19, where 7:22 is listed in recurrenceRefs; Luke 8:2 is carried there as a composite rather than made the source.

A five-word run whose next words diverge completely — 2 Chronicles 30:17 continues 'in the congregation that were not sanctified', 3 Nephi 7:26 'in the commencement of this year, that were baptized unto repentance'. The Chronicles verse is about Levites killing passover lambs for the ritually unclean at Hezekiah's passover; the Book of Mormon verse is a year-end tally of converts. The only tie is the existential 'there were many in the', which is bare English.

A five-word run and the only candidate the machine offered for the verse that announces the sign. “for the space of” does occur in exactly one KJV verse — the King James Bible otherwise says 'by the space of' and 'about the space of' — so the rarity is real and it is worthless. “the space of” occurs in exactly sixteen KJV verses and is the KJV's standing way of measuring any interval; Acts 19:8 measures three months of synagogue preaching at Ephesus, and the preposition in front of it is an accident of English. 3 Nephi 8 uses the formula four times over — three days at 8:3 and 8:23, three hours twice at 8:19 — and the one occurrence that carries a real borrowing is 8:19's, where the run is longer and lands on a KJV singleton (Acts 5:7, 'about the space of three hours'). This entry covers every 'for the space of' candidate in the chapter.

A five-word run and the top-ranked candidate for the verse. Numbers 25:1 is Israel at Shittim beginning to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab; 3 Nephi 8:3 is a people beginning to watch for a sign. 'The people began to' is a narrative hinge, not a phrase, and the Book of Mormon uses it constantly. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

exclusions.sharedText: in the fourth day of the
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter (rarity 3.04, a seven-word longest run) and it is a date. Zechariah 7:1 dates a prophecy to the fourth year of Darius and the fourth day of the ninth month; 3 Nephi 8:5 dates a storm to the thirty-fourth year, the first month, the fourth day. Both are the KJV's ordinal dating formula and the coincidence is the numeral 'fourth', which is the only rare word in the match. The same applies to 2 Chronicles 3:2, ranked below it for the same reason. The Book of Mormon dates its own chapters this way throughout (3 Nephi 1:1, 2:5, 4:5, 7:23 and the rest), so the formula cannot be a borrowing from whichever KJV verse happens to share a numeral with it — the standing exclusion at Helaman 1:1 makes this point for regnal dating and it holds here for calendar dating.

exclusions.sharedText: into the depths of the sea
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the sole candidate for the verse, and the senses are opposed at the only point that matters. “depths of the sea” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Micah 7:19, Psalm 68:22 and Matthew 18:6 — and Micah's is the one that is quoted: 'thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea', the closing image of a book about forgiveness, where what sinks is guilt and the sinking is mercy. 3 Nephi 8:9 sinks a city with its inhabitants in it and drowns them. Matthew 18:6 is closer in sense (a millstone and a drowning) and shares less wording, and Revelation 18:21, where an angel casts a millstone into the sea as a sign of 'that great city Babylon' thrown down, is closer still in situation and shares nothing at all. “were drowned” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 18:6 and Hebrews 11:29, and the second is the Book of Mormon's usual Red Sea source (see 1 Nephi 4:2) — the Egyptians drowned, which fits an Exodus-plague chapter, but 'the inhabitants thereof were drowned' shares no further word with it. Nothing here rises above the vocabulary any English writer would use for a city going under.

A five-word run of pure connective tissue. 'The whole face of the earth' is one of the Book of Mormon's own most-worn phrases and 3 Nephi 8 uses it or a variant at 8:12, 8:17, 8:18, 8:20 and 8:22; the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5 covers this class. Genesis 2:6 waters the whole face of the ground with a mist rising from the earth, which is a creation, not a destruction, and the only reason it ranked at all is that the Book of Mormon happens to have 'the whole face of the land was changed' in the same clause as a list of storms. Ezekiel 34:6's 'upon all the face of the earth', ranked at 8:18 for the same reason, is covered by this entry.

exclusions.sharedText: the earth and the inhabitants thereof
exclusions.reason: A six-word run, and it needs an entry rather than silence because Isaiah 40 is genuinely in play one verse earlier: 3 Nephi 8:13 is catalogued to Isaiah 40:4 by way of 1 Nephi 17:46, and a reader who sees the machine propose Isaiah 40:22 here will reasonably wonder whether the chapter is working through Isaiah 40 in order. It is not. Isaiah 40:22 is the grasshopper verse — God enthroned above the circle of the earth, stretching the heavens out as a curtain — and its 'the inhabitants thereof' is a genitive of the whole earth's population, while 3 Nephi 8:14's is a genitive of individual cities, repeated from 8:9 where the inhabitants of Moroni drown. 'Inhabitants thereof' occurs in the KJV too often to identify anything. The Isaiah 40 material this chapter actually uses is at 8:13, and it comes through the Book of Mormon, not straight off the page.

exclusions.sharedText: (the unprecedented earthquake and the fallen cities)
exclusions.reason: This is the register's most tempting entry for the chapter and the machine never proposed it. Revelation 16:18-19 is, on paper, 3 Nephi 8 in miniature: 'there were voices, and thunders, and lightnings; and there was a great earthquake, such as was not since men were upon the earth, so mighty an earthquake, and so great. And the great city was divided into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell.' The chapter has the thunders and lightnings (8:12, 8:17), the unprecedented convulsion (8:5, 8:7), the fallen cities (8:14) and a great city named twice in the lament (8:24, 8:25), and “since men were upon the earth” and “cities of the nations” are each KJV singletons. Not one of those singletons is reproduced. The Book of Mormon's superlative is 'such an one as never had been known in all the land', which is the shape of Exodus 9:24 and 11:6 and not of Revelation's 'such as was not since men were upon the earth'; its list is 'thunderings' with the definite article, which is Exodus 20:18's form and not Revelation's articleless 'thunders'; and its cities are sunk, burned and shaken rather than divided and fallen. The seventh bowl and the Nephite destruction are two descriptions of one kind of event, and a shared kind is not dependence. Filed at length so that a reader who reaches Revelation 16 on their own is told the catalogue got there and could not make the wording work.

A four-word run, and worth an entry because the surrounding verses of Nahum are a better fit than the ranked one and still not good enough. Nahum 1:3 says the LORD 'hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm' — and “in the whirlwind” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, this one, while 3 Nephi 8:16 has people 'carried away in the whirlwind'. Nahum 1:5-6 then has the mountains quaking, the earth burned at his presence and 'the rocks are thrown down by him', which is a KJV singleton and is three of this chapter's four disasters. But the Book of Mormon's rocks are 'rent in twain' and 'broken up', which are Matthew 27:51's and Helaman 14:22's words and not Nahum's, and its whirlwind carries people off rather than serving as God's road. The theophany of Nahum 1 and the destruction of 3 Nephi 8 share their furniture and none of their sentences.

A four-word run of connective English. Exodus 18:8 is Moses recounting to Jethro 'all the travail that had come upon them by the way'; 3 Nephi 8:23 is the destruction 'which had come upon them'. The phrase is the ordinary KJV way of saying that something happened to somebody and it carries no argument in either direction. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; listed only because it was the verse's second-ranked candidate and the verse itself carries a real link (Amos 8:3).

The mourners' cry is a city-lament in two parts, spoken 'in one place' and then 'in another place', naming a burned city (8:24) and a buried one (8:25) and each time with the demonstrative: 'that great city Zarahemla', 'that great city Moronihah'. The King James Bible's stock city-lament has exactly that form — 'Alas, alas that great city' at Revelation 18:10, 18:16 and 18:19, twice with the city's name appended ('that great city Babylon', 18:10 and 18:21) — and Revelation 18 laments a city burned (18:9, 'the smoke of her burning'), mourned by weeping and wailing (18:19), and thrown down into the sea like a millstone (18:21), which is 3 Nephi 8:8, 8:23 and 8:9 in order. It is nevertheless declined. “that great city” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses, three of them Jonah's Nineveh, and the demonstrative-plus-name construction is ordinary English that the Book of Mormon uses of its own cities elsewhere. More decisively, the one phrase the lament repeats verbatim in both halves is not Revelation's: it is 'before this great and terrible day', which the mediation test refers to Joel 2:31, and the rest of the cry is Helaman 13:33's scripted lament word for word. The lament's form is Revelation's; its words are Joel's and Samuel's, and the catalogue records where the words are. See the links at 3 Nephi 8:24 and 8:25.

exclusions.sharedText: (the mountain that falls on the mourners)
exclusions.reason: Typology pulls hard here and the wording will not bear it, which is the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' case again. On the way to the cross Jesus turns to the women of Jerusalem — 'weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children' — and tells them that they will say to the mountains, Fall on us, and to the hills, Cover us (Luke 23:28-30). 3 Nephi 8:25 is a crowd weeping in the crucifixion darkness for their mothers, their daughters and their children, who have been 'buried up in that great city Moronihah' — the city over which, at 8:10, the earth was carried up until 'there became a great mountain'. A mountain has literally fallen on and covered them, in the chapter that narrates the crucifixion, three verses after a lament shaped like Luke's. And there is not one shared word. mediation-check.py cannot even run the test properly: Luke 23:30 quotes Hosea 10:8 and reverses its verbs — Hosea has 'to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us', Luke has them the other way round — so the wording is decidable in principle, and 3 Nephi reproduces neither form, having no mountains address and no imperative at all. Recorded so that a reader who sees the type is told the catalogue saw it, could not settle which of Hosea and Luke it would point to if it were real, and declined it as dependence.

A five-word run and the chapter's top-ranked candidate at this verse, and it is the Book of Mormon's own standing phrase. 'Upon all the face of the earth/land' runs through the whole book from 1 Nephi onward and is covered by the standing exclusion filed in 1 Nephi; Ezekiel 34:6's scattered flock has nothing else in common with a voice heard after an earthquake. The verse's real business is the voice itself, which is adjudicated at 9:2 against Revelation 8:13.

A tempting candidate and very nearly the right one. “devil and his angels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:41, where they are the party for whom the everlasting fire was prepared — and 3 Nephi 9 has just burned four cities with fire. But the Book of Mormon's clause is 'the Devil laugheth, and his angels rejoice', and the verb is what decides it: Revelation 12:12 has the devil, the woe, the inhabiters of the earth and the rejoicing all in one verse, and 3 Nephi 9:2 has all four. Matthew 25:41 supplies only the possessive. The link is written at 9:2 against Revelation 8:13 with Revelation 12:12 composite; Matthew is recorded here because a reader who knows the singleton will expect to find it cited.

The phrase is this chapter's refrain — it occurs at 9:5, 9:6, 9:7 (three times), 9:8 and 9:10 — and it is King James boilerplate for a city and its population, which the machine ranked only because the surrounding words happened to align. Micah 6:12, proposed at 9:8 for the same string, falls with it. Neither Isaiah's grasshoppers nor Micah's liars has any further contact with a list of destroyed Nephite cities. This entry covers every 'and the inhabitants thereof' candidate in the chapter.

“the depths of the earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is why it ranked twice in this chapter (9:6 and 9:8), and the sense runs the opposite way. Psalm 71:20 is a prayer of confidence: 'thou … shalt quicken me again, and shalt bring me **up** again from the depths of the earth.' The depths there are the place God rescues a man out of, and the whole force of the verse is the ascent. 3 Nephi 9:6 and 9:8 use the same phrase for the descent — cities and their inhabitants 'buried up in the depths of the earth' so that their wickedness may never come up again. A singleton is strong evidence of a source only when the borrowing does something a reader of the source would recognise, and here the borrowing would have to reverse the one thing the psalm asserts. The chapter's word for what is buried is 'hid', and the psalm hides nothing.

“hills and valleys” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the temptation is that both verses are about the shape of a promised land. Deuteronomy 11:11 is the contrast drawn between Egypt, watered by foot, and Canaan, 'a land of hills and valleys' that drinks the rain of heaven — the topography is the blessing, evidence that God tends the land directly. 3 Nephi 9:8 makes hills and valleys by burying four cities and their inhabitants, so that the terrain is the grave and the erasure of a record. Same two nouns, opposite theology of landscape, and no third word shared. Recorded because the singleton is real and a reader will find it.

The highest-scoring machine candidate at 9:9 and again at 9:10, on a six-word run. “burned with fire” occurs in exactly seventeen KJV verses and is the King James Bible's ordinary description of a destroyed city — Jerusalem's gates at Nehemiah 1:3 and 2:17, the cities of Isaiah 1:7, Ziklag at 1 Samuel 30:3. Jeremiah 38:23 is Zedekiah being told he will cause Jerusalem to be burned, which is a warning to a king about his own city and not a divine announcement of completed judgement. Where this chapter's burning does have a source it is Revelation 18:8, 'she shall be utterly burned with fire', which is adjudicated at 9:3 with the rest of the Babylon cluster.

“more righteous than” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, and Ezekiel 16:52 is the only one that is a divine judgement oracle rather than a private admission (Genesis 38:26, 1 Samuel 24:17) or a complaint (Habakkuk 1:13). It is also full of this chapter's other keyword: 'thy sins that thou hast committed more abominable than they.' But the comparison is inverted at the point that matters. Ezekiel tells Jerusalem that Sodom and Samaria 'are more righteous than thou' — the comparative is an accusation levelled at the survivor. 3 Nephi 9:13 tells the survivors 'ye were more righteous than they', and uses the comparative as the reason they are alive. An identical construction doing the opposite work.

Five words of pure conditional syntax, and the top machine candidate at this verse. Genesis 34:15 is Jacob's sons setting the terms of Shechem's circumcision; nothing but the grammar of a conditional offer is shared. The same applies to Deuteronomy 15:11's 'of the land therefore' at 9:9. Listed once for both.

Worth recording because of what stands four verses later. 3 Nephi 9:18 quotes ten words of Revelation 22:13, and Revelation 22:17 — four verses on in the source — reads 'And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely', which sits close to 9:14's 'whosoever will come, him will I receive'. If the chapter were working through the end of Revelation in order, this would be the second stop. It is not enough: “whosoever will” occurs in exactly eleven KJV verses and is a bare relative construction, the Book of Mormon adds 'come' where Revelation has 'take', and there is no water, no thirst and no freely. The Alpha and Omega quotation at 9:18 stands on its own wording and does not need a neighbour.

The expectation is strong enough to need answering. This chapter is a voice out of darkness that identifies itself six times in eight verses — 'I am Jesus Christ', 'I am in the Father', 'I am the light and the life of the world', 'I am Alpha and Omega' — and the reader's ear goes to Exodus 3:14, the burning-bush self-naming and the Bible's foundational divine 'I am'. The wording will not bear it. Exodus 3:14 reads 'I AM THAT I AM … Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you', where the formula is absolute: the predicate of 'I am' is 'I am'. Every one of this chapter's formulas is predicated in the ordinary way — I am *X* — which is the construction of John's self-predications and of Revelation's, and both of those are present with their own verbatim wording (John 14:10 at 9:15, John 8:12 at 9:18, Revelation 22:13 at 9:18). There is no shared word beyond the copula, and the copula is not evidence. Recorded so that a reader who came to this chapter looking for Exodus 3 is told the catalogue looked too.

exclusions.sharedText: the earth and all things that
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and a real influence on the wording, but not the source of its grammar. Nehemiah 9:6 reads 'the earth, and all things that **are** therein', which is idiomatic and which the Book of Mormon does not have. The 1830 reads 'all things that in them **is**' — a singular verb on a plural antecedent, which is a King James solecism occurring in exactly two verses, Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24. Nehemiah probably supplies 'things'; Exodus and Acts supply the construction, and the link is written there. Recorded here because the machine ranks Nehemiah and a reader working from the 1920 text, where 'is' has been corrected to 'are', will find Nehemiah the better fit — which is precisely the effect CONVENTIONS §8 warns about.

exclusions.sharedText: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the
exclusions.reason: The best-known of Revelation's four self-identifications and the one most readers name, and it is excluded by a single syllable. Revelation 1:8 reads 'the beginning and the **ending**'; 3 Nephi 9:18 reads 'the beginning and the end', which occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 21:6 and 22:13. The link is written at 9:18 against Revelation 22:13 with 21:6 composite. This entry also discharges the Frederick row at this verse: `data/frederick-refs.json` records Revelation 1:8 as occurring near his discussion of 3 Nephi 9:18, which is a fact about the index's co-occurrence window and not a source proposal by him — his subject is the Gospel of John. Our reading places the wording at 21:6/22:13, and the difference is one word long and checkable.

The top two machine candidates at this verse, Acts 15:8 and Acts 4:31, both rank on the phrase 'the Holy Ghost' plus whatever happens to follow it. Acts 15:8's 'giving them the Holy Ghost, even as he did unto us' is Peter defending the Gentile mission at the Jerusalem council; the 'even as' that produced the match is the Book of Mormon's own comparative introducing the Lamanites, not a borrowed clause. Acts 4:31 shares only 'with the Holy Ghost'. The verse's real New Testament source is the Baptist's saying at Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16, adjudicated at 9:20.

The exclusion a reader is most likely to dispute, so it is written out. Psalm 51:16-17 is the Bible's classic preference of contrition over sacrifice — 'thou desirest not sacrifice … The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise' — and 3 Nephi 9:19-20 makes exactly that argument, abolishing sacrifice and substituting the broken heart. On subject matter Psalm 51 is unanswerable. On wording it is wrong, and the wording is what this catalogue records. Psalm 51:17 pairs the adjectives with the opposite nouns: broken *spirit*, contrite *heart*. 3 Nephi 9:20 has 'a broken heart and a contrite spirit', and “broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Psalm 34:18 — which also carries “contrite spirit” and carries the two in this order. The link is written at 9:20 against Psalm 34:18; Psalm 51 is where the thought comes from and Psalm 34 is where the words do.

exclusions.sharedText: for of such is the kingdom of
exclusions.reason: The third of the three synoptic forms and the only one the wording excludes. Matthew 19:14 ends 'for of such is the kingdom of **heaven**'; 3 Nephi 9:22 has 'the kingdom of God', and “of such is the kingdom of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 10:14 and Luke 18:16. Matthew's substitution of 'heaven' for 'God' is systematic across his Gospel, so this is a clean one-word test and it settles which pair of Gospels is in view. Mark and Luke themselves cannot be separated here — they are identical across the whole shared span — and the link at 9:22 names Mark with Luke composite for that reason.

A four-word run and the top-ranked candidate for the verse, and the senses are exactly opposed. “I will gather you” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Jeremiah 29:14, Ezekiel 22:19 and Ezekiel 22:21 — and Ezekiel 22:20, the verse the machine returned, is the middle of that image: Israel gathered as silver and brass and iron are gathered into a furnace, ‘so will I gather you in mine anger and in my fury, and I will leave you there, and melt you’. Ezekiel gathers in order to smelt. 3 Nephi 10:6 gathers as a hen gathers chickens under her wings, conditional on repentance, and the whole force of the verse is that this gathering is shelter rather than furnace. The gathering language of the verse is Matthew 23:37's and is adjudicated there; Ezekiel's is the same verb performing the opposite act.

“weep and howl” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, James 5:1 and — as two clauses rather than one phrase — Joel 1:5, so James is effectively the only place the collocation stands as a unit. The temptation is real: a rare two-word idiom, and a scene of public lamentation. But James 5:1 is a prophetic summons addressed to the guilty in advance of judgment — ‘Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you’ — and 3 Nephi 10:8 describes the spared grieving after judgment for kindred and friends already dead. The direction of time is reversed, the addressees are the opposite party, and the cause is bereavement rather than impending loss of wealth. The Book of Mormon has also used ‘lamenting and howling’ at 10:2 in the same sense, which suggests a narrator's own idiom for mass grief rather than a borrowing.

The three days of darkness that end at 3 Nephi 10:9 are the ninth plague, and a reader who reaches this verse will expect the catalogue to say so. It is said in the wrong chapter if it is said here. Exodus 10:22's ‘there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days’ has its verbal counterpart at 3 Nephi 8:20-23 — ‘thick darkness upon the face of all the land’, and the three days counted out there — where the darkness is described rather than dispersed. 3 Nephi 10:9 shares with Exodus only the numeral, in a clause about the darkness ending. Filed here so that the reader is sent to chapter 8 rather than told there is nothing; the Exodus link belongs to 8:20-23 and is adjudicated with that chapter.

“praise and thanksgiving” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is the kind of count that normally carries a row in this catalogue, and here it is arithmetic rather than evidence. Nehemiah 12:46 is an antiquarian aside inside the dedication of the wall — ‘in the days of David and Asaph of old there were chief of the singers, and songs of praise and thanksgiving unto God’ — with no contact of any kind with 3 Nephi 10:10 beyond the pair of nouns. The KJV pairs praise with thanksgiving constantly in other orders and other constructions (‘thanksgiving, and the voice of melody’, ‘the sacrifices of thanksgiving’, ‘praise unto our God’), so the singleton reflects one particular ordering of two of the commonest words in the psalter. The real borrowing in this verse is Jeremiah 31:13's ‘mourning into joy’, which is catalogued as a link.

exclusions.sharedText: drowned in the depth(s) of the sea
exclusions.reason: A tempting singleton that fails on a single letter. “drowned in the depth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 18:6, the millstone saying; and the Book of Mormon reads ‘drowned in the depths of the sea’, which is not Matthew's phrase. “depths of the sea” in the plural occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Psalm 68:22, Isaiah 51:10 and Micah 7:19 — none of which involves drowning, and the plural is the ordinary KJV form of the noun. This is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names: read the whole candidate, and check the inflection. The sense is also wrong in the way that matters. Matthew 18:6 is a hypothetical about what would be better for a man who offends a little one; 3 Nephi 10:13 is a list of literal deaths that literally did not happen to the survivors. Recorded because the singleton will be found by anyone who greps for it.

A five-word run, ranked second in the verse behind the Matthew 24:15 quotation that actually carries it, and it is pure KJV connective tissue. Judges 21:21 is the instruction to the Benjamites to lie in wait in the vineyards and seize the daughters of Shiloh as they come out to dance; 3 Nephi 10:14 is an appeal to a reader to test a catalogue of catastrophes against the prophets. Nothing is shared but the imperative string ‘and see, and, behold, if’, which is the KJV's standard way of introducing a condition to an addressee who is being told to look. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion on connective boilerplate at 1 Nephi 2:1; listed individually only because a five-word run in a verse that does contain a real quotation invites the wrong one to be catalogued.

“remnant of Joseph” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Amos 5:15's remnant is a remnant spared from a national judgment on condition of doing justice — which is very close to what 3 Nephi 10:12-17 is about, so the case deserves stating before it is declined. It is declined on distribution. The Book of Mormon's phrase is ‘a remnant of the seed of Joseph’, and “remnant of the seed” occurs in no KJV verse at all while occurring thirteen times in the Book of Mormon (1 Nephi 13:38-39, 3 Nephi 5:23-24, Alma 46:23-27, Ether 13:6-10, Mormon 5:24 and here). It is one of the book's own standing formulae, built on its own covenant argument about Joseph's coat, and the intervening ‘of the seed’ is exactly what separates it from Amos. A formula the Book of Mormon uses thirteen times cannot be sourced to a KJV verse it does not match.

A five-word run and the only candidate the machine returned for the verse, and it turns on an idiom that means two different things. Ezekiel 20:17 is God declining to destroy Israel in the wilderness — ‘neither did I make an end of them’ — where ‘make an end of’ takes a people as its object and means annihilate. Mormon's ‘I make an end of my sayings’ takes a discourse as its object and means stop talking; it is his standing colophon formula, used at the close of books and sections throughout. Two senses of one English phrasal verb, and no other contact.

The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter's opening verse, and it is a locative formula. 3 Nephi 11:1 reads “round about the temple which was in the land Bountiful”; Daniel 5:2 reads “the vessels … which his father Nebuchadnezzar had taken out of the temple which was in Jerusalem.” The five shared words are 'the temple which was in' followed by a place name, which is simply how the KJV specifies which temple is meant, and Daniel 5 — Belshazzar's feast, the desecration of the vessels, the writing on the wall — has nothing else in common with a crowd gathered to marvel at a landscape. Recorded because it ranked first and a reader scanning the machine output would meet it first.

The typological pull is real and the wording will not carry it. 3 Nephi 11:3 has a voice that 'did pierce them that did hear, to the centre … did pierce them to the very soul'; Hebrews 4:12 has the word of God 'sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit'. Both are about divine speech that penetrates, both name the soul, and 'pierce' occurs in only four KJV verses. But the shared vocabulary is one verb and one noun, in different grammatical roles, and Hebrews' distinctive machinery — the twoedged sword, the joints and marrow, the discerning of thoughts — is entirely absent. The verse's real borrowings are 1 Kings 19:11-12's structure of negations and Luke 24:32's burning heart, both catalogued as links at this verse; Hebrews 4:12 is what a reader expects to find and does not.

A tempting near-miss on rarity. 'White robes' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all in Revelation (6:11, 7:9, 7:13), and 'clothed in white' in exactly two, both also Revelation (3:5, 4:4, in each case 'clothed in white raiment'). But the KJV never writes 'a white robe' in the singular, and every Revelation occurrence is plural and collective — the martyrs under the altar, the innumerable multitude, the twenty-four elders — where 3 Nephi 11:8 dresses one descending figure. Mark 16:5's 'clothed in a long white garment' is the nearest single-figure parallel and shares only the adjective. No source can be identified below the level of 'white clothing marks a heavenly visitant', which is not a link. The verse's real borrowing is Luke 24:36, catalogued here.

The elements are present and the order is wrong. Acts 9:4 has Saul 'fell to the earth, and heard a voice saying unto him'; 3 Nephi 11:12 has the multitude fall to the earth after Christ has spoken and been seen. 'Fell to the earth' occurs in exactly three KJV verses. But the Damascus-road sequence is voice-then-prostration and its point is that the hearer cannot see; 3 Nephi's is see-then-hear-then-prostrate, and the falling is explicitly caused not by the voice but by recollection — 'for they remembered that it had been prophesied among them that Christ should shew himself unto them after his ascension into Heaven'.
