The prostration here is recognition, not blindness. Note that the 1830 'shew' was modernised to 'show' in 1920, so the verse does carry KJV orthography; it just does not carry Acts 9.

The exact trap ADJUDICATING §4 describes, with the added temptation that both verses mention Israel. Micah 5:2 reads 'out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel'; 3 Nephi 11:14 reads 'Arise and come forth unto me, that ye may thrust your hands into my side … that I am the God of Israel'. The five-word run is genuine, and it is a run across a clause boundary in one text and not in the other: in Micah 'unto me' is the Father's, and 'that' introduces a relative clause describing the ruler; in 3 Nephi 'unto me' is Christ's, addressed to a crowd, and 'that' introduces a purpose clause. The two 'me's are different persons and the two 'that's are different parts of speech. The verse's real sources are John 20:25-27 and Isaiah 54:5, both catalogued as links here.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when they had
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run and pure narrative boilerplate — the longest match in the chapter and the least informative, which is CONVENTIONS §9's point about the n-gram stream exactly. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1. Amos 7:2 concerns locusts eating the grass of the land. Recorded once here because the run length would otherwise make it look important to anyone reading the dossier; the other 'and it came to pass' matches in the chapter (11:1, 11:3, 11:4, 11:8, 11:9, 11:12, 11:13, 11:16, 11:18) are passed over in silence.

A real five-word run and a genuine collocation — 'at the feet of Jesus' is a KJV singleton at Luke 8:35, and John 12:3 has Mary anointing 'the feet of Jesus'. But the anointing at Bethany contributes nothing else, and the chapter's actual borrowing from the feet-of-Jesus material lies two verses later: 3 Nephi 11:19 has Nephi 'kiss his feet', and 'kissed his feet' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 7:38 — the sinful woman in the Pharisee's house, which is also the passage John 12:3 is habitually confused with. The link is catalogued at 11:19 against Luke 7:38. A reader who arrives at 11:17 expecting a feet-of-Jesus source should be sent there.

A five-word run of court protocol. Araunah 'bowed himself before the king on his face upon the ground'; Nephi 'bowed himself before the Lord'. The KJV uses this construction for approaching a superior throughout the historical books, and nothing else of 2 Samuel 24 — the census, the plague, the threshingfloor — is in view. The distinctive material in 11:19 is the kiss, not the bow, and it is catalogued as a link to Luke 7:38.

Four connective words. Psalm 89:24 reads 'in my name shall his horn be exalted', where the speaker is the LORD and the horn is David's; 3 Nephi 11:23 reads 'in my name shall ye baptize them'. The shared string is a prepositional phrase plus an auxiliary, and the Psalm's subject matter — the Davidic covenant and its faithfulness formula — is not in the chapter. The verse's real contacts are with Acts 8:36-39 and Acts 2:38, catalogued as a link here.

This one is not noise: 'they are they which' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 5:39, and the Book of Mormon reproduces it verbatim. It is filed here rather than as a link of its own because it is a relative construction rather than a content phrase, and because the sentence it sits in is governed by Mark 16:16 and by Paul's 'inherit the kingdom of God' — the borrowing is catalogued as part of the Mark 16:16 row at this verse, with John 5:39 in its composite. Worth noting for the Index Verborum that the 1830's 'they are they which' was modernised to 'who' in 1920, erasing the KJV form.

exclusions.sharedText: unto the ends of the earth
exclusions.reason: A live mediation question that the wording cannot settle, recorded because the machinery was run on it. Isaiah 49:6 reads 'that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth' and Acts 13:47, quoting it, reads 'for salvation unto the ends of the earth'; mediation-check.py returns one decisive point for Acts, on the plural 'ends'. But the plural is not diagnostic here: 'unto the ends of the earth' occurs in six KJV verses, four of them in the Psalms, so the Book of Mormon's plural could come from any of them or from none. Beyond those five words 3 Nephi 11:41 — 'go forth unto this people, and declare the words which I have spoken' — has no contact with Isaiah 49:6 or Acts 13:47 at all: no light, no Gentiles, no salvation, no servant. The commission's nearest relative is Acts 1:8's 'unto the uttermost part of the earth', which shares no wording either. Recorded so that a reader who runs the same check is told the catalogue ran it and declined the result.

exclusions.sharedText: baptize you with fire and with the Holy Ghost
exclusions.reason: The Baptist's promise, with the two elements transposed, and the catalogue adjudicates it in this book at 3 Nephi 9:20, where the risen Christ first makes it and where the inversion is argued at length. “With the Holy Ghost, and with fire” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 3:11 and Luke 3:16, both of which put the Holy Ghost first; the Book of Mormon's order, “with fire and with the Holy Ghost”, occurs in no KJV verse at all and is this book's standing form. 3 Nephi 12:1-2 is the same speaker using his own formula three chapters later, which ADJUDICATING §4 files here rather than as a second link. A reader who meets the phrase at 12:1 should be sent to 9:20.

exclusions.sharedText: the meek shall inherit the earth
exclusions.reason: The proposal is reasonable and the wording refuses it. Psalm 37:11 is the only Old Testament verse that holds the meek and the inheritance of the earth together — “But the meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace” — and it is the acknowledged background of Matthew 5:5. But “blessed are the meek” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is Matthew's. The psalm makes a prediction about a class; 3 Nephi 12:5 pronounces a blessing over them, in the beatitude form and in the beatitude's position between the mourners and the hungry. The link is at Matthew 5:5 with Psalm 37:11 recorded as its composite; this entry exists so that a reader who reaches for the psalm is told the catalogue reached for it too.

exclusions.sharedText: a broken heart and a contrite spirit
exclusions.reason: “Broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “contrite spirit” occurs in exactly two, so Psalm 34:18 is the only verse in the King James Bible holding both, and in the Book of Mormon's order — not Psalm 51:17, which readers reflexively name and which has the nouns crossed. That argument is made in full at 3 Nephi 9:20, where the same speaker first demands the sacrifice, and this verse is his own formula recurring within the same book eleven verses into a new discourse. Filed here under ADJUDICATING §4 with the reader sent to 9:20; the catalogue has also taken the pair to Psalm 34:18 at 2 Nephi 2:7, 2 Nephi 4:32 and Jacob 2:10.

exclusions.sharedText: (no parallel — the least commandments saying is absent)
exclusions.reason: Matthew 5:19 — “Whosoever therefore shall break one of these least commandments, and shall teach men so, he shall be called the least in the kingdom of heaven” — has no counterpart in the Sermon at the Temple, which runs straight from 12:18 (Matthew 5:18) to 12:20 (Matthew 5:20). Recorded because 12:20's replacement clause, “except ye shall keep my commandments, which I have commanded you at this time”, occupies the ground Matthew 5:19 covers and a reader may take it for a compressed rendering of that verse. It is not: nothing of Matthew 5:19's vocabulary survives — no breaking, no teaching, no least, no greatness — and the frame the Book of Mormon keeps (“except … ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven”) is verse 20's, whose closing eight words occur in exactly one KJV verse.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references Exodus 20:13 and Deuteronomy 5:17 at this verse, and the catalogue records the sixth commandment as a composite of the link rather than as its source, because the mediation test is decisive against it. Exodus 20:13 and Deuteronomy 5:17 consist, in the KJV, of the four words “Thou shalt not kill” and nothing else. Every other word of 3 Nephi 12:21 — the frame “Ye have heard that it hath been said by them of old time”, which occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all in Matthew 5, and the sanction “and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment”, whose central phrase occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both in Matthew 5 — is Matthew's. The Decalogue reaches this chapter through Matthew's quotation of it. The link is at Matthew 5:21.

Offered by the n-gram stream against 12:29's “suffer none of these things to enter into your heart”, and it is the wrong direction of travel. Matthew 15:19 is about what comes OUT of the heart and defiles a man — “out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries” — while 3 Nephi 12:29 is a commandment about what must not be let IN. The two verses share the heart and a vice list and nothing else; the Sermon at the Temple's own list at 12:22-28 (anger, insult, lust) is Matthew 5's, not Matthew 15's, and 12:29 is a Book of Mormon summary of the sayings it has just quoted rather than a borrowing from elsewhere in the Gospel.

Hardy cross-references Exodus 20:14 and Deuteronomy 5:18 here. On its own the verse cannot settle its own mediation — tools/mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence, because the commandment is worded identically in Exodus and in Matthew's quotation of it, and Deuteronomy's variant form (“Neither shalt thou commit adultery”) is the one the Book of Mormon does not have. The frame decides it: “by them of old time” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 5:21, 5:27 and 5:33, and in no Old Testament verse, and the Sermon at the Temple uses it at precisely those three points. A writer quoting the Decalogue directly would have no source for the phrase. The link is at Matthew 5:27.

Hardy cross-references Deuteronomy 24:1-4 here and the mediation test returns four decisive points against it. Deuteronomy has a long conditional about uncleanness found in a wife and instructs the husband to WRITE her a BILL of divorcement, give it in her hand and send her out of his house; 3 Nephi has none of the conditions, none of the delivery, and reads GIVE her a WRITING of divorcement. “Writing of divorcement” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 5:31 and Mark 10:4, and never in the Old Testament, which says “bill” in all three of its occurrences. The link is at Matthew 5:31.

Hardy cross-references Leviticus 19:12 and Numbers 30:2 here, and neither can be the source of the wording. Leviticus reads “ye shall not swear by my name falsely, neither shalt thou profane the name of thy God”; Numbers reads “he shall not break his word”. The Book of Mormon reads “Thou shalt not forswear thyself, but shalt perform unto the Lord thine oaths”, and “forswear” occurs in exactly one KJV verse in the whole Bible — Matthew 5:33. The mediation tool returns four decisive points for Matthew and none for either Old Testament candidate, including the connective “Again”. The link is at Matthew 5:33.

Isaiah 66:1 is where the throne and the footstool come from — “The heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool” — and a reader working from the Old Testament will propose it. The possessive settles it in one syllable. Isaiah's oracle is spoken by God in the first person and reads “my footstool”; Matthew reports it about God and reads “his”, and “for it is his footstool” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has “his”. The mediation tool returns three decisive points for Matthew 5:34-35 and none for Isaiah, and the Book of Mormon also lacks every word of Isaiah's continuation about the house and the place of rest. Isaiah 66:1 is recorded as the composite of the links at 12:34 and 12:35.

exclusions.sharedText: eye for eye, tooth for tooth
exclusions.reason: Hardy cross-references Exodus 21:23-24, Leviticus 24:19-20 and Deuteronomy 19:21 here — the three King James statements of the talion — and all three are articleless: “eye for eye, tooth for tooth”, which occurs in exactly three KJV verses. Matthew alone writes “An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and that is the Book of Mormon's form, articles and conjunction and all. Worth flagging for anyone re-running the check: tools/mediation-check.py reports the divergences as pointing both ways at this verse, because its aligner treats the stray indefinite articles as unmatched rather than as Matthean; the phrase count overturns that reading. The link is at Matthew 5:38.

Luke 6:29 is the Synoptic parallel and it is not the source. Luke reads “unto him that smiteth thee on the one cheek offer also the other”; Matthew reads “whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also”, and “smite thee on thy right cheek” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon has the right cheek, the verb “turn”, and Matthew's word order. The entry is filed as a class marker: at every point in this chapter where Matthew and Luke offer different wordings for the same saying — the cheek here, the coat and cloak at 12:40, the four commands of 12:44 — the Sermon at the Temple has Matthew's, and 12:41 reproduces a verse Luke does not contain at all.

Hardy cross-references Leviticus 19:18 here, and the verse's decisive half has no Old Testament source at all. Leviticus reads “thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD”; the Book of Mormon reads “thou shalt love thy neighbor, and hate thine enemy”, and “hate thine enemy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:43. No commandment to hate an enemy stands anywhere in the King James Old Testament, which is why Matthew's second clause has its own long literature. Whatever Matthew was quoting, what the Book of Mormon has is Matthew. The link is at Matthew 5:43.

exclusions.sharedText: (no parallel — the publicans saying is absent)
exclusions.reason: Hardy cross-references Matthew 5:46-47 at this verse, and the row records an absence rather than a borrowing: the Sermon at the Temple has no parallel to “For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same?” or to the salutation of brethren. There is not one shared distinctive word. The entry is written because the omission is the interesting fact — 3 Nephi 12:44-45 tracks Matthew 5:44-45 for fifty-seven words and 12:48 resumes at Matthew 5:48, so the gap is exactly two verses wide and exactly where the Judaean publicans stand. What fills it is 2 Corinthians 5:17, adjudicated as a link at 12:47. Hardy's pairing of the two references at one verse is the right pairing; this register separates them so that a reader is told which one is present and which is missing.

The clause 3 Nephi 13:1 puts in front of Matthew 6:1 opens “Verily, verily, I say”, and that formula occurs in exactly twenty-five KJV verses, every one of them in the Gospel of John — John 3:3 is simply the first. The observation is real and it is recorded in the link at 13:1 as part of that verse's significance, because a Matthean sermon introduced in Johannine idiom is worth a reader knowing about, and 3 Nephi 9 borrows from John repeatedly and demonstrably. But it is not a link to John 3:3 or to any other single verse. The double amen is the standing speech-formula of the risen Christ throughout 3 Nephi, used dozens of times outside any Johannine context; it is the speaker's own idiom, not a borrowing made here. Filed so that a reader who notices the seam is told the catalogue noticed it and declined to hang a source on it.

exclusions.sharedText: enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door
exclusions.reason: The standing Old Testament background proposed for Matthew 6:6, and therefore the parallel a reader is most likely to bring to 3 Nephi 13:6. Isaiah 26:20 reads “Come, my people, enter thou into thy chambers, and shut thy doors about thee: hide thyself as it were for a little moment, until the indignation be overpast”, and “enter thou into thy chambers” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The situation rhymes — go inside, shut the door, wait on God — and the wording does not. Isaiah has ‘chambers’ and plural ‘doors’; Matthew and 3 Nephi have ‘closet’ and a single ‘door’, and “enter into thy closet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “shut thy door” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both of them Matthew 6:6. Isaiah's shut door hides a people from wrath; Matthew's hides a man from applause. Whatever route Matthew took to Isaiah, 3 Nephi took to Matthew, and the link is filed there.

Hardy's cross-reference apparatus keys Matthew 6:10 to 3 Nephi 13:9, and the keying is correct for what his note is doing: he is marking that the Nephite prayer omits ‘thy kingdom come’, the first half of Matthew 6:10, and he offers a reading of the omission. 3 Nephi 13:9 itself contains no word of Matthew 6:10 — it is Matthew 6:9 verbatim — so under CONVENTIONS §6a the link goes where the wording is, at 3 Nephi 13:10, which reproduces the second half of Matthew 6:10 and is a KJV singleton (“Thy will be done in earth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse). This entry sends a reader from Hardy's verse to the catalogue's, and records that the row was discharged as an omission rather than as a borrowing. The audit tool flagged this row as a suspect on word-overlap grounds; the printed apparatus was checked directly and the keying is Hardy's own, not an extraction error.

exclusions.sharedText: Give us this day our daily bread
exclusions.reason: The companion to the entry at 13:9. Hardy keys Matthew 6:11 to 3 Nephi 13:10 in order to note that the Nephite prayer omits the petition for daily bread; the verse itself has nothing of Matthew 6:11 in it, and 3 Nephi 13:11 passes straight from ‘as it is in heaven’ to ‘And forgive us our debts’. There is no borrowing to catalogue and no verse to hang one on, so the row is discharged here. What is worth saying is that the two omissions are not random: they are the prayer's two petitions of request, and removing them leaves a prayer that asks God for nothing but forgiveness and rescue. That argument is made in the link at 13:10.

“anointest my head with oil” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the collocation of anointing with a head is rare enough that a reader meeting ‘anoint thy head, and wash thy face’ will think of the twenty-third Psalm. The senses are unrelated. Psalm 23:5 is about honour conferred by a host at a table prepared in the presence of enemies; Matthew 6:17, which 3 Nephi 13:17 reproduces, is about cosmetic ordinariness — grooming yourself so that nobody can tell you are fasting. The Psalm's anointing is meant to be seen and the Gospel's is meant to conceal. Two shared words, opposed purposes, and “when thou fastest” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is Matthew's; nothing else of Psalm 23 is present.

The New Testament's other treasure-and-corrosion passage, and a genuine temptation: James 5:2-3 reads “Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten. Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you”, where “the rust of them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “your gold and silver is cankered” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Moths, rust, corruption and hoarded wealth are all present, and James is the New Testament book whose sapiential register is closest to the Sermon on the Mount. But James has no thieves, no heaven, and no antithesis: he pronounces a woe on the rich, where Matthew and 3 Nephi set two kinds of treasury against each other across two balanced verses. “moth and rust” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “break through and steal” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and both are Matthew 6:19, which is where the link is filed.

exclusions.sharedText: For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also
exclusions.reason: “where your treasure is” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:21 and Luke 12:34, and in the King James Version the two are identical word for word — the only such pair in this chapter's material. The mediation tool reports, correctly, that no test is available. The verse is therefore assigned to Matthew on sequence rather than on wording: 3 Nephi 13:19-20 has Matthew's antithesis against a wholly different Lukan form at Luke 12:33, and 13:22 onward continues in Matthew's order. Recorded here so that the assignment is visible as a judgment rather than presented as a reading of the words.

exclusions.sharedText: The light of the body is the eye
exclusions.reason: “the light of the body is the eye” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:22 and Luke 11:34, and the clause is identical in both — so the opening of 3 Nephi 13:22 cannot by itself choose between them. Everything after it can. Matthew continues “if therefore thine eye be single, thy whole body shall be full of light”; Luke continues “therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light”. The Book of Mormon has Matthew's conditional, Matthew's tense, and no ‘also’. At 13:23 the divergence widens further — Luke has no equivalent of “how great is that darkness!” at all. Luke is displaced at every testable point and the link is filed at Matthew 6:22 and 6:23.

exclusions.sharedText: No man can serve two masters
exclusions.reason: The only non-Matthean candidate the n-gram stream produced anywhere in this chapter, and it ranked high (14.83, a thirty-three-word run) because Luke 16:13 is Matthew 6:24 with one word changed. That one word decides it: Luke reads “No servant can serve two masters” and Matthew reads “No man”. 3 Nephi 13:24 reads “No man”. The mediation tool cannot make this call — its common-word filter suppresses divergences turning on a word as frequent as ‘man’, so it reports no decisive divergence — and the reading was taken by eye, exactly the class of miss ADJUDICATING §4 warns about. Everything else in the two verses, including “God and mammon”, which occurs in exactly two KJV verses, is common to both, so this single noun is the whole of the evidence and it is sufficient.

exclusions.sharedText: yet your heavenly Father feedeth them
exclusions.reason: The Old Testament text behind the tradition, and not behind this verse. Psalm 147:9 reads “He giveth to the beast his food, and to the young ravens which cry”, and “he giveth to the beast his food” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; with Job 38:41 it is the scriptural warrant for God feeding birds that do not provide for themselves. Luke inherits it and keeps the allusion visible by naming ravens (Luke 12:24, “Consider the ravens”). Matthew generalises to “the fowls of the air” and loses it, and 3 Nephi 13:26 follows Matthew — including “gather into barns”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and “heavenly”, which Luke does not have. There is not one shared word with the Psalm. The entry is filed because the loss is itself informative: what 3 Nephi reproduces is not the tradition behind Matthew but Matthew's particular handling of it.

The queen of Sheba's inventory — “when the queen of Sheba had seen all Solomon's wisdom, and the house that he had built” — with its continuation at 10:5 through his table, his servants, his apparel and his ascent to the house of the LORD, and the same account at 2 Chronicles 9:3-6. This is what Solomon's glory consists of in the King James Bible, and it is the passage a reader should recover to feel the force of 3 Nephi 13:29; it is written into that link's significance for exactly that reason. It is not a link. “in all his glory” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 6:29 and Luke 12:27, and neither Kings nor Chronicles uses the phrase of Solomon or of anyone; there is no verbal contact between 1 Kings 10 and 3 Nephi 13:29 at all. Catalogued as a background, not as a source.

exclusions.sharedText: For after all these things do the Gentiles seek
exclusions.reason: Hardy keys Matthew 6:32 to 3 Nephi 13:31, and as at 13:9 the keying marks an omission rather than a borrowing: his note records that the Nephite text drops “for after all these things do the Gentiles seek” from Matthew 6:32. 3 Nephi 13:31 is Matthew 6:31 verbatim; the surviving half of Matthew 6:32 is adjudicated at 3 Nephi 13:32, where “your heavenly Father knoweth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. This row therefore sends a reader forward one verse and records the omission where Hardy puts it. The audit flagged the row as a suspect; the printed apparatus was read directly and the keying is Hardy's, not ours.

exclusions.sharedText: take no thought for the morrow
exclusions.reason: “Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the Old Testament's proverb about the morrow — the obvious background for a saying that tells its hearers to take no thought for it, and the verse James 4:13-14 develops. The thoughts are not the same thought. Proverbs forbids presumption about tomorrow's outcome; Matthew forbids anxiety about tomorrow's provision, and grounds the prohibition in a Father who feeds birds. The one word they share is ‘to morrow’. “no thought for the morrow” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the things of itself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Matthew 6:34, and the Nephite verse reproduces both.

exclusions.sharedText: Verily, verily, I say unto you
exclusions.reason: A real and interesting observation, filed here rather than as a link because the chapter is not its first use. “Verily, verily, I say unto you” occurs in exactly 20 KJV verses and every one of the twenty is in the Gospel of John; Matthew's Jesus never doubles the word. So the formula that introduces this Matthean chapter is Johannine, and 3 Nephi 14:1 is joining a saying from one Gospel to a formula from another. But the seam is not made here: the doubled “verily” is already the risen Christ's habitual formula in this book from 3 Nephi 11:29 onward (11:31, 11:35, 11:39, then 12:13, 12:14, 12:26, 12:32, 12:34, 13:1), so by chapter 14 it is the narrator's own idiom and not a fresh borrowing. ADJUDICATING §4: adjudicate at first use. A reader who meets it at 14:1 is sent to 3 Nephi 11:29. The count above is worth carrying to whichever chapter takes that row.

This entry stands for the whole Sermon on the Plain, and it is written out once here rather than eleven times through the chapter. Luke 6:20-49 and Luke 11:9-13 carry most of what 3 Nephi 14 says, and a reader who knows the synoptic problem will reasonably ask whether the Nephite Sermon might be closer to Luke anywhere. It is not, at any of the eleven verses where the two Gospels are worded differently. tools/mediation-check.py returns a decisive result for Matthew at 14:2 (three points), 14:3 (one: “considerest” not “perceivest”), 14:4 (three), 14:7 (one), 14:9 (two), 14:12 (two), 14:13 (four), 14:16 (four), 14:18 (two), 14:21 (three), 14:23 (four), 14:24 (one), 14:25 (four) and 14:27 (two), and at no verse in the chapter does it return a decisive result for Luke. Verses 8 and 10 are the only ones where the two Gospels do not differ, and they are recorded as undecidable in their own rows rather than assigned to Luke by default. At this verse specifically, Luke 6:37 reads “Judge not, and ye shall not be judged: condemn not, and ye shall not be condemned: forgive, and ye shall be forgiven”, three members where Matthew and 3 Nephi have one, and “condemn not” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is absent here. Individual Lukan candidates are filed separately below only where the divergence teaches something the general result does not.

A negative entry, recorded because a reader collating this chapter against Matthew 7 will notice the absence and should be told it was seen. 3 Nephi 14 reproduces Matthew 7:1-27 and stops; Matthew 7:28-29 — “the people were astonished at his doctrine: for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes” — has no counterpart anywhere in 3 Nephi. 3 Nephi 15:1 supplies its own conclusion instead, “when Jesus had ended these sayings he cast his eyes round about on the multitude”. The omission is intelligible on the Book of Mormon's own terms, since there are no scribes in the audience to be compared with, but it is worth recording that the transcription's boundaries are not arbitrary: it begins where Matthew's chapter begins and ends where Matthew's discourse ends, one verse before Matthew's chapter does.

“that which is holy” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:6 and Proverbs 20:25, and a two-verse rarity on a four-word phrase is the kind of count that normally earns a row. It does not here, because the senses have nothing in common. Proverbs 20:25 is about rash vows — “It is a snare to the man who devoureth that which is holy, and after vows to make enquiry” — where the holy thing is consecrated food eaten by the man who consecrated it, and the danger is to him. Matthew 7:6's holy thing is given away to those who will trample it, and the danger is to the thing and then to the giver. Nothing else of Proverbs 20 is anywhere near this chapter, and the whole of the rest of the verse is Matthew's, three King James singletons deep. Recorded so that the count is on file and the decision visible.

exclusions.sharedText: If ye then being evil know how to give good gifts unto your children
exclusions.reason: The only candidate the n-gram stream proposed in this chapter that is not from Matthew 7, and it scored 8.70 on a nineteen-word run — which is exactly what one would expect, because Luke 11:13 shares its first sixteen words with Matthew 7:11. The last dozen are where they part, and the Book of Mormon goes with Matthew at every point: “your Father which is in heaven” not Luke's “your heavenly Father”, and “good things to them that ask him” not Luke's “the Holy Spirit to them that ask him”. “good things to them that ask him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Worth recording twice over: first because it is the chapter's best illustration of CONVENTIONS §9 — a long contiguous run is a recall floor and not a ranking, and here the longest non-Matthean run in the chapter belongs to the source that is wrong; and second because tools/mediation-check.py cannot resolve this pair, returning “no decisive divergence” where three plain divergences exist. Its matcher scores the three adjacent replacements as “neither”. The Matthean reading here was made by eye against the two printed verses, and the tool's limitation is flagged in the link's provenance.

exclusions.sharedText: hewn down, and cast into the fire
exclusions.reason: “hewn down, and cast into the fire” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9 — so the eight-word run does not by itself say which of the three is in view, and the Book of Mormon has used the Baptist's form before (Alma 5:52 carries the axe clause, “the axe is laid at the root of the tree”, which belongs to Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9 and not to the Sermon). Here the Sermon's form is the right one on two grounds. The axe clause is absent, and the relative pronoun is Matthew 7:19's: “every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, because Matthew 3:10 reads “which bringeth not” and Luke 3:9 reads “every tree therefore which”. Luke 3:9 is excluded on the same evidence and is not filed separately.

Luke 13:26-27 is the closest thing the third Gospel has to Matthew 7:22-23, and it matters here because Luke, not Matthew, preserves the Old Testament wording behind the saying: Psalm 6:8 reads “Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity” and Luke 13:27 reads “depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity”, while Matthew 7:23 recasts the phrase as “depart from me, ye that work iniquity”. 3 Nephi has Matthew's recasting. tools/mediation-check.py returns four decisive points against Luke — “profess unto them” not “tell you”, “never knew” not “know”, no “not whence ye are”, and “that work” not “workers of” — and three against the Psalm. The positive finding is carried as a link at 14:23 with source Psalm 6:8 and mediation OT-via-NT; this entry records the third candidate that the same test disposes of.

Filed separately from the general Lukan entry because this is the one place where Luke's version is not merely shorter but tells a different story. Luke's wise man “digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock”, and what assails the house is one flood and one stream that beats “vehemently”. Matthew's man simply builds on rock, and three things come: rain, floods, winds. 3 Nephi has Matthew's three, in Matthew's order, with no digging and no “vehemently”, and it keeps them in that order again at 3 Nephi 18:13 outside the quoted block. “founded upon a rock” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, this one and Luke 6:48, which is why the pair is worth adjudicating rather than passing over.

“upon the sand” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 7:26 and Revelation 13:1, and the Book of Mormon has drawn on Revelation elsewhere often enough that a two-verse rarity deserves a look. There is nothing here. Revelation 13:1 is John standing on the seashore watching a beast rise out of the sea; the sand is where the seer stands, not what anything is built on. The whole of the surrounding verse is Matthew 7:26, and “shall be likened unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse.

“Concerning the law of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is why it ranked, and the rarity is an accident of the genitive: Daniel 6:5 reads “concerning the law of his God” and 3 Nephi 15:2 reads “concerning the law of Moses”, so the shared string is a preposition, an article and a noun that both sentences happen to complete differently. Daniel 6:5 is the satraps' conspiracy to find a charge against Daniel; 3 Nephi 15:2 is a crowd marvelling at a teaching. The real borrowing in this verse is 2 Corinthians 5:17, which the n-gram stream did not propose at all because the Book of Mormon's reported speech shifts Paul's present tense to a pluperfect and the contiguous window breaks at the verb.

A six-word run, and “covenant which I have made” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, so the candidate deserves an answer rather than silence. The senses are opposed. In Deuteronomy 31:16 the LORD tells Moses that after his death Israel will “break my covenant which I have made with them” — the clause exists to predict the covenant's rupture, and the verb governing it is “break”. In 3 Nephi 15:8 the same words are the subject of the opposite claim: “the covenant which I have made with my people, is not all fulfilled”, which is an assertion that the covenant is still running, in a verse whose whole point is to distinguish the covenant (unfinished) from the law (ended). Nothing else of Deuteronomy 31 is present, and the Book of Mormon's covenant language here is its own, running from 1 Nephi 22 through 3 Nephi 20-21.

exclusions.sharedText: I am the law, and the light
exclusions.reason: “Behold, I am the law, and the light” is a genuine echo of the Johannine self-declaration, and it is adjudicated in this book already: John 8:12 stands behind 3 Nephi 9:18, “I am the light and the life of the world”, and the same formula recurs at 3 Nephi 11:11. By the time it reaches 15:9 it is the speaker's established self-designation within the Book of Mormon rather than a fresh borrowing (ADJUDICATING §4), and what is new in 15:9 is not “the light” but “the law” — an addition with no King James model, made because the chapter is arguing that the law of Moses ends in a person. A reader who arrives here looking for John 8:12 should be sent to 3 Nephi 9:18. The links at 15:9 are for the two halves of the sentence that follow: Isaiah 45:22 with Amos 5:4, and Matthew 10:22 with John 10:28.

“Whom he had chosen” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 105:26 (Aaron) and Acts 1:2 (“the apostles whom he had chosen”), and the second of those has the right referent — a body of chosen apostles receiving commandments from the risen Christ, which is exactly the situation of 3 Nephi 15:11-24. It is still not enough. The four words are the ordinary English relative, the Book of Mormon carries the phrase as a fixed epithet for the Nephite twelve (3 Nephi 13:25, 18:26, 18:36, Moroni 2:1), and Acts 1:2's distinctive material — the ascension, the forty days, the Holy Ghost as the medium of the commandments — is absent here. Recorded because a reader who notices the Acts parallel should be told the catalogue noticed it and declined it.

exclusions.sharedText: when Jesus had spoken these words
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter after John 10:16, and a King James singleton: “when Jesus had spoken these words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 18:1, where it closes the farewell discourse and opens the passion. The temptation is real, because 3 Nephi 15:11 also stands at the join between a long address and what follows it. But the clause is not this verse's property — it is 3 Nephi's standing narrative formula for a transition, used at 13:25, here at 15:11, and again at 18:26, always followed by the speaker turning to “the twelve whom he had chosen” or “the disciples whom he had chosen”. It enters the book at 3 Nephi 13:25 and should be adjudicated there if anywhere; a reader who meets it at 15:11 is meeting the third occurrence of a house formula, not a borrowing from John 18. Note also that the formula's King James home is a verse the Book of Mormon shares nothing else with: no garden, no brook Cedron, no going forth.

The obvious source for a commission phrased as being “a light” to a people is the Servant text, Isaiah 49:6, and its New Testament citation at Acts 13:47 — and this is exactly the mediation case CONVENTIONS §7 exists for, so it was tested rather than assumed. tools/mediation-check.py on 3 Nephi 15:12 against Isaiah 49:6 and Acts 13:47 reports no decisive divergence and, more usefully, that the Book of Mormon reproduces neither candidate at any point where they differ: it has no “Gentiles”, no “salvation”, no “ends of the earth”, and its light is “unto this people”, which is the opposite of the Servant's outward direction. The wording follows the Sermon at the Temple's own localisation of Matthew 5:14 at 3 Nephi 12:14 (“the light of this people”), and the link is filed there. Worth recording because the Servant reading is the natural one and because 3 Nephi 16 does turn to the Gentiles four verses later, which makes the wrong source look even more plausible than it is.

A five-word run and a King James singleton — “the other tribes of the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — with a second hook that makes it more tempting than it should be: Numbers 36 is about inheritance passing between tribes, and 3 Nephi 15:13 has just said “this is the land of your inheritance”. The sense will not carry it. Numbers 36:3 is a legal objection about heiresses marrying outside their tribe and their land being reassigned; 3 Nephi 15:15 is about tribes of Israel the Father has “led away out of the land” and about whom the speaker was forbidden to tell the Jerusalem audience. The shared words are the ordinary English for naming tribes other than the ones in view, and the Book of Mormon's “other tribes” is its own category, taken up again at 15:20 and 3 Nephi 16:1-4 without any further contact with Numbers.

The shepherd oracle behind John 10:16 is Ezekiel's, and a reader tracing “one fold, and one shepherd” to its Old Testament root will arrive at Ezekiel 34:23 and 37:24. The catalogue's link is at John 10:16 and the mediation was decided rather than defaulted (CONVENTIONS §7). “One shepherd” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Ecclesiastes 12:11, Ezekiel 34:23, Ezekiel 37:24 and John 10:16 — and tools/mediation-check.py on 3 Nephi 15:17 against Ezekiel 37:24 and John 10:16 returns four decisive points for John and none for Ezekiel: the Book of Mormon has “other sheep I have, which are not of this fold”, “them also I must bring”, “they shall hear my voice” and “one fold”, and none of Ezekiel's David, servant, king over them, judgments or statutes. The oracle reaches 3 Nephi in its Johannine form and only in that form. Filed here so that Ezekiel 34 and 37 are not silently absent from a chapter that is manifestly about one flock under one shepherd.

A five-word run and a King James singleton — “the Gentiles should be” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the context is genuinely apt, since Ephesians 3 is Paul's account of a Gentile inclusion that was “hid” in earlier ages and revealed later, which is close to what 3 Nephi 15:22-23 says about the Jerusalem hearers' failure to understand. The verbal contact is nevertheless a subject, a modal and a copula, and the two sentences complete them incompatibly: Ephesians has the Gentiles becoming fellowheirs of the promise, and 3 Nephi has them being “converted through their preaching”, where “their” are the Nephite disciples. The Book of Mormon's own doctrine of Gentile conversion through a Nephite record is developed at length in 3 Nephi 16 and 20-21 with no further contact with Ephesians.

The best temptation in the chapter's register. “They supposed it had been” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, a five-word run, and both sentences are about disciples getting a supernatural identification wrong in the presence of Jesus. But the errors are of different kinds and the phrase's grammar shows it. In Mark 6:49 the disciples see something on the water and mistake a person for a class of being: “they supposed it had been a spirit”. In 3 Nephi 15:22 the Jerusalem hearers mistake the referent of a saying: “they supposed it had been the Gentiles”. Mark's “it” is a figure walking on the sea; the Book of Mormon's “it” is the phrase “other sheep”, and the object of the supposition is an interpretation, not an apparition. The idiom is the King James's ordinary way of reporting a mistaken supposition and nothing else of Mark 6 is present — no sea, no walking, no crying out, no fourth watch.

exclusions.sharedText: and they shall hear my voice ... that there may be one fold, and one shepherd
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter and a correct identification — 'one fold, and one shepherd' is a KJV singleton and it is reproduced intact. It is excluded here only because the chapter's use of John 10:16 is adjudicated two verses earlier, at 16:1, where the borrowing does something the machine cannot see: 'not of this fold' is rewritten as 'not of this land'. 16:3 restores the metaphor 16:1 dismantled, and the two verses are one movement. The reader who arrives at 16:3 should be sent to 16:1, and to 3 Nephi 15:17 and 15:21, where the same verse is quoted verbatim twice in the preceding chapter.

The run straddles a clause boundary and joins two unrelated phrases: 'scattered forth upon the face of the earth' + 'because of their unbelief'. Jeremiah 15:4 has 'removed into all kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh'. The scattering is a real thematic overlap, but the KJV's own verse for it in this chapter's argument is Leviticus 26:33 ('I will scatter you among the heathen'), which stands behind 16:8-11 and is adjudicated at 16:11, and the 'because of' clause belongs to Romans 11:20, adjudicated at 16:4 itself. The Jeremiah row is the machine finding a boundary.

A five-word run of pure command formula. John 15:17 is 'These things I command you, that ye love one another'; 3 Nephi 16:4 is 'And I command you that ye shall write these sayings'. Nothing is shared but the syntax of issuing an order, and the Book of Mormon uses that syntax continuously. Recorded rather than passed over in silence because this verse does carry a genuine Johannine borrowing — John 16:23's 'ask the Father in my name' — and a reader could reasonably suppose the two were connected. They are not; the John 15 candidate is boilerplate and the John 16 one is a KJV singleton.

The wrong half of the phrase, for the reason already given in the register at 3 Nephi 5:26: Jeremiah 49:36 reads 'the four quarters of heaven', not of the earth, and its winds scatter Elam rather than gather anyone. 3 Nephi 16:5 reads 'of the earth' and gathers. Repeated here because the machine ranks it afresh at every occurrence of the phrase and a reader arriving at this verse has not necessarily seen the entry at 5:26.

exclusions.sharedText: the four quarters of the earth
exclusions.reason: A KJV singleton and a real borrowing, adjudicated for this book at 3 Nephi 5:24, where the mediation test against Isaiah 11:12 is run and the choice of 'quarters' over Isaiah's 'corners' is shown to be decisive. 16:5 is Christ's own use of a phrase Mormon has already used as narrator eleven chapters earlier, in the same gathering sense and with the same reversal of Revelation's meaning — Revelation's four quarters are where Gog and Magog are gathered from to make war, the Book of Mormon's are where Israel is gathered from to be given a covenant. Nothing is added here that 5:24 does not already carry, and the standing exclusion at 3 Nephi 5:26 covers the same candidate.

Ranked at both 16:8 and 16:9, and 'come out from among them' is a KJV singleton, so the temptation is real — the more so because 2 Corinthians 6:17 is itself a citation of Isaiah 52:11, three verses past the block this chapter quotes at 16:18-20. The senses are opposed at the only point that matters. Paul's imperative is voluntary and self-protective: the believers are told to separate themselves from unbelievers, 'be ye separate, and touch not the unclean thing', and the promise attached is 'I will receive you'. 3 Nephi 16:8-9 is involuntary and punitive: the house of Israel 'have been cast out from among them, and have been trodden under feet by them'. One party leaves to stay clean; the other is expelled and trampled. Note also that the matching words are not the KJV's Isaiah at all — Isaiah 52:11 reads 'Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence' — so the phrase that produces the candidate is Paul's own rendering, and the Isaiah 52 adjacency, however striking, cannot be used to support the row. The genuine source of 16:9's clause is 1 Kings 9:7's 'will I cast out of my sight', adjudicated there.

This is the register's most interesting entry in the chapter and it has to be declined. 'Trodden under feet' — with the plural — occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 14:19 and Isaiah 28:3, against five for the singular 'trodden under foot'. 3 Nephi 16:8 has the plural, and both 1830 and 1920 read 'trodden under feet' there, so it is not an orthographic accident of the first edition. Seven verses later, at 16:15, the same book has the singular, 'trodden under foot', because it is quoting Matthew 5:13. The chapter therefore distinguishes the two KJV forms and uses each in a passage where that form is at home, which is the kind of fact that ordinarily makes a link. It does not make one here. Isaiah 28:3's plural belongs to 'the crown of pride, the drunkards of Ephraim' — the trodden party is Israel's own northern kingdom, undone by drink, and there is no Gentile in the verse. 3 Nephi 16:8's trodden party is Israel scattered by Gentiles who have 'come forth upon the face of this land'. Three words, opposed agents, and no second point of contact anywhere in Isaiah 28. What survives is worth recording without the link: whoever wrote 16:8 and 16:15 had both King James spellings available and did not mix them.

A five-word run inside a list of passive infinitives — 'to be smitten, and to be afflicted, and to be slain, and to be cast out' — where the shared material is the list's grammar. Esther 7:4's 'to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish' is the same construction and no more. Esther is pleading for the Jews before Ahasuerus and the verse turns on being sold; 3 Nephi 16:9 is God rehearsing what he has caused to be done to his own people. The list's real background is the covenant curse of Leviticus 26, which the following verses take up explicitly at 16:11.

Genuinely close in subject — Jeremiah 12:14 is God plucking his people out of their land because of evil neighbours — and still too little. The shared words are a first-person causative and the phrase 'my people', both of which the Book of Mormon uses constantly and this chapter uses six times. Jeremiah's clause is 'the inheritance which I have caused my people Israel to inherit', a possession; 3 Nephi 16:9's is 'I have caused my people ... to be smitten', an affliction. The verb's object is opposite in kind.

Five words of which four are function words. 'The mercies of the LORD' in Psalm 89:1 is the opening of a psalm of praise; 'the mercies of the Father unto the Gentiles' in 3 Nephi 16:9 is one term in a balanced pair with 'the judgements of the Father upon my people'. The pairing of mercy and judgement is the verse's real structure and it is not Psalm 89's.

'The whole earth' occurs in twenty-eight KJV verses and the rest of the run is connective. Daniel 7:23's fourth beast devours the whole earth and treads it down; 3 Nephi 16:10's Gentiles are lifted up 'above all the people of the whole earth'. Devouring the earth and being exalted above its people are different claims, and Daniel supplies no other word here. The verse's real intertext is Romans 11:21-22, which is where the row is written, at moderate and with a stated whyNot.

A five-word KJV singleton, which is ordinarily the strongest evidence this catalogue can produce, and it is worthless here. Revelation 17:1 is one of the seven vial-angels summoning John: 'Come hither; I will shew unto thee the judgment of the great whore that sitteth upon many waters.' 3 Nephi 16:12 is the Father addressing the house of Israel: 'I will shew unto thee, O house of Israel, that the Gentiles shall not have power over you.' The speaker, the addressee and the thing shown are all different, and nothing else of Revelation 17 is anywhere near. The phrase is simply the King James formula for one party undertaking to show another something, and its being a singleton is arithmetic rather than significance — compare the standing entry at Helaman 1:1. The 1830 spelling 'shew', which 1920 modernized to 'show', is worth recording as KJV orthography surviving in the first edition, but it attests the translation's general idiom and not this verse.

'Hearken unto my voice' is one of the King James Bible's commonest covenant formulas and 'hear my voice' alone occurs in eleven verses. Exodus 18:19 is Jethro offering Moses administrative advice; 3 Nephi 16:15 is God stating the condition on which he will let Israel tread the Gentiles down. The verse's actual borrowing, seventeen consecutive words of Matthew 5:13, sits immediately after this run and is adjudicated at the verse.

exclusions.sharedText: for the Lord hath comforted his people
exclusions.reason: A genuine seven-word agreement, and displaced. 'Hath comforted his people' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 49:13 and Isaiah 52:9, so the clause alone cannot choose between them — but the rest of 3 Nephi 16:19 decides it without ambiguity. The Book of Mormon reads 'Break forth into joy, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem ... he hath redeemed Jerusalem'; Isaiah 49:13 reads 'break forth into singing, O mountains ... and will have mercy upon his afflicted'. 'Break forth into joy' and 'waste places of Jerusalem' are each KJV singletons and each belongs to 52:9. The candidate is recorded because Isaiah 49 is quoted at length elsewhere in the Book of Mormon (1 Nephi 21, 2 Nephi 6), so a reader has reason to expect it here, and because the two verses are close enough that the machine cannot separate them.

exclusions.sharedText: when Jesus had spoken these words
exclusions.reason: The dossier's highest-ranked candidate in the chapter, a seven-word verbatim run, and “when Jesus had spoken these words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — John 18:1, the sentence that takes Jesus over the brook Cedron into the garden. The temptation is real because the chapter that follows is full of passion-narrative material: kneeling, prayer, groaning, weeping. It is nevertheless the Book of Mormon's own narrative formula. The clause appears at 3 Nephi 12:1, 13:25, 14:1, 15:11, 17:1 and 18:26 — six times in seven chapters, five of them before this verse — and the wider form 'had spoken these words' runs through 1 Nephi as well. By CONVENTIONS §4 a phrase a narrator has adopted is adjudicated at first use and not re-borrowed each time it recurs, and first use in this book is 3 Nephi 12:1. The KJV singleton status is arithmetic: the King James Bible had occasion to write this particular six-word chain once, and the Book of Mormon writes it whenever Jesus stops speaking. The genuine link at this verse is to Matthew 26:18, on 'my time is at hand', which is not a formula anywhere.

John 13:21 is proposed on a four-word run of narrative formula, 'when Jesus had thus', and would be pure noise but for its second clause: 'he was troubled in spirit, and testified'. Nine verses later the Book of Mormon has Jesus troubled (17:14), and a reader who has both verses in view will want to join them. The join is declined here and made at 17:14 instead, where the wording decides it. 3 Nephi 17:14 reads 'groaned within himself … Father, I am troubled', which reproduces John 11:38's reflexive construction and John 11:33's pairing of groaning with being troubled, and addresses the Father as John 12:27 does; John 13:21 has neither the groan nor the Father, and its trouble is over Judas. The 17:5 candidate is the same formula that produced the John 18:1 entry above and carries the same weight.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when he had
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run and the top-scoring candidate at this verse, and it is the standing case: 'and it came to pass that when he had' is the Book of Mormon's continuous narrative connective and the KJV's, and Ezekiel 10:6 is about the man clothed in linen taking fire from between the cherubim. Listed rather than passed over in silence only because the rank is conspicuous and because it sits directly on top of one of the chapter's strongest links — the real source at 17:9 is Acts 5:16, which shares four words and a KJV singleton. This is the pilot's finding about the n-gram stream (CONVENTIONS §9) in one verse: the longest run and the true source are not the same candidate, and are not close.

A five-word run, ranked first at this verse, and the senses are opposed at the only point that matters. Matthew 27:20 reads 'the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus'; 3 Nephi 17:13 reads 'he commanded the multitude that they should kneel down upon the ground'. The KJV verse is the one place in the passion narrative where somebody instructs a crowd what to do with Jesus and the instruction is to kill him; the Book of Mormon verse is Jesus instructing a crowd to kneel before he prays for them. Shared are a definite article, a noun the KJV uses ninety times, and a subjunctive. Nothing else of Matthew 27 is anywhere near this chapter.

“because of the wickedness of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 28:20, and the thematic fit is not absurd: the Deuteronomic curse falls on Israel for wickedness, and 3 Nephi 17:14 has Jesus troubled 'because of the wickedness of the people of the house of Israel'. But the rarity is an artifact of the exact preposition chain and nothing else. 'Wickedness' appears in more than a hundred KJV verses, 'the wickedness of' in dozens, and Deuteronomy's own near-parallels at 9:4 and 9:5 read 'for the wickedness of these nations' — the same claim with a different preposition. What the Book of Mormon shares with Deuteronomy 28:20 is five words of ordinary causal English and the general idea that Israel's wickedness has consequences, which is the premise of most of the Old Testament. The verse's real dependence is Johannine and is adjudicated as such.

Recorded because it is a KJV singleton and singletons are the evidence this catalogue leans on hardest, so one that should be declined needs to be shown being declined. “I am troubled” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 38:6 — 'I am troubled; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long' — and 3 Nephi 17:14 has the clause exactly. But Psalm 38 is a penitential psalm and the trouble is the speaker's own: his sin, his wounds, his friends standing aloof. The Book of Mormon's Jesus is troubled about somebody else's wickedness, and the sentence he says it in addresses the Father, which the psalm never does. The Johannine passages adjudicated at this verse — John 11:33's 'he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled', John 11:38's 'groaning in himself', John 12:27's 'Now is my soul troubled … Father' — supply the groan, the reflexive, the trouble and the address together, and the psalm supplies only the third of those. A rare string in the wrong grammatical person is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names, and this is a clean instance of it.

exclusions.sharedText: Jesus had made an end of
exclusions.reason: The best machine proposal in the chapter and it is still displaced. Matthew 11:1 reads 'when Jesus had made an end of commanding his twelve disciples', which gives a five-word run with the right subject, and it ranked first here. But the Book of Mormon's clause is 'made an end of PRAYING', and the KJV has that phrase in exactly two verses — 1 Kings 8:54 and 2 Chronicles 7:1, the two accounts of Solomon's dedication of the temple. “made an end of commanding” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 49:33 and Matthew 11:1, and neither is about prayer. This is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 describes as the window closing one word early: the run is longest through 'end of' and the word that follows it is what identifies the source. Once the Solomon verses are in view the rest of the chapter reorganises around them — kneeling, rising, fire from heaven at 17:24, the people prostrate and worshipping at 17:10 — which is the argument made at the link.

Typology pulls hard and the wording will not bear it, which is the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' case again. 3 Nephi 17:23 reads 'Behold your little ones', and the King James Bible's one Christological use of that construction is from the cross: 'Woman, behold thy son!' (John 19:26), answered by 'Behold thy mother!' (19:27) — the verses in which Jesus, dying, consigns a child and a parent to one another. A chapter this saturated in Johannine material (11:33, 11:35, 1:51, 15:16, 14:28, 19:35 are all adjudicated here) makes the parallel tempting, and the sense is even apt, since Jesus is presenting children to the multitude as their charge. It is declined because 'behold' plus a possessive is not distinctive: the KJV uses 'Behold thy' and 'Behold your' dozens of times, of kings, mothers, sons, gods and calves, and there is no second point of contact — no cross, no consignment, no naming of a person to a person. Recorded so that a reader who sees the crucifixion scene here is told the catalogue saw it and would not write it.

The machine's top candidate at the closing verse, on a five-word run, and it deserves writing up because the coincidence has a second layer that makes it look like a finding. Numbers 26:37 gives the census of the sons of Ephraim as 'thirty and two thousand and five hundred', and 3 Nephi 17:25 numbers its multitude at 'about two thousand and five hundred souls' — and the Book of Mormon's people are Josephites, so a reader may well feel that a Josephite head-count has been taken from a Josephite census. It has not. The shared string is a numeral, and it is not even the same numeral: Numbers reads thirty-two thousand five hundred and the Book of Mormon reads two thousand five hundred, so the run is produced by chopping the KJV's number in the middle. Numbers 26 is a wilderness muster of fighting men by tribe; 3 Nephi 17:25 counts 'men, women and children' who have just seen angels. The chapter's real numbering formula is Acts 2:41's 'about three thousand souls', which shares the approximation, the unit and the syntax, and which is adjudicated at this verse.

A five-word run and the second-ranked candidate in the verse, and both halves are boilerplate. Leviticus 24:23 is Moses ordering the blasphemer taken out of the camp and stoned; 3 Nephi 18:1 is Jesus asking for bread and wine. ‘Commanded … that they should bring forth’ is the KJV’s ordinary syntax for a relayed order and the Book of Mormon uses it continuously. The first-ranked candidate in the same verse, Matthew 16:20 (‘his disciples that they should’), is the same phenomenon and is covered here rather than listed twice; it recurs at 18:8 for the same reason.

The top-scoring candidate in the verse and it is the machine reading syntax as content. Matthew 27:20 is the chief priests persuading the crowd to ask for Barabbas and destroy Jesus; 3 Nephi 18:2 is Jesus seating a crowd for a meal. The four shared words are ‘the multitude that they should’, which is simply how the KJV introduces an instruction given to a crowd. The real source of this verse is the feeding-miracle seating formula — “commanded the multitude to sit down” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 14:19 and Matthew 15:35 — and the link is filed there. Worth an entry because the machine ranked a Passion verse first in the chapter that institutes the sacrament, which is exactly the trap CONVENTIONS §9 describes.

“the gates of hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 16:18, so the candidate is as rare as candidates get, and the borrowing is real — but it is not first made here. 3 Nephi 11:39-40 has already welded Matthew 16:18 to Matthew 7:24-27 in almost these words: ‘whoso buildeth upon this, buildeth upon my rock; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against them … is not built upon my rock, but he buildeth upon a sandy foundation, and the gates of hell standeth open to receive such, when the floods come, and the winds beat upon them.’ 18:12-13 is that sentence again, and Matthew 16:18 is adjudicated at 3 Nephi 11:39 (see also 3 Nephi 11:40 for Matthew 7:26). A reader who arrives at 18:13 should be sent there. What remains fresh at 18:13 — the restored ‘rain’, which 11:40 dropped and Matthew 7:25/27 has — carries the link written at this verse to Matthew 7:27, and discharges Hardy’s cross-reference. Note also the 1830 reading, ‘the gates of hell is already open to receive them’, with a singular verb and ‘already’ for ‘ready’; 1920 prints ‘the gates of hell are ready to receive them’.

A six-word run and the only candidate the machine offered in this verse, and it is as opposed in sense as a match can be. Ezekiel 16:33 is the prophet’s figure of Jerusalem as a whore who pays her lovers ‘that they may come unto thee on every side for thy whoredom’; 3 Nephi 18:22 forbids the disciples to turn anyone away from the assembly. Nothing is shared but the infinitive of approach. The verse’s actual source is the Synoptic children saying — “forbid them not” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Matthew 19:14, Mark 10:14 and Luke 18:16 — and the link is filed at 18:22 accordingly.

exclusions.sharedText: what ye have seen me do
exclusions.reason: The best entry in this register and it has to be written out, because a reader who finds it will assume the catalogue missed it. “ye have seen me do” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and the other one is Abimelech at mount Zalmon: he cuts a bough, lays it on his shoulder, and tells his men ‘What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done’ — after which they pile boughs against the tower of Shechem and burn a thousand men and women alive inside it (Judges 9:49). 3 Nephi 18:24 reads ‘Behold I am the light which ye shall hold up — that which ye have seen me do.’ The formula is identical, the situation is a leader making his own performed act the pattern for his followers, and the outcomes are a massacre and a lamp. The rarity is real and the coincidence is a coincidence: nothing else in Judges 9 is present, and the Book of Mormon’s sentence has a much closer home in John 13:15 (“I have given you an example” occurs in exactly one KJV verse), which is filed as the link at 18:16.

‘Hold up your light, that it may shine unto the world’ is the Sermon’s lamp saying, and “let your light so shine” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:16 — but 3 Nephi has already transcribed that verse in full at 12:16, where it is adjudicated as a certain quotation. 18:24 is the same speaker citing his own earlier sermon back to the same audience, which is the recurrence case of ADJUDICATING §4 and not a fresh borrowing. The same applies to ‘Behold I am the light which ye shall hold up’: “I am the light” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, John 8:12 and John 9:5, and John 8:12 is already adjudicated at 3 Nephi 9:18 and 11:11. Both belong here as cross-references rather than as rows. What is genuinely new at 18:24 — ‘hold up’, which is in no KJV verse in this sense — is the Book of Mormon’s own contribution and cannot be catalogued as dependence.

exclusions.sharedText: When Jesus had spoken these words
exclusions.reason: A four-word run reproducing a KJV singleton exactly — “When Jesus had spoken these words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 18:1 — and it is still boilerplate, because the Book of Mormon has made it boilerplate. The phrase appears six times in the 1830 text, all of them in this one visit: 3 Nephi 12:1, 13:25, 14:1, 15:11, 17:1 and 18:26, where it marks each turn of the discourse from one audience to another. A formula the narrator uses six times in seven chapters is his transition device, not a borrowing from the verse that happens to share it; John 18:1’s own continuation is Jesus crossing the Cedron into Gethsemane, which has nothing to do with any of the six. The entry is written rather than passed over in silence because the KJV rarity is genuine and will keep re-ranking this candidate.

“return and repent” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joel 2:14, which is why the machine ranked it, and the rarity is arithmetic rather than distinctive: the two verbs are the standard KJV pair for turning back to God and the Bible simply had occasion to put them in this order once. Joel 2:14 is a question about whether the LORD will relent and leave a grain offering behind him — ‘Who knoweth if he will return and repent’, where the subject of both verbs is God and ‘repent’ means to change a purpose. 3 Nephi 18:32’s subject is an excommunicated man and ‘repent’ means contrition. Same two words, opposite grammatical subject, opposite sense of the second verb.

The Isaiah 6:10 healing formula, in its New Testament rather than its Old Testament form, and it is adjudicated at 3 Nephi 9:13 rather than here. `mediation-check.py` run on this verse against Isaiah 6:10 and Matthew 13:15 returns one decisive point — the Book of Mormon has the New Testament’s ‘I should heal them’, a first-person divine healer, against Isaiah’s agentless ‘be healed’ — so the mediation is settled and it is settled the same way it was at 9:13, which has the fuller sentence (‘return unto me, and repent of your sins, and be converted, that I may heal you’) and the second decisive divergence as well. 18:32’s ‘they will return and repent, and come unto me … and I shall heal them’ is the same speaker’s same formula nine chapters later, which is the recurrence case of ADJUDICATING §4. Note one caution about the tool at this verse: its ‘backbone’ of shared words (heart, ears, eyes, lest, see, hear, understand) is computed between the two candidates and not against the Book of Mormon, and 18:32 has almost none of them — the decisive point stands, the backbone does not corroborate it here.

A five-word run split across a clause boundary in Jude and therefore meaningless. Jude 1:10 reads ‘these speak evil of those things which they know not: but what they know naturally, as brute beasts’ — the machine’s window has closed over the colon, joining the end of one clause to the start of the next. 3 Nephi 18:32’s ‘ye know not but what they will return and repent’ is a single idiom for uncertainty. This is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 calls the window closing one word early, in its other form: the window opening one clause too soon.

The top-ranked candidate in the verse, on the strength of ‘and it came to pass, when Jesus had made an end of’, and it is two formulas in a row. “made an end of” occurs in exactly thirty-eight KJV verses and is the King James Bible’s standard way of closing a speech or a task; the Book of Mormon uses it throughout. Matthew 11:1’s own continuation — Jesus departing to teach and preach in the cities — has nothing to do with 3 Nephi 18:36, where he touches the twelve one by one and confers the Holy Ghost. Two nearer candidates exist and neither carries: Matthew 7:28, where “ended these sayings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, is the wrong verb, and Genesis 49:33, the only other verse with ‘made an end of commanding’, is Jacob dying. The verse’s real content is the laying on of hands, filed as a link at 18:37 against Acts 8:17-19.

“he departed from them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 19:9, and the verse is Paul withdrawing from the synagogue at Ephesus because ‘divers were hardened, and believed not, but spake evil of that way’, taking the disciples off to the school of Tyrannus. 3 Nephi 18:39 is the Ascension. The shared words are the plainest English for leaving a group and the senses are opposed — Acts 19:9 is a separation caused by unbelief and followed by two more years of teaching; 18:39 is a departure into heaven witnessed by believers. The verse’s genuine sources are registered with the link at 18:38: “a cloud received him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 1:9, and “carried up into heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:51.

exclusions.sharedText: every man his wife and his children
exclusions.reason: The chapter's top-ranked machine candidate and a five-word run, and the senses are opposed. In 1 Samuel 30:22 the men of Belial propose that the two hundred who did not fight be given back their wives and children and nothing else — the clause is a formula of exclusion from spoil, spoken by the worst men in David's company and immediately overruled by him. In 3 Nephi 19:1 it describes an orderly, blessed dispersal after Christ's ascension. Nothing else of the verse is present, and taking one's own household home is not a distinctive act needing a source.

Recorded because a reader who knows the Fourth Gospel will propose it and should be told the catalogue saw it. John 7:53 — “And every man went unto his own house” — is the KJV's one verse of that shape, and its setting is a genuine parallel: a multitude divided about Jesus disperses, and the very next clause has Jesus going up the mount of Olives. 3 Nephi 19:1 has Jesus ascending into heaven and the multitude dispersing to their homes. But the wording will not carry it. The Book of Mormon reads “did return to his own home”, and “his own home” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — John 19:27, the beloved disciple taking Mary away from the cross — which is a different verse, a different phrase and an unrelated sense. What is actually shared with John 7:53 is “every man” and the idea of going home, and the register at 1 Nephi 1:5 covers connective matter of that weight.

exclusions.sharedText: the Father in the name of
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the highest-scoring candidate at 19:6 and 19:8, and it is the Book of Mormon's own liturgical formula rather than a borrowing. “Pray unto the Father in the name of Jesus” occurs four times in this chapter alone (19:6, 19:7, 19:8, and the pattern behind 19:9) and has been the prescribed form since 3 Nephi 18:19-21, where Christ commands it. Ephesians 5:20 is about giving thanks always for all things, and shares no content word beyond the two nouns the formula requires. This entry covers every “Father in the name of” candidate in the chapter.

The n-gram stream ranked Isaiah 11:16 because it contains “came up out of the”; its next word is “land”, and the sentence is about Israel's highway from Assyria in the day it came up out of the land of Egypt. The Book of Mormon's next word is “water”. The borrowing at this verse is catalogued to Acts 8:39, where “come up out of the water” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. A model instance of the window closing one word early (ADJUDICATING §4).

“Angels came and ministered unto him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 4:11, the close of the temptation in the wilderness, and 3 Nephi 19:14 reads “angels did come down out of heaven, and did minister unto them”. The rarity is misleading: the shorter “ministered unto him” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses and covers servants, women and the myriads of Daniel 7:10, so what is rare is only the collocation with “angels”, which the King James Bible has just twice (Matthew 4:11 and Mark 1:13, of the same episode). Against that, the Book of Mormon has already used this exact sentence eighteen verses earlier — 3 Nephi 17:24, “they were encircled about with fire; and the angels did minister unto them” — so 19:14 is the narrator repeating his own clause from the same visit, not reaching for Matthew. The 1830's “do bear record” (1920: “did bear record”) is preserved for the same reason it matters at 19:33: the present tense is the writer's, not a source's.

exclusions.sharedText: and commanded them that they should
exclusions.reason: A six-word run of pure command-report syntax. Mark 6:8's object is a staff, no scrip, no bread and no money for the mission of the twelve; 3 Nephi 19:16's is kneeling down on the earth. The same standing exclusion covers Matthew 16:20 at 19:17 (“his disciples that they should”), where Matthew's object is telling no man that he was the Christ.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when they had
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run and the longest in the chapter, and it is entirely the “and it came to pass” formula plus a temporal subordinator. The standing exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 2:1 covers it; it is named here only because nine words invites a second look. Amos 7:2 concerns the locusts finishing the grass of the land. The same applies to Mark 2:23 at 19:31.

The best-looking machine proposal in the chapter and it must be discharged carefully, because “bowed himself to the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “bowed himself to the earth” occurs in none — so the Book of Mormon's clause is closer to Genesis 33:3 than to anything else in the King James Bible. It is still not the source. Genesis 33:3 is Jacob approaching Esau, bowing seven times in fear of a brother he has cheated; there is no prayer in it, no withdrawal, and no second party. The link at this verse is to Matthew 26:39 and its sequel, on the strength of the chapter's reproduction of Gethsemane's whole six-movement structure at 19:19, 19:24, 19:27, 19:30, 19:31 and 19:35 — where the posture clause stands in the slot Matthew fills with “fell on his face” and Mark with “fell on the ground”. The Book of Mormon's substitution of “the earth” for either is what produced the Genesis match, and it is a substitution, not a citation.

Five words of petitionary boilerplate. Acts 24:4 is Tertullus flattering Felix — “that I be not further tedious unto thee, I pray thee that thou wouldest hear us of thy clemency a few words” — where “I pray thee” is the ordinary courtesy of address, not prayer at all. 3 Nephi 19:21 is Christ petitioning the Father for the Holy Ghost. The idiom is common to both because English uses one verb for both senses.

Four words in a chapter that says “pray unto” eleven times. 2 Chronicles 6:34 is Solomon's dedicatory prayer asking that Israel's prayers toward the temple be heard when the army goes out to war; the shared material is a verb, a preposition and a pronoun. Worth naming only because 19:22 is doctrinally the most exposed verse in the chapter — “they pray unto me because I am with them” — and a reader may expect a source behind it. The catalogue finds none; the argument the verse is making is answered from John 20:28 at 19:18, not from Chronicles.

Four words of narrative pointing, and the verse's top-ranked candidate only because the surrounding phrase “upon them and behold they were” is uncommon. Genesis 40:6 is Joseph finding Pharaoh's butler and baker sad in the morning. The real borrowings at 19:25 are catalogued to Numbers 6:24-26 and Mark 9:3.

A five-word run, and Isaiah 60:21 does end “the work of my hands, that I may be glorified”. But the Book of Mormon's clause is “that I may be glorified in them”, and “I am glorified in them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — John 17:10, four verses from the John 17:9 sentence that 3 Nephi 19:29 reproduces for thirteen consecutive words. The prepositional phrase Isaiah lacks is exactly the phrase that decides it. Registered here so that a reader following the n-gram scores is sent to the link at this verse.

The Book of Mormon's clause is “their soul shall never hunger nor thirst, but shall be filled”, and the two KJV candidates for a hunger-and-thirst promise are Revelation 7:16, “They shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more”, and John 6:35, “he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst”. John wins on two counts. “Never hunger” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is John 6:35; Revelation has “hunger no more”, a different construction. And Revelation 7:16 accounts for a third of the Book of Mormon verse and nothing else in it — the first two thirds are about eating a bread that is a body and drinking a wine that is blood, which is John 6:54-56 and is absent from Revelation 7 entirely. The link is written at John 6:35 with John 6:54 and 6:56 as composite.

exclusions.sharedText: from the east, and from the west
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter's first fifteen verses, on a ten-word run, and it is the wrong one of the two verses that share the phrase. “From the east and from the west” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 107:3 and Luke 13:29. Psalm 107:3 is a gathering — “And gathered them out of the lands, from the east, and from the west, from the north, and from the south” — and 3 Nephi 20:13 is a gathering: “shall the remnants … be gathered in from the east, and from the west, and from the south, and from the north.” Luke 13:29 is a banquet scene, and the people who come from the four quarters in it do so in order to “sit down in the kingdom of God” while the sons of the kingdom are thrust out; the verb is not gathering and the sense is exclusion, not restoration. A moderate link is written at Psalm 107:3 instead, with the caveat that the Book of Mormon's order of the quarters (east, west, south, north) matches neither candidate.

“Powers of heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 21:26, which makes it the strongest-looking candidate a rarity search returns for this verse and makes it worth refusing in writing. Luke's clause is “the powers of heaven shall be SHAKEN” — the cosmic dissolution of the Olivet discourse, listed alongside men's hearts failing them for fear. 3 Nephi 20:22's clause is “the powers of heaven shall be IN THE MIDST OF THIS PEOPLE; yea, even I will be in the midst of you” — a promise of presence in a verse about establishing a New Jerusalem. The one shared phrase is doing opposite work in the two verses: in Luke the heavenly powers are the thing destabilized, here they are the thing granted.
