The catalogue writes an echo at Revelation 21:2 for this verse's “New Jerusalem” instead, and records that the remainder of the verse has no verbal source it can identify — Ezekiel 37:26-27 and Zechariah 2:10-11 are the nearest in sense and share no wording.

exclusions.sharedText: A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me
exclusions.reason: Stephen quotes the prophet-like-unto-Moses oracle at Acts 7:37 in wording identical to Peter's at Acts 3:22 for its first twenty-one words — “raise up unto you of your brethren” occurs in exactly these two KJV verses and nowhere else — so the machine proposes both and the choice has to be made on what follows. Acts 7:37 stops at “him shall ye hear”; Acts 3:22 continues “in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you”, and 3 Nephi 20:23 has those twelve words in full. Acts 3 then supplies the sanction clause that occupies the second half of the Book of Mormon verse — “every soul, which will not hear that prophet, shall be destroyed from among the people” (Acts 3:23) — for which Acts 7 has no equivalent at all. The link is written at Acts 3:22 with Acts 3:23 and Deuteronomy 18:15, 18-19 as composite. This is the same disposition the pilot reached at 1 Nephi 22:20, where the identical pair of candidates arose.

exclusions.sharedText: break forth into … for the LORD hath comforted his people
exclusions.reason: Isaiah 49:13 is the other KJV verse that joins a breaking-forth to the clause “for the LORD hath comforted his people”, and a reader arriving at 3 Nephi 20:34 with a concordance will meet it. It reads “break forth into SINGING, O mountains”; Isaiah 52:9 reads “Break forth into JOY, sing together, ye waste places of Jerusalem”, and the Book of Mormon has joy, the singing together and the waste places — “break forth into joy” and “waste places of Jerusalem” are each KJV singletons at Isaiah 52:9. Isaiah 49:13 also has no Jerusalem redeemed in it, which is how 3 Nephi 20:34 ends. The same displacement was filed at 3 Nephi 16:19, where the corpus quotes the same verse without alteration; it is repeated here because a reader browsing chapter 20 has no reason to look at chapter 16's register.

A genuine mediation candidate and the most interesting refusal in the chapter, because it is refused on the evidence rather than on the sense. Isaiah 52:11 reads “touch NO unclean thing”; 2 Corinthians 6:17 quotes it as “touch NOT the unclean thing”; and 3 Nephi 20:41 reads “touch NOT that which is unclean”, whose negative is Paul's and not Isaiah's. That is exactly the kind of one-word divergence on which the pilot's sixteen OT-via-NT rows were decided, so it deserves a hearing. It loses on volume. mediation-check.py returns three decisive points and all three favour Isaiah: the Book of Mormon opens “Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence”, where Paul has “Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord”; it keeps “from thence”, which Paul drops; and it keeps the whole of “go ye out of the midst of her; be ye clean, that bear the vessels of the Lord”, eighteen consecutive words for which Paul substitutes “and I will receive you”. One shared negative against eighteen shared words. The link is written at Isaiah 52:11 as direct-OT, and the shared “not” is recorded in that row's provenance as a sense-agreement with Paul that is not a verbal borrowing from him.

A trap of the exact kind ADJUDICATING §4 warns about, and one that a rarity check run on the Book of Mormon's own wording walks straight into. 3 Nephi 20:44 reads “As many were ASTONISHED at thee”; Isaiah 52:14, its source, reads “As many were ASTONIED at thee”. The Book of Mormon's participle is therefore not in Isaiah 52:14 at all, and “astonished at thee” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Ezekiel 26:16, 27:35 and 28:19 — every one of them in the oracles against Tyre. The parallel is an artifact of a modernized spelling: “astonied” is the King James form and occurs in ten of its verses, “astonished” is what displaced it, and every edition of the Book of Mormon has the later word. Nothing else in 3 Nephi 20:44 is Ezekiel's, and the twenty words after the participle — “his visage was so marred more than any man, and his form more than the sons of men” — are Isaiah 52:14 verbatim, carrying the KJV singleton “his visage was so marred”. Ezekiel 26:16 and 28:19 are covered by this entry and not listed separately.

A tempting row, and the temptation is worth recording. 'Give you a sign' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 7:14 — 'Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign' — and 3 Nephi 21:1-7 is a sustained discourse about a sign given by the Lord himself. But the verbal contact will not carry it. 3 Nephi reads 'I give unto you a sign', with the KJV's own commonest dative marker inserted, and 'sign' is otherwise unremarkable; the Book of Mormon uses 'give unto you a sign' at Helaman 14:2 as well, where Samuel the Lamanite announces the birth of Christ, and that verse would be the natural home for an Isaiah 7:14 link if one were to be written. Nothing else of Isaiah 7 is present here: no virgin, no conception, no Immanuel, and no threatened king. Filed rather than written because typology is doing all the work and the wording almost none — the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry in 1 Nephi is the model.

exclusions.sharedText: and verily I say unto you
exclusions.reason: The chapter's top-ranked candidate at its first verse, and it is the discourse marker Christ uses in four verses of this chapter alone (21:1, 21:2, 21:3 with 'verily' doubled, and 21:26). 'Verily I say unto you' occurs in dozens of KJV verses; Luke 13:35 ranked only because the preceding 'and' happens to be there too. Covered by the standing formulaic exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 1:5; listed here because it is the top-scoring row of the chapter and a reader checking the register at 21:1 should be told why it was passed over.

A five-word run and a genuine KJV singleton — 'harden their hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 11:20 — and the senses are exactly opposed, which is what makes it register content rather than noise. In Joshua 11:20 the hardening is God's own act, performed ON the Canaanites so that they will attack Israel and be destroyed without mercy: 'it was of the LORD to harden their hearts, that they should come against Israel in battle, that he might destroy them utterly.' In 3 Nephi 21:6 the hardening is the Gentiles' own, it is the thing that must NOT happen, and the alternative offered is repentance, baptism and adoption into Israel. God hardens in order to destroy; the Father waits to see whether they will harden and hopes they will not. The Book of Mormon also uses 'harden their hearts' as a standing idiom throughout, so the singleton is a coincidence of English word order rather than a route.

Recorded because the route exists and the row still fails. 'Shew my power' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 9:17 — Pharaoh raised up 'that I might shew my power in thee, and that my name might be declared throughout all the earth' — and Romans 9-11 is demonstrably in play in this discourse: 3 Nephi 16:4 draws on Romans 11:25 and 16:10 on Romans 11:22, both adjudicated. Romans 9:17's logic is also 3 Nephi 21:6's logic, that God uses an unwilling nation as the instrument by which his name reaches everyone else. But 3 Nephi reads 'shew forth his power', which is a different construction with a different possessive, and 'shew forth' by itself appears in fifteen KJV verses. Two content words in common is not enough to name a source, and writing the link would be building a verbal case to justify a thematic one.

exclusions.sharedText: which are of the house of
exclusions.reason: A six-word run scoring 1.25, and it is a collision of two stock phrases. 'The house of Israel' is the chapter's refrain, in six of its twenty-nine verses (21:1, 21:4, 21:6, 21:7, 21:20, 21:23), and 'which are of the house of' completes it in the ordinary way; 1 Corinthians 1:11's 'them which are of the house of Chloe' is a Corinthian household and has nothing else in common with a covenant made to Israel. The real link at this verse is Ezekiel 24:27, adjudicated.

This one has to be declined explicitly, because Revelation 15:3 is the source of the pilot's flagship link at 1 Nephi 1:14 and 'great and marvellous' is the phrase it supplied. It occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3. But by 3 Nephi it is no longer a borrowing: the Book of Mormon uses 'great and marvellous' twenty-four times across every book, and it is settled corpus idiom long before this chapter. What is genuinely borrowed at 21:9 is Isaiah 29:14's 'a marvellous work among', a KJV singleton, to which the corpus formula has been prefixed as an intensifier. The link is written at 21:9 against Isaiah 29:14 and Acts 13:41; Revelation supplies only the adjective pair, and its adjudication belongs at 1 Nephi 1:14, where it is.

'Cut off from among' occurs in eleven KJV verses, almost all of them the Levitical and Numbers formula for excision from the congregation, and Leviticus 20:17 ranked here on 'they shall be cut off'. The Priestly formula is certainly the ultimate background of the idiom, but it is not the proximate source at this verse and the machine cannot see why. 3 Nephi 21:11's sanction descends by a traceable route: Acts 3:23 reads 'destroyed from among the people'; 1 Nephi 22:20 changed 'destroyed' to 'cut off' and 3 Nephi 20:23 repeated the change; 21:11 inherits it. The link is written against Deuteronomy 18:19 with Acts 3:23 composite and mediation OT-via-earlier-BoM. Leviticus 20:17's own subject — a man who marries his sister — has nothing to do with it.

exclusions.sharedText: delivered unto the Gentiles and shall
exclusions.reason: A five-word run, and the sense is inverted in a way worth naming. Luke 18:32 is the third passion prediction: 'he shall be delivered unto the Gentiles, and shall be mocked, and spitefully entreated, and spitted on'. Christ is the thing handed to the Gentiles, and what follows is his humiliation. In 3 Nephi 21:11 Christ is the speaker, what is brought forth unto the Gentiles is a book, and the power to bring it is given rather than surrendered. The shared string is 'unto the Gentiles and shall', which is grammar. Recorded because the surface pairing of Christ, the Gentiles and a handing-over is exactly the kind of coincidence a reader might mistake for a source.

A cross-reference, filed so that a Hardy row is discharged where a reader will look for it. Hardy's footnote at 3 Ne 21.11 carries the citation 'Mic 5.8-15' alongside Deuteronomy 18:19 and Acts 3:23, on the ground that 'cut off' is the term connecting the Mosaic sanction to the Micah oracle, where it recurs six times. That observation is right and it is taken up in the link written at this verse, but the Micah quotation itself does not begin until 21:12; there is no Micah wording in 21:11 beyond the two words the two passages share. The catalogue therefore writes a link at each of 21:12, 21:13, 21:14, 21:15, 21:16, 21:17, 21:18 and 21:21 against Micah 5:8, 5:9, 5:10, 5:11, 5:12, 5:13, 5:14 and 5:15 respectively, so that each verse of the quotation can be seen doing its own work, and sends a reader from 21:11 to 21:12 for the start of it. Hardy's own convention is to hang a multi-verse citation on one verse of the span, as he does again at 21:13 for Micah 5:8-9.

exclusions.sharedText: in the midst of them as
exclusions.reason: Six words, and every one of them is supplied by the verse the Book of Mormon is actually quoting. Micah 5:8 reads 'in the midst of many people as a lion'; 3 Nephi 21:12 reads 'in the midst of them, as a lion'. Isaiah 25:11's Moabite spreading his hands to swim is an artifact of the shortened phrase matching. The link is written at 21:12 against Micah 5:8.

exclusions.sharedText: for it shall come to pass in that day, saith the
exclusions.reason: An eleven-word run, the longest non-Micah run in the chapter, and it is entirely the KJV's prophetic dating formula. 'And it shall come to pass in that day, saith the LORD' opens Jeremiah 30:8, Micah 5:10, Hosea 2:16, Zechariah 13:2 and many more; the reason it appears verbatim at 3 Nephi 21:14 is that Micah 5:10 is being quoted, and Micah 5:10 has it. Jeremiah 30:8's content — breaking a yoke from a neck — is not present. Filed rather than passed over in silence only because eleven words is long enough that a reader might wonder.

Five words, and they belong to Micah 5:12, which this verse is quoting almost entire: 'out of thine hand; and thou shalt have no more soothsayers'. Deuteronomy 3:2's 'into thy hand; and thou shalt do unto him as thou didst unto Sihon' is a delivery of an enemy, the opposite transaction. The link is written at 21:16 against Micah 5:12.

'Shall be done away' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:10, and the eschatological sense there — 'when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away' — sits well with a verse about the vices of the last days being abolished. The count is real and the row still fails, because the phrase is standing Book of Mormon idiom: 'done away' appears in eleven Book of Mormon verses across six books, including three others in 3 Nephi alone (9:19, 11:30, 12:47). A KJV singleton that the corpus has naturalized is evidence about the corpus's English, not about this verse's source. Worth recording in data/kjv-phrases.json as an Index Verborum entry rather than as a link.

The best of several New Testament vice-list candidates and still not a link. 'Envyings' occurs in exactly two KJV verses (2 Corinthians 12:20, Galatians 5:21) and 'strifes' in four, and 2 Corinthians 12:20 is the only KJV verse holding both — 'debates, envyings, wraths, strifes, backbitings, whisperings, swellings, tumults'. But the two words are not adjacent there, and the four other items in the Book of Mormon's list are not Paul's: 'lyings', 'deceivings', 'priestcrafts' and 'whoredoms', of which 'priestcrafts' occurs in no KJV verse at all. This is the corpus's own recurring vice-list, run at 2 Nephi 26:21, 3 Nephi 16:10, 3 Nephi 30:2, 4 Nephi 1:16 and Alma 16:18 with much the same members; 3 Nephi 16:10, twenty pages earlier in the same discourse, is its nearest neighbour. A catalogue of dependence should not attribute a house formula to the one Pauline verse that shares two of its nouns.

'Beloved Son' occurs in ten KJV verses, six of them the voice from heaven at the baptism and the transfiguration, and the speaker at 3 Nephi 21:20 is the Father — so the pairing is not accidental. But it is not new here. 3 Nephi 11:7 is the Father's voice at the theophany that opens this entire visit: 'Behold, my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased, in whom I have glorified my name, hear ye him', which is Matthew 17:5 almost word for word, and that verse is where the link is adjudicated. By 21:20 the title is the discourse's established way of referring to Christ in the Father's mouth. The sanction clause of this verse — 'them will I cut off from among my people' — is likewise the second use of 21:11's, and it is adjudicated there.

Five words, and 'the remnant of Jacob' has been in front of the reader continuously since 21:12, where it entered as the opening phrase of the Micah 5:8 quotation. Isaiah 10:21's 'The remnant shall return, even the remnant of Jacob, unto the mighty God' is a different oracle about a different remnant, and nothing else of Isaiah 10 is present. The word 'unto' completing the run belongs to 'unto whom I have given this land'. The chapter's use of the phrase is adjudicated at 21:12 against Micah 5:8, with 3 Nephi 16:14 in recurrenceRefs.

exclusions.sharedText: scattered upon all the face of the
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and the top candidate at this verse, and it is the Book of Mormon's own dispersion formula, adopted at 1 Nephi 10:12 and used continuously thereafter; the standing exclusion filed in 1 Nephi covers it, and a near-identical entry stands at 3 Nephi 9:1. Ezekiel 34:6 reads 'my flock was scattered upon all the face of the earth' and 3 Nephi 21:24 reads 'scattered upon all the face of the land', which is the corpus's habitual substitution. The real intertext of 21:23-24 is the New Jerusalem, adjudicated at 21:23.

'Powers of heaven' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 21:26 — 'the powers of heaven shall be shaken' — with Matthew 24:29's 'the powers of the heavens' and Mark 13:25's 'the powers that are in heaven' beside it. All three are the cosmic collapse of the Olivet discourse, where the shaking of the heavenly powers is a terror preceding the Son of man. 3 Nephi 21:25 is its opposite: 'then shall the power of heaven come down among them; and I also will be in the midst', a descent that constitutes the gathered city rather than dissolving the sky. The first edition also reads the singular 'power', which is in no King James verse at all, though Hardy's apparatus records the plural in the Printer's Manuscript; and the sentence is in any case a restatement of 3 Nephi 20:22, 'the powers of heaven shall be in the midst of this people; yea, even I will be in the midst of you', which is where the phrase enters this discourse.

Five words. Leviticus 25:30 concerns a house inside a walled city that is not redeemed within the year: it 'shall not go out in the jubile', meaning it does not revert to its original owner at the jubilee. The subject is a building and 'go out' is a technical term of property law. 3 Nephi 21:29's 'they shall not go out in haste' is Isaiah 52:12's second-Exodus departure and is adjudicated there. The row is a clean example of the trap named in ADJUDICATING §4 — the window closes one word early, and the next word is 'the jubile'.

Worth the entry because the coherence is better than the wording. “also to the Gentiles” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 11:18, and that verse is the moment the Jerusalem church concedes that the Gentiles are inside the covenant — which is precisely the inference 3 Nephi 23:2 draws from Isaiah ('he spake as touching all things concerning my people which are of the house of Israel; therefore it must needs be that he must speak also to the Gentiles'). But the shared string is four function words with one content word in it, the syntax is unrelated (Acts has 'hath God also to the Gentiles granted repentance unto life'; 3 Nephi has an infinitive complement of 'speak'), and nothing else of Acts 11 is anywhere near. The verse's other candidate, Matthew 18:7's 'it must needs be that', is a Book of Mormon connective used at twenty-one places in the corpus and is covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

A cross-reference rather than a rejection. 23:3's 'all things that he spake, hath been, and shall be' is the second and third terms of Revelation 1:19's threefold division of what a seer is to write, but the verse that actually carries the King James wording is the next one: 23:4's 'write the things which I have told you' against Revelation 1:19's “write the things which”, a singleton. The link is adjudicated at 23:4 and the significance field there argues 23:3 as part of it. A reader who arrives at 23:3 should go to 23:4.

exclusions.sharedText: and is baptized ... the same shall be saved
exclusions.reason: “and is baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 16:16, and so does “is baptized shall be saved”, so the machine is right that the phrase is here. It is not a fresh borrowing. Mark 16:16 is adjudicated for this book at 3 Nephi 11:33, where Christ states his doctrine and reproduces both limbs of Mark's antithesis; 23:5 is the same speaker reusing his own formula twelve chapters later, with 'believeth' replaced by 'hearken unto my words, and repenteth'. It is recorded in the composite and recurrenceRefs of the Deuteronomy 18:19 row at this verse, which is where the new material is. 'The same shall be saved' by itself occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:13 and Mark 13:13, both of enduring to the end, and neither is in view.

The highest-scoring machine candidate anywhere in this chapter, and it is pointing at the wrong verse. “arise from the dead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 5:14, which is why it ranked; but the sentence it belongs to is a baptismal or hymnic fragment addressed to a sleeper ('Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light') and has no saints, no appearing, and no resurrection narrative. The verse's real source is Matthew 27:52-53 by way of Helaman 14:25, adjudicated at this verse. The coincidence is nonetheless worth one line: Matthew 27:52 describes its risen saints as 'the saints which slept arose', and the KJV's only other pairing of sleep with rising from the dead is the Ephesians verse the machine found.

A five-word run that is a singleton in both directions — “and his disciples answered” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “his disciples answered him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, both Mark 8:4, and the clause occurs once in the whole Book of Mormon, here — and it is still narrative boilerplate. The KJV's usual form is 'his disciples said unto him' (five verses) or 'answered and said'; Mark 8:4 happens to be the one place it inverts them, and the rarity is arithmetic rather than distinctive. The senses are also opposed: Mark's disciples answer with the obtuse question that shows they have forgotten the first feeding, while 3 Nephi's answer correctly and confirm the prophecy. The reply itself, 'Yea, Lord', occurs in exactly five KJV verses and identifies no source.

exclusions.sharedText: How be it that ye have not
exclusions.reason: Registered because the rebuke is unmistakably synoptic in shape and the wording will not quite carry it. 'How is it that ye ...?' is the King James Jesus' standing form of reproach to his disciples — Mark 4:40 'how is it that ye have no faith?', Mark 8:21 'How is it that ye do not understand?', Matthew 16:11, Luke 12:56 — and 3 Nephi 23:11 is exactly that: Christ turning on the disciples over a failure they should not have made. But “how is it that ye” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses, which is too many to identify a source, and the Book of Mormon does not have the phrase. Both 1830 and 1920 read 'How be it that ye have not written this thing', a construction in no KJV verse; the KJV's 'howbeit' is one word and adversative, not interrogative. A reader who hears Mark here is hearing a register, not a borrowing.

The chapter's other arithmetic singleton: “it was written according” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Esther 8:9, in the course of a hundred-and-twenty-word clause about Mordecai's decree being copied out to a hundred and twenty-seven provinces in every province's own writing. The shared four words are a passive verb and a preposition. Filed with the Genesis 50:12 entry above: 23:13 is a one-sentence compliance notice and it will match any KJV verse that reports an order carried out.

“according as he commanded” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 50:12 — 'And his sons did unto him according as he commanded them' — and the singleton is worthless. It is the King James Bible's ordinary compliance formula in a slightly less common inflection ('as the LORD commanded', 'according to all that ... commanded'), and Genesis 50:12 is Jacob's burial. 3 Nephi 23:13 records a scribal correction. No content word beyond 'commanded' is shared.

exclusions.sharedText: expounded all the Scriptures ... expounded unto them
exclusions.reason: A cross-reference, not a rejection. 23:14's 'when Jesus had expounded all the Scriptures in one ... he commanded them that they should teach the things which he had expounded unto them' repeats the fusion of Luke 24:27 and Mark 4:34 that is adjudicated eight verses earlier at 23:6, where the argument for it is made. The one element 23:14 adds, 'in one', is not from either source and is not from any KJV verse. Later occurrences of the same construction at 3 Nephi 24:1 and 3 Nephi 26:1 are cross-referred from 23:6 as well. The chapter's other candidates here, Matthew 13:53 and Matthew 19:1, are the eight-word run 'and it came to pass that when Jesus had', which is the KJV's own discourse-closing formula and the Book of Mormon's commonest connective; the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 covers it.

The chapter's opening candidate and a four-word run, and it is the n-gram stream at its least useful. 2 Chronicles 20:24 is Judah looking out from the watch tower of the wilderness at the dead bodies of Moab and Ammon; 3 Nephi 26:1 is Christ expounding scripture. The words they share are a preposition, an article and a noun. The real source of this verse is in neither the candidate list nor anywhere near it: “expounded all things” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 4:34, and “unto the multitude” occurs in exactly four, of which the only one about Jesus teaching is Matthew 13:34 — which is Mark 4:34's own Synoptic parallel. Both links are filed at 26:1.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references Malachi 4:1-2 here, and the reference is right as a back-pointer and wrong as a verbal one. 3 Nephi 26:2 reads 'These Scriptures which ye had not with you, the Father commanded that I should give unto you' — a demonstrative pointing back at the Malachi text transcribed at 3 Nephi 24-25, which is where the catalogue has collated it verse by verse (Malachi 4:1 at 3 Nephi 25:1, Malachi 4:2 at 25:2). Verse 2 itself shares not one word with Malachi 4. This is CONVENTIONS §6a's second bullet: a study edition is right to tell its reader what 'these scriptures' means at the point the phrase occurs, and a catalogue of verbal dependence puts the link where the wording is. The row is discharged, and a reader who arrives at 26:2 from Hardy is sent to 25:1-2. Note that this verse sits at the chapter boundary where our own extract of Hardy formerly mis-keyed the Malachi 4:1-2 and 4:2 notes across 25/26; the correction stands in data/hardy-corrections.json and the current keying is the printed apparatus's.

exclusions.sharedText: the one on the one … and the other on the other
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter, tied with 2 Samuel 2:13, and a six-word run in each — and it is a King James correlative idiom with no content. The construction is 'the one on the one side, and the other on the other side', and the KJV uses it for whatever happens to be paired: Aaron and Hur propping up Moses' hands at Rephidim (Exodus 17:12), Joab's men and Abner's men facing each other across the pool of Gibeon (2 Samuel 2:13), the cherubim, the pillars, the doorposts. 3 Nephi 26:5 uses it of the two resurrections 'being on a parallel', and changes the noun that governs it from 'side' to 'hand', which neither KJV verse has. Nothing else of either verse is present. The verse's real dependence is on John 5:29, filed as a link at 26:5, where both halves of the antithesis are KJV singletons.

A five-word run and a genuine near-miss, which is why it needs writing out rather than passing over. “things which Jesus did” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Luke 9:43, John 11:45 and John 21:25 — and the machine ranked the wrong one of the three. John 11:45 is the crowd at Bethany who saw the raising of Lazarus and believed; the phrase there is about witnessed deeds producing faith. 3 Nephi 26:6 is about deeds that cannot be got into a book, which is John 21:25's subject and only John 21:25's: 'there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one …'. The link is filed at 26:6 against John 21:25.

“hundredth part” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 5:11, where it is the rate of interest the nobles are made to restore to their brethren, and the standing wrong-sense exclusion for it was filed at Words of Mormon 1:5 and repeated at Jacob 3:13. It is Mormon's own measure of what will not fit in a record — six occurrences across the Book of Mormon, five of them his — and not a borrowing from a chapter about usury. What the verse does borrow is the idiom around the fraction rather than the fraction itself: “things which Jesus did” occurs in exactly three KJV verses and “should be written” occurs in exactly one, both of them John 21:25, which is filed as a link at this verse.

Worth an entry because the rarity is real and misleading: “made manifest unto them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. That verse is Paul quoting Isaiah 65:1 — 'I was made manifest unto them that asked not after me' — and its whole force is that the manifestation went to people who had made no approach and had no faith, which Paul applies to the Gentiles against Israel. 3 Nephi 26:9 is the exact inverse: the greater things are made manifest only to those who have first received the lesser and believed, and are withheld from the rest 'unto their condemnation' (26:10). The one KJV verse with the phrase says revelation is unearned by definition; the Book of Mormon verse says it is conditional. A four-word run with the argument reversed is a coincidence of English, not a borrowing. The temptation is sharpened by 26:8's 'from the Gentiles', which is Romans 10-11's subject — and that is a reason to say why we declined it rather than to accept it.

The register's best entry in this chapter, because the string match is exact and the grammar is opposite. “the LORD forbid” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — 1 Samuel 24:6, 1 Samuel 26:11 and 1 Kings 21:3 — and in all three it is an optative oath formula meaning 'God forbid that I should', spoken by a man refusing to do something: David refusing to strike Saul, twice, and Naboth refusing to sell the inheritance of his fathers. 1 Kings 21:3 even matches the object pronoun, 'The LORD forbid it me'. In 3 Nephi 26:11 the same four words are a plain past indicative with the Lord as the grammatical subject — Mormon was about to write the whole record 'but the Lord forbid it, saying, I will try the faith of my people'. Somebody actually did the forbidding. The situational rhyme is close enough to tempt (a man refusing to hand over his fathers' inheritance; an abridger refusing to hand over his fathers' record) and it is a rhyme, not a dependence.

A five-word run and a KJV singleton — “for the space of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the catalogue has declined it twice already, at 2 Nephi 25:13 and Mosiah 7:1, for the reason ADJUDICATING §4 names: the run ends one word early. Acts 19:8 continues 'months', of Paul disputing in the Ephesian synagogue; 3 Nephi 26:13 continues 'days'. The phrase is in any case one of Mormon's commonest connectives, occurring some sixty-five times across the Book of Mormon, and cannot be a fresh borrowing here. This entry covers the candidate for the rest of 3 Nephi.

“great and marvellous” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and Revelation 15:3, and the catalogue treats it as a genuine borrowing — it is adjudicated at 1 Nephi 1:14 and at a dozen places since. Within 3 Nephi it is first adjudicated at 4:32 and argued again at 5:8 and 5:18, so by ADJUDICATING §4 its reappearances in this book are the same narrator using his own adopted formula rather than fresh borrowings. 26:14 ('great and marvellous things') and 26:16 ('utter marvellous things') are two such reappearances; the argument for the family is at 3 Nephi 4:32. Recorded here rather than passed over in silence because the 1830 spelling 'marvellous' is the KJV's and is modernized in 1920, so a reader working from the first edition will see the match and should be told where it is adjudicated.

The chapter's second-highest-scoring candidate and a four-word exact run in the 1830 text, which is the point worth recording: 1830 reads 'shewed' and 1920 reads 'showed', so the match is exact in the first edition and half-lost in the modern one (CONVENTIONS §8). It is still not a borrowing. Acts 7:26 is Stephen's summary of Moses going out on the second day and finding two Hebrews fighting — 'he shewed himself unto them as they strove' — and the verb there means he came into their view uninvited and was rebuffed. 3 Nephi 26:15 is the risen Christ appearing to disciples who are expecting him. 'Shew oneself unto' is the ordinary King James idiom for appearing to somebody (Leviticus's leper to the priest, 1 Kings's Elijah to Ahab), and its concentration here is a fact about the 1830 orthography, not about Acts 7.

Four words, and typology pulls at them: Genesis 22:15 is the angel of the LORD calling to Abraham out of heaven the second time, immediately after the binding of Isaac, to swear the covenant — a second heavenly word confirming what the first had demanded, in the King James Bible's most-read scene of a father and a son. 3 Nephi 26:15 is a chronological note about Christ's second ascension. The shared words are 'heaven', 'the second time', and nothing else; the Book of Mormon's clause is 'after he had ascended into Heaven the second time', where Genesis's is 'called unto Abraham out of heaven the second time'. Direction of motion, speaker and subject all differ. Filed so that a reader who sees the Abrahamic pattern knows the catalogue looked and declined it.

Recorded for its negative result, which is the useful kind here. 3 Nephi 26:21 names the community — 'they which were baptized in the name of Jesus, were called the church of Christ' — and a reader will reasonably look for a King James warrant. There is none: “the church of Christ” occurs in no KJV verse. The nearest is Romans 16:16's plural, 'the churches of Christ salute you', which is a greeting from congregations rather than a name for the body, and the King James Bible otherwise says 'the church of God' (eight KJV verses, including 1 Corinthians 1:2) or simply 'the church'. So the name this verse gives the church is not the King James Bible's, and the catalogue should say so plainly rather than reach for Romans 16:16. The verse's actual dependence is on the Acts baptismal formula, filed as a link at 26:17. The 1830 'which' is corrected to 'who' in 1920.

exclusions.sharedText: stood in the midst of them, and saith unto them
exclusions.reason: A ten-word run and the second-ranked candidate at this verse, and “stood in the midst of them” is a KJV singleton at Luke 24:36. It is nonetheless not adjudicated here. The catalogue files that borrowing at 3 Nephi 11:8, where the risen Christ first descends and stands in the midst of the multitude and where the Emmaus and upper-room material of Luke 24 is worked through at length (11:3 takes Luke 24:32, 11:14 takes John 20:27). 27:2 is the same narrator using the arrival formula he adopted sixteen chapters earlier for the same person doing the same thing, and ADJUDICATING §4 files a within-book repeat at first use. A reader who arrives at 27:2 and sees Luke 24:36 in it has seen correctly; the argument is at 11:8. The fresh borrowing at this verse is the question that follows, Matthew 20:32, which is linked.

exclusions.sharedText: this is the thing that ye shall do
exclusions.reason: A five-word run and the only candidate the machine offers at this verse. Judges 21:11 is the order to slaughter Jabesh-gilead — “Ye shall utterly destroy every male, and every woman that hath lain by man” — and 3 Nephi 27:7 is “whatsoever ye shall do, ye shall do it in my name”. The overlap is the bare English of instruction, “ye shall do”, doubled in each verse by accident of construction: the Book of Mormon doubles it because it is building an anaphora on “in my name”, Judges because it is glossing a vow. No content word is shared. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion for connective boilerplate, and written out because the ranking is high enough that a reader working from the dossier would meet it.

Hardy cross-references Matthew 16:18 at this verse, and the association is sound at the level a study edition works at: 27:8 is the founding statement about what makes a church Christ's, and Matthew 16:18 is the KJV's one verse in which Christ says “I will build my church”. But the verbal contact here is two words, “my church”, in a verse whose argument is about naming rather than building — “how be it my church, save it be called in my name?” — and “upon this rock I will build my church” is already adjudicated in this book at 3 Nephi 11:39, where the Book of Mormon has the rock, the building and the gates-of-hell clause together. Putting the link where the wording is (CONVENTIONS §6a) sends it to 11:39; a reader at 27:8 is sent there from here. What 27:8 does add to 11:39 is the naming argument, which has no Matthew 16 warrant at all: Matthew 16:18 never says the church is called anything.

Hardy also cross-references Matthew 7:24-27 here, the wise and foolish builders, and the pull is real because 27:8-11 turns entirely on what a church is “built upon” — the gospel, or the works of men, or the works of the devil. The wording will not carry it. Matthew 7:24-27's distinctive vocabulary is the rock, the sand, the rain, the floods, the winds, the house and the great fall, and 3 Nephi 27:8-11 has none of the seven; what it shares is the participle “built upon”, which is ordinary English. The parable itself is adjudicated in this book twice already, at 3 Nephi 14:24-27 where it is transcribed whole and at 3 Nephi 11:40 and 18:13 where its closing verses are applied. The Matthew 7 contact that this chapter really does make is elsewhere: 27:11's “hewn down and cast into the fire” from 7:19, and 27:29 and 27:33 from 7:7-8 and 7:13-14, all of which are linked.

The top-ranked candidate at this verse on a five-word run, and it is the wrong half of the sentence. What 1 Timothy 1:15 contributes is “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners”, and “came into the world” is a formula the KJV uses of Christ at John 1:9, 6:14, 11:27, 12:46, 16:28, 18:37 and 1 Timothy 1:15 — too widely spread to identify a source, and used in the Book of Mormon constantly. The purpose clause is where the borrowing is, and it is Johannine, not Pauline: “to do the will of my Father, because my Father sent me” answers to John 6:38 and John 4:34, which are linked at this verse. 1 Timothy's purpose clause, saving sinners, is not in 3 Nephi 27:13 at all.

exclusions.sharedText: what ye have seen me do
exclusions.reason: The register's best entry in this chapter, because the run is genuinely long — “ye have seen me do”, five words — and because a reader who finds it will assume the catalogue missed it. Judges 9:48 is Abimelech on mount Zalmon: he cuts a bough from a tree, lays it on his shoulder, and tells his men “What ye have seen me do, make haste, and do as I have done” — whereupon they each cut a bough, pile them against the tower of Shechem and burn about a thousand men and women alive inside it. 3 Nephi 27:21 is “the works which ye have seen me do, that shall ye also do”, spoken to the twelve about their ministry. The clause is identical and every term of the situation is inverted: the model is a usurper, the imitation is an atrocity, and the point of the sentence in Judges is speed rather than fidelity. The real source of the construction is John 14:12, the only KJV verse with “the works that I do shall he do also”, which is linked here; Judges 9:48 is what an n-gram window returns when a very ordinary English clause happens to have been used once by Abimelech.

A five-word run, and both verses attach a promise to a conditional — 2 Peter 1:10 “if ye do these things, ye shall never fall”, 3 Nephi 27:22 “if ye do these things, blessed are ye, for ye shall be lifted up at the last day”. The shared string is the conditional itself and nothing else: 2 Peter's “these things” are the virtues of the ladder in 1:5-7, the Book of Mormon's are the works of 27:21, and the apodoses share no word. “If ye do these things” is not a KJV singleton in any useful sense; it is how English joins a condition to a consequence. Note that the genuine 2 Peter contact in this chapter is at 27:27, where “what manner of persons ought ye to be” is a singleton at 2 Peter 3:11 and is linked.

A five-word run made entirely of an interjection and a quantifier. Luke 11:41 ends the woe about the outside of the cup — “give alms of such things as ye have; and, behold, all things are clean unto you” — and 3 Nephi 27:26 is “behold, all things are written by the Father”. The predicate, which is the only part that carries meaning, is different in each. Filed rather than passed over in silence because the run ranks in the chapter's top twenty-four and because a reader might expect the catalogue to have considered the cup-and-platter material given how much of Matthew 23 and Luke 11 the Book of Mormon uses elsewhere; it does not use it here.

exclusions.sharedText: whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name
exclusions.reason: By some distance the highest-scoring candidate in the chapter — an eight-word run on a KJV singleton, “whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name” standing in exactly one verse, John 16:23 — and it is not adjudicated here because the catalogue has already adjudicated it in this book. 3 Nephi 18:20 has the same clause and carries the link as a certain quotation; 3 Nephi 16:4 carries a second, weaker use. 27:28 is the third occurrence within one book of a formula the speaker has made his own, which is the case ADJUDICATING §4 files at first use. It is worth noting what 27:28 adds and what it does not: it prefixes “And now I go unto the Father”, which is a KJV singleton at John 14:28 and already adjudicated at 3 Nephi 17:4, and which is also the second half of John 14:12 — the verse linked seven verses earlier at 27:21. The chapter is holding one Johannine sentence open across those seven verses, and that observation is recorded in the note at 27:21 rather than as a fourth row on John 16:23.

exclusions.sharedText: for silver, and for gold, and for
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and the highest-ranked machine candidate at this verse, and it is a list. 2 Chronicles 32:27 inventories Hezekiah's treasuries — “for silver, and for gold, and for precious stones, and for spices, and for shields” — and 3 Nephi 27:32 is “they will sell me for silver, and for gold, and for that which moth doth corrupt”. The run is produced by the KJV's way of coordinating a series with a repeated preposition, and it survives seven words only because both series happen to begin with the same two metals, which is the order the KJV always uses. Nothing of Hezekiah is here. The verse's real sources are Matthew 6:19, whose “thieves break through and steal” is a singleton and which supplies the third member of the Book of Mormon's list, and John 17:12; both are linked. The betrayal price behind “sell me for silver” is Matthew 26:15's thirty pieces, recorded there as a composite rather than as a separate row, since the Book of Mormon has neither the number nor the KJV's verb.

exclusions.sharedText: when Jesus had ended these sayings
exclusions.reason: “And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings” is a KJV singleton at Matthew 7:28, and 3 Nephi 27:33 opens with it almost verbatim. The link is filed at 3 Nephi 15:1, where the same formula closes the sermon at the temple in the position Matthew 7:28 occupies in the Sermon on the Mount, and where it is adjudicated as a certain quotation. Here it is the same narrator reaching for the same closing formula at the end of a different discourse, and it is the fourth thing in this chapter drawn from the closing verses of Matthew 7 — the formula, the strait gate, the ask-and-receive saying, the tree hewn down. The formula itself carries no fresh argument; the material it introduces does, and 27:33's two links are on that.

Typology pulls and the arithmetic refuses. Nine of the twelve ask to live ‘unto the age of man’ (28:2) and are told they shall come to Christ ‘after that ye are seventy and two years old’ (28:3). The King James Bible has exactly one verse fixing the age of man — Psalm 90:10, ‘The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years’ — and it is the obvious source for a promise pegged to a human lifespan. But the Book of Mormon’s number is seventy-two, which is neither of Psalm 90:10’s two figures, and it shares not one word with the verse: no ‘threescore’, no ‘days of our years’, no ‘labour and sorrow’. A borrowing that adopted the psalm’s idea would have adopted its round number, which is the whole point of the psalm’s number. Recorded so that a reader who reaches for Psalm 90 is told the catalogue reached for it too and put it down.

exclusions.sharedText: and said unto them, What will ye
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and the longest in the chapter, and it is the wrong Matthew 26 verse. Matthew 26:15 is Judas at the chief priests: ‘And said unto them, What will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you?’ 3 Nephi 28:4 is Christ turning to the three: ‘and said unto them, What will ye that I should do unto you?’ The senses are inverted at every point — in Matthew the speaker is the betrayer, the addressees are the buyers, and the question is what he will be paid; in 3 Nephi the speaker is the one about to be departed from, the addressees are his disciples, and the question is what he will give. The run is the KJV’s ordinary formula for introducing direct speech plus two words of an interrogative, and the real source of the sentence is the question of Matthew 20:32 and Mark 10:51 in the setting of Mark 10:36, where the link is filed. Worth the entry because Matthew 26 does supply this chapter: 28:35 takes ‘if he had not been born’ from Matthew 26:24, nine verses further on, and a reader who notices that will want to know whether we considered 26:15. We did, and it is coincidence.

A five-word run scoring 2.00, and ‘the kingdom of my father’ is the phrase a Christian text uses for heaven without needing a source. Its one KJV occurrence is Ziba slandering Mephibosheth to David — ‘To day shall the house of Israel restore me the kingdom of my father’ — a lie told to steal an estate during Absalom’s revolt, and it is the only sentence in the King James Bible where the phrase appears. Nothing whatever connects it to a promise of the kingdom made to disciples who will not taste of death. The verse’s real borrowings are from 1 Corinthians 15:52-53 and they are filed at 28:8; this candidate ranked only because the KJV happens to have had one occasion to write the phrase and it was a usurper’s.

A five-word run and pure connective tissue. Numbers 31:5 is a muster roll — ‘there were delivered out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand of every tribe’ — where ‘delivered’ means handed over for service, not rescued. The Book of Mormon’s sense is rescue, and the verse’s real link is to Psalm 71:20, whose ‘depths of the earth’ is a KJV singleton and is filed at 28:20.

Four words of KJV boilerplate for priestly service; Numbers 1:50 is the appointment of the Levites over the tabernacle and its vessels, and what they minister unto is the tabernacle itself. The verse’s adjudicated link is the Revelation 14:6 formula that follows in the same clause.

exclusions.sharedText: the Father in the name of
exclusions.reason: A six-word run that is the standing Christian formula for prayer and thanksgiving, used throughout the Book of Mormon and throughout the New Testament; Ephesians 5:20 ranked only because its particular arrangement of the words is uncommon. Nothing else of Ephesians 5 is present. The distinctive contact in this verse is ‘as the angels of God’, a KJV singleton at Matthew 22:30, and the link is filed there.

Cross-reference, not a rejection. ‘Yea, even among the Gentiles shall there be a great and marvellous work wrought by them’ is Isaiah 29:14’s ‘a marvellous work and a wonder’, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse and which the Book of Mormon has been quoting since 1 Nephi; within 3 Nephi it is adjudicated at 21:9, where the Gentiles and the marvellous work stand in the same sentence as here. This is the narrator reusing a formula already established in his own book (ADJUDICATING §4), so the row is not written twice. The 1830 text spells it ‘marvellous’ at 28:31, 28:32 and 28:33, and ‘judgement’ at 28:31, 28:32 and 28:40, both KJV spellings modernised in 1920 — the first edition shows the borrowing more plainly than the current text does. A reader arriving at 28:32 should be sent to 3 Nephi 21:9.

exclusions.sharedText: their bodies, that they might not
exclusions.reason: The best trap in the chapter, because it is the right book and the wrong verse. Daniel 3 genuinely stands behind 28:21 — three men thrice cast into a furnace and unharmed — so a six-word run out of Daniel 3:28 looks like confirmation. It is not. Nebuchadnezzar’s sentence is about what Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego did before the fire: they ‘yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God’, an act of defiant obedience with the body offered up. 3 Nephi 28:38 is about what was done to the three Nephites afterwards: ‘there was a change wrought upon their bodies, that they might not suffer pain nor sorrow’, a divine alteration with the body received. The shared string is a possessive noun plus the KJV’s commonest purpose clause, and the two ‘might nots’ govern opposite things — refusal to serve, inability to suffer. The verse’s real source is 1 Corinthians 15:51-53, filed at 28:8 and recurring here, at 28:37, 28:39 and 28:40.

exclusions.sharedText: made with the children of Israel
exclusions.reason: The chapter's top-scoring machine candidate, on a six-word run, and “made with the children of Israel” is in fact a KJV singleton — which is exactly why the register has to explain the rejection rather than assume it. The rarity is arithmetic. Every word of the run is ordinary: 'the children of Israel' is the King James Bible's standard designation for the nation and appears in hundreds of verses, and 'made with' is the ordinary verb for cutting a covenant. That 2 Chronicles 6:11 is the only verse in which the two happen to meet is shown by its own synoptic parallel, 1 Kings 8:21, which says the same thing about the same ark with 'which he made with our fathers' — the formula is variable, so its one fixed instance identifies nothing. The senses are unrelated besides: 2 Chronicles 6:11 is Solomon reporting that the covenant is inside the ark he has housed, 3 Nephi 29:1 is Mormon announcing that its terms are beginning to be kept in the last days. Note also that the Book of Mormon's subject is 'the Father', which is not KJV covenant language anywhere.

The machine matched 'the lands of their' against Leviticus 26:36's 'the lands of their enemies', which is the wrong noun in the wrong sense — Leviticus is describing Israelites scattered and terrified in foreign territory, 3 Nephi 29:1 their restoration to their own. 'Lands of their inheritance' in the plural is a Book of Mormon formula and not a KJV phrase; the KJV says 'the land of your inheritance' or 'his inheritance', in the singular. Filed because Leviticus 26 genuinely does stand behind this chapter's theology of a remembered covenant (26:42, 'then will I remember my covenant with Jacob'), so a reader may reasonably expect a link here, and the catalogue's answer is that the theology is shared and the wording is not.

Acts 3:21 is where the catalogue adjudicated this epithet in this book, at 3 Nephi 5:1, and it recorded 2 Peter 3:2 there as the alternative it could not exclude on the wording alone. At 29:2 the wording does decide: the Book of Mormon has the noun 'words', which 2 Peter 3:2 has and Acts 3:21 lacks, and lacks 'by the mouth of all his', which Acts 3:21 has. tools/mediation-check.py returns 2 Peter 3:2 on both points. What settles it beyond the string is the company the phrase keeps — the same sentence goes on to forbid saying that the Lord delays his coming, which is 2 Peter 3:4's scoffers answered by 2 Peter 3:9, two and seven verses after 3:2. The link is written at 29:2 to 2 Peter 3:2; Acts 3:21 remains the right reading at 5:1, where the totalising 'all' is present and the scoffing context is not.

A tempting near-miss and the register should say so. Psalm 2:1 is the one KJV verse that puts 'imagine' and 'vain' in a single clause, and it puts them in the mouth of exactly this chapter's audience — 'Why do the heathen rage, and the people imagine a vain thing?' — with the object of the raging being the LORD and his anointed. But the two words are doing different jobs in the two verses. In the psalm the vain thing is the plot, and its vanity is the poet's verdict on it; in 3 Nephi 29:3 the vanity is what the scoffers allege of God's words, and the sentence forbids the allegation. Nothing else of Psalm 2 is present, and 'vain' occurs in 102 KJV verses. The link at 29:3 goes to Zechariah 8:17 instead, on 'imagine … in your hearts', which is the construction the Book of Mormon actually has; Psalm 2:1 is recorded in that row's provenance as a possibility rather than dismissed.

'The doings of the land' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Leviticus 18:3, which is why a four-word window ranked it, and the sense is the opposite of what 3 Nephi 29:4 needs. Leviticus 18:3 forbids Israel to imitate the doings of Egypt and Canaan; 'doings' there is a word for other people's abominations, and that is how the KJV uses it almost everywhere — 'the evil of your doings', 'the fruit of his doings', 'according to his doings will he recompense him'. 3 Nephi 29:4-5 makes the doings God's own and the offence contempt for them. 'Doings of the Lord' occurs in no KJV verse at all; the closest the King James Bible comes is 'his doings' of God at Psalm 9:11 and Isaiah 12:4, where the verb is 'declare' and the sense is praise. This is a Book of Mormon usage, and the register should say that plainly rather than let a rare-string match stand in for one.

'Woe unto him that' occurs in exactly five KJV verses and Isaiah 45:9 is the one whose subject fits — 'Woe unto him that striveth with his Maker' is a woe on contending with what God is doing, which is 3 Nephi 29:5's charge. It is declined as a source for two reasons. First, the wording stops at the formula: the Book of Mormon continues 'that spurneth at the doings of the Lord', which shares nothing with 'striveth with his Maker', and the potter-and-clay figure that occupies the rest of Isaiah 45:9 is absent from 3 Nephi 29 entirely. Second, the mediation test is empty. Romans 9:20 reworks Isaiah 45:9 into 'who art thou that repliest against God', and tools/mediation-check.py finds the Book of Mormon following neither form at any point of divergence — it has neither Isaiah's clay nor Paul's thing formed, neither 'striveth' nor 'repliest'. A verse whose NT reworking and OT original are equally absent is not the source of the sentence. The chapter's woe-series is instead catalogued as a figural link to Isaiah 5's, where the offences match.

A four-word run and a genuine rarity — 'revelations of the Lord' in the plural is 2 Corinthians 12:1's phrase — and it is the wrong kind of revelation. Paul's plural is his own visions, introduced with an apology for boasting of them ('It is not expedient for me doubtless to glory') and followed by the third heaven and the thorn in the flesh. 3 Nephi 29:6's plural is the category of divine self-disclosure whose continuance is being denied. Nothing of 2 Corinthians 12 is present. The verse's real source is one chapter of Paul, but the other letter: 1 Corinthians 12's inventory of gifts, strung on 1 Corinthians 14:6's serial 'or by', which is where the link is filed.

'Get gain' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:13, and it is the Book of Mormon's standing term for corrupt religious and civil profit. It is not adjudicated afresh here: the argument was made at 2 Nephi 26:20 and, within this book, at 3 Nephi 6:10, where James 4:13-5:6 supplies the merchants, the boastings and the condemning of the just across a whole paragraph. At 29:7 the phrase arrives alone, with none of James's surrounding material, and is a writer using his own established formula. The 1830 form 'for to get gain' is worth noting for a different reason and is discussed in the John 17:12 row at this verse: the first edition attaches the gain to the denial and keeps the KJV's 'for to' before the infinitive, and 1920 moved the phrase and dropped 'for'.

1 Kings 9:7-8 is where the catalogue has twice put the Book of Mormon's hissing — at 1 Nephi 19:14 and at 3 Nephi 16:9, both on the compound 'a hiss and a byword', which is 9:7's 'a proverb and a byword' with 9:8's hissing substituted for 'proverb'. A reader arriving at 29:8 will expect the same source and should be told why it is not used. 29:8 does not have the compound. It has 'hiss' as a finite verb in a list of three things the Gentiles are told to stop doing, with the Jews as its direct object, and the 1 Kings verses give a noun in a formula about a desolate house at which passers-by are astonished. The KJV supplies the required grammar in exactly one place, Lamentations 2:15-16, where enemies hiss at the daughter of Jerusalem, and the link is filed there.

'Which he hath sworn' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the KJV singleton is a trap here. Leviticus 6:5 is about a man who has sworn falsely over property he denied holding, and the clause introduces the restitution he owes plus a fifth part. 3 Nephi 29:8's clause is 'he will do unto them according to that which he hath sworn', where the swearer is the Lord and the oath is the covenant with Israel. The two uses share four words and no situation, and the rare string is an accident of English: the KJV's ordinary way of saying what 29:8 says is an oath sworn to the fathers — 'The oath which he sware to our father Abraham' (Luke 1:73), 'which thou hast sworn unto our fathers from the days of old' (Micah 7:20) — and the Book of Mormon uses none of those forms. Filed because a rarity count run without reading the verse would put this in the catalogue.

exclusions.sharedText: to the right hand or to the left
exclusions.reason: The phrase occurs in exactly ten KJV verses and Deuteronomy 5:32 heads the commonest family of them — Deuteronomy 17:20, 28:14, Joshua 1:7 and 23:6, 2 Kings 22:2 and the rest — in all of which the sense is 'do not stray from the law'. That is the family a reader or a machine will reach for first, and it is the wrong one: in every member of it the person who might turn is the one addressed, and what he must not turn from is the commandment. 3 Nephi 29:9 has the Gentiles trying to turn the Lord's hand, not their own feet. The link is filed at 2 Samuel 14:19, the tenth occurrence and the only one where the idiom means that what the king has already spoken cannot be deflected — 'none can turn' is a KJV singleton there — which is the sense 29:9 requires.

The most tempting of the machine's proposals in this chapter, because the situation is right and the wording is not. Acts 14:15 is Paul and Barnabas at Lystra, preaching to a Gentile crowd 'that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God' — a Gentile audience, an imperative to turn, and the living God, which is exactly the three things 3 Nephi 30 does. But the only shared string is 'the living God, which', and the 'which' is a relative pronoun attached to different antecedents in the two verses (Paul's introduces the creator; the Book of Mormon's introduces a command given to Mormon). 'The living God' occurs in thirty KJV verses. The verse's actual borrowing is the fuller title 'the Son of the living God', which Acts 14:15 does not have, and the Gentile-turn idiom is accounted for at 30:2 by Zechariah 1:3-4 and Romans 15:11. Written up at length because a reader who notices the Lystra parallel should be told the catalogue noticed it and declined it on the wording.

A six-word run and the highest longest-run candidate in the verse, and it is the wrong title. Mark 1:1 and Matthew 1:1 both give 'Jesus Christ, the Son of —' and neither completes it with 'the living God': Mark has 'the Son of God', Matthew 'the son of David'. The Book of Mormon's clause is 'Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God', and that full phrase belongs to exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 16:16 and John 6:69, where the link is written. Recorded because the run length invites the mistake: the machine ranks Mark 1:1 above Matthew 16:16 on contiguity, and contiguity is measuring the generic half of the phrase. The same entry covers Matthew 1:1 and 2 John 1:3, which share the same generic run.

exclusions.sharedText: wicked ways ... my people, which are
exclusions.reason: A real two-point contact with one verse, and it loses on a pronoun. 2 Chronicles 7:14 is one of only two KJV verses containing 'wicked ways' and one of only two containing 'my people, which are', and 3 Nephi 30:2 has something answering to both — 'from your wicked ways' near its opening and 'numbered with my people, which are of the house of Israel' at its close. The temptation is strong because Solomon's verse is the King James Bible's standing promise that repentance is answered by forgiveness. But the Book of Mormon reads 'your wicked ways', and 2 Chronicles reads 'their wicked ways'; the only KJV verse with 'your wicked ways' is Ezekiel 20:44, which is where the link sends the phrase, inside Zechariah 1:4's frame. The second contact is likewise displaced: 'my people, which are' in 2 Chronicles completes as 'called by my name' and in Exodus 3:7 as 'in Egypt', while the Book of Mormon's clause is about Gentiles being counted in with Israel, which is Romans 15:10's 'Rejoice, ye Gentiles, with his people' — the verse immediately before the source of this verse's opening vocative. 2 Chronicles 7:14 is adjudicated as a link elsewhere in the corpus, at Mosiah 29:20.

The vice list of this verse — lyings, deceivings, whoredoms, secret abominations, idolatries, murders, priestcrafts, envyings, strifes — is the corpus's own recurring catalogue, and it was adjudicated for this book at 3 Nephi 21:19, where the same Pauline candidate was declined. The reasoning there governs here and is not repeated: 2 Corinthians 12:20 is the only KJV verse holding both 'envyings' and 'strifes', but the two are not adjacent in it, and the members that carry the Book of Mormon's list are not Paul's — 'priestcrafts' occurs in no KJV verse at all. The same list runs at 2 Nephi 26:21, 3 Nephi 16:10, 3 Nephi 21:19, 4 Nephi 1:16 and Alma 16:18. A reader who arrives at 30:2 and recognises Galatians 5:19-21 or 2 Corinthians 12:20 is sent to the register entry at 21:19.

“deceivings” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 2:13, which is the strongest kind of evidence this catalogue recognises and it still fails, for two reasons. First the sense: 2 Peter's 'deceivings' are the revelries of false teachers who feast at the church's love-feasts — 'sporting themselves with their own deceivings while they feast with you' — and the word there is a noun for dissipation, not for lies told to somebody. The Book of Mormon's 'lyings and deceivings' is a pair of nouns for acts of deception, and is fixed as such by the word it is coupled to. Second the distribution: 'deceivings' appears in five Book of Mormon verses across four books (3 Nephi 1:22, 21:19, 30:2, Alma 16:18, Mormon 8:31), always in the same vice list and never near anything else of 2 Peter 2. A King James hapax that the corpus has naturalised into a standing formula is evidence about the corpus's English, not about this verse's source — the same finding as the 'done away' entry at 3 Nephi 21:19.

Typology pulls hard here and the wording will not bear it. Ezekiel 36:25-27 is the Old Testament's water-and-Spirit passage and the standard proof text behind Christian baptism: sprinkled clean water, cleansing 'from all your filthiness, and from all your idols', then a new heart, then 'I will put my spirit within you'. 3 Nephi 30:2 has the same three movements in the same order — turn 'from all your wickedness and abominations', be baptized, be filled with the Holy Ghost — and even shares Ezekiel's list of idols. But the only shared string is the connective 'and from all your', and the Book of Mormon's sequence is fully accounted for by Acts 2:38, which has all four of its members in its order and shares its actual vocabulary ('remission', 'Holy Ghost'). Recorded so that a reader who sees Ezekiel 36 behind this verse is told the catalogue saw it and put the link where the words are.

“and come unto me” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 45:18 and Isaiah 55:3, which is why it ranked. Genesis 45:18 is Pharaoh telling Joseph to fetch his family down to Egypt for the fat of the land, and nothing in it is a summons to repentance. Isaiah 55:3 is much closer in kind — 'Incline your ear, and come unto me: hear, and your soul shall live; and I will make an everlasting covenant with you' — an imperative to hear, an invitation to come, and a covenant, which is the shape of this chapter. It is not written as a link because 'come unto me' is the settled idiom of this book, used at 3 Nephi 9:14, 12:19, 12:23, 18:25 and 27:20 and adjudicated at 9:22 against Isaiah 45:22 and Matthew 11:28, and because Zechariah 1:3's 'Turn ye unto me' already stands inside the construction this verse borrows. Registered for both verses under Genesis 45:18, the one the machine proposed.

Worth recording precisely because the reading it would produce is attractive. “numbered with” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Isaiah 53:12 and its quotation at Mark 15:28 ('he was numbered with the transgressors'), and Acts 1:17 and 1:26 (Matthias numbered with the eleven). Isaiah 53:12 is in the Book of Mormon in full at Mosiah 14:12, so the phrase is demonstrably available to the corpus, and the inversion almost writes itself: the one who was numbered with the transgressors ends the book by offering to number the Gentiles with his people. The catalogue declines it. Two words is not enough to carry a source when the second of them is 'with', the Book of Mormon has none of the surrounding language of either Isaiah 53 or Acts 1, and the clause it does complete — 'numbered with my people' — is answered by Romans 15:10 in the same catena that supplies this verse's opening vocative, which needs no inversion to explain it. mediation-check.py was run on Isaiah 53:12 against Mark 15:28 and returned no decisive point, Mark reproducing Isaiah verbatim in the shared span, so even had the link been written the mediation could not have been settled.

Filed as a figural link when this chapter was adjudicated, with an explicit withdrawal condition: 'Withdraw this row if the 3 Nephi 10:5 quotation of Matthew 23:37 turns out on adjudication to be independent of chapter 7.' It has. 3 Nephi 10:4-5 quotes Matthew 23:37 on its own verbal evidence — mediation-check.py decides Matthew over Luke 13:34 on two independent points (“gathereth” not “doth gather”, “chickens” not “brood”) — with no reference to this verse. The structural observation stands and is recorded at 3 Nephi 10:4's recurrenceRefs (which lists 3 Nephi 7:14 is not among them, correctly: 7:14 shares no wording with Matthew 23:37 at all, only the narrative fact of prophets stoned). Stoning prophets is a commonplace of the prophetic literature (2 Chronicles 24:21, Hebrews 11:37) and the Book of Mormon has its own idiom for it; there is nothing left to attach a link to once the structural argument is withdrawn.

A six-word run and the top-ranked candidate for the verse. “in the name of Jesus” is the King James formula for apostolic action and 4 Nephi 1:1 and 1:5 use it as such — baptized in the name of Jesus, miracles worked in nothing save the name of Jesus. Acts 5:40 is the Sanhedrin forbidding the apostles to speak in that name, which is a prohibition, not a practice; nothing else of the verse is present. The corpus uses the phrase continuously from 3 Nephi onward and cannot be borrowing it from the one verse the n-gram stream happened to rank.

exclusions.sharedText: upon all the face of the
exclusions.reason: A six-word run, and a standing exclusion covers it: 'upon all the face of the earth/land' is Book of Mormon connective tissue used at 1:2, 1:23 and 1:46 of this chapter alone. Ezekiel 34:6 is a scattering oracle and 4 Nephi 1:2 is a conversion notice; the shared words are a preposition, an article and a noun.

exclusions.sharedText: rich and poor ... free and bond
exclusions.reason: A tempting entry and it has to be written out, because a reader who finds it will assume the catalogue missed it. 4 Nephi 1:3 abolishes two social pairs in one clause — 'there were not rich and poor, bond and free' — and the King James Bible pairs those same two pairs in exactly one verse: “rich and poor” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, and Revelation 13:16 is the only one that continues 'free and bond'. But the order is inverted (the Book of Mormon's own “bond and free” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses), the context is opposed at the only point that matters — Revelation enumerates the categories in order to say the beast marks every one of them, 4 Nephi enumerates them in order to say they ceased to exist — and Revelation 13:16's actual subject, the mark in the right hand or forehead, has no counterpart here. The idea's real King James home is Galatians 3:28, where “bond nor free” is abolished and 'ye are all one in Christ Jesus'; that verse is recorded as a composite on the Acts 4:32 row and its 'all one' resurfaces at 1:17.

Typology pulls hard and the wording will not quite bear it. A covenant people multiplying rapidly in a land after a deliverance is Exodus 1:7 — 'the children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty' — and 4 Nephi 1:10 reads 'did wax strong, and did multiply exceeding fast'. The elements are all there and none of them is contiguous: “waxed exceeding” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 1:7 and Daniel 8:9, and the Book of Mormon has neither, splitting 'wax' onto 'strong' and 'exceeding' onto 'fast'. tools/mediation-check.py was run against the New Testament form, Acts 7:17 ('the people grew and multiplied in Egypt'), and returned one decisive point for Exodus on the strength of 'waxed exceeding' — but that is the very phrase the Book of Mormon does not reproduce, so the verdict decides between two candidates neither of which is demonstrably present. Recorded so that a reader who sees the Exodus pattern is told the catalogue saw it and declined it.

The model case for this category in the chapter. “fasting and prayer” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and 4 Nephi 1:12 has it exactly: 'continuing in fasting and prayer'. A singleton match on a devotional phrase in a devotional verse looks decisive until the source verse is read. 1 Corinthians 7:5 is Paul on conjugal duty — 'Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.' The phrase names a temporary abstention from marriage, and 'come together again' in that verse means resuming it. 4 Nephi 1:12 uses the same three words for a congregation's ordinary devotion and then says they were 'meeting together oft'. The collocation of fasting with prayer is unavoidable in English and the Book of Mormon uses it throughout; the singleton is an accident of the KJV's preferring 'prayer and fasting' everywhere else.

A five-word run made entirely of articles, a preposition and 'people'. Esther 3:8 is Haman denouncing a scattered people to Ahasuerus; 4 Nephi 1:13 is a peace notice. Nothing content-bearing is shared.

The machine's proposal for the verse, on a four-word run, and it is superseded. “the love of God” occurs in exactly twelve KJV verses, so the phrase alone points nowhere; what the Book of Mormon adds is the verb, and “dwelleth the love of God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 John 3:17, where the love of God dwelling in a man is tested by whether he shares his goods with a brother in need. Romans 8:39's love of God is the love from which nothing can separate us — a different proposition, in a different grammatical relation, with no dwelling in it. The link is written at this verse to 1 John 3:17.

exclusions.sharedText: passed away and there was no
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the highest-scoring candidate for the verse, and it is an artifact of two independent formulas colliding. 4 Nephi dates every paragraph by years that pass away and denies contention in every one of its golden-age verses, so 'passed away, and there was no contention' is simply those two habits meeting. Revelation 21:1's 'were passed away; and there was no more sea' is the dissolution of the first heaven and the first earth. The senses are not merely different but incompatible: in Revelation the passing away is the end of the old order and the beginning of the new, in 4 Nephi it is the calendar. Worth the entry because 4 Nephi 1:18 is also the verse in which the first generation from Christ passes away, which makes the eschatological reading momentarily attractive.

exclusions.sharedText: died and his son ... in his stead
exclusions.reason: “in his stead” occurs in exactly seventy-three KJV verses and is the King James Bible's standing succession formula, almost always 'reigned in his stead'. 4 Nephi 1:19-21 and 1:47 use it four times for a succession of record-keepers rather than kings — 'kept it in his stead', 'kept the record in his stead' — which is a genuine adaptation of a regnal formula to a scribal one, and worth noticing, but it is not dependence on 1 Chronicles 19:1 or on any other single verse. This entry covers every 'in his stead' candidate in the chapter.

“get gain” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, James 4:13, and 4 Nephi 1:26's 'churches unto themselves, to get gain' will attract the candidate. The catalogue adjudicated the phrase at Alma 11:20 and filed a standing exclusion there and at 3 Nephi 29:7; the reasoning is unchanged here. James 4:13 is about merchants presuming on tomorrow, and the Book of Mormon uses 'get gain' as a fixed idiom for priestcraft from 2 Nephi 26:29 onward. A reader of this verse is sent to Alma 11:20.

A five-word run of function words. Leviticus 6:5 is restitution law — restoring a thing 'unto him to whom it appertaineth' — and 4 Nephi 1:27 is about administering what is sacred 'unto him to whom it had been forbidden'. The two clauses are opposite in force, one about restoring property to its owner and one about giving holy things to a man debarred from them, and share no content word.

exclusions.sharedText: the prisons were rent in twain
exclusions.reason: A real borrowing, adjudicated elsewhere. 'The prisons were rent in twain' fuses Matthew 27:51's phrase with Acts 16's episode, and the argument is made in full at Alma 14:27, where prison walls fall on the men who built them; 3 Nephi 28:19 records it re-entering in Mormon's hand for these same three disciples. 4 Nephi 1:30 is Mormon narrating that episode a second time within a few pages, in the same hand, so the row is a cross-reference rather than a third link. A reader of this verse is sent to Alma 14:27 and 3 Nephi 28:19.

“harden their hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Joshua 11:20, and “hardened their heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 12:40 — which is genuinely awkward here, because the rest of 4 Nephi 1:31 is drawn from John 7:1 and John 12:37 and the John 12:40 form would complete the set. The Book of Mormon's plural 'hearts' matches Joshua, not John, and hardening of hearts is standing Book of Mormon idiom under a standing exclusion filed at 3 Nephi 1:22 and 3 Nephi 21:6. The catalogue therefore declines to press the John 12:40 contact and says so on the link at this verse: mediation for the hardening clause specifically is left undecided rather than resolved by the company it keeps.

The second occurrence in four verses, within one chapter; the standing exclusion at 3 Nephi 1:22 and the entry at 4 Nephi 1:31 cover it. Recorded so the register's coverage of the phrase in this chapter is complete.

exclusions.sharedText: over all the face of the
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the same standing formula excluded at 1:2. Genesis 41:56 is the famine over all the face of the earth; the Book of Mormon uses the phrase for the spread of the Gadianton robbers. Nothing but the prepositional formula is shared.

A four-word run and pure numeral. 4 Nephi dates by years from the coming of Christ in almost every verse, and 'three hundred and five' happens to coincide with the first four words of Daniel 12:12's 'thousand three hundred and five and thirty days'. The parallel is arithmetic, and the same reasoning was filed against 1 Chronicles 26:31 at Helaman 1:1. This entry covers every regnal- or year-numeral candidate in the chapter.

'Ammaron, being constrained by the Holy Ghost' invites two candidates and takes neither. “constraineth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses: Job 32:18, 'the spirit within me constraineth me', which is Elihu compelled to speak, and 2 Corinthians 5:14, 'the love of Christ constraineth us'. Job's is the closer, pairing a spirit with the verb, but the Book of Mormon's participle is passive where Job's verb is active, the constraint in Job is toward speech where Ammaron's is toward concealment, and the corpus uses 'constrained by the Spirit' as its own idiom elsewhere. Two words in a different voice and an opposed action.

exclusions.sharedText: remnant of the house of Jacob
exclusions.reason: “remnant of Jacob” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Isaiah 10:21, Micah 5:7 and Micah 5:8, and “remnant of the house of” occurs in exactly three, none of them with Jacob. The formula reaches 4 Nephi through this corpus's own transcription of Micah 5:8, which is adjudicated at 3 Nephi 16:14, 3 Nephi 20:16 and 3 Nephi 21:12; by the time Ammaron hides the records it is settled Book of Mormon vocabulary for the covenant people's future. A reader of this verse is sent to 3 Nephi 20:16.

The second of the two KJV verses that read “I perceive that thou art” — the phrase occurs in exactly 2, John 4:19 and this one — and it ranked because a five-word run is a five-word run. It is the wrong one, and the register should say why rather than leave a reader to wonder whether we noticed it. Acts 8:23 is Peter's sentence of judgment on Simon Magus: 'For I perceive that thou art in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity.' “gall of bitterness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Ammaron's clause is the opposite act — an old man commissioning a child he judges fit to keep the national record — and its grammar is different besides. John 4:19 completes the phrase with an article and a character noun, 'a prophet', which is exactly what Mormon 1:2 does with 'a sober child'; Acts 8:23 completes it with a prepositional phrase. The link is filed at this verse to John 4:19.

A four-word run and a genuine KJV singleton — “twenty and four years” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — which is precisely why it needs an entry rather than silence, since a singleton is the strongest evidence this catalogue normally has. Here the rarity is arithmetic and nothing else. The King James Bible states ages and reign-lengths in the 'twenty and four' pattern constantly and simply had occasion to write this particular numeral once, in a regnal notice for Baasha of Israel. Mormon 1:3 is Ammaron telling a ten-year-old when to come back for the plates. Nothing is shared but a number in the KJV's ordinary way of writing numbers, and the same standing objection covers 'about ten years of age' at 1:2 and 'fifteen years of age' at 1:15, where Luke 8:42's 'about twelve years of age' scores for the same reason.
