The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter at 2.00, and “the whole face of the” does occur in exactly one KJV verse. It is still nothing: Genesis 2:6 is the mist watering the whole face of the ground before there was rain, and Mormon 1:7 is a land covered with buildings. 'The face of the land' and 'all the face of the earth' are among the Book of Mormon's most heavily used narrative formulae, and the catalogue already carries standing exclusions for them at Helaman 11:18 and 3 Nephi 8:12 for Genesis 2:6, and at Alma 29:2, Helaman 11:32, Helaman 16:22, 3 Nephi 9:1 and 3 Nephi 21:24 for Ezekiel 34:6. This entry extends both to the book of Mormon, and covers 1:13's 'upon the face of the whole land' and 1:19's 'upon all the face of the land' (Ezekiel 34:6, rarity 1.35) without listing them separately.

The strongest-looking candidate in the chapter by every mechanical measure — a six-word run, rarity 3.00, and “of thirty thousand” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and it is the register's standard cautionary case. 2 Chronicles 35:7 is Josiah's passover: the king gives the people thirty thousand lambs and kids from his own substance, so that a nation which has forgotten the feast can keep it. Mormon 1:11 is a muster: the Nephites gather 'a great number of men, even to exceed the number of thirty thousand' and spend the year beating the Lamanites. The shared string is a numeral in the KJV's fixed idiom for stating a total, and the two things counted are a flock offered in worship and an army raised for war. Nothing else of 2 Chronicles 35 is present. Recorded at length because the machine ranked it first and a reader running the same search will find it first too.

A four-word run that scored at two separate verses in this chapter (1:16 and 1:17), which is usually a sign that the phrase is the writer's own connective habit rather than a borrowing — Mormon says 'I were forbidden that I should preach unto them' twice in consecutive verses. Ephesians 3:8 is Paul on the grace given him 'that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ', which is the assertion of a commission; Mormon 1:16 is the withdrawal of one. The verse does have a real source proposed in this catalogue, but it is Ezekiel 3:26 and the case rests on the silencing, not on the infinitive.

Worth an entry because a reader will look for a source for 'sorceries, and witchcrafts, and magics' and should be told the catalogue looked too. No KJV verse has the triad, and the KJV has no noun 'magics' at all. “sorceries” occurs in exactly 5 KJV verses (Isaiah 47:9, 47:12, Acts 8:11, Revelation 9:21, Revelation 18:23) and “witchcrafts” in exactly 3 (2 Kings 9:22, Micah 5:12, Nahum 3:4), and the two words never meet. The two closest situations are attractive and neither yields wording: Revelation 9:21, where a plagued people do not repent of their sorceries, and Micah 5:12, where the LORD cuts off witchcrafts and soothsayers from a people he is about to purge — Micah 5 being a chapter Hardy's apparatus does bring to bear later in this book, at Mormon 5:24 for Micah 5:8. A single shared noun in each case, and no syntax, so there is nothing to catalogue as dependence.

‘And notwithstanding I being young, was large in stature, therefore the people of Nephi appointed me that I should be their leader.’ The King James Bible has a type-scene here — the young man of exceptional build who is made head of the nation's armies, Saul ‘higher than any of the people from his shoulders and upward’ (1 Samuel 9:2), David going out against the Philistine while Saul asks ‘whose son is this youth?’ (1 Samuel 17:55) — and the machine offered the second of those at Mormon 2:27 on the run ‘go forth against the’. Neither verse supplies a word of Mormon 2:1. The phrase the verse actually uses is not biblical at all: ‘large in stature’ is in no KJV verse, and it occurs three times in the Book of Mormon, at 1 Nephi 2:16 and 4:31 of Nephi and here of Mormon. The model is internal, and it is 1 Nephi 4:31 specifically — ‘a man large in stature, and also having received much strength of the Lord’ — because the other half of that self-description turns up twenty-five verses later at Mormon 2:26, in the negative. The borrowing is adjudicated there, at the Isaiah 14:10 row; a reader who arrives at 2:1 expecting Saul or David should be sent to it.

A four-word run that ranked twice in this chapter, at 2:3 and again at 2:16, and both times it is the Book of Mormon's regnal-style dating formula colliding with the KJV's. 2 Kings 12:6 dates the repair of the temple to ‘the three and twentieth year of king Jehoash’; Mormon 2:3 and 2:16 date battles to ‘the three hundred and twenty and seventh year’ and ‘the three hundred and forty and fifth year’. Mormon 2 dates itself this way seven times (2:2, 2:3, 2:9, 2:15, 2:16, 2:22, 2:28), which is by itself proof that the formula is the book's own habit and not a reach for the one KJV verse that shares four of its words. This entry covers every ‘in the three hundred and Nth year’ candidate in the chapter.

The candidate scores on three overlapping four-word windows and two of them are ‘and it came to’ and ‘it came to pass’, which the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5 already covers. What is left is ‘take possession of the’, Jezebel telling Ahab to go down and take Naboth's vineyard now that Naboth is dead. Mormon 2:4 is an army occupying a city it will be driven out of in the same verse, and the same phrase returns at 2:27 for the recovery of the lands of inheritance; it is ordinary English for seizing property and points at nothing.

exclusions.sharedText: and came to the land of
exclusions.reason: A six-word run, and a travel formula on both ends. Jeremiah 40:12 is the scattered Jews returning to Judah under Gedaliah; Mormon 2:6 is a defeated army marching to the land of Joshua on the west seashore. ‘Came to the land of’ is how the KJV moves people between places and how the Book of Mormon does the same; nothing else of Jeremiah 40 is present. Worth noting only because this chapter really does draw on Jeremiah — three times, at 2:15 twice and 2:27 — and none of it is here.

‘We did gather in our people as fast as it were possible, that we might get them together in one body.’ “in one body” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Romans 12:4, Ephesians 2:16 and Colossians 3:15 — and all three are Paul's ecclesial figure, the church as a single body with many members, in Ephesians reconciled to God ‘by the cross’. Mormon 2:7 is a military concentration: an army gathering its scattered people into one place before the enemy arrives. The phrase is identical and the referent is opposed — Paul's one body is made out of people who were not one, Mormon's is a defensive formation. The same clause recurs at 2:21 with ‘as much as it were possible’ and the same reason applies.

A five-word run and the highest-scoring candidate in the first half of the chapter, and it is the right string on the wrong scene. Exodus 1:7 is Israel multiplying in Egypt — ‘fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty; and the land was filled with them’ — which is a blessing and the beginning of a nation. Mormon 2:8 is ‘the land was filled with robbers and with Lamanites’ followed by ‘blood and carnage spread throughout all the face of the land’, which is the end of one. The verse the wording and the scene both point at is Genesis 6:11, ‘the earth was filled with violence’, and the link is catalogued there; “filled with violence” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 6:11 and 6:13.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when
exclusions.reason: An eight-word run, the longest in the chapter, and it is entirely ‘and it came to pass that when’ — the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5. The same window ranks again at 2:26 against Amos 7:2 with a nine-word run. Neither Paul's trance in the temple nor Amos's locusts has anything else in common with Mormon 2. Recorded once, at length, because a run this long looks like evidence and is not: the n-gram stream is a recall floor, not a ranking (CONVENTIONS §9), and in this chapter its two longest runs are both boilerplate while the two strongest links in the chapter — Nehemiah 4:14 at 2:23 and Isaiah 14:10 at 2:26 — scored nothing at all. This entry covers the Acts 22:17, Amos 7:2, Jeremiah 13:11, Genesis 40:16, Daniel 6:26, 2 Samuel 17:17, Revelation 10:8, 1 Samuel 13:11, Acts 27:39, Job 10:21 and Daniel 9:20 candidates in this chapter, all of which rank on connective boilerplate alone.

A four-word run that ranks at both 2:19 and 2:27, and it is a real content phrase, which is why it needs an entry rather than silence. Jeremiah 44:3 is the LORD's charge against the Judahites in Egypt — ‘Because of their wickedness which they have committed to provoke me to anger, in that they went to burn incense’ — a specific indictment of a specific idolatry. Mormon uses the phrase twice as the ground of his own grief, not of God's anger: ‘wo is me, because of their wickedness: for my heart has been filled with sorrow because of their wickedness’. The chapter's genuine Jeremiah contacts are elsewhere and are catalogued: Jeremiah 45:3 at this verse, for the lament, and Jeremiah 16:4 and 8:20 at 2:15. Jeremiah 44 is not among them.

The machine's best candidate in the second half of the chapter, on a five-word run, and it is displaced by a better one. 2 Chronicles 20:13 is Judah standing before the LORD to pray before Jehoshaphat's battle, ‘with their little ones, their wives, and their children’ — a congregation, not a muster, and no one in it is told to fight. Mormon 2:23 is an exhortation to fight, and the KJV verse that exhorts men to fight for that list is Nehemiah 4:14, where “your wives, and your houses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The link is catalogued there, with the argument from the ‘houses … homes’ doublet.

Four words, and the senses are opposed on the point the verse turns on. Deuteronomy 7:7 explains why the LORD chose Israel although they were ‘the fewest of all people’: election is not a reward for strength. Mormon 2:26 explains why a Nephite army that had just stood against fifty thousand with thirty thousand, and driven them, was nonetheless finished — ‘the strength of the Lord was not with us: yea, we were left to ourselves’. Deuteronomy denies that numbers matter to a people God has chosen; Mormon reports what happens to a people God has stopped upholding. The verse's real sources are Isaiah 14:10 and, behind it, Judges 16, and they are catalogued at this verse.

exclusions.sharedText: come unto me and be ye baptized
exclusions.reason: A cross-reference, not a rejection (PLAN §3, ruled 2026-09-07). The machine ranked Isaiah 45:22 here on 'unto me and be ye', and the contact is real: the Lord's command to Mormon — 'repent ye, and come unto me and be ye baptized' — is the first half of a formula whose second half arrives at the end of the chapter, 'all ye ends of the earth to repent' (3:22). The Book of Mormon has both halves in one sentence at 3 Nephi 27:20, in the record Mormon abridged, and Isaiah 45:22 stands behind that. The link is therefore adjudicated at 3:22, where the vocative that carries it actually appears, and a reader who arrives at 3:2 should be sent there. Note also that 'and be ye baptized' occurs in exactly 0 KJV verses; nothing in this half of the formula is King James English.

This one has to be written out because the rarity count looks decisive and is not. 'Harden their hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Joshua 11:20, 'For it was of the LORD to harden their hearts, that they should come against Israel in battle, that he might destroy them utterly' — and the context is a startlingly good fit for Mormon 3, where hardened hearts (3:3) produce a march to battle (3:10) and end in being cut off from the face of the earth (3:15). The count is nevertheless worthless here, because the phrase is one of the Book of Mormon's most heavily worn formulas: it occurs in thirty-five verses spread across every book from 1 Nephi to Ether. A formula used thirty-five times cannot be evidence of dependence on the one KJV verse that happens to share it. The agency also differs at the point that matters: in Joshua it is the LORD who hardens, in Mormon 3:3 the people harden their own hearts against him. Filed as the model case for a KJV singleton that a Book of Mormon commonplace has neutralised.

exclusions.sharedText: that they should gather themselves together
exclusions.reason: The chapter's highest-scoring machine candidate, a six-word run, and pure formula. Ezra 10:7 proclaims that the children of the captivity 'should gather themselves together unto Jerusalem' for a covenant assembly; Mormon 3:5 musters an army at the land Desolation to hold a narrow pass. 'Gather themselves together' is the King James Bible's standing phrase for any assembly of people, and the Book of Mormon uses it continuously in exactly this military sense throughout the war narratives. Nothing else of Ezra 10 is present.

'Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria, and preached Christ unto them' against 'the Lamanites did come down to the city of Desolation to battle'. The shared string is a preposition, a direction and the ordinary way of naming a city in English. Covered by the standing formulaic exclusion; listed only because it ranked in the chapter's top twenty-four.

'Utterly refuse' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and a reader who runs the count will find it: Exodus 22:17, 'If her father utterly refuse to give her unto him, he shall pay money according to the dowry of virgins' — the seducer's fine in the covenant code. Mormon uses the phrase twice in six verses (3:11, 3:16), which is the only place in the Book of Mormon it occurs, so the rarity is real at both ends. The senses have nothing whatever in common. Exodus 22:17 is a father withholding a daughter from a marriage and being compensated in silver; Mormon 3:11 is a general resigning a command. The adverb is the KJV's ordinary intensifier for a refusal and would be reached for by anyone writing in that register. Recorded at length because the double singleton is exactly the shape of evidence this catalogue accepts elsewhere, and here it means nothing.

Tempting and declined. 'Poured out my soul' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hannah's answer to Eli at 1 Samuel 1:15 — a woman of a sorrowful spirit pouring out her soul before the LORD and taken for a drunkard. Mormon 3:12 reads 'my soul had been poured out in prayer unto my God all the day long', and the situation rhymes: unavailing prayer, misread by the people it is offered for. But the Book of Mormon's clause is passive where Hannah's is active, the possessive differs, and the book pours out souls elsewhere without any Samuel vocabulary (Alma 46:17, Mosiah 26:14). What is left is a shared metaphor that the Psalms use too (42:4, 62:8). The love-of-God clause is where this verse's link is; see the Romans 8:39 row.

The same trap as the Joshua 11:20 entry at 3:3, one verse of the King James Bible and seventeen of the Book of Mormon. 'Hardness of their hearts' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:5, where Jesus is grieved at it in the synagogue before healing the withered hand; it occurs in seventeen Book of Mormon verses from 1 Nephi 2:18 onward, as the book's standing explanation for any failure of preaching. Mormon 3:12 is one of the seventeen. The catalogue does hold a Mark 3:5 link — at 1 Nephi 17:53, for 'stretch forth thine hand', which is the half of the verse a formula has not swallowed.

The machine's only candidate at the chapter's most important verse, and it is boilerplate sitting next to a certain quotation. 'Cut off' is the covenant code's standing penalty formula and the Book of Mormon's standing threat; Leviticus 20:17 is a prohibited-degrees law about a man and his sister. The verse's actual borrowing is the clause before it, 'Vengeance is mine, and I will repay', adjudicated as a quotation of Romans 12:19. Recorded so that a reader who sees only the machine's proposal at 3:15 knows the catalogue looked past it.

exclusions.sharedText: unto all the ends of the earth
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and the longest in the chapter, which is what got it ranked. 'All the ends of the earth' occurs in exactly seven KJV verses (Psalm 65:5, 67:7, 98:3, Proverbs 30:4, Isaiah 26:15, 45:22, 52:10) and in twenty-three Book of Mormon verses, eight of which carry it as the vocative 'all ye ends of the earth'. Isaiah 26:15 is about the enlargement of the nation and has nothing else in common with a passage about two benches of twelve judges. The one Isaiah verse of the seven that does bear on this chapter is 45:22, and it is adjudicated at 3:22, where the imperative that identifies it appears.

A four-word run, and 'according to their works' occurs in exactly three KJV verses (2 Corinthians 11:15, Revelation 20:12, 20:13) with Revelation 2:23's second-person variant beside them — a genuinely rare formula, and one the Book of Mormon has already fixed for itself. 3 Nephi 27:15, in the record Mormon abridged, has the risen Christ say men shall 'be judged according to their works', and Mormon 6:21 repeats the phrase with the judgement seat attached. The judgment-of-works material in this chapter is adjudicated at 3:20, where the whole composite stands (2 Corinthians 5:10, Romans 14:10, Ecclesiastes 12:14); the Apocalypse is not needed for it and nothing else of Revelation 2 or 20 is present.

'The gospel of Jesus Christ' at Mark 1:1 against 'the Gospel of Jesus Christ, which ye shall have among you'. The phrase is the New Testament's ordinary name for the thing and the Book of Mormon's too, and Mark 1:1 contributes nothing else. The verse's real borrowings are two clauses later — 'whom they slew' and 'the very Christ' — and both are adjudicated.

A four-word run and a KJV singleton — “their armies to battle” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the singleton is arithmetic rather than evidential. The King James Bible narrates armies going to battle constantly and simply had occasion to phrase it with this possessive once. 1 Samuel 17:1 is the muster before David and Goliath; Mormon 4:1 is the Nephites' opening offensive of the year 363, and nothing else of 1 Samuel 17 is present — no champion, no single combat, no defiance. The Book of Mormon uses the same construction throughout the war books (Alma 43, Mormon 2-6), so it is the corpus's own military idiom, not a borrowing from the one KJV verse that shares the possessive.

The machine's highest-ranked candidate at three separate verses of this chapter (4:2, 4:7, 4:13), on the strength of “take possession of the” plus “and it came to pass”. It is boilerplate on both sides. 1 Kings 21:15 is Jezebel telling Ahab to seize Naboth's vineyard; the Book of Mormon phrase is its standard verb for the capture of a fortified city and occurs across Alma and Mormon dozens of times. The only feature that could tempt is that Naboth's vineyard is a seizure by murder and Mormon 4 is a chapter of seizure by massacre, but there is no shared vocabulary beyond the formula and no vineyard, no false witness, no prophetic sentence. This entry covers 4:7 and 4:13 as well; they are not listed individually.

exclusions.sharedText: boast of their strength ... in their own might
exclusions.reason: NOT a rejection — a placement note. Mormon 4:8's “they did again boast of their strength; and they went forth in their own might” is the Book of Mormon's boasting-in-own-strength doctrine, whose KJV footing was argued at Helaman 4:13 (“their boastings in their own strength, they were left in their own strength”), where the noun “boastings” is a King James singleton at James 4:16. Mormon 4:8 has the verb, not the noun, so the singleton that carries the Helaman row is not present here and a fresh link would rest on nothing. “Their own strength” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses and “own strength” in exactly two, Psalm 21:13 and Amos 6:13, neither of which is about a nation boasting after a victory. Deuteronomy 8:17's “the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth” — also a singleton — was weighed as the alternative and declined: it is about wealth, not arms, and shares no word with 4:8. A reader who wants the biblical background of this sentence should be sent to Helaman 4:13.

“Every heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 21:7, and the temptation is sharp, because Ezekiel 21 is the sword-song — “A sword, a sword is sharpened, and also furbished” — and is therefore the KJV chapter closest in subject to Mormon 4. But the predicate is exactly inverted. Ezekiel's every heart shall MELT, with all hands feeble and all knees weak as water, at the mere news that the sword is coming; Mormon's every heart WAS HARDENED, so that they delighted in the shedding of blood continually. Ezekiel describes a people undone by the prospect of slaughter; Mormon describes a people who have acquired a taste for it. Two words, opposed verbs, and the whole difference between the two chapters' anthropology lies in that opposition. Recorded because the singleton would otherwise look overlooked, and because the inversion is more interesting than the parallel would have been.

“It is impossible for the tongue to describe, or for man to write a perfect description” is an inexpressibility topos, and the King James Bible has two famous ones: John 21:25, whose “the world itself” is a singleton — “even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written” — and Romans 8:26's “groanings which cannot be uttered”, also a singleton. Neither is present in any word. John's topos is about superabundance of good (the deeds of Jesus), Romans' about prayer beyond language; Mormon's is about the unspeakability of atrocity, which the KJV never has occasion to say. The Book of Mormon uses the figure repeatedly in its own words (3 Nephi 17:17, “no tongue can speak”), so it is a corpus habit rather than a borrowing. Recorded because a reader meeting a sentence about what cannot be written will think of John 21:25, and should be told the catalogue thought of it too.

NOT a rejection — a cross-reference. 4:14 is the first of the chapter's two child-sacrifice notices (“did take many prisoners of women and of children, and did offer them up as sacrifices unto their idol gods”), and it is the one a reader will stop at. Its wording, however, is the Book of Mormon's own: “idol gods” is in no KJV verse, and “sacrificed unto” alone occurs in ten, too many to identify a source. The KJV wording appears at 4:21, “sacrificed unto idols”, against Psalm 106:38's “sacrificed unto the idols of Canaan”, which is a King James singleton — so the link is filed there, where the words are (CONVENTIONS §6a), and covers both notices. Ezekiel 16:20-21 and 2 Kings 17:17 were weighed here and share no wording with either verse.

“They were not numbered, because of the greatness of their number” is the innumerable-army topos, and the KJV has a well-stocked shelf of it: Judges 6:5 and 7:12's Midianites “as grasshoppers for multitude ... without number”, 1 Kings 3:8's people “that cannot be numbered nor counted for multitude”, Genesis 32:12's sand of the sea. “Not be numbered” is even a KJV singleton, at Genesis 16:10. None of them is here. Every KJV instance pairs the countlessness with a simile — grasshoppers, sand, stars — and Mormon 4:17 supplies no simile at all, only the flat tautology that they could not be counted because there were too many. The candidate is a topos held in common, not a text used, and the Gideon parallel that the topos suggests (a small covenant force against an innumerable host) is precisely the shape Mormon 4 refuses: there is no Gideon here and the small force loses.

A four-word run scoring at the top of the verse, and the two senses of “beat” have nothing to do with each other. Exodus 39:3 is the making of the high priest's ephod: “they did beat the gold into thin plates, and cut it into wires, to work it in the blue, and in the purple, and in the scarlet.” Mormon 4:19 is a rout: “an exceeding sore battle fought in the land Desolation, in the which they did beat the Nephites.” Metalworking against military defeat, with the object supplying the whole difference. Worth the entry only because “beat ... into thin plates” sits so close to the Book of Mormon's own governing metaphor of engraved plates that a reader running a concordance on plates and beating will land here; there is no connection, and the plates of Mormon 4:23 are taken up, not hammered.

“Great slaughter” occurs in fifteen KJV verses and is the standard formula of the conquest and early monarchy narratives — Joshua at Gibeon, Jephthah at Minnith, Samson hip and thigh, David against the Philistines. No single verse can be the source and none is proposed. It is worth recording what the formula does here rather than where it comes from: in the KJV the great slaughter is almost always inflicted BY the covenant people ON the nations, and the one conspicuous exception, 1 Samuel 4:10, is the day the ark was taken. Mormon 4:21 puts the covenant people on the receiving end of their own scriptural idiom, and follows it immediately with their children sacrificed to idols. The reversal is the interesting fact; a link is not.

The top-ranked candidate in the first half of the chapter, and “fled to the city” is a genuine KJV singleton, which is why it ranked. It is also the only reason it ranked. Numbers 35:32 is manslaughter law: a killer who has fled to a city of refuge may not buy his way home before the high priest dies. Mormon 5:3 is an army in retreat holding a fortified position — 'the Lamanites did come against us as we had fled to the city of Jordan'. Refuge is the one idea the two share and the Book of Mormon does not use the word or the institution; the city of Jordan is a garrison, not an asylum, and it is defended rather than dwelt in. A four-word run of the plainest possible English about running to a walled town.

A five-word run and pure dating formula. 1 Kings 6:1 dates the founding of the temple to the four hundred and eightieth year from the Exodus; Mormon 5:6 dates a Lamanite offensive to the three hundred and eightieth year from the sign of Christ's birth. The Book of Mormon dates in this manner throughout the book of Mormon — 4:7, 4:10, 4:16, 5:5, 6:5 — and the resemblance is that both books count years and both had occasion to write the ordinal 'eightieth'. This entry covers every 'in the Nth year' candidate in the chapter; they are not listed individually. Compare the standing exclusion at Helaman 1:1.

Worth the register because the wording is rarer than it looks and the sense is exactly inverted. “the flight” as an abstract noun occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Amos 2:14 — 'Therefore the flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not strengthen his force, neither shall the mighty deliver himself' — and Mormon 5:7 uses the same abstract noun twice in one sentence and pairs it with swiftness both times: 'they whose flight were swifter than the Lamanites did escape, and they whose flight did not exceed the Lamanites, were swept down and destroyed'. Amos and Mormon are describing the same event, the rout of a nation's army, in the same rare grammatical form. But Amos's whole point is that speed will not save anyone — the flight perishes FROM the swift — and Mormon's whole point is that speed was precisely what saved the men who had it. A borrowing that reversed the proposition would have to show some other contact to be credible and there is none: no shared verb, no shared subject, nothing of Amos 2:14-16's catalogue of the strong, the mighty, the archer and the horseman. Recorded so a reader who notices the singleton is told the catalogue noticed it and declined it.

The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter by rarity and it should not be accepted. “because of the wickedness of” does occur in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 28:20, but the count is an accident of the preposition: 'for the wickedness of' occurs repeatedly (Deuteronomy 9:4, 9:5, Jeremiah 12:4 and others) and the sense is identical. The pull here is thematic rather than verbal, and it is a real pull — Deuteronomy 28 is the curse chapter whose promised destruction, scattering and being 'a byword among all nations' is the plot of Mormon 5 — but the phrase Mormon actually writes is a subordinate clause of apology to his readers, 'that ye might not have too great sorrow because of the wickedness of this people', not a statement of divine cause. Where this chapter does borrow a covenant-curse chapter, it borrows Leviticus 26 and it borrows it distinctively; see the link at 5:20.

The most tempting exclusion in the chapter. “remnant of these” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the setting is not remote: Joshua 23 is a leader's farewell address warning a covenant people that if they turn aside the LORD will no longer drive out the nations before them, which is structurally what Mormon 5 is. But the referent of the remnant is opposed in the two texts, and it is the referent that does all the work. Joshua's 'remnant of these nations' is the surviving Canaanites, the foreign population Israel is forbidden to intermarry with; Mormon's 'remnant of these people' is his own destroyed nation's descendants, the audience the record is being written for and the object of the book's hope. One is what the covenant people must not cleave to; the other is what the covenant will be kept for. Beyond the four words there is no contact — no marriages, no driving out, no snares and scourges — and 'the remnant of' is in any case the Book of Mormon's standing term for the seed of Lehi, used at 5:12, 5:24, 7:1 and throughout 3 Nephi.

A five-word run across a clause boundary in both texts and nothing else whatever. Judges 19:25 is the Levite putting his concubine out of the door at Gibeah; Mormon 5:12 is a statement that wickedness will not bring the record forth to its intended readers. The match is 'brought her forth unto them; and they' against 'will not bring them forth unto them; and they', which is the machine matching two pronouns and a preposition. Listed only because it ranked, and because a five-word run in a register that elsewhere treats five-word runs as evidence should be shown to have been looked at.

Ezekiel 14:22 is more interesting than the usual n-gram noise because it is about a remnant and a coming forth — 'behold, therein shall be left a remnant that shall be brought forth … behold, they shall come forth unto you, and ye shall see their way and their doings' — in a chapter about a land given to destruction, and Mormon 5:13 is about a record coming forth after a land has been destroyed. But Ezekiel's subject is people and Mormon's is plates, and the five shared words are 'behold they shall come forth', which is the ordinary King James way of announcing that anything is about to appear. The remnant theme in this chapter is adjudicated where it has wording behind it, at 5:24.

The machine offered Matthew 26:63, where Caiaphas adjures Jesus 'by the living God' to say 'whether thou be the Christ, the Son of God' — which puts all of Mormon 5:14's elements on the page but distributes them differently. The Book of Mormon has the completed title 'the Son of the living God', which occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 16:16 and John 6:69, and not at Matthew 26:63, where 'the living God' belongs to the oath and not to the title. The link is adjudicated at 5:14 on John 20:31 for the purpose clause and Matthew 16:16 for the title; see there. Jeremiah 43:1, also proposed for this verse on 'the LORD their God', is the bare King James possessive formula and is passed over.

Mark 6:6 is Jesus marvelling at Nazareth's unbelief; Mormon 5:15 is a prophecy that his people will become dark and loathsome 'because of their unbelief and idolatry'. The four words are shared and nothing else is: no marvelling, no mighty works, no city. Where the unbelief of Mormon 5 does have a plausible scriptural background it is Romans 11:20, 'because of unbelief they were broken off', and that is recorded not as a verbal link but as one point of contact inside the figural link on Romans 11 filed at 5:19. Ecclesiastes 2:12, also proposed here on 'even that which hath been', is connective boilerplate.

exclusions.sharedText: (Christ as shepherd of a straying people)
exclusions.reason: A typological expectation the wording will not bear, in the pattern of the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry in 1 Nephi. Mormon 5:17 says the Lamanites 'were once a delightsome people, and they had Christ for their Shepherd; yea, they were led even by God, the Father', and 1 Peter 2:25 says 'ye were as sheep going astray; but are now returned unto the Shepherd and Bishop of your souls' — the same figure of a people that had a shepherd and left him, with the direction of travel reversed. There is no shared wording beyond the noun. 'Shepherd' as a title for God or Christ is spread across Psalm 23:1, Psalm 80:1, Isaiah 40:11, Ezekiel 34, John 10:11, Hebrews 13:20 and 1 Peter 5:4, and nothing in Mormon 5:17 selects among them. Recorded because the verse invites the identification and the catalogue should be seen to have declined it.

The highest-scoring candidate at the head of the chapter, and the pairing is genuinely affecting: Esther pleads “how can I endure to see the destruction of my kindred?” and Mormon opens “I finish my record concerning the destruction of my people, the Nephites.” But the shared run is four ordinary words and the fifth word diverges — Esther has “kindred”, Mormon has “people” — and the two sentences do opposite work. Esther's is a plea made while the destruction can still be stopped, and it is stopped; Mormon's is a colophon written after it has happened, in the past tense, by the man who watched. Nothing else of Esther 8 is present. Recorded because a reader who notices the phrase should be told the catalogue noticed it too.

A four-word run, and “desired of him” occurs in only two KJV verses (Acts 9:2 and 1 John 5:15), so the machine ranked it. But it is the opening of the same sentence whose main clause is Luke 1:74's — “desired of him that he would grant unto us that we might” — and the eight-word run there is a KJV singleton. The whole borrowing is adjudicated at Mormon 6:2 against Luke 1:74. Saul asking the high priest for letters to Damascus contributes nothing further; the verbal contact is the bare KJV idiom for making a request of a superior, which is what both sentences happen to be doing.

The second-highest-scoring candidate in the chapter and a real trap, because “fall into the hands of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Hebrews 10:31, “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” — and Mormon 6:6 is a fearful sentence about things falling into hands. The senses do not meet at any point. Hebrews is about a person falling under the judgment of God, which is the worst thing that can happen to an apostate; Mormon 6:6 is about sacred records falling under the custody of an enemy who would burn them, which is a logistical fear about objects. Nor is the phrase Mormon's borrowing: “fall into the hands” occurs six times in the Book of Mormon (Alma 43:10, 43:11, 56:50, 59:11, Mosiah 21:19 and here), five of them in the war chapters and every one of them about materiel or ground changing sides. It is this book's ordinary military idiom, and the KJV singleton is an accident of how rarely the KJV needed the plural.

A five-word run and pure KJV boilerplate for a civilian population; the catalogue's standing exclusion on connective formulae covers it. Worth naming only because 2 Chronicles 20 is the Jehoshaphat narrative in which the assembled families do not have to fight at all — “ye shall not need to fight in this battle” — which is the exact inverse of Mormon 6:7, where the wives and children stand in the line and are killed. The inversion is interesting and it is not evidence: the phrase is Judahite muster language, and the verse's real borrowing is Hebrews 2:15's “fear of death”, adjudicated as a link at this verse.

The machine matched four connective words, but the reason to write this up is typological, and it is the strongest typological pull in the chapter. Judges 19-21 is the Bible's one narrative of a whole tribe of Israel being hunted to near-extinction by its own brother tribes, ending with a remnant of six hundred men and a national lament — and Mormon 6 is the Book of Mormon's account of a whole branch of the house of Israel being hunted to extinction by its own brother nation, ending with a remnant of twenty-four and a lament. The wording will not carry it. Judges 20:48 shares nothing distinctive with Mormon 6:8; “smote them with the edge of the sword” does not appear in Mormon 6, whose weapons list at 6:9 is its own; and the surviving numbers, six hundred against twenty-four, are not in any relation. Filed here on the Exodus 2:2 “goodly” model (CONVENTIONS §5): the type is visible, the catalogue saw it, and it declined to catalogue it as dependence.

exclusions.sharedText: with the sword, and with the
exclusions.reason: “with the sword and with the” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 27:8, so a six-word run scores high; but the two lists are different kinds of list. Jeremiah's is the prophetic triad of judgments — sword, famine, pestilence — three agencies by which God consumes a nation that will not serve Babylon. Mormon's is an inventory of hardware: sword, bow, arrow, axe, “and with all manner of weapons of war.” Neither famine nor pestilence appears in Mormon 6, and no weapon appears in Jeremiah 27:8 but the sword. The shared string is the KJV's way of running any list at all. Note also that “weapons of war” is not available as evidence here: it occurs 44 times in the Book of Mormon, overwhelmingly in Alma, and is this book's own standing phrase. Its one genuinely relevant KJV occurrence, 2 Samuel 1:27, is taken up as part of the David-lament link adjudicated at Mormon 6:13.

exclusions.sharedText: (the wounded commander of a last stand)
exclusions.reason: Not proposed by any machine stream, and written up because it is the parallel a reader is most likely to arrive at unaided. Josiah is the last good king of Judah; he goes out to a battle he is warned against, is shot by archers, is carried wounded from the field, and dies — after which Jeremiah composes a lament for him and the lamentations become an ordinance in Israel (2 Chronicles 35:20-25). Mormon is the last righteous commander of the Nephites; he goes out to a battle he knows is the last, is wounded and left for dead among his ten thousand, survives, and composes the lament. The correspondence extends to the lamenting prophet being Jeremiah, whose 9:1 does stand behind Mormon 6:16. But there is no verbal contact: 2 Chronicles 35:23 reads “the archers shot at king Josiah; and the king said to his servants, Have me away; for I am sore wounded”, and Mormon 6:10 reads “I fell wounded in the midst; and they passed by me that they did not put an end to my life”. The only shared word is “wounded”. “Wounded in the midst” occurs in no KJV verse. The Megiddo–Cumorah reading is worth a reader's time and is not dependence; where the wording does bear, at “fallen … in the midst”, the source is 2 Samuel 1:25 and the link is at 6:13.

Proposed identically at 6:11 and 6:12 and covering both. A four-word run whose match is an artifact of 1830 grammar: the first edition writes “the ten thousand of my people which were hewn down” where 1920 writes “who”, and the relative pronoun is what makes the run. Romans 9:25 is Paul quoting Hosea on the calling of a people that were not a people — an oracle of inclusion — against a verse counting corpses from a hilltop. The same entry disposes of Ezekiel 45:5's “the ten thousand of”, also proposed at both verses: Ezekiel is measuring a Levitical land allotment in cubits, and Mormon is naming a military division. Neither is a source for the other; both are the KJV's ordinary way of attaching a number to a genitive.

“judged according to” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 24:6 and 1 Peter 4:6, and the machine offered the latter. It is the wrong half of the phrase. Mormon 6:21 reads “to be judged according to your works”, and “according to your works” — second person plural — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 2:23; 1 Peter 4:6 continues “according to men in the flesh”, which is not a judgment by works at all but a contrast between human and divine reckoning. tools/mediation-check.py run on Mormon 6:21 against Psalm 62:12 and Revelation 2:23 returns the point decisively: the Book of Mormon has “your works”, not the Psalm's “his work”. The clause is adjudicated as part of the composite link at Mormon 6:21. The same entry disposes of Ephesians 4:21's “so be that ye”, proposed at the same verse, which is the bare KJV conditional.

The second-ranked candidate in the chapter and the one a careful reader is most likely to accept, because the typology is nearly perfect. Genesis 49:28 closes Jacob's deathbed blessing — “All these are the twelve tribes of Israel: and this is it that their father spake unto them, and blessed them” — and Mormon 7:1 is the last surviving Nephite's final words to the house of Israel, introduced with “and this is the words which I speak.” A dying patriarch, the house of Israel, and a formula announcing that what follows is his speech. But the verbal contact is the four words “of Israel and this is”, which is an accident of two ordinary clauses abutting, and the two formulas are not the same formula: Genesis 49:28 is a narrator's retrospective summary of a speech already given, Mormon 7:1 is a speaker's own prospective announcement of a speech about to be given. Nothing else of Genesis 49 is present — no tribes, no blessing, no naming. The chapter's real source for its address to the remnant is Isaiah 46:3, linked at this verse, and Isaiah 46:3 happens to open with “O house of Jacob”, which is where the patriarchal resonance actually comes from.

Filed because the anaphora is the most conspicuous formal feature of the chapter and a reader will want to know whether the catalogue tested it. Mormon 7:2-5 open four consecutive verses with “Know ye that ye…”, and “know ye that” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: 1 Kings 22:3 (Ramoth in Gilead is ours), Psalm 100:3, Luke 21:31 and Hebrews 13:23 (Timothy is set at liberty). Only Psalm 100:3 is a summons to a people to know a fact about who they and their God are — “Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people” — which is the exact rhetorical situation of Mormon 7:2, “Know ye that ye are of the house of Israel.” The temptation is real and the wording will not bear it: three words, all of them common, and no second point of contact anywhere in the psalm. The Book of Mormon uses “know ye” freely elsewhere without any psalm in view. Recorded so that the register shows the anaphora was examined and declined, not overlooked.

“ye cannot be saved” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 15:1 and Acts 27:31, and both are, like Mormon 7:3, the apodosis of a conditional stating a necessary precondition of salvation: “Except ye be circumcised after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved”; “Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.” Mormon 7:3 has the identical shape — “ye must come unto repentance, or ye cannot be saved.” Rejected on sense, and the sense is not merely different but reversed. Acts 15:1 puts the sentence in the mouths of the Judaisers precisely so that the council of Acts 15 can strike it down; the verse exists in the New Testament as a claim to be refuted, and its content is a ritual requirement laid on Gentile converts by a party the apostles rule against. Acts 27:31 is Paul on the deck of a foundering ship talking about staying aboard, and is not soteriological at all. A four-word run whose one plausible source is a sentence its own book contradicts is not a borrowing worth cataloguing, though a reader who finds it is owed the account.

“weapons of war” occurs in exactly nine KJV verses and is the King James Bible's ordinary term for military equipment, so no single verse can be named on the phrase alone. The one that tempts is 2 Samuel 1:27, the last line of David's lament over Saul and Jonathan — “How are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished!” — because Mormon 7 stands immediately after Mormon 6:17-22, this catalogue's most sustained lament over a fallen army, and the transition from lamenting the fallen to naming the weapons of war is the transition David makes. But 2 Samuel 1:27 is an exclamation over weapons destroyed with their owners, and Mormon 7:4 is an imperative to living men to put theirs down; there is no shared verb, no shared syntax, and “weapons of war” is a phrase the Book of Mormon uses dozens of times in the war chapters without any lament attached. The genuine borrowing in this verse is the “delight… in the shedding of blood” construction of Psalm 68:30 plus Hebrews 9:22, linked at the verse.

A four-word run and a genuine machine hit: Revelation 15:2 has “them that had gotten the victory over the beast”, and Mormon 7:5 has “he hath gained the victory over the grave.” The construction is the same and Revelation is the only KJV verse that carries it. It is superseded all the same. “the victory” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, of which 1 Corinthians 15:57 — “thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” — stands four words from “sting of death” and nine from “swallowed up in victory”, both of which Mormon 7:5 also has, and 1 Corinthians 15:55 assigns the victory specifically to the grave, which is Mormon's object. Revelation supplies a preposition; 1 Corinthians supplies the sentence. Adjudicated at this verse as 1 Corinthians 15:55 with 15:54, 15:56 and 15:57 as composite.

exclusions.sharedText: by the ___ of the Father he hath risen again
exclusions.reason: A near miss worth recording because the miss is in one word and the word is decisive. “glory of the Father” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 6:4: “like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.” Mormon 7:5 reads “by the power of the Father he hath risen again”, and “power of the Father” occurs in no KJV verse at all. The setting also invites the identification, since Romans 6:4 grounds the resurrection in baptism and Mormon 7:8 and 7:10 both command baptism. But the substitution of power for glory removes the only rare element the verse had, and the Book of Mormon's construction is a commonplace of its own idiom rather than of the King James Bible's. “risen again” occurs in six KJV verses, none of them attached to the Father. Rejected, and the reader sent to the 1 Corinthians 15:54-57 complex linked at this verse, which accounts for the rest of the sentence.

“stand before the judgment seat” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 14:10, and “judgment seat of Christ” in exactly two, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10; Mormon 7:6's “raised to stand before his judgement seat” has real contact with both. It is not adjudicated here. This catalogue links the Romans / 2 Corinthians composite at Mormon 3:20, earlier in this same book and in the same narrator's voice, where the verse carries the whole fusion — 2 Corinthians's “must”, Romans's “stand”, and 2 Corinthians's tail about receiving according to what is done, whether good or bad — and where mediation-check.py's divergences pointing both ways are set out in full. ADJUDICATING §4 governs: a phrase a narrator has adopted is adjudicated at first use within a book, and 7:6 has only the barest form of it, three words with no distinguishing feature. A reader who arrives at 7:6 should be sent to Mormon 3:20, and to Mormon 6:21 and 3:22 in the same chain. The link written at 7:6 is for a different source, 1 Corinthians 15:54's “brought to pass”.

The highest-scoring candidate the machine offered for this verse, on a five-word run, and it is the wrong sentence entirely. Genesis 16:12 is the angel's oracle about the unborn Ishmael: “he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him; and he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren.” The KJV's idiom there means to live alongside or in defiance of one's kin, not to be admitted to anyone's company, and it is a prophecy of perpetual hostility. Mormon 7:7's clause is a promise of heaven — “to dwell in the presence of God in his kingdom.” Nor is there a better biblical source to substitute: “in the presence of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 1:19 (Gabriel standing there) and Hebrews 9:24 (Christ appearing there for us), and neither uses the verb dwell or refers to the destiny of the redeemed. The clause is the Book of Mormon's own. The adjudicated link at this verse is to the triadic formula at its end.

Acts 10:48 (“commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord”) and Acts 5:40 (“not speak in the name of Jesus”) both scored above Acts 2:38 on the machine's ranking of this verse, on six-word windows. Both are superseded by Acts 2:38, linked here, on a point the windows cannot see: Mormon 7:8 begins “Therefore repent, and be baptized”, and “Repent, and be baptized” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:38, which then continues into the same “in the name of Jesus” the other two candidates share. Acts 10:48 reads “of the Lord”, not “of Jesus”, and Acts 5:40 has no baptism in it at all. A standing instance of CONVENTIONS §9: the longest run is not the best source.

One of the register's better entries for this book, because the phrase is rare, the doctrinal setting is adjacent, and the sense is exactly inverted. “first covenant” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Hebrews 8:7 and Hebrews 9:1, and in both it is a technical term for the Sinai covenant considered as superseded: “if that first covenant had been faultless, then should no place have been sought for the second”; “then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary”, the sanctuary Hebrews 9:8-9 goes on to call a figure now passing away. Mormon 7:10 uses the phrase for the opposite purpose: “ye are numbered among the people of the first covenant”, offered as a standing reason why the addressees should believe and be baptised. Hebrews' first covenant is the one its readers must be argued out of; Mormon's is the one his readers are to be told they still belong to. Related vocabulary in the same verse points elsewhere and is likewise declined — “seed of Jacob” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Psalm 22:23, Isaiah 45:19, Jeremiah 33:26) and none of them is about a covenanted remnant, and “it shall be well with” occurs in exactly seven and is a KJV commonplace. The verse's adjudicated links are to Matthew 3:11 and to the baptism narrative.

'As a scroll' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 34:4 and Revelation 6:14, and Revelation is the better-known of the two and stands in a chapter this book has already used at Mormon 5:22. It is nonetheless not the source. Revelation reads 'the heaven departed as a scroll when it is rolled together', with the participial clause trailing after the noun; Isaiah reads 'the heavens shall be rolled together as a scroll', with the participle before it, and Mormon 9:2 has Isaiah's order exactly as Mormon 5:23 does. The same displacement was recorded at 5:23 and the two occurrences agree, which is what makes the reading settled rather than incidental. Revelation 6:14 is retained as `composite` on the Isaiah row rather than as a source.

'A god which is not a God of miracles' against 'he is not a God of the dead, but of the living'. The five shared words are the whole of the case, and the predicate nouns are unrelated. What makes the candidate worth an entry rather than silence is that Luke 20 really is in play in this passage — but one verse later and by a different route. Mormon 9:11's 'the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob' carries the New Testament punctuation of the divine title found at Luke 20:37 and its three Synoptic parallels and at no Old Testament verse, and Mormon 9:8 tracks Mark 12:24. So the Synoptic resurrection controversy is behind this stretch of the chapter, and the machine has picked the wrong verse of it. 'God of miracles' occurs in no KJV verse and is the Book of Mormon's own phrase, established at 2 Nephi 27:23 and denied by the opponents of 2 Nephi 28:6; the syntax 'is not a God of X' needs no source.

exclusions.sharedText: the earth and all things that
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the highest-ranked candidate the machine produced for this verse. Nehemiah 9:6 is a creation doxology and the resemblance is real, but its clause is 'the earth, and all things that are therein', with the relative and the plural verb, while Mormon 9:11 reads 'all things that in them is' — the KJV's own inverted construction with the singular verb, which occurs at Exodus 20:11 and Acts 4:24 and nowhere else. The 1830 preserves the singular; the 1920 corrected it to 'are' and in doing so erased the quotation. So the verse's creation clause is adjudicated against Exodus 20:11 with Acts 4:24 as the undecidable alternative, and Nehemiah 9:6 is displaced by a form that matches at the one point where the KJV's English is peculiar.

exclusions.sharedText: man was created of the dust of the earth
exclusions.reason: The expectation pulls hard here — the verse names the creation of the heavens and the earth, the creation of man from dust, and the working of miracles, in that order, so a reader will supply Genesis 1-2 without being asked. The wording will not bear it. Genesis 2:7 reads 'the LORD God formed man of the dust of the GROUND'; 'the dust of the ground' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and 'of the dust of the earth' occurs in exactly one, which is Job 14:19 and is about erosion. Mormon 9:17 has neither of the KJV's collocations joined to the KJV's verb: 'man was created of the dust of the earth'. Nor does 'by his word the heaven and the earth should be' reproduce any of the three candidate creation-by-word verses — Psalm 33:6 ('by the word of the LORD were the heavens made'), Hebrews 11:3 ('the worlds were framed by the word of God') and 2 Peter 3:5 ('by the word of God the heavens were of old') — although 2 Peter 3 is demonstrably open elsewhere in this chapter (9:2, 9:6), which is why the case was tested rather than assumed. Recorded so that a reader who sees Genesis here is told the catalogue saw it too and declined it; the doctrine is common to every English Bible and no verse of any of them is being followed.

exclusions.sharedText: the Father in the name of
exclusions.reason: The machine ranked Ephesians 5:20 at 9:6, 9:21 and 9:27 on the strength of 'the Father in the name of', which in Ephesians is part of 'giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ' — a thanksgiving formula, not a petition formula. Mormon 9:21 and 9:27 are both about asking, and the KJV's asking formula is John's: 'whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name' at John 16:23, where 'shall ask the Father' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. That link is adjudicated at 9:21 and cross-referenced at 9:27. This entry covers the Ephesians 5:20 candidate at all three verses; it is not listed again.

exclusions.sharedText: shall be saved but he that
exclusions.reason: A six-word run in a verse that reproduces the whole of Mark 16:16 word for word, seventeen consecutive words with nothing altered. Proverbs 28:18 shares the connective spine ('shall be saved: but he that is perverse') and nothing else; it is not about baptism, belief or damnation. Recorded only because a six-word run inside a verbatim quotation of another verse is the clearest possible demonstration of what CONVENTIONS §9 says about the n-gram stream — it is a recall floor, not a ranking, and it will happily rank a proverb second inside a sentence that is already a complete quotation of something else.

Hardy's apparatus records Mark 16:15-18 at Mormon 9:25 with the observation that the wording exactly matches. The reference is right and the keying is his convention, not our parser's error: he attaches a cross-reference for a quoted span to the last verse of the span, and the span here is 9:22-25 — Moroni introduces the quotation at 9:22 with a speech formula and does not close the reported speech until 9:25. But 9:25 itself contains no Mark 16 wording at all. It reads 'whosoever shall believe in my name, doubting nothing, unto him will I confirm all my words, even unto the ends of the earth', which is Moroni's own extension of the promise and whose one rare phrase, 'doubting nothing', is a King James singleton from Acts 10:20 and is adjudicated at 9:21 with John 16:23. So the links are filed where the wording is (CONVENTIONS §6a, second bullet): Mark 16:15 at Mormon 9:22, Mark 16:16 at 9:23, and Mark 16:17 and 16:18 both at 9:24. Each of those four rows cites Hardy at 9.25 and says what his apparatus does. A reader who comes to 9:25 looking for Mark 16 is sent to the three verses above it.

Genuinely tempting, and it has to be written out. Mormon 9:26 is a chain of five rhetorical questions about the works of the Lord — 'who can stand against the works of the Lord? Who can deny his sayings?' — and Psalm 106:2 is the Bible's own rhetorical question of that shape: 'Who can utter the mighty acts of the LORD? who can shew forth all his praise?' The shape matches and the sense does not: the Psalm's question is a confession of inadequate praise, and Moroni's is a threat to opponents. The shared string is five connective words. The verse's real borrowing is at its end, where 'all ye that are despisers of the works of the Lord, for ye shall wonder and perish' takes Acts 13:41 in its Septuagint form against Habakkuk 1:5's Hebrew one, and that link is adjudicated here. Psalm 106:2 supplies neither the accusation nor the rare words.

Five connective words, 'than that which we have', shared between Moroni's 'that ye may learn to be more wise than that which we have been' and Paul's 'preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you'. Nothing content-bearing is shared: Galatians 1:8 anathematises anyone who alters the gospel, Mormon 9:31 asks not to be condemned for the imperfections of the record. The 1830 grammar of the Book of Mormon clause ('more wise than that which we have been', where a modern hand would write 'than we have been') is what produced the run, and the 1920 edition deleted the relative — so the match exists only in the first edition and is an artifact of its syntax, not of a source.

Recorded as a negative finding because a reader will look. Mormon 9:32-34, the passage on the characters, the reformed Egyptian, the altered Hebrew and the prepared means of interpretation, is the most-discussed paragraph in the chapter and it has no King James contact whatever — not a phrase, not a collocation, not a formula. Every other verse of Mormon 9 that makes a claim about God, judgment, miracle or prayer is built out of borrowed English, and the three verses that make a claim about the plates themselves are built out of none. That contrast is worth recording in the register precisely because it is invisible to the catalogue's positive apparatus, which can only list what it found.

The chapter's top-ranked candidate and a genuine KJV singleton — “creation of the world” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and it should still be declined. The singleton is arithmetic rather than distinctive: the King James Bible's ordinary idiom for the same idea is 'the foundation of the world', which it writes ten times, and it simply had occasion to write 'creation of the world' once. Romans 1:20 is an argument that God's invisible attributes are inferable from created things, and it uses the phrase adverbially, 'from the creation of the world', meaning ever since. Ether 1:3 uses it as the title of a section of a record — 'the first part of this record, which speaketh concerning the creation of the world, and also of Adam'. Nothing else of Romans 1 is anywhere near. If anything the verse tells against KJV dependence at this point, since it reaches for the collocation the KJV almost never uses.

'And Ahah was the son of Seth', matched against 'which was the son of Seth, which was the son of Adam'. The Luke 3 contact is real and is adjudicated in this chapter, but not here: the case rests on the ascending form of the whole genealogy (link at 1:6) and on the one clause that adopts Luke's relative construction (link at 1:32). At 1:10 the shared words are a name the Book of Mormon needs for its own list and the four-word chain 'was the son of', which stands in 23 KJV verses. A reader sent here by the machine should read the rows at 1:6 and 1:32. The same disposal covers the 1 Samuel 14:51 match at 1:19 — see that entry.

'And Kish was the son of Corom', matched against 'And Kish was the father of Saul; and Ner the father of Abner was the son of Abiel.' A four-word run with a proper name in it, which is why it ranked, and the name is the whole of the resemblance. Saul's father Kish is a Benjaminite whose sole narrative function is to lose the asses that send his son to Samuel; Ether's Kish is the twelfth name up a Jaredite king-list and has no story attached at this point in the record at all. The verses agree because both are genealogical notices containing a Kish, and the KJV happens to phrase its notice with the same four function words the Book of Mormon uses twenty-five times in this chapter. This entry also covers the general question of whether the chapter's formula is the Chronicler's: 1 Chronicles 6:33-38 and Ezra 7:1-5 do run ascending 'son of' chains, but they are verbless appositions — 'the son of Joel, the son of Shemuel' — and Ether 1 uses a finite clause each time. The form is argued at 1:6 and the one verbal agreement is at 1:32.

exclusions.sharedText: scattered upon all the face of the earth
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run, the longest in the chapter, and a genuine KJV singleton — but it is the Book of Mormon's own dispersion formula, adjudicated as a composite element at 1 Nephi 10:12 and excluded as a repeat at 1 Nephi 13:39, 1 Nephi 14:14, 3 Nephi 5:24, 3 Nephi 21:24 and elsewhere; the standing exclusion filed in 1 Nephi covers it. What is worth recording is what happens here and nowhere else in the corpus. This is the one verse in the Book of Mormon that narrates the event the formula describes, and at that verse the formula displaces its own scriptural source: Genesis 11:8 and 11:9 both read 'scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth', and Ether 1:33, in a sentence that has just quoted Genesis 11:9's 'confound the language', writes 'scattered upon all the face of the earth' instead — Ezekiel's word order, and the corpus's. The verse takes its event from Genesis and its words for the event from its own house style. The link at this verse is Genesis 11:9; see also Psalm 95:11 for the oath clause.

exclusions.sharedText: a large and a mighty man
exclusions.reason: The brother of Jared is introduced as 'a large and a mighty man', and the Genesis chapter immediately preceding the tower gives the only mighty man of the region: 'And Cush begat Nimrod: he began to be a mighty one in the earth' (10:8). The temptation is strong and the setting is right. But 'mighty man' is one of the KJV's commonest epithets, standing in dozens of verses, and Genesis 10:8-9 reads 'a mighty one' and 'a mighty hunter before the LORD' — not 'a mighty man' — while 'large' has no counterpart at all. The Nimrod material belongs to Ether 2:1, where the valley of Nimrod is named outright and where Hardy's apparatus keys Genesis 10:8-9; it is adjudicated there and not here.

A five-word run of pure connective tissue. 'It may be that' stands in eight KJV verses and Paul's is about wintering at Corinth. The verse's real business is the intercession formula, which is adjudicated at 1:38 against Joel 2:14 and Jonah 3:9 and which takes 1:36's 'turn away his anger' as its first half.

Five words spanning a clause boundary in both verses — Ether's 'inquire of the Lord whether he will drive us out', Paul's 'shall he receive of the Lord, whether he be bond or free'. The 'whether' governs different things and no content word is shared. Batched with it: 2 Kings 3:11's 'enquire of the LORD that we may', which is the KJV's standard oracle-seeking formula (Genesis 25:22, 1 Samuel 9:9, 1 Kings 22:5 and a dozen more) and identifies no source. The link at this verse is Hebrews 11:8.

Five words of KJV connective phrasing, in a verse about the passover of the resident alien. 'According to the word of the Lord' and its variants run through the whole Book of Mormon; covered by the standing boilerplate exclusion.

exclusions.sharedText: it came to pass that the Lord
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and the top candidate at this verse; it is 'and it came to pass', which is the type case of the standing exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 2:1. Joshua 1:1 shares nothing else with the Lord's hearing of the brother of Jared.

A genuine KJV singleton — “both male and female” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the sense is exactly opposed, which is what makes it worth an entry rather than silence. Numbers 5:3 is the law of the camp: 'Both male and female shall ye put out, without the camp shall ye put them; that they defile not their camps.' The phrase there governs expulsion of the unclean. In Ether 1:41 it governs the gathering-in of livestock for a voyage. Same four words, opposite direction of travel, and the machine ranked it first because the string is unique. The inventory Ether 1:41 is actually reproducing is Noah's, Genesis 6:19-21, where the creatures are 'male and female' and come 'after their kind' and food is gathered; the link is written there. The Genesis 7:16 candidate at the same verse — “male and female of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — is superseded by the same row, which takes 6:19-21 as the source because Ether follows the loading command and not the boarding notice.

exclusions.sharedText: and there will I meet thee
exclusions.reason: Worth recording because it is the kind of near-miss a careful reader will notice and the register should be seen to have noticed. Ether 1:42 has God appoint a rendezvous — 'And there will I meet thee' — and the KJV has a formula for God appointing a rendezvous: “there I will meet with thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 25:22, with 'where I will meet with thee' at Exodus 30:6 and 30:36 and 'there I will meet with you' at Exodus 29:42-43. But that formula is the sanctuary formula without exception: every occurrence is the mercy seat, the altar of incense or the door of the tabernacle, and it means the place where God will be permanently available to Moses, not a place to be at on a particular day. Ether's is a map reference. The word order differs too — 'there will I meet thee' against 'there I will meet with thee' — and the preposition the KJV never omits is omitted. Declined.

Four words, and in Genesis they introduce the curse on the serpent while in Ether they mark the completion of an obedient errand. The KJV writes 'because thou hast done this' at Genesis 3:14 and Genesis 22:16 with opposite valuations, which is a fair measure of how little the string carries. Batched with the same verse's Joel 3:2 match, 'down into the valley': the phrase stands in exactly two KJV verses and Joel's is the valley of Jehoshaphat, a place of judgment on gathered nations, where Ether's is a nameless valley northward that is a stage on a journey. The link at this verse is Micah 2:13.

The chapter's second-ranked candidate at this verse and its direction is reversed: “will I bless thee” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 63:4 and Psalm 145:2, and in both of them the speaker blessing is the worshipper and the one blessed is God. Ether 1:43 is God blessing a man. The clause belongs to the Abrahamic promise adjudicated at this verse against Genesis 12:2, where the KJV reads 'and I will bless thee'. Batched with the remaining machine candidates at 1:43, none of which shares a content word that construes: Leviticus 20:23 on 'the nation which I', Genesis 17:7 on 'thee and thy seed' (a real element of the promise, but the promise is fixed on Genesis 12:2 by the great-nation clause), Ezekiel 7:27 on 'I will do unto', Daniel 1:3 on 'seed and of the', Ezra 9:15 on 'thee because of this', and Ezekiel 34:6's dispersion formula for the fourth time in the chapter — see the entry at 1:33.

exclusions.sharedText: gathered … of every kind … into vessels … fish
exclusions.reason: Not proposed by the machine and tempting enough that it should be recorded as considered and declined. Read Ether 2:1-2 straight through and three rare KJV items fall in Matthew's order: 'gathered together … of every kind' (“of every kind” occurs in exactly 2 KJV verses, 1 Chronicles 28:14 and Matthew 13:47), then a vessel prepared (“into vessels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 13:48), then 'the fish of the waters'. Matthew 13:47-48 is the dragnet: 'a net, that was cast into the sea, and gathered of every kind: which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away.' Fish, of every kind, vessels — in that sequence, in one two-verse parable, and nowhere else in the KJV. It still fails, on referents. The Book of Mormon's 'of every kind' attaches to flocks gathered male and female, not to fish; its vessel is a water-tank for carrying live fish on a journey, not a sorting basket on a shore; and its fish are being preserved where Matthew's good fish are being selected and the rest thrown away. The parable is an image of the last judgment separating the righteous from the wicked, and Ether 2:1-3 is an inventory that separates nothing — the whole point of the manifest is that everything comes. The shared items are three, they are rare, and each is doing a different job in each text. The verses' real source is the ark manifest of Genesis 6:19-7:3, which is adjudicated as a link at 2:3.

A better temptation than the Samson row, because the shared element is not merely connective: both verses bring a people down into a named valley, and named valleys are not common. Joel 3:2 reads 'I will also gather all nations, and will bring them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat, and will plead with them there for my people and for my heritage Israel.' The senses are opposed at the load-bearing point. Joel's valley is the valley of decision (3:14), the nations are gathered into it to be judged and the sickle is put in because their wickedness is great; Ether's valley is a staging ground from which a favoured company departs before a judgment, and the Lord who comes down into it comes to give travel directions. Joel gathers the nations in; Ether sends one family out. The valley's name is also doing entirely different work in each — 'Jehoshaphat' is glossed by Joel as 'the LORD judgeth', 'Nimrod' is glossed by Ether as the mighty hunter of Genesis 10:9, and that gloss is where the verse's real borrowing lies (see the link at 2:1). Worth recording because the harvest-of-wrath imagery Joel 3:13 supplies does bear on this chapter — at 2:15, where 'fully ripe' is adjudicated to Revelation 14:18, which is itself rewriting Joel.

The machine's top-ranked candidate for the verse (rarity 2.00, a five-word run) and pure artifact. Judges 14:7 is Samson going down to Timnath to talk with the Philistine woman he means to marry: 'And he went down, and talked with the woman; and she pleased Samson well.' Ether 2:4 is the Lord coming down into the valley of Nimrod and talking with the brother of Jared out of a cloud he cannot be seen through. The shared string is 'down, and talked with the', of which every word is connective; the run scores because English puts those five words in that order whenever anyone descends and speaks. Nothing else of the Samson narrative is anywhere near this chapter. The real source of the verse's descent-and-speech is the cloud theophany of Numbers 11:25 and Exodus 33:9, which is adjudicated as a link at 2:4.

exclusions.sharedText: (that quarter where there never had man been)
exclusions.reason: A typological expectation with nothing under it, filed on the model of the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry in 1 Nephi. The Jaredites are sent 'into that quarter where there never had man been', and the KJV's formula for a place no man has occupied belongs almost entirely to two objects: the colt whereon never man sat (Mark 11:2, Luke 19:30) and the sepulchre wherein never man was laid (Luke 23:53, John 19:41). “never man” occurs in 5 KJV verses and four of them are those. The pull is real — a virgin land entered by a chosen remnant is a resurrection image, and this chapter will bury its travellers in the deep and raise them again at 2:24 — but the wording will not carry it. The Book of Mormon's construction is 'where there never had man been', which shares only the two commonest words of the KJV's 'wherein never man', and the Gospel formula is always about a receptacle prepared for a single sacred occupant, never about territory. Recorded so that a reader who feels the type is told the catalogue felt it too and declined it.

exclusions.sharedText: it came to pass … that the Lord did bring
exclusions.reason: 'The Lord did bring Jared and his brethren forth even to that great sea' against 'the LORD did bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their armies'. The five-word run is 'it came to pass … that the Lord did bring', and it is the exodus formula, which the Book of Mormon uses continuously and which the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 2:1 covers for 'and it came to pass'. The exodus framing of this journey is real and is catalogued where it has wording to stand on — at 2:5, where Deuteronomy 1:33's going-before, cloud and pitching of tents are reproduced, and at 2:23, where the pillar of fire is explicitly withheld. Exodus 12:51 adds nothing those rows do not have and its distinctive matter (the armies, the selfsame day, the land of Egypt) is absent. This entry also covers Joshua 1:1, which the machine returned twice in this chapter on 'it came to pass that the Lord', and Amos 7:2 at 2:4 on 'and it came to pass, that when they had'.

A five-word run and one of the register's better entries, because the coincidence is not in connective tissue but in a specified interval. Acts 5:7: 'And it was about the space of three hours after, when his wife, not knowing what was done, came in' — the three hours between Ananias's death and Sapphira's arrival, after which she lies to Peter and is carried out dead. Ether 2:14: three hours in which the Lord chastens the brother of Jared for four years of not calling on his name, at the end of which he is forgiven. Both intervals are three hours; both stand between a fault and its reckoning; and there the resemblance stops. In Acts the three hours are dead time whose only function is that Sapphira does not yet know, and the reckoning is a death sentence; in Ether the three hours are the chastening itself, and the reckoning is forgiveness within one verse. The KJV's other 'space of three' is months (Acts 19:8), which the machine also returned. Neither is a source. What the three hours in Ether 2:14 are doing is fixing the scale of a rebuke, and the KJV has no verse that does that.

exclusions.sharedText: to call upon the name of the Lord
exclusions.reason: An eight-word run, the longest in the verse, and it cannot bear a link because the phrase is stock in both corpora: “call upon the name of the Lord” occurs in 5 KJV verses (Genesis 4:26, Psalm 116:13, 116:17, Zephaniah 3:9, Romans 10:13) and the Book of Mormon uses it constantly. Recorded rather than passed over in silence because of where it falls. Genesis 4:26 is the primeval history's note that 'then began men to call upon the name of the LORD', and this chapter is saturated with Genesis 4-11 — Nimrod at 2:1, the ark manifest at 2:3, Genesis 6:3 quoted verbatim at 2:15, the ark's door and window at 2:17 and 2:23. A rebuke for NOT calling on the name of the Lord, delivered in a chapter working through Genesis in order, sitting next to the KJV verse that reports when men began to, is a pattern a careful reader would want to weigh. It does not survive the count: five KJV verses is not a source, and the Book of Mormon's own usage is dense enough that the phrase would be here whatever Genesis said. The chapter's Genesis dependence is catalogued where the wording is rare.

exclusions.sharedText: in them there is no light
exclusions.reason: Not a rejection but a cross-reference, of the kind ruled admissible at Mosiah 11:14. The brother of Jared's first complaint, 'in them there is no light', is the same six words as Isaiah 8:20's KJV singleton 'there is no light in them', in a different order. The link is written at 2:22, where the complaint is repeated in Isaiah's own word order — 'behold, there is no light in them' — because that is where the borrowing is demonstrable rather than merely present. A reader arriving at 2:19 and finding nothing should be sent three verses on rather than told there is no contact here; there is, and it is the same contact.

Considered and declined, and worth the entry because the coincidence is exact where it is exact. “dash them in pieces” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 2:9 — 'thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel' — and it is the KJV's only verse in which something is dashed in pieces AND is a vessel. Ether 2:23 is about vessels and uses 'dashed in pieces' in the same breath. But the grammar refuses it: what will be dashed in pieces in Ether is the windows, and the vessels are the thing the windows would be set into, so the two rare terms sit on opposite sides of the sentence from where Psalm 2 puts them. The senses are opposed as well — Psalm 2:9 is the Son shattering rebellious nations with an iron rod, Ether 2:23 is a shipwright's objection about glazing — and “dashed in pieces” itself occurs in 4 KJV verses (Exodus 15:6, Hosea 10:14, 13:16, Nahum 3:10), all of them massacres. There is no route from any of them to a window. The verse's real sources are Genesis 6:16 and Exodus 13:21, both adjudicated as links at 2:23.

A five-word run and the machine's third candidate for the verse: 'I will bring you up out of the affliction of Egypt unto the land of the Canaanites.' The words are right and the verse is not. Exodus 3:17's motion is up out of Egypt into Canaan, a geography with no sea in it and no depths; the run scores because 'I will bring you up' is a common divine promise. Ether 2:24's clause is 'I will bring you up again out of the depths of the sea', and its distinctive elements are 'again' and 'the depths of the sea', neither of which Exodus 3:17 has. Both are KJV singletons elsewhere — “from the depths of the sea” at Psalm 68:22, which is also a first-person promise of the Lord to bring his people back out of the sea, and “bring me up again” at Psalm 71:20. The link is written at 2:24 to Psalm 68:22 with Psalm 71:20 as composite.

The machine returned Matthew 20:32 at both 2:23 and 2:25 as the top candidate, on the four words 'What will ye that I'.
