Matthew's form is 'What will ye that I shall do unto you?' and the Book of Mormon's is 'What will ye that I should do' — 'should', not 'shall', which is Mark's. “that I should do unto thee” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 10:51, the question put to blind Bartimaeus whose answer is 'that I might receive my sight'. The link is written at 2:23, the question's first occurrence, with Matthew 20:32 and Mark 10:36 recorded as composite because the Book of Mormon's plural 'ye' is theirs and its 'I should do' is Mark 10:51's. This entry sends a reader at 2:25 — where the question is asked a second time, and where the Lord finally completes it with 'that ye may have light' — to the adjudication at 2:23 rather than repeating it.

A four-word run and the joint top-ranked candidate in the chapter, and it is bare narrative connective. “Went forth unto the mount” differs from “went forth unto the spring of the waters” in everything but the movement verb and two function words. Elisha is healing a water source at Jericho; the brother of Jared is climbing a mountain with molten stones. This entry stands for the whole class of “went forth / go forth unto” matches in Ether 3 — 2 Samuel 13:39 at 3:21 among them — which are not listed individually, per CONVENTIONS §5.

“out of a rock” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 15:46, and a singleton in a chapter this saturated deserves an answer rather than silence. The temptation is real and it is specifically theological: Mark 15:46 is the burial, a body of flesh laid in a place hewn out of a rock and closed with a stone, and Ether 3 is a chapter about stones worked out of a rock in which the Lord's flesh is seen and a record is sealed up. A reader who finds the singleton will build that reading. The catalogue declines it on the verb. Mark's tomb is hewn — cut away, subtractive, a cavity — and Ether 3:1 and 3:3 both read moulten, which is the opposite operation and is the whole physical point of the verse, since only melting produces stone “white and clear, even as transparent glass”. Strip the verbs and what remains is rock, out of, and the article. Nothing else of Mark 15 is anywhere in the chapter: no burial, no linen, no sepulchre, no rolling. The genuine link at 3:1 is Exodus 34:4, where a man works stone and carries it up a mountain, and Revelation 21:21 for the glass; the Markan echo is an accident of the commonest preposition in English meeting the commonest word for stone.

Not a machine proposal but the association a well-read reader brings, and it needs recording because it survives further into the chapter than most. “white stone” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 2:17, where the overcomer is given a white stone “and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it” — a stone that carries writing only its recipient can read. Ether 3 has sixteen white stones, and twenty-two verses later two stones are sealed up with a text “in a language that they cannot be read”, to be interpreted only by the gift they carry. The convergence of white stone, private writing and privileged reading is striking. It is also assembled from two different places in the chapter, and the wording will not bear it: Ether 3:1's stones are “white and clear”, an optical description of transparency required by their purpose, and they are not the two stones of 3:23, which are never called white. Revelation 2:17's stone bears a name, not a script; nobody interprets it; and the whole point of Ether's stones is that they make another text legible rather than carrying a text themselves. Filed so that a reader who assembles the parallel is told the catalogue assembled it too and declined it. The real Revelation contact in this verse is 21:21's transparent glass, which is catalogued as a link.

The five-word match is “the earth and the LORD”, which straddles a clause boundary in both verses and is therefore not a phrase at all: in Ezekiel it joins “the LORD hath forsaken the earth” to “and the LORD seeth not”, and in Ether it joins “had fallen to the earth” to “and the Lord said unto him”. Ezekiel 9 is the marking of Jerusalem for slaughter. The real source at 3:7 is Joshua 7:10, whose “Get thee up; wherefore liest thou thus upon thy face?” the machine stream could not see because the Book of Mormon's wording modernises it.

Four words of which three are function words. Genesis 46:29 has Joseph presenting himself to his father at Goshen; the shared string is the reflexive plus the dative plus a conjunction, and it will attach to any sentence in which somebody shows himself to somebody else. The genuine contact for “shewed himself” in this chapter is the post-resurrection idiom of John 21:1, which is catalogued as a link at 3:17 where the phrase is fullest.

The model exclusion for this chapter, because the rarity is genuine and misleading in equal measure. “my sons and my daughters” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 31:28, and “sons and daughters” without the possessives occurs in exactly twenty-six, most of them the begetting formula of Genesis 5 and 11. So the machine correctly reports a five-word singleton — and the singleton is Laban complaining to Jacob that he was not allowed to kiss his grandchildren goodbye. The sense is not merely different but domestic and aggrieved, and nothing else of Genesis 31 is within reach. The verse's real sources are catalogued: John 1:12 supplies the adoption clause, with three separate KJV singletons of its own (“believe on his name”, “power to become”, “become the sons of God”), and 2 Corinthians 6:18 supplies the daughters in the King James Bible's one formula for the pair as divine promise, “ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty”. Note the general lesson: a possessive-plus-plural singleton is almost always an artifact of the possessives, and the count to run is the one without them.

Five function words. Leviticus 5:17 is the guilt offering for an unwitting sin; Ether 3:17 is Moroni excusing the brevity of his abridgement. This entry covers the same class of match at 3:21, where “these things which ye have” pulled Acts 8:24, Deuteronomy 1:18 and John 8:38, and where “the time cometh that” pulled John 16:2. None is listed separately.

A four-word run that exists only in the 1830 text, which is worth stating for its own sake: the first edition reads “the many great works which the Lord had shewed unto him” and the 1920 edition prints “showed”, so the modern text no longer matches the KJV string at all and a search of the current edition would not find this candidate (CONVENTIONS §8). Having said that, the match is not a borrowing. 2 Chronicles 7:10 is the dismissal of the people after the dedication of Solomon's temple, glad for “the goodness that the LORD had shewed unto David”; shew unto is the King James Bible's ordinary construction for divine favour displayed to a person, and Ether uses it four times in this chapter alone (3:13, 3:17, 3:18, 3:26). The real Chronicles-shaped question at 3:18 is not verbal, and the chapter's substantive links stand elsewhere.

exclusions.sharedText: it came to pass that the Lord
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and the longest in the chapter, and it is the Book of Mormon's own most-used sentence opener meeting the King James Bible's. It scored twice, here and at 3:28, on the same string. Covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; recorded once here only because the run length will otherwise look like an oversight to anyone reading the dossier. Joshua 1:1 is the commissioning of Joshua after Moses' death and has nothing to do with either verse.

A five-word run of pure donation formula: Jeremiah 45:5 promises Baruch “thy life will I give unto thee for a prey”, which is a rescue from the fall of Jerusalem and shares nothing with Ether 3:23 but the verb and its pronouns. The candidate is superseded rather than merely rejected. The King James Bible has one verse in which God promises to give a man stone — Exodus 24:12, “Come up to me into the mount, and be there: and I will give thee tables of stone”, a singleton — and that is the sentence Ether 3:23 is built on, in a chapter that has been running the Sinai ascent since 3:1. The link is catalogued there.

“And when the Lord had said these words” is the Book of Mormon's standard resumption after reported speech and it appears twice in this chapter, at 3:13 and 3:25. Acts 28:29 is the Jews departing from Paul's lodging in Rome. Covered by the standing formulaic exclusion; the neighbouring 1 Kings 4:34 candidate at the same verse (“of the earth which had”) is a clause-straddling match of the same kind and is not listed separately.

The best-looking rejected candidate in the chapter, and the one the register exists for. “shewed unto him all” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 4:5 — “And the devil, taking him up into an high mountain, shewed unto him all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time” — and Ether 3:25 reads “the Lord shewed unto the brother of Jared all the inhabitants of the earth”. Syntax, verb, spelling, quantifier and the mountain all agree, and the 1830 “shewed” makes the agreement exact where the 1920 “showed” would hide it. It is still the wrong verse, and for a reason a catalogue should be able to state: in Luke the shower is the devil, the showing is the second temptation, the content is dominion offered for worship, and the correct response is refusal. In Ether the shower is the Lord, the showing is the reward of unequalled faith, and the content is not offered but disclosed. A panorama shown from a mountain by a tempter and a panorama shown from a mountain by God are the same stage business in opposite plays. The link at this verse is Deuteronomy 34:1, where “the LORD shewed him all the land” from the top of Pisgah — one of only two KJV verses reading “the LORD shewed him” — which keeps the chapter's Moses frame and gets the agent right.

The chapter's top-ranked machine candidate and pure connective tissue. “the children of men” is one of the Book of Mormon's commonest phrases and “come unto” one of its commonest verbs; the run is an accident of their meeting. Exodus 3:13 is Moses asking God for a name to give Israel, and shares no content word with a verse about writings withheld from publication. Covered in principle by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5 and listed here only because it heads the ranking for this chapter and a reader checking our work will meet it first.

A five-word run scoring 2.00, and it is a speech-introduction formula in both texts. Micaiah is promising Ahab's messenger that he will say only what the LORD tells him; Moroni is introducing a divine oracle about when the sealed record goes to the Gentiles. The Book of Mormon uses “saith the Lord” and its variants continuously — three more times inside this chapter alone (4:7 twice, 4:8) — so no single KJV verse can be the source of the formula. Note also that the 1830's “For the Lord saith unto me” is present tense where the 1920 reads “said”, which is a variant worth having but bears on the editorial history, not on any borrowing.

exclusions.sharedText: the heavens and of the earth
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate at this verse — a seven-word run, rarity 3.00 — and it is genuinely present: “the Father of the heavens and of the earth” has Genesis 2:4's double genitive, which the KJV's more usual “heaven and earth” does not. But it is the smaller half of the verse's borrowing. The clause that follows, “and all things that in them is”, carries a grammatical fossil of Exodus 20:11 (the singular verb surviving a pluralised subject) that identifies its source beyond argument, and it is where the link is catalogued; Genesis 2:4 is recorded there as a composite. A reader who arrives at this verse through the machine ranking is sent to the Exodus 20:11 row.

Two candidates rank at this verse on the same string, Jeremiah 17:15 and 1 Chronicles 10:13, and “the word of the LORD” occurs in exactly 255 KJV verses. It is the King James Bible's standing designation for a prophetic communication and cannot point at any one of them. This entry covers both. The real borrowing at 4:8 is “let him be accursed”, which occurs in two KJV verses and is catalogued to Galatians 1:8; the machine could not see it because Galatians 1:8's surrounding words are entirely different, which is CONVENTIONS §9's point about the n-gram stream being a recall floor.

The most tempting rejection in the chapter and the reason this register exists. “so as by fire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — 1 Corinthians 3:15, “he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire” — and Ether 4:9 ends “the inhabitants thereof shall pass away, even so as by fire”. A four-word King James singleton reproduced with one word changed is normally decisive evidence, and here it is not, because the two verses use the fire for opposite purposes. Paul's fire tries a man's work, destroys the work, and lets the man through; the adverbial “yet” is doing the whole job, conceding a loss in order to affirm a salvation. Ether 4:9's fire is the instrument by which the inhabitants of the earth are removed, and its “even” intensifies a threat rather than qualifying a rescue. Nothing else of 1 Corinthians 3 is anywhere near this verse — no builders, no foundation, no gold and stubble, no day that declares it — and Ether 4:9's three clauses are otherwise a catalogue of cosmic authority (heavens opened and shut, earth shaken) with no soteriology in them at all. Recorded at length so that a reader who runs the rarity count and finds the singleton is told the catalogue found it too, and why it declined. The link at this verse is placed on Joel 3:16 instead, on the shaking.

The machine matched “that i am and” against “I AM THAT I AM: and”, and the temptation is real, because Ether 4:12 is a chain of divine self-predications (“I am the Father, I am the light, and the life”) and Exodus 3:14 is the one KJV verse where the divine name is a self-predication. But the shared words are not doing the same work. In Ether 4:12 “that I am” is the object of a verb of believing — “he that will not believe me, that I am” — an ellipsis for believing in the speaker's existence or identity; in Exodus 3:14 “THAT” is a relative and the phrase is a name given to Moses to repeat. The Book of Mormon's absolute “I am” self-predications in this verse are Johannine in form (see the John 14:6 row), not Mosaic, and the chapter shows no other contact with the burning bush.

“For good cometh of none, save it be of me” states in the Lord's own voice what Mark 10:18 and Matthew 19:17 state as a question — “Why callest thou me good? there is none good but one, that is, God”. The proposition is the same and the phrase “none good but one” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both of them that saying. It is excluded on two counts. There is no shared distinctive wording at all: “none” and “good” are the only common words and their syntax differs entirely. And the sense is inverted at the point that matters most — the synoptic saying deflects the title away from the speaker, and Ether 4:12 claims it for him. A Book of Mormon verse in which Christ says that all good comes of him is doing the opposite of the verse in which Christ declines to be called good. Recorded because a reader who knows the synoptic saying will think of it here.

“The knowledge which is hid up because of unbelief” invites Colossians 2:3, “in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge”, and “the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Two words in common is not enough, and the two hidings are of different kinds: Paul's knowledge is hidden *in Christ* as a location, permanently and by nature, while Ether 4:13's is hidden *from* a people, contingently, and released on repentance. The concealment language in this passage is adjudicated two verses later, at 4:15, where “hid up from the foundation of the world” has a real KJV background in Matthew 13:35's “kept secret from the foundation of the world” — a hiding that is likewise a withholding from those who will not receive, and that carries the parable theory the chapter is working with. A reader at 4:13 is sent there.

A five-word run scoring 2.00 across a clause boundary, and every word of it is connective. Ether 4:15's “...from the foundation of the world from you; yea, when ye shall call upon the Father” and Isaiah 1:15's “I will hide mine eyes from you: yea, when ye make many prayers” happen to place the same three particles in the same order. There is a faint thematic overlap — both concern prayer that God will or will not hear — but Isaiah 1:15 refuses the prayers of bloody hands and Ether 4:15 promises to hear the broken-hearted, and the resemblance does not survive the second clause. A textbook case of the n-gram stream scoring rare boilerplate (CONVENTIONS §9).

exclusions.sharedText: upon all the face of the
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and a stock KJV locution for extent — “upon all the face of the earth” at Genesis 1:29, 7:3, 8:9, 11:4 and elsewhere. Ezekiel 34:6 ranked only because its noun is “earth” and the surrounding words happen to align; the Book of Mormon's phrase is “upon all the face of the land”, which is its own standing formula, used dozens of times across the corpus. No contact with Ezekiel's scattered flock.

exclusions.sharedText: repent all ye ends of the earth, and come unto me
exclusions.reason: The call that opens 4:18 looks Isaianic — “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 45:22) is the KJV's one summons of the earth's ends to salvation, and the resemblance of shape is close. But “the ends of the earth” occurs in 28 KJV verses and “ye ends of the earth” in none of them, while the Book of Mormon has the vocative exactly, in the risen Lord's mouth, at 3 Nephi 9:22: “therefore repent, and come unto me ye ends of the earth, and be saved.” Ether 4:18 reproduces that sentence's three verbs in that order — repent, come unto me, be saved — with baptism inserted. The proximate model is the corpus's own, and the Isaiah verse stands behind 3 Nephi 9:22 rather than behind this one. Filed here rather than as a low-confidence link because the link that matters at 4:18 is the seventeen-word reproduction of Mark 16:16 in the second half of the verse.

exclusions.sharedText: shall be saved: but he that
exclusions.reason: A six-word run, and “shall be saved but he” occurs in exactly two KJV verses — Proverbs 28:18 and Mark 16:16. The machine ranked both and they are not equivalent candidates: Proverbs shares a bare antithetical formula, Mark shares seventeen consecutive words including the singleton “shall be damned”. Recorded so the register shows the pair was seen and resolved, not that the second-ranked candidate went unexamined.

‘Touch them not’ occurs in no KJV verse, and the typological pull here is strong enough to be worth resisting in writing. A holy object that may not be handled is 2 Samuel 6:6-7 — Uzzah putting forth his hand to the ark and dying for it — and a sealed record forbidden to the unauthorised is close enough to that story that a reader will think of it. But the wording will not carry any of it: 2 Samuel has ‘put forth his hand to the ark of God, and took hold of it’, with no prohibition uttered at all. Of the six KJV verses reading ‘touch not’, Colossians 2:21 is an ascetic slogan Paul is quoting in order to reject it, 2 Corinthians 6:17's object is ‘the unclean thing’, and 1 Chronicles 16:22 and Psalm 105:15 protect the Lord's anointed, i.e. persons; the remaining two, Lamentations 4:15 and Luke 11:46, are further off still. None is about a sacred artefact, and none shares a distinctive word with Ether 5:1. Recorded so that a reader who sees the ark here is told the catalogue saw it and declined it; compare the standing Exodus 2:2 ‘goodly’ entry, which is this failure mode's model case.

A window artifact, and instructive as one. Moroni writes ‘except by and by it shall be wisdom in God’, in which ‘by and’ ends one idiom and ‘by it shall be’ is not a phrase at all — the four-word run straddles the seam. Jeremiah 49:17 and 1 Kings 9:8 both read ‘every one that passeth by it shall be astonished’, where ‘by it’ means past the ruined house. The two ‘by’s are different words doing different jobs. Both candidates are excluded on the same ground and neither is listed twice.

‘By and by’ occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Matthew 13:21, Mark 6:25, Luke 17:7, Luke 21:9 — which is rare enough to tempt, and the idiom is unmistakably of the KJV's period, so it is real evidence for the register the Book of Mormon is writing in. It is not evidence for any one verse, and it points the wrong way besides. In all four KJV instances ‘by and by’ means *immediately* (‘the end is not by and by’; ‘give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist’). Moroni's ‘except by and by it shall be wisdom in God’ requires the later English sense, *in due course*, which the KJV never has. The phrase is diagnostic of the 1830 text's idiom and not of a borrowing; it appears in five verses of the 1830 text (3 Nephi 27:11, Alma 32:42, 55:11, 55:14 and here). No source verse is identifiable and none should be proposed.

The chapter's top-ranked candidate at 5:1 and a five-word run, and it is pure connective tissue. Psalm 45:1's ‘I speak of the things which I have made touching the king’ and Moroni's ‘I have told you the things which I have sealed up’ share a relative-clause frame and not one content word: no speaking, no king, no sealing, no writing. The window is long only because ‘the things which I have’ is a shape English sentences fall into. This entry covers the same run wherever it recurs in the chapter.

Three machine candidates at 5:3 and one at 5:4 rest on this phrase alone — 2 Corinthians 6:7, 1 Peter 1:5, 2 Corinthians 13:4, and at 5:4 the six-word run against 1 Corinthians 1:24, where ‘the power of God and’ is a KJV singleton only because the next words are ‘the wisdom of God’. ‘By the power of God’ is a New Testament commonplace with no distinctive attachment, and the Book of Mormon uses it continuously. Nothing else of any of these verses is present: 1 Corinthians 1:24 is about the scandal of the cross to Jews and Greeks, 1 Peter 1:5 about being kept unto salvation. The rarity scores here are arithmetic, not evidence. This entry covers all four.

2 John 1:9 and 1 John 2:22 both end with ‘the Father and the Son’ and both scored well here. They are superseded. Ether 5:4 does not name two persons but three — ‘the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Ghost beareth record’ — and the KJV has exactly one sentence in which three named divine persons bear record, 1 John 5:7, four chapters from one of these candidates and one chapter from the other. The link is filed at 5:4 to 1 John 5:7; 2 John 1:9's polemic about abiding in the doctrine of Christ and 1 John 2:22's about the antichrist share the two-person formula and nothing else. Luke 2:25's ‘and the Holy Ghost’ and Luke 12:53's ‘the son and the father’ are covered by the same reasoning and are not listed separately.

‘For a testimony against’ occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Matthew 10:18, Mark 6:11, Mark 13:9, Luke 9:5 — and all four are the same saying: shake the dust off your feet, or be dragged before governors, ‘for a testimony against them’. The verbal contact with ‘shall stand as a testimony against the world’ is closer than anything Deuteronomy offers, so a reader working from strings alone would land here. It is the wrong place. The synoptic testimony is a gesture made by departing missionaries against a town that refused them; Ether 5:4's is a written record deposited to be produced at the last day, which is Deuteronomy 31:19-26's procedure and no one else's. The link is filed at 5:4 to Deuteronomy 31:26, figural and with its own whyNot, and this entry sends a reader who came for the string to the row that has the argument.

Three synoptic candidates — Matthew 24:3, Mark 13:4, Luke 21:7 — all the same question at the head of the same discourse, ‘Tell us, when shall these things be?’ There the words are an interrogative asking about timing; in Ether 5:4 they are the subject and auxiliary of ‘shall these things be established’, which the catalogue adjudicates to Deuteronomy 19:15 by way of 2 Corinthians 13:1. The run is real and the parse is wrong, which is the same failure as the 5:1 ‘by it shall be’ entry: a contiguous window is blind to where the clause boundaries are. All three are excluded together.

exclusions.sharedText: the Father in the name of
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate at 5:5 and a six-word run, and the senses do not touch. Ephesians 5:20 is about thanksgiving — ‘giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ’ — where ‘in the name of’ modifies the giving of thanks and the Father is its recipient. Ether 5:5 is about access: ‘if it so be that they repent and come unto the Father in the name of Jesus’, where the name licenses an approach that repentance has made possible. The shared string is the KJV's ordinary way of attaching a name to an act directed at the Father, which is why it is long; it identifies a construction, not a source. The catalogue's reading of the verse is filed to John 14:6, the KJV's one verse about coming unto the Father, where the exclusivity Ether 5:5 implies is stated outright.

‘Into the kingdom of God’ occurs in ten KJV verses, six of them the camel-and-the-needle saying in its three synoptic forms and its immediate repetitions. The verb is the difficulty as much as the count: nine of the ten read *enter* into the kingdom of God and the tenth (Matthew 21:31) *go* into it, while Ether 5:5 has *received* into the kingdom of God, which is in no KJV verse. Nothing points at John 3:5 or at any of the other nine. Recorded because the phrase is prominent enough in the verse that its absence from the link list would otherwise look like an oversight.

A KJV singleton, a five-word run, and the top-scoring candidate in the verse — and a textbook instance of the trap CONVENTIONS §9 describes, where rare boilerplate outranks real evidence. ‘And now, if I have found favour in thine eyes’ is David's excuse, relayed by Jonathan, for missing Saul's table; the singleton status comes from the accident that the KJV's many ‘if I have found favour’ formulas are prefaced ‘and now’ exactly once. Ether 5:6's continuation is ‘if I have no authority for these things’ — a negation, a different verb, and a challenge rather than a petition. The next word after the run diverges and the sense diverges with it, which is the ‘window closes one word early’ failure (ADJUDICATING §4).

The most tempting rejection in the chapter, and it is rejected narrowly. ‘Ye shall see me’ occurs in exactly three KJV verses, John 16:16, 16:17 and 16:19, which are three recitals of one saying — ‘a little while, and ye shall not see me: and again, a little while, and ye shall see me’ — so the rarity is one saying, not three attestations. The thematic fit is genuine: a speaker who is about to be absent promises his hearers a future seeing at which their present perplexity will be resolved, and Moroni, writing from the far side of his own death, tells his reader ‘ye shall know that I have authority when ye shall see me’. But the words are four of the commonest in the language in their commonest order, John's saying is inseparable from its ‘a little while’ frame and Moroni has no trace of that frame, and John's promised seeing is a reunion in joy (16:22) where Moroni's is an appearance before God's judgment. What the verse actually reaches for at that point is Revelation 20:12's ‘stand before God’, a KJV singleton, and that is where the link is filed. Recorded here rather than passed over because a reader who hears John 16 in the sentence has heard something real, and should be told the catalogue heard it and weighed it.

The chapter's top-ranked candidate at this verse and it is an accident of English word order. Ether 6:2 has 'the brother of Jared came down out of the mount, and he did put forth the stones'; Judges 3:27 has 'he blew a trumpet in the mountain of Ephraim, and the children of Israel went down with him from the mount, and he before them'. The shared run straddles a clause boundary in both and consists of an article, a noun the Book of Mormon has already used four times in Ether 3 for Shelem, and a pronoun. Ehud's muster after the killing of Eglon has no contact of any kind with the lighting of the barges. Covered here rather than passed over in silence only because it is the sole candidate the machine offered for a verse that does have a genuine source, adjudicated at 6:3.

Ether 6:4 ends 'commending themselves unto the Lord their God'; Numbers 6:2 has men and women who 'separate themselves unto the LORD' by the vow of a Nazarite. The four words are a reflexive pronoun and a prepositional phrase, and the verbs they attach to are unrelated — commending is entrusting, separating is consecrating. Nothing else of the Nazarite legislation is anywhere near this chapter. The Jeremiah 3:7, Amos 7:2 and Joshua 5:8 candidates at this same verse are 'and it came to pass' and 'had done all these things' and are covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

A four-word run and a real one: 'And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam'. But 'the LORD God caused' is the KJV's ordinary way of narrating any divine act with a causative verb, and the object here is a surgical anaesthetic in Eden. The temptation is worth naming because the chapter genuinely is running Genesis — but it is running Genesis 7-11, not Genesis 2, and the borrowing at this verse is 'the face of the waters' and 'a wind', both of which come from the flood. Filed as wrong-sense rather than formulaic because a reader who noticed that Ether 6 is a creation-and-flood chapter might reasonably take the Eden verse for evidence of it.

exclusions.sharedText: upon the waves of the sea
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter and the one most likely to tempt a reader, because it shares six consecutive words with Ether 6:5 and because both sentences are about God and the sea. It is declined on distribution and on sense. “waves of the sea” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Job 9:8, Psalm 93:4, Isaiah 48:18 and Jude 1:13 — which is not rare enough to identify a source for a phrase this ordinary, and the preposition that completes the run is doing opposite work in the two texts: Job's God treads upon the waves, walking on them in sovereignty, while Ether's Jaredites are tossed upon them, helpless. Job 9:8 is a hymn to divine transcendence in a speech about the impossibility of contending with God; Ether 6:5 is a report of a voyage. The verse's real source is adjudicated at 6:5 (Genesis 8:1, with Genesis 7:18), and the storm sequence it belongs to at 6:7 (Psalm 107).

“the fierceness of” occurs in exactly ten KJV verses and in nine of them the genitive is anger, wrath or indignation; the tenth, Jeremiah 25:38, has 'the fierceness of the oppressor'. Ether 6:6 has 'the fierceness of the wind'. The Book of Mormon has taken a KJV idiom for the intensity of rage and applied it to weather, which is a small stylistic observation and not a dependence on any one verse. Jeremiah 25:38's lion forsaking his covert has nothing to do with a storm at sea.

'Because of the mountain waves which broke upon them' against 'Because of the mountain of Zion, which is desolate, the foxes walk upon it'. The match ends exactly where the content begins: Lamentations' next word is 'of', introducing a genitive, and Ether's next word is 'waves', making 'mountain' an attributive adjective — a use the KJV never makes of the word. 'Mountain waves' is not a biblical construction at all, which is the interesting fact here and the reason the entry is written: the most vivid image in the Jaredite storm is one of the few phrases in the chapter with no King James background.

Typology pulls hard here. Isaiah 43:2 — 'When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned' — is the Bible's standing promise that water will not hurt the covenant people, and Ether 6:7 says 'there was no water that could hurt them'. But there is not one distinctive shared word. Isaiah's verbs are pass, overflow, walk, burn; Ether's are hurt, encompass, cry, bring forth. “no water” occurs in exactly seventeen KJV verses and every one of them is about drought or an empty pit, which is the opposite problem. Recorded so that a reader who sees the Isaiah promise behind the barges is told the catalogue saw it too and declined it; the deliverance language at this verse comes from Psalm 107:28, adjudicated at 6:7.

exclusions.sharedText: the Lord all the day long
exclusions.reason: A six-word run, and the second-highest score in the chapter, and worthless. “the day long” occurs in exactly thirteen KJV verses, spread across Deuteronomy, the Psalms and Proverbs, and it attaches indifferently to boasting, mourning, being plagued, coveting and being killed. Proverbs 23:17's own sentence is 'be thou in the fear of the LORD all the day long', a warning against envying sinners; Ether 6:9 is a doxology on a boat. The run scores because 'the LORD' happens to precede the adverbial in Proverbs, which is a fact about the two English word orders. The verse's real contact is Psalm 68:32, adjudicated at 6:9.

'And the brother of Jared also begat sons and daughters' reproduces, word for word, a clause that stands in exactly eighteen KJV verses, all but one of them in the antediluvian genealogy of Genesis 5 and the post-flood genealogy of Genesis 11 (the exception is 2 Chronicles 24:3). That is a real signal and not a coincidence — a chapter that has just crossed a flood and landed is now generating a genealogy in the exact formula Genesis uses on the far side of its own flood — but it cannot be keyed to any single verse, and the formula is the KJV's rather than any one passage's. The observation is adjudicated at 6:18, where it belongs to the Genesis 8-11 sequence argument as a whole. A reader who arrives at 6:15 looking for its source should go there.

'Before they went down to their graves' against 'So they went down to Bethel'. Four words of pure motion-verb-plus-preposition, and the destinations could hardly be further apart: Elisha refusing to leave Elijah on the road to Bethel, and two old men contemplating their burial. Ether 6:19 and 6:21 use the idiom twice in three verses because 'go down to the grave' is the King James way of saying die — “go down to the grave” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 2:6 and Job 21:13, neither of which is in view. Recorded because 2 Kings 2 is a live route in this corpus (1 Nephi 3:15, 1 Nephi 4:2) and a reader might reasonably expect it to be one here.

“a king over them” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, and this is the other one: 'And they had a king over them, which is the angel of the bottomless pit, whose name in the Hebrew tongue is Abaddon.' Listed because the rarity argument at 6:22 depends on the count, and a reader checking it will find this verse and should be told why it was set aside. Judges 9:8 supplies the whole clause the Book of Mormon has — anointing, a king, over them — while Revelation 9:11 supplies only the last four words and supplies them of the locusts of the fifth trumpet. There is a genuine thematic irony in the fact that the KJV's only two kings-over-them are a bramble and Abaddon, and the 6:22 link's significance field makes that point without needing this verse as a source.

A tempting one, and worth setting out because two independent things point at it. Genesis 21:11, 'And the thing was very grievous in Abraham's sight because of his son', is the KJV's one sentence in which a father finds a proposal about his son grievous, and Ether 6:23 is 'this was grievous unto them' said of a proposal to make one of their sons a king. “grievous in” occurs in exactly three KJV verses and two of them are this Abraham scene. But the syntax will not carry it: the KJV construction is invariably 'grievous in the sight of' someone, and the Book of Mormon has 'grievous unto them', which is not a KJV idiom at all. And the sense is wrong at the point that matters — Abraham grieves at losing a son, the brother of Jared grieves at one of them being crowned. The 1 Samuel 8:6 parallel, where 'the thing displeased Samuel, when they said, Give us a king', is much the closer situational match and is adjudicated at 6:19; the verse's own borrowing is Revelation 13:10, adjudicated at 6:23.

The strongest exclusion in the chapter and the one a careful reader would most likely accept. “to be their king” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Acts 13:22, 'he raised up unto them David to be their king' — and Ether 6:25 has 'he commanded them that they should constrain no man to be their king'. A four-word singleton in a chapter about making a king is exactly the shape this catalogue normally accepts, and Acts 13 is already a live route in the corpus: Mosiah 29:23 is built out of Acts 13:10, and Acts 13:21, one verse before the singleton, is the New Testament's only retelling of Israel's demand for a king. It is nevertheless declined, for two reasons. The run is a singleton by arithmetic rather than by diction — four of the commonest words in English, in the only order that makes an infinitive of them, and the KJV simply had few occasions to write it. And the sense is not merely different but inverted: Acts 13:22 is God raising a man up to the throne, Ether 6:25 is a father forbidding anyone to be forced onto it. The kingship borrowing in this passage is Judges 9:8, adjudicated at 6:22, and the refusal sequence Judges 9:9-15, adjudicated at 6:26; a reader who arrives at 6:25 should go to both. Noted for a future sweep: if Acts 13:21-22 turns out to stand behind other Jaredite accession formulas, this entry should be revisited.

Ether 6:25 in the 1830 reads 'the first born of the brother of Jared' as two words, which is how Exodus 11:5 spells it in its second occurrence — 'from the first born of Pharaoh that sitteth upon his throne' — and how 1920 does not, having normalised the Book of Mormon to 'firstborn'. That orthographic agreement is worth recording under CONVENTIONS §8, and it is all there is: 'the firstborn of' is the KJV's standard genitive and Exodus 11:5 is the death of the Egyptian firstborn, which has no bearing on a Jaredite who declines a crown. The Titus 3:2 ('no man to be'), Genesis 37:11 ('him but his father') and 2 Kings 11:17 ('king and the people') candidates at this verse are connective and are passed over under the standing exclusion.

A five-word run whose fifth word is 'to', and the two continuations are 'prosper' and 'commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab'. The Book of Mormon uses 'the people began to' as a narrative hinge throughout — it is one of Mormon's and Moroni's commonest transitions — and Numbers 25:1 is the apostasy at Shittim. No contact. Recorded only because it scored 1.50 and is the top candidate at the verse.

'For all the goodness that the LORD had done for David his servant, and for Israel his people' — and the context is genuinely apt, since 1 Kings 8:66 dismisses the people joyful and glad of heart after a king has dedicated the temple. But the five shared words are the ordinary way of saying what God did for someone, and what identifies Ether 6:30's source is the phrase in front of them, 'how great things', which 1 Kings 8:66 does not have. Adjudicated at 6:30 as 1 Samuel 12:24 in the wording of Mark 5:19; the Mark 5:19 candidate the machine ranked first at this verse is not excluded but is recorded there as the composite and as the live alternative.

The top-ranked candidate at 7:2 and at 7:4, on a six-word run, and it is the King James Bible's genealogical boilerplate. “he begat sons and daughters” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, but the phrase without the pronoun occurs in eighteen, and every one of them is Genesis 5 or Genesis 11 — the antediluvian and post-Babel descent lists. That is a formula, not a source: the KJV writes it once per generation for sixteen generations precisely because it carries no information. The Book of Mormon uses it the same way, four times in this chapter alone (7:2, 7:4, 7:12, 7:26), and it enters Ether earlier still, at 6:15-16, so 7:2 is not even its first Jaredite occurrence. The second machine proposal here, 2 Chronicles 24:3 (Jehoiada's two wives), is the same string in a narrative with nothing else in common. Numbers 26:62 was also proposed, for 'twenty and three', which in that verse is a Levite census figure in thousands. What Ether 7:1-2 does with its numbers is argued at the Judges 10:4 link on this verse; the begetting formula is not part of that argument.

The machine's only candidate at 7:3, and it is the right chapter of the Bible for the wrong reason. Genesis 37:3 reads 'because he was the son of his old age', and “son of his old age” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — a genuine rarity, but a different construction from the one Ether has. The Book of Mormon's string is 'begat Kib in his old age', and “in his old age” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 21:2 and Genesis 21:7, both of them Isaac's birth to Abraham. The link is written at this verse to Genesis 21:2, and the Isaac context is what makes it worth writing; Joseph's coat contributes nothing.

A four-word run and a real temptation, because both verses are about a son set against his father and a household divided. The senses are opposed at the only point that matters. Matthew 10:35 is Christ describing the cost of discipleship — the division is caused by the gospel, the divided son is in the right, and the saying is a warning issued by the one who causes it. Ether 7:4 is a prince of thirty-two raising an army to depose his father and put him in captivity, an act the chapter treats as the first crime in Jaredite history and the fulfilment of a prophecy of bondage. Matthew's variance is a consequence of righteousness; Corihor's is rebellion. Nothing else of Matthew 10 is present, and the daughters and mothers-in-law that make up the rest of the verse have no counterpart. The real borrowing in this verse is at its other end — 'drew away many people after him', Acts 5:37 — and is catalogued as a link.

The highest-scoring candidate at 7:10, and it is the regnal accession formula, which the KJV uses of nearly every king of Israel and Judah. Shallum the son of Jabesh contributes nothing but the syntax of beginning to reign; his month in Samaria has no counterpart here. The Book of Mormon's use of the KJV's dynastic formulary is a real feature of this chapter and is adjudicated as a structural link at 7:3, to the Edomite king-list of Genesis 36:31-39, on the grounds that no single one of the sixty-three 'reigned in his stead' verses can be named as a source. This candidate is superseded by that row.

This entry has to be written because the count is seductive and wrong. “in the stead of his” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 22:13, where Abraham offers the ram 'for a burnt offering in the stead of his son' — and Ether 7 is a chapter about fathers, sons, and one son taking a father's place. A reader who runs the phrase will find a singleton attached to the Bible's central substitution scene and will be tempted to catalogue it. The rarity is arithmetic, in exactly the way the register's Helaman 1:1 entry describes. 'In his stead' and 'in the stead of' are among the KJV's commonest constructions — “reigned in his stead” alone occurs in exactly 63 KJV verses — and the string here is long only because 'his father' happens to follow, as 'his son' happens to follow in Genesis 22:13. The two verses share a preposition and a possessive. Ether 7:10 is a succession notice; Genesis 22:13 is a sacrifice. The succession formula itself is adjudicated at 7:3.

A six-word run, the top candidate at 7:11, and the sense is inverted. Ezekiel 34:6 is the indictment of the shepherds of Israel: 'my flock was scattered upon all the face of the earth, and none did search or seek after them.' The phrase there measures a catastrophe of dispersal caused by rulers who failed. Ether 7:11 reads 'he did spread his kingdom upon all the face of the land, for the people had become exceeding numerous' — the same words measuring a good king's dominion over a growing people. Scattering against spreading, abandonment against government, earth against land. The Book of Mormon uses 'upon all the face of the earth' in the Ezekiel sense elsewhere and it is covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; what is recorded here is that its appearance at 7:11 is the opposite sense and is not a borrowing from Ezekiel. The verse's real KJV contact is 'did execute judgement in righteousness', which is adjudicated at 7:1 with this verse in recurrenceRefs.

Recorded because a reader will notice it and should be told the catalogue noticed too. Ether 7 names two Jaredite princes after figures of Genesis 1-11 — Noah at 7:14 and Nimrod at 7:22 — in a book whose founding event is the confounding of tongues at Babel. The Nimrod case is catalogued as a link at 7:22, because Genesis 10:10 attaches a kingdom to that name and Ether 7:22 has this Nimrod dispose of one, so the borrowing does argumentative work. The Noah case will not carry the same weight. There is no shared wording of any kind: Ether 7:14-18 gives its Noah a rebellion, a battle, a captive king and a murder in the night, and Genesis gives its Noah an ark, and the only point of contact is four letters. Worse, the sense runs backwards — the KJV's Noah is the one just man in a generation of violence, and Ether's is the usurper who takes a king captive and is killed in his own house. The Book of Mormon's other wicked King Noah, at Mosiah 11, raises the same question, and it is a question for that book rather than this one. Filed here at insufficient-verbal rather than wrong-sense because there is no verbal contact to have a sense at all.

A genuine KJV singleton — “carried him away” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — and the sequence is close: the chief priests bind Jesus, carry him away, deliver him to Pilate, and he is put to death; Noah takes Shule the king, carries him away captive, and is about to put him to death. It is displaced rather than rejected. Jeremiah 52:9 accounts for the whole of Ether's clause and not three words of it: “took the king and carried” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and Ether 7:17 has the object ('the king'), the verb pair, the qualifier 'captive' and a named destination, which is the Babylonian deportation formula entire. Mark 15:1 has no 'king', no 'captive' and no destination. The link is written at this verse to Jeremiah 52:9 with Mark 15:1 named in its provenance, so a reader who finds the singleton is not left thinking it went unseen.

This is the entry the Judges 3:26 Ehud case in Helaman is the model for: the typology pulls hard and the wording will not bear it. Ether 7:18 is a night rescue from prison on the eve of an execution — Noah is 'about to put him to death', the sons of Shule enter the house by night, kill him, break down the door of the prison and bring their father out — and the King James Bible has one famous scene of that shape, Acts 12: Herod means to bring Peter forth after Easter, the angel comes 'the same night', the chains fall off and the iron gate opens of its own accord. The shared elements are the eve of execution, the night, the door and the deliverance. There is not one shared distinctive word, and the difference is doctrinal rather than incidental: Acts 12's whole point is that no human agency is involved, the keepers are asleep and the gate opens by itself, whereas Ether's deliverance is a homicide and a broken door. A second candidate has to be recorded with it. 2 Kings 11 has the usurper who holds a throne against its rightful occupant slain by a counter-coup and the true king enthroned — Athaliah killed, Joash crowned — which is Ether 7:18-19's plot exactly, and 2 Kings 11:17 was in fact proposed by the machine at 7:19 on 'the king and the people'. It likewise has no verbal contact: Ether shares with 2 Kings 11 no phrase longer than the definite article. Both are recorded here so that a reader who sees either type is told the catalogue saw it and declined to catalogue it as dependence. Either would become a link if a distinctive phrase were found; neither has one.

The top candidate at 7:18 on a five-word run, and it is pure syntax. Acts 20:3 has Paul 'about to sail into Syria' when the Jews lay wait for him; Ether 7:18 has Noah 'about to put him to death' when the sons of Shule break into his house. The construction marks an interrupted intention, which is the commonest possible narrative use for it, and the two intentions have nothing in common. Nothing else of Acts 20 is present.

A five-word run consisting of two nouns and three articles. 2 Kings 11:17 is Jehoiada's covenant between the LORD, the king and the people; Ether 7:19 is a note that the people under Shule's reign prospered. The pairing of a king with his people is not a phrase anyone borrows. The chapter's real relation to 2 Kings 11 — the usurper slain, the rightful king restored — is discussed in the exclusion at 7:18, where it is declined for want of verbal contact.

Worth an entry only because of what the spelling shows. “favour in the eyes of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 15:25 — David, fleeing Absalom's rebellion, sending the ark back with Zadok, 'if I shall find favour in the eyes of the LORD' — and Ether 7:22 reads 'he did gain favor in the eyes of Shule', in a chapter that is itself a chain of rebellions against a father. The singleton is arithmetic all the same: the KJV's ordinary idioms are 'found grace in the eyes of' and 'found favour in the sight of', which between them run to dozens of verses, and the one occurrence of this variant is an accident of which noun and which preposition happened to meet. The verb is wrong as well — the KJV never 'gains' favour, it finds it. The negative datum is the useful part: the 1830 spells the word 'favor', not the KJV's 'favour', and CONVENTIONS §8 cuts both ways. Where 1830 keeps a KJV spelling that is evidence of copying; where it does not, as here, it is evidence that this phrase was not being copied from a King James page.

The best entry in this chapter's register and the highest-scoring candidate in the chapter. “which gave power unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does the shorter “gave power unto”: Revelation 13:4, 'they worshipped the dragon which gave power unto the beast'. Ether 7:25 reads 'he did execute a law throughout all the land, which gave power unto the prophets that they should go whithersoever they would'. Five consecutive words on a KJV singleton is normally decisive evidence in this catalogue, and here it is worthless, because the two sentences are opposites at every joint. In Revelation the giver is the dragon, the receiver is the beast, and what is conferred is the authority to make war on the saints and to be worshipped in God's place; the verse is the KJV's compressed statement of illegitimate power. In Ether the giver is a king acting by law, the receivers are prophets, and what is conferred is nothing but freedom of movement — the right to go where they will and say what they were sent to say. Revelation's clause describes a delegation of tyranny; Ether's describes a statute protecting speech. The grammatical coincidence is complete and the sense is inverted, which is precisely the shape CONVENTIONS §5 asks to be written up at length rather than passed over: a reader who runs the phrase will find the singleton, and must be told that the catalogue found it first and rejected it.

Proposed at 7:27 for a four-word run, and the run is the whole of it. 2 Kings 8:4 is Gehazi telling the king of Israel 'all the great things that Elisha hath done' — a servant entertaining a court with prophet anecdotes. Ether 7:27 has Shule remembering 'the great things that the Lord had done for his fathers in bringing them across the great deep into the promised land': the agent is God and not a prophet, the beneficiaries are the ancestors and not the hearer, and the content is a founding deliverance. The verse's contacts are catalogued as a link to Judges 2:7, whose 'great works of the LORD, that he did for Israel' supplies the thought, with 1 Kings 8:66 in composite for the exact run “the Lord had done for”, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse.

exclusions.sharedText: and came and dwelt in the
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter and a six-word run, and it is narrative connective tissue. Genesis 13:18 is Abram moving his tent to the plain of Mamre and building an altar; Ether 8:2 is a son who has rebelled against his father going to live in the land of Heth before buying half a kingdom with flattery. The shared string is 'and came and dwelt in the', which is how the King James Bible says that somebody moved house — it does the same work at Genesis 13:18, and the Book of Mormon uses relocation formulas of this kind continuously through the Jaredite king-list. Nothing of Abram's altar, tent, or promise is present, and no content word beyond the verbs is shared.

Already excluded at Ether 7:4 on the same four-word run and for the same reason; the entry is repeated here because the machine proposes it again and a reader working verse by verse will meet it again. Matthew 10:35 is Christ describing the division his coming makes within households — the man set at variance against his father is being separated by loyalty to Christ, and the saying is a warning about the cost of discipleship. Ether 8:2 is a prince raising a rebellion to depose and imprison his own father for the kingdom. The verbal overlap is the preposition and the kinship noun; the senses have nothing in common.

This one is genuinely tempting and worth the space. Jeremiah 17:11 is the KJV's proverb about ill-gotten power: 'so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool.' Ether 8 is precisely a story about getting a kingdom not by right, and 8:4 says that Omer 'was in captivity the half of his days' — a life measured out in halves, in a chapter whose other half-measure is the half of the kingdom. But the sense is inverted at the decisive point. In Jeremiah the man whose days are cut in half is the one who took what was not his; in Ether 8:4 the man whose days are halved is the rightful king who was robbed, and the usurper Jared keeps his gains until his own daughter's plot unmakes them. If Jeremiah 17:11 stood behind any verse of this chapter it would have to stand behind Jared, and it does not stand behind Jared verbally either. Recorded so that a reader who notices the proverb is told the catalogue noticed it and declined it.

A four-word run with opposed referents. In Acts 9:29 the Grecians go about to slay Saul because he disputes boldly in the name of the Lord Jesus, and the narrative's sympathy is entirely with the intended victim, who escapes to Tarsus. In Ether 8:6 the men about to slay Jared are his own brothers putting down an armed rebellion against their father, and the narrative's judgment falls on the man whose life is spared: sparing him is what allows everything in the rest of the chapter to happen. The phrase is the KJV's ordinary way of saying that a killing was imminent.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when they had
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run, the longest in the chapter, and entirely covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5. 'And it came to pass that when they had' is the Book of Mormon's ordinary narrative hinge; Amos 7:2's continuation is locusts finishing the grass of the land and the prophet interceding for Jacob, and Ether 8:6 is a night battle ending in a plea for a life. Listed rather than passed over in silence only because its length makes it the top-ranked candidate for the verse and a reader may wonder why it is not a link.

A rarity coincidence worth registering and not worth cataloguing. 'His kinsfolks' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 1 Kings 16:11 and 2 Kings 10:11, and both are dynastic massacres — Zimri destroying the house of Baasha, Jehu destroying the house of Ahab, in each case killing the dead king's kinsfolk along with his priests and his great men. Ether 8:13 gathers 'all his kinsfolks' into a house to plot a dynastic massacre, which makes the coincidence arresting: the same rare noun, the same political operation, in the same three verses of the King James Bible. But the roles are exactly reversed. In Kings the kinsfolk are the victims of the purge; in Ether they are its instrument, and they survive it. Since the word is one noun and the reversal is total, the case cannot be argued as dependence. The Judges 15:12 link at this verse is where the verbal evidence actually is.

'Whoso should divulge whatsoever thing Akish made known unto them, the same should lose his life.' 'Shall lose his life' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 8:35 and Luke 17:33, and 'lose his life' in four, all four of them the same saying of Jesus about losing one's life for his sake and finding it. The construction Ether uses even keeps Mark's resumptive pronoun — 'the same shall save it' / 'the same should lose his life'. It is refused because the saying is a paradox about voluntary self-loss for the gospel's sake and Ether 8:14 is a penalty clause in a murder contract: the life lost is taken by the conspirators, not laid down, and it is lost for keeping a secret rather than for confessing Christ. Recorded because the shared string is genuinely rare and a careful reader could be caught by it. The oath's real source is at Matthew 5:34-36, catalogued as a link on this verse.

'They were kept up by the power of the devil … to keep them in darkness.' Acts 26:18 is the KJV's one verse joining the two ideas: Paul is sent 'to open their eyes, and to turn them from darkness to light, and from the power of Satan unto God'. The conjunction of darkness with a satanic power is thus not common KJV property, and the temptation to link is real. But 'power of the devil' occurs in exactly zero KJV verses — the KJV says 'power of Satan' — and nothing else of Acts 26:18 is present: no eyes opened, no turning, no forgiveness, no inheritance. What Ether 8:16 has is the Book of Mormon's own standing idiom for the secret combinations, 'works of darkness' and the devil's power, which runs from 2 Nephi 9:9 through Helaman 6:28-30 and reaches this verse from inside the book. Declined at any confidence for want of verbal contact.

'Neither doth he will that man should shed blood, but in all things hath forbidden it, from the beginning of man.' The claim being made is a claim about Genesis — that the shedding of human blood was prohibited from the outset — and the KJV states the prohibition once, at Genesis 9:6, 'Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed: for in the image of God made he man.' That verse is the Bible's foundational homicide statute, it binds a pre-Israelite world, and this catalogue has already used it as the source of Nephi's objection at 1 Nephi 4:10, where the wording was genuinely reproduced. Here it is not. 'Should shed blood' occurs in exactly zero KJV verses; 'sheddeth man' is a Genesis 9:6 singleton and Ether does not have it; the image of God, the talionic clause, and Noah are all absent. And the doctrine does not quite fit either: Genesis 9:6 is given after the flood, whereas Ether 8:19 dates the prohibition 'from the beginning of man', which is Helaman 6:29's phrase and the Book of Mormon's own antediluvian chronology of the secret combinations. Refused as a link and recorded here because the doctrinal fit is close enough to tempt.

A five-word run with opposite polarity. Proverbs 10:3 is a promise — 'The LORD will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish' — where the verb governs a harm God prevents. Ether 8:22 is a threat: 'the Lord will not suffer that the blood of his saints … shall always cry unto him from the ground … and yet he avengeth them not', where the verb governs a delay God will not extend. The KJV construction 'the LORD will not suffer' is the ordinary way of saying God will not permit something, and the two verses do not permit the same thing. The real sources of this verse are Genesis 4:10 and Revelation 6:10, catalogued as a link here.

A five-word run of judgment boilerplate. Psalm 92:7's wicked spring as the grass and flourish only 'that they shall be destroyed for ever'; Ether 8:22's nation that upholds secret combinations 'shall be destroyed'. The clause is the KJV's standard predicate for the fate of the wicked and the Book of Mormon's too — it is the burden of the whole book of Ether and of Moroni's editorial voice throughout. No content word beyond the verb is shared and the Psalm's grass image, which is what makes the Psalm distinctive, is absent.

'Yea, even the sword of the justice of the eternal God, shall fall upon you, to your overthrow and destruction.' The image is unmistakably scriptural and Deuteronomy 32:41-43 is its likeliest biblical home — 'If I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment, I will render vengeance to mine enemies' — the more so because Deuteronomy 32:43, 'he will avenge the blood of his servants', stands behind the vengeance language of the preceding verse. But 'sword of the justice' occurs in exactly zero KJV verses, and the sword of God's justice is a Book of Mormon fixture rather than a King James one: Alma 26:19, Alma 60:29 and Helaman 13:5 all have it, and Moroni is using the book's own phrase. Declined as a biblical link for want of any shared string; recorded so that a reader who reaches for Deuteronomy 32 is told why the catalogue did not.

Hardy's apparatus cross-references Genesis 4:1-12 at this verse alongside Genesis 3:1-7, and the reference is a fair one for a study edition: Ether 8:25 says the devil 'hath caused man to commit murder from the beginning', which is a summary of Cain. But this catalogue puts links where the wording is (CONVENTIONS §6a), and the Cain material of Ether 8 is verbal in two other places. At 8:15 Cain is named outright and the predicate attached to him, 'a murderer from the beginning', is a five-word KJV singleton — from John 8:44, not from Genesis 4. At 8:22 and again at 8:24 the blood of the slain cries from the ground for vengeance, which is Genesis 4:10 verbatim in its distinctive words ('blood crieth' is a KJV singleton), and mediation-check.py confirms Ether has the Genesis form rather than Hebrews 12:24's. Both are catalogued as links. Ether 8:25 itself reaches Cain through a summary phrase with no Genesis wording in it, so the row is discharged here by cross-reference: a reader sent to this verse by Hardy should go to 8:15 for Cain and to 8:22 for Abel's blood. The Genesis 3 half of Hardy's row is answered by the link at this verse, with the note that the verbal contact is at Genesis 3:13 rather than in 3:1-7.

'That they may come unto the fountain of all righteousness and be saved.' 'Fountain of' occurs in fifteen KJV verses and the metaphorical ones are well distributed — the fountain of living waters (Jeremiah 2:13), of life (Psalm 36:9, Proverbs 13:14, Proverbs 14:27), of Jacob, of Israel, of tears. None of them is a fountain of righteousness, and no KJV verse joins the noun to that abstraction. The Book of Mormon does it three times — 1 Nephi 2:9, where Lehi wishes Laman were 'continually running into the fountain of all righteousness', here, and again at Ether 12:28 — so Ether 8:26 is drawing on Lehi's phrase rather than on any one biblical fountain. Recorded to show that the candidate was considered and to say where the phrase actually comes from.

exclusions.sharedText: his sons and his daughters, and all his
exclusions.reason: This one is genuinely tempting and deserves an entry rather than silence, because Genesis 36 is a live source for the book of Ether: the Edomite king-list at Genesis 36:31-39 is adjudicated at Ether 7:3 as the structural model for the Jaredite dynastic chronicle, so a second contact with the same chapter would be a real finding. It does not survive inspection. Genesis 36:6 is Esau moving his household away from Jacob, and the shared string is a family inventory — sons, daughters, household — that the King James Bible writes the same way every time it writes one (Genesis 46:7, Job 1:2, and so on). Ether's own clause continues 'and all his household', where Genesis has 'and all the persons of his house'; the one distinctive element of Genesis 36:6, that Esau departs 'from the face of his brother Jacob', has no counterpart here, and Omer departs from a son-in-law, not a brother. The chapter's use of Genesis 36 is the formula 'reigned in his stead', which is covered by the standing treatment at Ether 7:3.

exclusions.sharedText: that he should depart out of
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and one of the two highest-scoring candidates in the chapter. It is an accident of two different idioms colliding: John 13:1's clause is 'that he should depart out of this world unto the Father', of Jesus at the last supper knowing his hour is come, and the whole force of the sentence is in the words Ether does not share. Ether 9:3 is a man leaving a country. Nothing else of John 13 is anywhere near this verse, and the real borrowing in the sentence is the dream-warning that precedes the departure, which is Matthew 2:12's and is adjudicated as a link at this verse. Worth noting for completeness that 'depart out of the land' is itself a KJV singleton, at Deuteronomy 9:7, of the Exodus — but that verse is a rebuke about provoking the LORD in the wilderness and shares nothing else here either, so the phrase is filed as ordinary English rather than as a borrowing from either candidate.

exclusions.sharedText: came to a place which was
exclusions.reason: A six-word run to Gethsemane, and pure narrative connective. 'They came to a place which was named Gethsemane' and 'came to a place which was called Ablom' share nothing but the King James way of introducing a place-name, and the two places have nothing to do with each other. This entry covers the same construction wherever it recurs in the Jaredite chapters.

Not a machine candidate, and recorded because it is the kind of coincidence that will tempt a later reader who runs a concordance. 'Gave audience' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 15:12, where the Jerusalem council keeps silence and gives audience to Barnabas and Paul — that is, listens to them. Ether 9:5 has Jared 'giving audience to his people' as he sits on his throne, which is the modern courtly sense: a monarch receiving petitioners. The two senses are not merely different, they are converse — in Acts the audience is the assembly, in Ether the audience is granted by the king. The phrase in Ether is nineteenth-century English that happens to have a King James homonym, and cataloguing it as a borrowing would misrepresent both texts.

A six-word run consisting almost entirely of a kinship term. 'Father in law' occurs across the Jethro narrative and Judges and Ruth; Exodus 18:24 is Moses taking Jethro's advice about delegating judgment, and Ether 9:5 is Akish having Jared beheaded. The candidate is an artifact of a four-word noun phrase being counted as four words.

1 Kings 8:39 is Solomon at the dedication of the temple, asking God to judge each man because 'thou only knowest the hearts of all the children of men'; Ether 9:6 says a secret society 'had corrupted the hearts of all the people'. The shared words are a quantifier and a body part. The interest of Ether 9:6, if it has one, is that it makes the corruption total in the way Genesis 6:5 does, and Genesis 6:5 is already adjudicated as a link elsewhere in this book (Ether 3:2).

The chapter's most instructive machine miss. Joshua 7:5 was ranked here because it shares five words with the verse, but its hearts 'melted, and became as water' after the rout at Ai — that is, the people are afraid. Ether 9:10's hearts are won over, which is the opposite operation performed on the same organ. The real source is 2 Samuel 15:6, where Absalom 'stole the hearts of the men of Israel', a KJV singleton the n-gram stream could not see because Ether substitutes 'won' for 'stole' and 'of the people' for 'of the men of Israel', leaving no contiguous window long enough to score. A textbook case of CONVENTIONS §9: the true source is invisible to contiguous matching and a wrong-sense candidate ranks in its place.

The highest-scoring candidate in the chapter, returned three separate times (at 9:14, 9:21 and 9:22), and it is the regnal formula rather than a verse. 'Reigned in his stead' occurs in exactly sixty-three KJV verses; 2 Chronicles 1:8 ranked because it happens to have the infinitive form Ether uses, but nothing else of Solomon's prayer is present. The formula is adjudicated for the whole book at Ether 7:3, as a structural link to the Edomite king-list of Genesis 36:31-39 — the King James Bible's one unbroken chain of the formula outside the regnal histories of Israel and Judah, and the only one belonging to a people outside the covenant. This entry covers every occurrence of the formula in chapter 9: 9:6, 9:14, 9:21, 9:22, 9:25 and 9:27. They are not listed individually.

'Omer began to be old; nevertheless, in his old age he begat Emer.' The phrase is a KJV phrase — it occurs in exactly two verses, Genesis 21:2 and 21:7, both of the birth of Isaac — and it is a real borrowing, but it is not a fresh one. It is adjudicated at its first Jaredite occurrence, Ether 7:3, where the argument is set out in full and the recurrences at 7:7 and 7:26 are recorded. This is the fourth use within the same book and the same narrating hand, so under CONVENTIONS §4 it is Moroni using his own formula rather than reaching again for Genesis. Recorded here so that a reader working through chapter 9 verse by verse is sent to Ether 7:3 rather than shown nothing.

A duration. Acts 19:10 measures Paul's teaching in the school of Tyrannus; Ether 9:15 measures how long Omer lived after abdicating. 'By the space of' is the King James way of expressing an interval and the Book of Mormon uses it continuously — 9:12 has 'for the space of many years' and 9:16 'in the space of sixty and two years' in the same run of verses. This entry covers all of them.

A window that closes across a clause boundary. 2 Chronicles 34:8 has Josiah purging 'the land, and the house' — the house being the temple, which he then sends men to repair. Ether 9:16 reads 'take the curse from off the land, and the house of Emer did prosper', where 'the house' begins a new subject and means a dynasty. The match is between the end of one clause and the start of another and there is no contact of any kind between the two verses.

exclusions.sharedText: of gold and of silver and
exclusions.reason: A close call and worth recording as one. Daniel 11:43 is the only KJV verse with the string 'of gold and of silver and', which is exactly Ether 9:17's order of the metals, and it goes on to 'all the precious things of Egypt'. What decides against it is the construction of the third item: Ether has 'and of precious things', repeating the preposition, which is a King James singleton at 2 Chronicles 21:3 and is not Daniel's phrasing. Daniel also supplies no context — it is the king of the north's plunder in an apocalyptic campaign — where 2 Chronicles 21:3 supplies a father distributing wealth among royal sons in the verse before one of them kills all his brothers, which is the situation Ether 9 is in. The link is filed at 2 Chronicles 21:3.

A typological expectation the wording will not bear, and the model for this kind of entry is the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' case in 1 Nephi. Everything about the position of Ether 9:16-20 says Deuteronomy 8: a people made rich in a land given them, a warning attached about forgetting the giver, and — twelve verses later — the two wilderness terrors of Deuteronomy 8:15, serpents and drought, arriving in that order. But the catalogue itself is not written in King James English at any point. 'Silks' occurs in no KJV verse; 'horses and asses' occurs in no KJV verse; 'useful', which Ether uses twice in 9:18-19, occurs in no KJV verse; and the animals of 9:19 include three that are not in any Bible. Deuteronomy 8:13's own terms are 'herds', 'flocks', 'silver' and 'gold' multiplied, and Ether shares only the two metals, which are shared with twenty-nine other KJV verses. The Deuteronomy 8 contact in this chapter is real and is adjudicated where it is verbal — at 9:31, on Deuteronomy 8:15's pairing of fiery serpents with drought, the only such pairing in the King James Bible. It is not adjudicated here, and a reader who feels the Deuteronomic shape of 9:16-20 is right about the shape and should be told the vocabulary does not support it.

exclusions.sharedText: choice above all other lands; ripened in iniquity; the fulness of my wrath
exclusions.reason: Ether 9:20 restates the land covenant in the terms the book established at Ether 2:8-12, where it is adjudicated: 'ripened in iniquity' answers to Genesis 15:16's 'the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full', which is the link filed at Ether 2:10. None of the three signature phrases here is King James English on its own — 'choice above all other lands', 'fulness of my wrath' and 'pour out his blessings' each occur in no KJV verse — so there is nothing to adjudicate at this verse that has not been adjudicated at Ether 2. Recorded so that a reader stopping at 9:20, which is the chapter's theological centre, is sent to Ether 2:10 rather than shown an empty apparatus.

A numeral. 'Forty and two years old' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is Ahaziah's age at accession; Ether 9:24 has Coriantum living to a hundred and forty-two. The King James Bible writes every number this way, so any Jaredite age will collide with some regnal notice, and the collision carries no information. The genuine reading of 9:24 — the three-part Abrahamic death sequence of Genesis 23:1, 25:1 and 25:7 — is filed as a link at this verse, and it would be unaffected if Coriantum had died at any other age.

Methuselah's age against Com's reign of forty-nine years. The shared string is a numeral and a conjunction. Genealogical arithmetic in King James English will always produce these; the entry stands for all of them in chapter 9.

'The famine was over all the face of the earth' against 'the people had spread again over all the face of the land'. The phrase is one the Book of Mormon uses continuously, and it is covered by the standing exclusion on connective boilerplate. Recorded here only because the coincidence is sharper than usual — Genesis 41:56 is about a famine and Ether 9 is four verses from one — and a reader might reasonably wonder. The famine link in this chapter is at 9:30, to Deuteronomy 11:17 and Acts 11:28, neither of which is Joseph's.

The King James Bible's pit is Joseph's — 'cast him into a pit' occurs in exactly one verse, Genesis 37:24, and 'into a pit' in exactly three, the other two being sabbath-day livestock. None of them holds a prophet, and Ether 9:29's pits do. The nearest King James situation is Jeremiah 38:6, where Jeremiah is let down into a miry dungeon and left, but the KJV calls it a dungeon and not a pit, and Ether shares no wording with it. The verse's real borrowing is its grammar rather than its furniture: 'and some of them they cast into pits' reproduces the resumptive construction of Luke 11:49, a King James singleton, and that is where the link is filed. Recorded because a reader who knows Genesis 37 will see a pit here and should be told the catalogue looked and declined.

The best of the machine's proposals in the second half of the chapter and the one hardest to dismiss. Jeremiah 14 is headed 'the word of the LORD that came to Jeremiah concerning the dearth' — one of only seven KJV verses using that word — and 14:4-6 has no rain, ground that is chapt, and beasts wandering and failing for want of grass, which is close to Ether 9:30-31's drought and fleeing flocks. Two things decide against it. First, Ether's tense-and-preposition pattern is Deuteronomy's, not Jeremiah's: Jeremiah has 'no rain in the earth', Ether has 'no rain upon the face of the earth', and Deuteronomy 11:17's 'that there be no rain' with 'lest ye perish quickly' matches Ether's second clause ('destroyed exceeding fast') that Jeremiah has no counterpart for. Second, Jeremiah 14's animals fail and die where Ether's flee and are pursued, which is the Numbers 21 serpent material and not a drought motif at all. The drought link is filed at Deuteronomy 11:17 with 2 Chronicles 7:13; a later adjudicator who wants to reopen Jeremiah 14 should do it on 14:1's 'dearth', not on 14:4.

Ezra 3:13 is the shout at the foundation of the second temple, so loud that 'the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping'. Ether 9:33's people cannot pass a road held by serpents. The shared four words are a negated modal and a subject. The verse's genuine source is Hosea 2:6 — 'hedge up' is a KJV singleton and Ether takes both halves of the construction — and the link is filed there.

A narrative hinge. Exodus 32:1's people see that Moses is delayed and make a calf; Ether 9:34's see that they must perish and repent. The two outcomes are opposite and the shared words are a clause opener the King James Bible uses whenever a crowd reacts to something.

Not a machine candidate; recorded because the collocation is distinctive enough to catch a reader's eye and the sense is inverted. In the King James Bible, carcases falling is a judgment formula about human beings: 'your carcases, they shall fall in this wilderness' (Numbers 14:32), quoted in the New Testament at Hebrews 3:17 of the generation that perished for unbelief. Ether 9:34's carcases are the beasts' — cattle that died on the flight south — and the people eat them. The direction of the horror is opposite: Numbers has a people whose own bodies are left in the desert, Ether has a people kept alive by bodies that are not theirs. There is also no verbal contact worth the name, since Ether spells it 'carcasses' and the construction is 'devour the carcasses of them which fell by the way'. The Numbers material that is genuinely in play in these verses is the serpent plague of Numbers 21:6-7, filed as a link at 9:31.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that when they had
exclusions.reason: A nine-word run and the longest in the chapter, and it is entirely 'and it came to pass' plus a temporal clause opener. Covered by the standing exclusion filed at 1 Nephi 2:1. The candidate is recorded only because its length will make it look important to anyone re-running the machine streams over this chapter. Numbers 25:1, ranked alongside it on 'and the people began to', is the same case and is covered by this entry.

The machine ranked this run at 10:4 and again at 10:30, and Genesis 22:13 is not a succession verse at all — it is the ram caught in a thicket, offered 'in the stead of his son'.
