The Book of Mormon's phrase is the dynastic formula, and the formula is already adjudicated for this book: “reigned in his stead” occurs in exactly 63 KJV verses, and the catalogue files the borrowing as a genre borrowing at Ether 7:3, against the Edomite king-list of Genesis 36:31-39. Ether 10 uses the formula five times (10:4, 10:13, 10:17, 10:18, 10:30) and every one of them is covered by that row. A reader who arrives at 10:4 should be sent to Ether 7:3, not given a ram.

exclusions.sharedText: over all the face of the
exclusions.reason: The highest-scoring candidate at this verse and pure Book of Mormon connective tissue. 'Upon the face of the land', 'over all the face of the land' and 'the whole face of the land' are among the record's most frequent formulae, used at 10:4 and again at 10:21 in this chapter alone; Genesis 41:56 is a famine spreading over the face of the earth, and 10:4 is a population spreading over the land after one. The King James phrase is common and the Book of Mormon's use of it is continuous. Covered by the standing formulaic exclusion; listed here only because it topped the candidate list.

exclusions.sharedText: cause to be put to death
exclusions.reason: A five-word exact run, and “cause to be put to death” is a KJV singleton — on the face of it the strongest possible evidence, and it is rejected anyway. The rarity is arithmetic, in the way the Helaman 1:1 'fortieth year of the reign' entry describes: the King James Bible says 'put to death' something over a hundred times and simply had occasion to attach this particular causative auxiliary once. Nothing else of Luke 21 is present. Luke 21:16 is the persecution prophecy — betrayal by parents, brethren, kinsfolks and friends, and the martyrdom of some disciples; Ether 10:6 is a tyrant executing men who refuse forced labour. The senses are not opposed, which is why the candidate is tempting, but neither is there any recoverable context that would repay the reader: the disciples' informers and the king's prisons have nothing to say to each other. The verse's real borrowing is at 10:5, from Matthew 23:4.

exclusions.sharedText: he was cut off from the
exclusions.reason: The top-scoring candidate at this verse, and the phrase it matches is not a biblical phrase at all. “cut off from the presence” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses. 'Cut off from the presence of the Lord' is one of the Book of Mormon's own standing formulae, first used at 1 Nephi 2:21 and settled at 2 Nephi 5:20 for the curse on the Lamanites, then used throughout the record; its proximate model is internal, not King James. 2 Chronicles 26:21 supplies 'he was cut off from the' and then diverges into 'the house of the LORD' — Uzziah the leper barred from the temple, which is exclusion from a building rather than from a presence, and a punishment for presumption in worship rather than, as here, for whoredoms. Recorded so that a reader of 10:11 is told the formula was recognised and traced inside the Book of Mormon rather than outside it.

exclusions.sharedText: in gold, and in silver, and in
exclusions.reason: Three candidates share this seven-word run at 10:12 — Exodus 35:32, Exodus 31:4 and 2 Chronicles 2:7 — and all three are commissions to a master craftsman whose third metal is brass. Ether 10:12's third, fourth and fifth items are grain, flocks and herds, which belong to Deuteronomy 8:12-13's warning catalogue and not to any craftsman's commission; the link at this verse is written to Deuteronomy 8:13 for that reason. The Exodus material is genuinely present in this chapter, but eleven verses later, at 10:23 and 10:27, where 'work', 'brass', 'curious' and 'all manner of work' actually appear. Both sources are in Ether 10; each is filed where its own words are.

'And in his old age he begat Levi.' The phrase occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 21:2 and 21:7, both of them the birth of Isaac, and the catalogue adjudicates the borrowing for this book at Ether 7:3, where it is used three times of a dynasty fathering its own deliverer in captivity. Ether 10:14 is the same situation exactly — a deposed king begetting sons and daughters in prison, and begetting in his old age the son who will make war and recover the kingdom (10:15). No fresh row is written here because the argument is made at 7:3 and the phrase has not changed hands; this entry exists so that a reader browsing 10:14 is sent there.

exclusions.sharedText: after the death of his father
exclusions.reason: The top candidate at this verse. 'After the death of his father' is ordinary King James narrative connective — the run is long only because both texts are chronicles and both had to say the same unremarkable thing. 2 Chronicles 22:4 is Ahaziah doing evil because the house of Ahab were his counsellors after his father died; Ether 10:15 is Levi serving in captivity after his father's death and then making war to take the kingdom. No distinctive vocabulary, no recoverable context.

The machine's only candidate here, and the phrase is real — “good old age” occurs in exactly four KJV verses. But Gideon is the wrong one of the four. Judges 8:32 is a death notice whose sequel is Judges 8:33-9:5: the nation goes whoring after Baalberith as soon as Gideon is dead, and Abimelech kills seventy brothers on one stone to take the succession. Ether 10:16-17 is the opposite in every particular — the father anoints his successor himself, and the successor 'did that which was good in the sight of the Lord, all his days'. 1 Chronicles 29:28, David's death notice, is the King James verse that holds a good old age and an orderly royal succession in one sentence, and the link at 10:16 is written there.

“the whole face of the” is a KJV singleton, which is why it ranked, and the singleton is a mist. Genesis 2:6 is the vapour that went up from the earth and watered the whole face of the ground before there was rain or a man to till it — an image of emptiness before habitation. Ether 10:21 is the same phrase used for the reverse: 'the whole face of the land northward was covered with inhabitants'. The word after the shared run differs too ('ground' against 'land'), and the Book of Mormon's 'whole face of the land' is one of its own recurrent formulae. A singleton whose sense inverts and whose next word diverges is not a source.

This is the typological pull of the whole chapter and the wording will not bear it, which makes it the entry most worth writing. Ether 10 is a king-list about taxation, corvée, prisons and rebellion; 1 Samuel 8:11-18 is the King James Bible's set-piece on what a king will do to a people, and Ether 6:19-23 has already borrowed its opening move (1 Samuel 8:5, the demand for a king), so the source is demonstrably in this record's hands. 1 Samuel 8:12 even runs agriculture into armament in the order Ether 10:25-27 does — 'to ear his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war'. But the only shared content word is 'reap'; Ether has 'weapons of war', which occurs in nine KJV verses, and not 'instruments of war', which occurs in three and is 1 Samuel's phrase. And the sense is inverted at the point that matters: 1 Samuel 8 is about a king conscripting his subjects' labour, whereas the subject of Ether 10:25-27 is the people themselves, in the reign the chapter calls the most blessed and prosperous it knows. The Samuel material governs 10:5-10, where the taxes and the prisons are; it does not govern the prosperity catalogue. Recorded so that a reader who sees the type is told the catalogue saw it and declined it.

The second half of the same temptation. Ether 10:25-27 moves in three verses from tools 'both to plough and to sow, to reap and to hoe' to 'all manner of weapons of war', which is the direction of Joel 3:10 ('Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruninghooks into spears') and the reverse of Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3. There is no verbal contact at all: the King James word in all three verses is 'plowshares', a noun, and Ether's is 'plough', a verb, and no other term is shared. The sequence is also an artifact of the list's own logic — a catalogue of manufactures that runs from farming to cloth to tools to weapons is ordered by subject matter, not by allusion. Filed rather than passed over in silence because the swords-and-ploughshares figure is the first thing a reader of these three verses is likely to reach for.

“weapons of war” occurs in nine KJV verses spread across Deuteronomy, Judges, 2 Samuel, Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which is too wide a distribution to point at any one of them, and Ezekiel 32:27 — the uncircumcised mighty gone down to hell with their weapons of war, their swords under their heads — has nothing else in common with a manufacturing inventory. The genuine borrowing in this verse is the other half of it, 'all manner of work of exceeding curious workmanship', which is Bezaleel's vocabulary from Exodus 35:32-35 and is adjudicated at 10:23 with 10:27 in its recurrenceRefs.

'They were in a land that was choice above all lands, for the Lord had spoken it.' Jeremiah 2:2 supplies only the five-word connective 'in a land that was' and then reads 'not sown', of the wilderness Israel followed God through — the opposite kind of land in the opposite kind of sentence. The Book of Mormon's phrase here is its own: 'choice above all lands' and 'choice above all other lands' occur nowhere in the King James Bible and repeatedly in this record, from 1 Nephi 2:20 through Ether 1:38, 2:7, 2:10 and 9:20. What is King James in Ether 10:28 is the promised-land material behind it, and that is adjudicated at 10:23 against Deuteronomy 8:7-9, with 10:28 in its recurrenceRefs.

“forty and two years” is a KJV singleton — 2 Chronicles 22:2, Ahaziah's age at accession — and it is rejected on the arithmetic. Ether 10 uses the number three times, at 10:8 (Riplakish's reign), 10:15 (Levi's captivity) and 10:32 (Com's half-kingdom), for three different kings and three different kinds of period, none of them an age; a numeral a chapter reaches for three times independently is that chapter's habit and not a borrowing. 2 Chronicles 22:2 is in any case one of the King James Bible's known arithmetical cruxes, since 2 Kings 8:26 gives Ahaziah's age as twenty and two — which is a reason to be more careful with the verse, not less. The same entry covers 'the half of the kingdom' in this verse: it occurs in three KJV verses, all of them Ahasuerus offering Esther a gift (Esther 5:3, 5:6, 7:2), where the sense is a king's extravagant promise and not, as here, a usurper's seizure by war.

exclusions.sharedText: came also in the days of
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and one of the chapter's highest-scoring candidates, and it is pure dating formula on both sides. Jeremiah 1:3 is a superscription fixing a prophet's ministry to two reigns; Ether 11:1 is the abridger's standing way of attaching an episode to a king, used again at 11:12 ('in the days of Ethem') and 11:20 ('in the days of Coriantor') and throughout Ether 6-10. A formula the Book of Mormon uses continuously cannot be a borrowing from the one KJV verse that happens to share its wording. This entry covers the 'in the days of X' candidates at 11:7, 11:12 and 11:20 as well; they are not listed individually.

Four words of narrative connective tissue introducing an arrival. John 19:39's arrival is Nicodemus with the myrrh and aloes for the burial of Jesus; Ether 11:1's is a body of prophets. Nothing but the verb and its adverb is shared, and the real link at this verse is to Acts 26:20 later in the same sentence.

exclusions.sharedText: (prophets sheltered from a régime that is killing them)
exclusions.reason: Written up at length because a reader who knows the Elijah cycle will see it here and should be told the catalogue saw it too. Ether 11:2 has prophets who cannot stay among a people that wants them dead and who are taken in by a man with power; 1 Kings 18:4 has Obadiah hiding a hundred prophets by fifty in a cave and feeding them with bread and water while Jezebel cuts off the prophets of the LORD — and Ether 11:5, three verses later, has a royal brother who 'did cause that all the prophets which prophesied of the destruction of the people, should be put to death', which is Jezebel's act exactly. Jeremiah 26 offers the same shape with a closer legal setting: the people demand Jeremiah's death (26:8-11), Urijah the prophet actually is executed (26:20-23), and Ahikam's hand is with Jeremiah 'that they should not give him into the hand of the people to put him to death' (26:24). The wording will not bear either. 1 Kings 18:4 shares no distinctive string with Ether 11:2, and Jeremiah 26:24's 'into the hand of the people' is not what Ether says. The verbal source at this verse is Luke 19:47, where 'the people sought to destroy' is a KJV singleton, and the Elijah and Jeremiah material is a type the chapter conforms to rather than a text it quotes.

Four words of inceptive auxiliary. Genesis 9:20's continuation is 'husbandman' and Ether 11:4's is 'exceeding great war'; the shared material is a tense, not a phrase. 'There began to be' is among the Book of Mormon's most frequent constructions and is covered by the standing exclusion on connective boilerplate.

The best refusal in this chapter's register, because the rarity is genuine and would tempt anyone: “a great curse” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 23:14. The senses are not merely different, they are structurally opposed. In Acts the curse is an oath men bind upon themselves — forty conspirators swearing to eat nothing until they have murdered Paul — so the curse is an instrument of the killing and its subject is the killers by their own choice. In Ether 11:6 the curse is a sentence pronounced from outside upon a land and its inhabitants, testified by the prophets the people are about to kill, and its subject is the killers against their will. Acts' curse is a means; Ether's is a consequence. Nothing else of Acts 23 is present, and the surrounding material at 11:6 comes from Daniel 12:1 and Jeremiah 8:1-2. Worth noting for the record that the chapter does borrow from Acts elsewhere — 11:1 takes Acts 26:20 — which makes the coincidence here more tempting and no more real.

A five-word run of inceptive boilerplate whose completions are opposite in every respect: Numbers 25:1 continues 'to commit whoredom with the daughters of Moab' and Ether 11:8 continues 'to repent of their iniquity'. The Israelite apostasy at Shittim has no other contact with this verse. Where Ether 11:8 does have a source it is Judges 2:18, adjudicated as part of the Judges 2 row at 11:13.

Four words of subordinating connective. Numbers 11:29 is Moses wishing all the LORD's people were prophets; Ether 11:12 is prophets announcing an extermination. The real contact at this verse is 'utterly destroy them from off the face of the earth', adjudicated to Amos 9:8.

A genuine candidate and a close one — Ezekiel 20:8's 'they rebelled against me, and would not hearken unto me' shares four words and the sense — but it is superseded. Ether 11:13 reads 'would not hearken unto their words', and “would not hearken unto their” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 2:17, where the object is 'their judges'. Ether has the possessive construction Ezekiel lacks. The Judges 2 reading also explains the neighbouring verses, which Ezekiel 20 does not: 11:8's relenting mercy is Judges 2:18 and the chapter's each-reign-worse-than-the-last movement is Judges 2:19. See the link at 11:13.

“reign in his stead” is a KJV singleton in that exact form only because the King James Bible almost always writes the past tense; “reigned in his stead” occurs in sixty-three verses and 'in his stead' in seventy-three. It is the regnal-annals formula of Kings and Chronicles, and the Book of Mormon has been using it since Ether 7:3 — 8:1, 9:22, 9:25, 10:18 and again here. A formula that recurs continuously through a book cannot be a borrowing from any single verse of the source it is imitating wholesale. Solomon's speech at Gibeon has no other contact with Ether 11:14. The same reason covers the 'all his days' and 'begat' candidates through 11:9-19.

“a mighty man” occurs in seventeen KJV verses and is the Bible's standing epithet for a warrior; 1 Chronicles 12:4's Ismaiah the Gibeonite is a name in a muster roll of David's men at Ziklag. Ether 11:15's man is anonymous, rises 'in iniquity' out of a secret combination, and fights the king. The three shared words are an epithet plus a preposition, distributed across the historical books, and they point at no verse in particular.

Five words of connective. John 9:16's division among the people is a dispute over whether a sabbath healer is of God; Ether 11:15's is an armed rebellion over power and gain. 'Because of' is doing all the work of the match.

“there arose a mighty” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the next word decides everything: Luke's is 'famine' and Ether's is 'man'. This is the trap ADJUDICATING §4 names — the window closing one word early — in its purest form, because the shared four words are a complete grammatical unit and the divergence is entirely in the noun. Luke 15:14 is the turn of the prodigal parable, a famine in a far country reducing a son to want; Ether 11:15 is a usurper rising out of a secret combination to take half a kingdom by battle. Recorded because the run is long and the ranking high, and because 'a mighty famine' and 'a mighty man' will keep re-proposing themselves to any n-gram stream.

The candidate is right and the verse is wrong. “obtain the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 11:21, and Ether 11:18 is in fact its closest match in sense — an outsider with no claim overthrows a reigning king and takes the throne, which is what Daniel's 'vile person' does. But the phrase enters the Book of Mormon at Ether 11:10 and is used at 11:11 and 11:16 before it reaches here, and ADJUDICATING §4 asks for the adjudication at first use. The link is written at 11:10 with 11:11, 11:16, 11:18 and 13:24 in its recurrenceRefs, and it argues there that the chapter takes the phrase on a lawful succession and arrives at Daniel's sense by this verse. A reader who found the parallel here should read the row at 11:10.

“great and marvellous” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3, and the 1830 text preserves the KJV's double-l spelling that the 1920 edition modernised to 'marvelous' — so the temptation is real and CONVENTIONS §8 would ordinarily make something of it. But 'great and marvellous things' is a Book of Mormon formula long before Ether 11:20: it stands at 1 Nephi 1:14, Alma 9:6, 3 Nephi 17:16-17, Mormon 8:34 and, within this book, at Ether 4:15, where the catalogue adjudicates the sentence to 2 Corinthians 3:13-16 and Matthew 13:35. Ether 12:5 uses it again five verses after this chapter closes. A phrase the abridger has adopted as his own is not a fresh borrowing on each outing, and the Revelation 15 material that is adjudicated in this catalogue — the six-word run at 1 Nephi 1:14 — is a different phrase from a different clause of the verse. Cross-reference only: see Ether 4:15.

“to possess the land” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses — Deuteronomy 11:31, Joshua 1:11, Joshua 18:3, Judges 2:6, Judges 18:9, Nehemiah 9:15 and Amos 2:10 — and it is the standing Deuteronomic idiom for entering Canaan, used by the Book of Mormon throughout its own land-covenant material. No one of the seven is identifiable as the source. The distinctive content of Ether 11:21 is not the possession but the manner of it, 'after the manner which he brought their fathers', which is adjudicated to Amos 9:7.

exclusions.sharedText: until the going down of the sun
exclusions.reason: A seven-word run and the top-scoring candidate in the chapter's opening, and it is a KJV time-expression. Ether 12:3 says Ether cried 'from the morning, even until the going down of the sun', a merism for a whole day of preaching; Exodus 17:12 says Moses' hands were steady until sundown while Israel fought Amalek. The phrase is the Bible's ordinary way of saying 'all day' (Deuteronomy 16:6, Joshua 8:29, 10:27, 2 Chronicles 18:34), and nothing else of Exodus 17 is present — no hands, no stone, no battle, no Aaron and Hur. The machine's second proposal here, 2 Samuel 24:15's 'from the morning even', is the other half of the same merism and is covered by this entry.

Five contiguous words and a pure KJV logical connective. Matthew 18:7 uses it of the necessity of offences coming into the world; Ether 12:7 uses it of the necessity that some had faith before Christ showed himself. The Book of Mormon uses 'it must needs be' constantly (2 Nephi 2:11 is the famous one) and the construction carries no signal. Nothing of Matthew 18's woe-saying is present.

Six shared words spanning 'glorified the name of the Father'. The real source of this verse is Hebrews 6:4, adjudicated as a link at 12:8 on the strength of a KJV singleton ('heavenly gift'); 'the name of the Father' is the commonest phrase in Christian English and Matthew 28:19's baptismal formula supplies none of the verse's content — no baptism, no nations, no teaching. Recorded because the run is long enough to tempt.

The machine's five-word run is real and the verse is wrong. Acts 13:52 says the disciples were 'filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost' — no baptism, no fire. Ether 12:14's 'baptized with fire and with the Holy Ghost' is the Matthew 3:11 / Luke 3:16 saying, and it is adjudicated as a link at this verse against Matthew 3:11, with the note that the Book of Mormon has inverted the KJV's order of the two elements and that the proximate model is its own earlier form at 3 Nephi 9:20.

This is the entry a reader running rarity counts will otherwise think we missed. 'Wrought miracles' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is the strongest kind of evidence this catalogue recognizes — and the verse is Revelation 19:20, where the miracles are the false prophet's, wrought before the beast, deceiving those who received the mark. Ether 12:16 reads 'all they which wrought miracles, wrought them by faith', which is the opposite valuation of the identical phrase. The rarity is an accident of the KJV's preferring 'did miracles', 'wrought signs' and 'shewed wonders' elsewhere; it is not evidence of contact. The genuine source of the verse's thought is Hebrews 11:33's 'wrought righteousness', within the catalogue already linked at 12:13.

exclusions.sharedText: which he had spoken unto him
exclusions.reason: A six-word run of pure relative-clause boilerplate. Jeremiah 36:4 is Baruch taking dictation; Ether 12:20 is the brother of Jared holding God to a promise. The only content word in common is 'spoken'. The Book of Mormon writes 'which he had spoken unto him' and its variants throughout, and no phrase of Jeremiah 36 beyond the connective appears.

Five words of speech-frame. The coincidence is slightly more interesting than usual, because Revelation 7:14's answer concerns robes washed white in blood and Ether 12:38 will speak of garments unspotted with blood — but the two are fifteen verses apart, the shared string belongs to neither idea, and the garment material at 12:38 is adjudicated there against Acts 20:26 and Jude 1:23. The frame itself is the KJV's standard formula for a reported dialogue and carries no signal.

Five words, scoring as highly as 2 Corinthians 12:9 in the same verse, and worthless. Ezekiel 39:10 says the Israelites shall take no wood out of the field because they will burn the weapons of Gog for fuel; Ether 12:26 says the meek shall take no advantage of Moroni's weakness. The shared string is the negative of an English verb of taking and stops exactly where the sense begins. The verse's real source, 2 Corinthians 12:9, is a link at 12:26 and rests on a KJV singleton.

Zechariah 1:9's angel says 'I will shew thee what these be'; Ether 12:27's Lord says 'if men come unto me, I will shew unto them their weakness'. The shared run straddles a clause boundary — the end of Moroni's 'come unto me' and the start of a new sentence — which is the signature of a false positive in a contiguous-window matcher. The machine's paired proposal of Psalm 101:2 ('O when wilt thou come unto me?') is the same accident and is covered here. The 1830 'shew' for 1920 'show' is evidence about the chapter's register, not about these verses.

exclusions.sharedText: and I will shew unto the
exclusions.reason: Six contiguous words, the longest run the machine found in this verse, and it is a bare announcement-of-disclosure formula: Daniel will shew the king the interpretation, the Lord will shew the Gentiles their weakness. Daniel 2 supplies no other element — no dream, no image, no wise men. The genuine source of Ether 12:28 is 1 Corinthians 13:13, whose triad is a KJV singleton and is adjudicated as a link here.

'Fountain of living waters' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 2:13 and 17:13, and a reader who sees 'the fountain of all righteousness' at Ether 12:28 will reach for them. The phrase is not Jeremiah's: it is the Book of Mormon's own, coined at 1 Nephi 2:9 where Lehi wishes Laman were like a river 'continually running into the fountain of all righteousness' — a verse whose source is Isaiah 48:18 and which is adjudicated in 1 Nephi 2. Ether 12:28 is using the book's internal formula, not the prophet's, and Jeremiah's fountain is in any case a thing forsaken rather than a thing arrived at.

The machine's top candidate at both 12:32 and 12:33, on five words of quotation-frame: Moroni twice says 'I remember that thou hast said that thou hast…', Solomon says 'the place whereof thou hast said that thou wouldest put thy name there'. The construction is how the KJV reports God's own prior speech and it is doing the same job in both texts, which is why it matches and why it means nothing. The paired proposal of Psalm 104:8 ('the place which thou hast founded') is the same accident and is covered here. Both verses have real sources — John 14:2 at 12:32, John 10:17-18 at 12:33 — and both are adjudicated as links.

Recorded so that the John 3:16 link at this verse is not read as careless. 'Love the world' in the Johannine letters is a prohibition — 'Love not the world, neither the things that are in the world. If any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him' — and a reader alert to Johannine idiom will notice that Ether 12:33 predicates of Christ what 1 John forbids to Christians. The two senses of 'world' are different (the created order and its inhabitants versus the present age and its appetites) and the KJV keeps them apart by context, not by vocabulary. The verse's source is John 3:16, which is where the KJV says God loved the world.

Five words spanning 'I prayed unto the Lord that he would give unto the Gentiles grace'. Psalm 22:8 is the mockers' taunt at the cross, 'He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him'. The shared string is the ordinary English frame for a petition and the two verses have opposite speakers — a prophet praying and enemies jeering. Nothing of Psalm 22 is present. The 'it came to pass that the Lord…' matches the machine also ranked in this verse and at 12:37 (Joshua 1:1) are covered by the standing connective exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5.

A genuinely tempting four-word run in a chapter about faith and sight, and the senses are opposed at the decisive point. John 20:29 is a rebuke: 'because thou hast seen me, thou hast believed: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed' — seeing is the lesser condition. Ether 12:37 is a commendation: 'because thou hast seen thy weakness, thou shalt be made strong' — seeing is the qualifying act. The object differs too; Thomas sees the risen Christ, Moroni sees his own inadequacy. The chapter does engage John 20:29's problem, but it does so at 12:19, where those who saw with their eyes what they had beheld with an eye of faith 'were glad', and that verse is linked to John 8:56.

The machine ranked Numbers 14:14 on 'face to face and that', where the 'and that' belongs to Moroni's next clause and to Numbers' list of things the nations have heard. 'Face to face' occurs in eleven KJV verses and identifies nothing on its own. The construction that does identify a source is 'face to face' immediately followed by an as-a-man simile, which occurs in exactly one KJV verse — Exodus 33:11, 'as a man speaketh unto his friend' — and Ether 12:39 has it, 'even as a man telleth another'. The link is filed at this verse against Exodus 33:11, with Deuteronomy 34:10 noted beside it.

The highest-scoring candidate in the verse on a five-word run, and it is a preface formula on both sides of the match. Luke 1:3 is a historian telling Theophilus he has had 'perfect understanding of all things from the very first'; Ether 13:2 is Moroni saying that Ether 'truly told them of all things, from the beginning of man'. Both are prefatory claims to comprehensive knowledge, which is why the words line up, and neither shares a distinctive term with the other — 'from the very first' and 'from the beginning of man' are different phrases. The verse's real borrowing is the flood clause, adjudicated at Genesis 8:8.

“the place of the” occurs in exactly 22 KJV verses and Ezekiel 41:9 is a measurement of a side chamber's wall. Recorded only because it ranked first for a verse whose actual content — the New Jerusalem descending — is one of the most heavily biblical sentences in the book, and a reader should be able to see that the machine had nothing to do with finding it. The link is at Revelation 3:12.

A five-word run made entirely of function words plus the divine name. “like unto the” occurs in exactly 17 KJV verses; 2 Chronicles 33:2 is Manasseh doing evil 'like unto the abominations of the heathen'. Ether 13:8 builds a holy city 'unto the Lord, like unto the Jerusalem of old'. The run crosses the comma that separates the two clauses in the Book of Mormon's own sentence, which is the standard failure mode of a contiguous-window matcher and is worth naming here because the same shape recurs throughout the war chapters.

This one is worth writing out, because the sense is closer than the wording and a careful reader could take it. “the house of Joseph” occurs in exactly 11 KJV verses, and Joshua 18:5 is a land allotment: 'the house of Joseph shall abide in their coasts on the north.' Ether 13:8 is also a land allotment to the house of Joseph — 'the remnant of the house of Joseph shall be built upon this land; and it shall be a land of their inheritance'. So the two verses share a subject, a verb position and a subject matter. What they do not share is anything distinctive: Joshua is dividing Canaan into seven parts among the tribes that have not yet received one, and 'shall abide in their coasts' is not 'shall be built upon this land'. The Book of Mormon's phrase for the tribe is in any case its own — “the seed of Joseph” occurs in no KJV verse, and Ether 13:6-11 uses it four times.

Not a rejection of the source but a record of where it sits. Isaiah 65:17 is the ultimate origin of the new heaven and new earth and is retained as a composite on the link at 13:9; it is not the proximate source, because tools/mediation-check.py returns two decisive points against it. Isaiah reads the plural 'new heavens' and “a new heaven” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 21:1; and Isaiah's second clause is 'the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind', where the Book of Mormon has the passing-away that is Revelation's. 2 Peter 3:13, the other KJV verse with the phrase, fails the same singular/plural test. Filed here so that a reader who arrives at Ether 13:9 with Isaiah in hand is told the catalogue tested it and why it lost.

exclusions.sharedText: and they shall be like unto
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the second-ranked candidate for the verse, and it is a coincidence of connective tissue. Lamentations 1:21 ends 'thou wilt bring the day that thou hast called, and they shall be like unto me' — Zion wishing her enemies the treatment she has had. Ether 13:9's clause is 'and they shall be like unto the old', the new heaven and new earth compared to the ones they replace. Nothing but the comparative formula is shared. The verse's sources are Revelation 21:1 and 2 Corinthians 5:17, both adjudicated.

The most interesting rejected candidate in the chapter. “and they are they” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “they are they which” occurs in exactly one, and both are John 5:39 — 'Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me.' Ether 13:10 and 13:11 use that exact construction twice in two verses, and 13:12 uses a third variation of it. So the machine is pointing at a genuine KJV singleton, twice. It is still the wrong verse. The construction Ether is running is the identification formula of Revelation 7:13-14 — 'These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb' — which supplies not only the syntax but the whitened garments, the Lamb's blood and the question the formula answers, all of which Ether 13:10 has and John 5:39 has none of. What John 5:39 contributes is a warning about the method: 'are they which' occurs in exactly 16 KJV verses and the four-word window happens to isolate the one where the preceding conjunction matches.

“the blood of the Lamb” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 7:14 and 12:11, and the machine proposed 12:11 at both 13:10 and 13:11. It is the wrong one of the two. Revelation 12:11 is a victory over the accuser — 'they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony' — with no garments and no washing in it. Revelation 7:14 has the garments made white, which is the clause Ether 13:10 and 13:11 are both using, and “white in the blood of the Lamb” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The link is filed at 13:10 against Revelation 7:14 and the same phrase at 13:11 is that link's second occurrence in two verses.

A citation in the printed study apparatus that cannot be right as printed, and the row is discharged here rather than by a manufactured link. The note attached to 'from the north countries' reads, on the page, 'That is, the lost tribes; see Jer 15.16; 31.8'. Jeremiah 31:8 is exactly what the note describes — 'I will bring them from the north country, and gather them from the coasts of the earth' — and is adjudicated as a link at this verse. Jeremiah 15:16 is 'Thy words were found, and I did eat them; and thy word was unto me the joy and rejoicing of mine heart', which has no northern gathering, no lost tribes and no verbal contact with Ether 13:11 anywhere in its context. The verse the note is plainly reaching for is Jeremiah 16:15, 'The LORD liveth, that brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north, and from all the lands whither he had driven them' — the same digits transposed. Checked against text/hardy-msi-raw.txt before filing, so this is a fault in the printed citation and not in our verse-walker; it is the same class as the 2 Nephi 17:17 citation already recorded in data/hardy-corrections.json. A separate and smaller point belongs to us: our extract of this note kept only its first reference and dropped '31.8', and the same truncation of a second book-less reference shows at Ether 13:7, where the page reads 'Gen 46.1–7; 49.33' and data/hardy-refs.json holds only the first.

Typology pulls hard and the wording will not bear it, on the model of the Exodus 2:2 'goodly' entry in 1 Nephi. Ether is rejected by his people, cast out, and lives in a rock while a king he has prophesied against destroys the nation; he comes out by night to watch and goes back in. That is close to Elijah at Horeb — 'he came thither unto a cave, and lodged there' — and closer still to Obadiah hiding a hundred prophets by fifty in a cave during Ahab's purge, 1 Kings 18:4, and to the Judges-era Israelites who 'made them the dens which are in the mountains, and caves' at Judges 6:2. But there is no shared wording at all. “cavity” occurs in no KJV verse; it is not a King James word, and the King James word for the thing is 'cave' or 'hole of the rock'. Recorded so that a reader who sees the hidden-prophet type is told the catalogue saw it and declined to catalogue it as dependence.

“by day and by night” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, which is why it ranked, and the singleton is arithmetic rather than distinctive: the King James Bible says the same thing constantly as “day and night”, which occurs in exactly 28 KJV verses, and simply had occasion to double the preposition once. Ether 13:13 does not even reproduce the phrase — it reads 'he hid himself in the cavity of a rock by day, and by night he went forth', where the two prepositions belong to two different clauses and the run crosses the comma between them. Isaiah 28:19 is the overflowing scourge passing over morning by morning; nothing else of it is present.

exclusions.sharedText: the word of the Lord came
exclusions.reason: “the word of the LORD came” occurs in exactly 92 KJV verses and is the Bible's standard prophetic commissioning formula; Jeremiah 25:3 ranked only because it also happens to sit next to a regnal year, which Ether 13:20 does too ('And in the second year, the word of the Lord came to Ether'). Neither the year nor the formula is evidence. This entry covers the same candidate wherever it recurs in Ether 13-15.

exclusions.sharedText: upon all the face of the
exclusions.reason: “upon all the face of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 34:6, and the singleton is worthless here: the KJV writes 'upon the face of the earth' constantly and doubled the quantifier once. The Book of Mormon uses 'upon all the face of the land' as its standing formula for a condition that has become general, and this chapter alone has it at 13:25, 13:26 and 13:31, which is why Ezekiel 34:6 ranked for three consecutive verses. This entry covers all of them. The scattered flock of Ezekiel 34 does bear on the Book of Mormon elsewhere and is adjudicated where it does.

“for the space of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “the space of two years” occurs in exactly one, so the machine ranked Acts 19:8 at 13:28 and Acts 19:10 at 13:31 — two adjacent verses of Acts against two verses of a Jaredite war. Both singletons are arithmetic. 'The space of' as a duration formula is spread across Acts 5:7, 19:8, 20:31 and James 5:17 and is ordinary King James English for an interval; the Book of Mormon uses it throughout its war narratives. Acts 19 is Paul in the school of Tyrannus. This entry covers both verses.

The typological expectation is strong enough that declining it has to be written down. Ether 14 opens with 'a great curse upon the land, because of the iniquity of the people' and proceeds to siege, burned cities, unburied dead and national extinction, which is the programme of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 in order. Deuteronomy 28:29-31 is the closest the KJV comes to the specific form the curse takes here — 'thou shalt be only oppressed and spoiled evermore, and no man shall save thee … thine ox shall be slain before thine eyes, and thou shalt not eat thereof … and thou shalt have none to rescue them' — property removed from a man's hands with no redress. But there is not one shared distinctive word, and the Book of Mormon's curse is not the Deuteronomic list: it is a specific and non-biblical thing, the disappearance of tools and swords laid down, which the record has already used at Helaman 13:31-36 ('their treasures … become slippery') and will use again at Mormon 1:18. Deuteronomy's curses take away crops, health, children and freedom; none of them makes objects vanish off a shelf. The land-curse frame is the Book of Mormon's own, established at Ether 2:8-11 for this land specifically, and it does not need Deuteronomy to explain it. Recorded so that a reader who reaches for Leviticus 26 or Deuteronomy 28 here is told the catalogue reached for them too and could not make the wording bear it.

The highest-scoring candidate on the opening verse and it is connective tissue. 'Because of the iniquity of the people' is one of the Book of Mormon's commonest editorial formulas, and 'the iniquity of the' is a KJV genitive chain that carries no source with it. Lamentations 4:6 is about Sodom's overthrow being quicker and kinder than Jerusalem's siege; nothing else in it touches Ether 14. Covered by the standing exclusion on connective matches (CONVENTIONS §5) and listed only because it ranked first here.

Worth an entry because the borrowing-and-lending pair is Deuteronomic and the chapter is a curse chapter, so the pull is real. Deuteronomy 28:12 and 15:6 make lending-without-borrowing the sign of blessing, and 28:44 makes the reverse the sign of curse; if Ether 14:2 were following that frame it would say the Jaredites were reduced to borrowing. It says the opposite of both: nobody lends and nobody borrows, because credit itself has become impossible. That is a third state Deuteronomy never describes, and the verbal contact is two ordinary words that the KJV uses of Israelite neighbours (Exodus 22:14) and Egyptian jewels (Exodus 3:22, 11:2) as readily as of covenant blessing. The clause is doing the Book of Mormon's own work — showing what the slippery-treasures curse does to exchange — and does not need Deuteronomy 28 to be read.

A genuine KJV singleton in an opposed sense, and the kind of match a careful reader will find and wonder about. “did cleave unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse: 'But ye that did cleave unto the LORD your God are alive every one of you this day' — the survivors of Baal-peor, defined by what they held onto. Ether 14:2 reads 'every man did cleave unto that which was his own, with his hands', and every man in it dies. The inversion is neat enough to be tempting and that is exactly why it is not evidence: 'cleave unto' is ordinary KJV register (thirteen verses), the past-tense auxiliary 'did' is the Book of Mormon's default narrative form on nearly every verb in this chapter ('did cleave', 'did march', 'did smite', 'did pursue', 'did burn'), and the three-word string is therefore produced by the text's own grammar rather than by Deuteronomy. Where the KJV's verb takes God as its object and means covenant fidelity, the Book of Mormon's takes movable property and means a man's fists closed on it.

Rarity 1.50 and a five-word run, and it is a prepositional accident. Psalm 89:25 is the Davidic covenant — 'I will set his hand also in the sea, and his right hand in the rivers' — where the right hand is imperial reach. Ether 14:2's right hand is holding a sword hilt. The run exists because both sentences happen to put a body part in a place. No other contact.

exclusions.sharedText: for the space of two years
exclusions.reason: Dating boilerplate, and this entry covers the same candidate wherever it recurs in the chapter — 14:7 ('for the space of two years', Acts 19:10 again) and 14:26 ('for the space of three days', Acts 19:8). 'For the space of' is the King James Bible's standard way of measuring a duration and the Book of Mormon's too; Acts 19 ranks only because Paul's Ephesian residence happened to last two years. A Jaredite pretender's exile in the wilderness of Akish and a two-year preaching in the school of Tyrannus have nothing else in common. No further 'space of' candidates in this chapter are listed individually.

Top candidate on the verse and pure syntax. Luke 22:56 is the servant girl noticing Peter by the fire; Ether 14:9 is a high priest murdering a king on his throne. The four-word run is the English for observing somebody in a seated posture. Recorded because the verse is a striking one — regicide on the throne, in one sentence — and a reader may expect the catalogue to have found something for it. There is a real biblical type here (Ehud and Eglon at Judges 3:20, Ish-bosheth at 2 Samuel 4:5-7, Sennacherib at 2 Kings 19:37) but Ether 14:9 gives it eighteen words and no distinctive vocabulary at all; nothing in the KJV can be shown to stand behind them.

The joint highest-scoring candidate in the chapter at rarity 2.00, and worthless. 'The face of the land' and 'the face of the earth' are among the Book of Mormon's most frequent phrases, and 'the whole face of the' is that phrase plus a quantifier; the chapter uses it four times in six verses (14:19, 14:21, 14:22, 14:23). Genesis 2:6 is the mist that watered the ground before it rained. Covered by the standing exclusion on connective matches; listed once here because of its rank, and this entry covers 'upon all the face of' at 14:23 (ranked to Ezekiel 34:6) as well.

“shedding of blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 9:22 — 'without shedding of blood is no remission' — and Ether 14:22 uses the phrase twice in a single clause, 'from the shedding of blood, to the shedding of blood', which looks like the strongest kind of evidence until it is counted against the Book of Mormon itself. The phrase occurs in thirteen Book of Mormon verses, most of them the Nephite war chapters (Alma 26:24, 48:14, 48:16, 48:23, 52:4, 58:28) where it means exactly what it means here, warfare, and where it is already fixed vocabulary long before Ether. Whatever Hebrews 9:22 contributed to the Book of Mormon's idiom, it contributed elsewhere; a reader wanting the atonement sense should look at Alma 34:13, which is the verse that argues about remission of sins. Ether 14:22's doubling is a rhetorical figure on a house phrase, not a quotation.

The most seductive candidate in the chapter and it has to be declined at length. “the scent thereof” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hosea 14:7, and Ether 14:23 uses it twice — a KJV singleton reproduced twice in a single verse is normally decisive. Three things defeat it. First, the sense is not merely different but perfectly opposed: Hosea 14:7's scent is the fragrance of restored Israel, 'as the wine of Lebanon', in the chapter where the nation is healed after the sword; Ether 14:23's is the stench of unburied corpses that keeps a whole land awake. Second, the Book of Mormon has its own precedent for the phrase in precisely this sense — Alma 16:11, the corpses of Ammonihah, 'so great was the scent thereof, that the people did not go in to possess the land … for many years' — which is the same word, the same referent, and the same consequence of a land made uninhabitable by its own dead. Ether 14:23 is following Alma 16:11, not Hosea. Third, 'thereof' is not evidence of anything: it is an 1830 tic used three more times in this chapter alone ('the hilt of his sword thereof' 14:2, 'the cities thereof' 14:17, 'in the stead thereof' 14:16), and the 1920 edition deleted two of those three as redundant, which is the editors' own testimony that they read it as a verbal habit rather than as borrowed language. 'Scent' plus the Book of Mormon's default possessive produces this string without any help from Hosea.

This is the chapter's best-looking machine candidate and the register is the right place for it. “the fulness of his” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 20:22 ('in the fulness of his sufficiency he shall be in straits'), and the very next verse supplies the missing noun: “fury of his wrath” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Job 20:23. So Ether 14:25's 'the Lord did visit them in the fulness of his wrath' can be read as a fusion of two consecutive KJV singletons, in a Joban speech about the portion of the wicked man whose prosperity turns to destruction — a very attractive reading, and wrong. 'The fulness of his wrath' is a Book of Mormon formula with a history: 1 Nephi 22:17, 2 Nephi 1:17, and — decisively — Ether 2:8 and 2:9, twelve chapters earlier in this same book, where it is the technical term for what comes on any nation that possesses this land and will not serve God ('they shall be swept off when the fulness of his wrath shall come upon them … when they are ripened in iniquity'). Ether 14:25 is the fulfilment notice for Ether 2:9 and quotes it, not Job. Note the incidental finding: the KJV never says 'fulness of his wrath' at all — it says 'fierceness of his wrath' — so the Book of Mormon's phrase is its own coinage, and where that coinage came from is a question for 1 Nephi 22:17, not for this verse.

exclusions.sharedText: (two armies, facing high ground, a valley between)
exclusions.reason: A cross-reference as much as an exclusion. The staging of 14:28-29 is 1 Samuel 17:1-3 exactly — one army in the valley of Corihor, the other encamped in the valley of Shurr by the hill Comnor, the challenger gathering his forces on the height and calling the other side out to fight — and it comes eighteen verses after a man of great stature (14:10) and ten after the cry 'Who can stand before the army of Shiz?' (14:18). The Goliath frame is real and is argued in this catalogue, but it is argued where the wording is: see the links at 14:10 (2 Samuel 21:20 and 1 Samuel 10:23) and 14:18 (Deuteronomy 9:2). Verse 28 itself shares not one distinctive word with 1 Samuel 17 — the Book of Mormon's armies pitch tents in valleys and gather on hills throughout Alma without any help from the Philistines — so no link is filed here. A reader who sees David and Goliath in this chapter is seeing something the catalogue also sees, two verses earlier.

“sound a trumpet” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the Sermon on the Mount forbidding it: 'when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do.' Ether 14:28's trumpet is a battlefield challenge sounded from a hill to invite an opposing army down. Nothing but the collocation is shared, and the collocation is the only way English says the thing. The KJV's own war-trumpets are blown, not sounded (Numbers 10:9, Judges 6:34), which is what makes Matthew 6:2 the singleton; the Book of Mormon's verb choice is not a borrowing but a nineteenth-century idiom the translation uses freely.

exclusions.sharedText: the second time ... the third time
exclusions.reason: Rarity 1.39 on a triple repetition, and the KJV verse behind it is Elijah on Carmel telling his servants to drench the altar: 'Do it the second time … Do it the third time.' Ether 14:29's threefold repetition is three failed assaults on a hill. Both texts use the KJV's ordinal formula for a thing done three times, which is the whole of the resemblance; the formula is not distinctive enough to carry a source, and the Book of Mormon uses it independently whenever it counts anything (compare the second and third watches, the second and third times messengers are sent). Nothing of Carmel — no altar, no water, no fire, no contest of gods — is present.

exclusions.sharedText: (the wounded king carried out of the battle)
exclusions.reason: The type-scene pulls and the wording will not bear it, so it goes in the register rather than the catalogue. Coriantumr takes many deep wounds, loses his blood, faints and is 'carried away as though he were dead'; Ahab is smitten between the joints of the harness, tells his driver 'carry me out of the host; for I am wounded', is stayed up in his chariot, and 'the blood ran out of the wound' until he dies at even (1 Kings 22:34-35). Four elements in common and not one shared phrase — “as though he were dead” occurs in no KJV verse, and neither does “deep wounds”. The decisive objection is the outcome. The Ahab scene exists to kill the king the prophet condemned; Ether 14:30 exists to not kill him, because 14:24 has just cited the oracle that Coriantumr should not fall by the sword, and his survival of an apparently mortal wounding is the oracle working. Acts 14:19, where Paul is stoned and dragged out 'supposing he had been dead' and then gets up, is the closer analogue for the survival, and it is no closer verbally. The catalogue declines both.

The highest-ranked candidate at this verse and a five-word run, and it is the King James Bible's ordinary way of naming a population. 2 Chronicles 20:13 is Judah standing before the LORD with their little ones to pray for deliverance; Ether 15:2 is Coriantumr counting two millions of his own dead. The Book of Mormon uses the enumeration constantly, including twice more in this chapter (15:15, and 'men, women and children' in the same verse), so no single KJV verse is in view. Nothing else of 2 Chronicles 20 is present.

exclusions.sharedText: repent of the evil which he had done
exclusions.reason: A six-word run and the top-scoring candidate in the chapter, and it is the Book of Mormon's own idiom rather than Jeremiah's. Ether 2:15 already reads 'the brother of Jared repented him of the evil which he had done', thirteen chapters earlier in the same book, so 15:3 is repeating a formula the book set for itself at its beginning. The KJV verse is also the wrong shape: in Jeremiah 26:19 it is the LORD who 'repented him of the evil which he had pronounced', a withdrawn judgment, not a man repenting of what he did. The real link at this verse is to Psalm 77:2, where the soul refuses to be comforted; see the adjudication there.

exclusions.sharedText: (a hill with a Hebrew name where the nations are gathered for the last battle)
exclusions.reason: Written out because every reader who knows Revelation will propose it. Ether 15:11-15 gathers an entire people to a named hill for a battle nobody survives, and Revelation 16:16 gathers the kings of the earth 'into a place called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon' — har megiddo, the hill of Megiddo, a Hebrew hill-name for the same event. The typological fit is as close as it gets. The wording is not there at all: Ether has 'the hill Ramah' and Revelation has 'Armageddon', and the two share no English word. The apocalyptic gathering IS catalogued in this chapter, one verse later and on verbal grounds, against Revelation 20:8, whose 'gather them together to battle' is a KJV singleton; a reader who came here for Armageddon should go to Ether 15:12. Ramah's own KJV background is adjudicated at 15:11 against Jeremiah 31:15.

exclusions.sharedText: upon all the face of the
exclusions.reason: A six-word run, and 'upon all the face' is technically a KJV singleton — which is exactly the failure mode CONVENTIONS §9 warns about, rare boilerplate scoring high. The KJV's phrase is 'upon all the face of the earth' (scattered sheep); the Book of Mormon's is 'upon all the face of the land', which is its standing formula for the whole territory and which it uses hundreds of times across the corpus. Ezekiel 34's shepherds and flock are nowhere in Ether 15. This entry covers the same match at 15:14 and 15:15.

'For the space of' is the King James Bible's standard duration formula and it appears at Acts 13:20, 19:8, 19:10, 20:31 and elsewhere with whatever numeral the context requires. Nothing connects the four hundred and fifty years of the judges to the Jaredites' four years of mustering except the word 'four'. This entry covers every 'space of' candidate in the chapter except 15:27, which is filed separately because its numeral matches.

exclusions.sharedText: which were upon the face of the
exclusions.reason: The longest shared run at this verse, seven words, and pure connective tissue on both sides. Numbers 12:3 is the parenthesis about Moses being meeker than all the men upon the face of the earth; Ether 15:14 is four years spent conscripting everyone left alive. The shared string is a relative clause and a locative formula, and the Book of Mormon writes it as reflexively as the KJV does. Covered in part by the Ezekiel 34:6 entry above; recorded separately because the run is long enough to tempt.

This one deserves the argument, because 'men women and children' is a KJV SINGLETON and the singleton is an extermination verse: 'we utterly destroyed them ... utterly destroying the men, women, and children, of every city.' A chapter about the extermination of a nation, using the KJV's one phrase for the extermination of a population, looks decisive. It is not, on two grounds. First, the Book of Mormon uses the phrase eight times, three of them in Ether alone (6:3 of the Jaredites crossing the sea by shining stones, 14:31, and here), so it is a house idiom and not a borrowing. Second, the sense inverts: Deuteronomy's men, women and children are the slaughtered inhabitants of a captured city, and Ether's are the army — 'both men, women and children being armed with weapons of war, having shields, and breast-plates, and head-plates.' The horror of Ether 15:15 is precisely that the noncombatants of the KJV formula have become combatants. Recorded rather than linked, but a reader who wants to press it has the counts here.

exclusions.sharedText: and it came to pass that on the morrow
exclusions.reason: Nine words, the longest run in the chapter, and every one of them boilerplate. 'And it came to pass' is covered by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5; 'on the morrow' is the KJV's ordinary next-day marker and Ether 15 uses it six times (15:8, 15:17, 15:21, 15:23, 15:24, 15:26, 15:29). Aaron's budded rod has nothing to do with the second day of a war of annihilation. This entry covers the same string at 15:29 (Amos 7:2) and the 'on the morrow' matches at Acts 23:32 and Acts 10:23.

A five-word run and the second-rarest candidate in the chapter, and the coincidence is entirely in the auxiliary verbs. Paul has determined not to make another visit to Corinth 'in heaviness', a decision about pastoral timing; Coriantumr writes to the man who is exterminating his people begging him not to come again to battle and offering him the kingdom. Both sentences say 'would not come again to' because both are about declining a second arrival, and there the resemblance stops — no content word is shared, and nothing else of 2 Corinthians 2 is anywhere near Ether 15.

A five-word run, and Joshua 7:5's 'the hearts of the people melted, and became as water' after the rout at Ai is a real defeat-of-a-nation verse, so the proposal is not silly. But the shared string is a generic possessive, the melting is absent from Ether, and the verse's actual borrowings are elsewhere and much rarer: 'the blindness of their minds' from Ephesians 4:18, whose 'the blindness of' is a KJV singleton, and 'the hardness of their hearts' from Mark 3:5, likewise a singleton, both catalogued at 15:19 along with the Genesis 6:3 formula behind 'the spirit of the Lord had ceased striving'. Joshua 7:5 is superseded.

The nearest paraphrase of Ether 15:22's sense in the whole KJV — men drunk on something that is not wine — and it occurs in exactly two verses, Isaiah 29:9 and 51:21, both of them oracles about a people staggering under judgment. It loses to Isaiah 49:26 on syntax and on corpus history. Ether reads 'drunken with anger, even as a man which is drunken with wine', which is the construction 'drunken with X, as with wine'; Isaiah 29:9 and 51:21 have no 'as with' comparison, and Isaiah 49:26 does — 'drunken with their own blood, as with sweet wine'. Isaiah 49:26 is also the verse the Book of Mormon has already quoted twice (1 Nephi 21:26, 2 Nephi 6:18) and interpreted once, at 1 Nephi 22:13, as a prophecy of a people warring among themselves until its own sword falls on its own head. See the link at 15:22.

'space of three hours' is a KJV SINGLETON, which is why it ranked, and it is one of the cleanest illustrations in this book of why a singleton is not by itself an argument. The KJV verse is the interval between Ananias's death and Sapphira walking in, a piece of narrative clock-work in a story about lying to the Holy Ghost; Ether 15:27 is the length of the last engagement of a war, after which fifty-nine men faint from blood loss. The rarity is arithmetical — the KJV measures duration with 'the space of' constantly (Acts 13:20, 19:8, 20:31, James 5:17) and simply had occasion to write 'hours' once. No content word beyond the numeral is shared.

A four-word run straddling a clause boundary in both texts, which is the signature of a false positive. Amos 9:4 is the LORD commanding the sword to slay the exiles; Ether 15:29 has the last survivors fighting again with the sword. 'The sword' is the most heavily used weapon-noun in both books — 'fall by the sword' alone occurs in twenty-four KJV verses — and it cannot point at a source. The Amos 7:2 candidate at the same verse is covered by the Numbers 17:8 entry above.

exclusions.sharedText: (a headless body raised on its hands before falling)
exclusions.reason: A manual temptation, and typologically it is a strong one. 'Shiz raised upon his hands and fell; and after that he had struggled for breath, he died' is one of the strangest sentences in the Book of Mormon, and the King James Bible has one image close to it: Dagon in 1 Samuel 5:4, fallen on his face before the ark with his head and both the palms of his hands cut off upon the threshold — a beheaded figure and its hands, on the ground, in a scene about a god who cannot stand. The wording will not carry it. Ether shares nothing with 1 Samuel 5:4 but the word 'hands', and its verbs, 'raised upon' and 'struggled for breath', are not KJV language at all: 'struggled' is a KJV singleton and it is Rebekah's twins in the womb (Genesis 25:22), and 'for breath' occurs nowhere. Recorded so that a reader who sees Dagon is told the catalogue saw him and declined.

'Fell to the earth' occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Joshua 7:6, 2 Samuel 1:2 and Acts 9:4, and the coincidence that one of the three sits four verses from the singleton this chapter does borrow — 'leaned upon his', 2 Samuel 1:6 — makes it look like a second draw on the same page. It is not. 2 Samuel 1:2's man falls to the earth to do obeisance before David; Ether 15:32's Coriantumr falls unconscious from blood loss and 'became as if he had no life'. The senses are unrelated and the phrase is common. The genuine 2 Samuel 1 borrowing is catalogued at 15:30, and the closest wording to 'as if he had no life' is 1 Nephi 4:7's Laban 'fallen to the earth' drunk before his beheading, which is inside the corpus and is discussed there.
